News.title: 'Piddington isn't a protest — it's the next stop on America's grievance politics tour'
News.content:
Britain has a remarkable talent for importing America’s most tiresome inventions just as the Americans themselves are starting to look for the receipt.

We got drive-through coffee, gender-reveal parties, Black Friday and people saying “reach out” when they mean “ring”. Now another container appears to have cleared customs: masked nationalism, Christian branding and political grievance packaged for social media. Next stop: Piddington.

The sleepy Oxfordshire village has become the latest immigration flashpoint after residents backed a symbolic referendum to “leave” Britain over plans to house up to 1,200 male asylum seekers at a nearby former military site.

And now Daniel “Danny Tommo” Thomas, leader of Patriot Platform, has indicated that thousands of his goons could descend on the area and remain for days in an attempt to stop migrants being moved in. You can almost imagine the tour T-shirt: Dover. Portsmouth. Piddington. Coming soon to an angry community near you.

‌



Residents in tiny village Piddington holding referendum on leaving the UK amid migrant row READ MORE :

View 5 Images Piddington, where opposition to plans for asylum accommodation has turned the Oxfordshire village into the latest focus of Britain’s immigration tensions (Image: PA Wire/PA Images)

View 5 Images Masked members of Patriot Platform during one of the group’s demonstrations as it seeks to build support around immigration flashpoints

This is the model America has already perfected: identify the grievance, locate the cameras, mobilise online, arrive in numbers and make certain there is enough footage for Telegram before moving on to the next flashpoint.

Call it grievance tourism. No Ticketmaster required here - just a flag, a phone and preferably a balaclava. Where local people see a difficult argument about asylum accommodation, national activists see a ready-made stage. Piddington risks becoming the latest stop on a travelling political roadshow where somebody else’s village provides the scenery and somebody else’s anxiety provides the content.

‌



Anyone familiar with America’s hard-right street movements could be forgiven for thinking the cosplay container had simply arrived several years late.

Patriot Platform describes itself as a “Christian national resistance movement”. Its emergence has involved black-clad, masked demonstrations, anti-migrant slogans and Christian-nationalist imagery. America road-tested parts of this formula years ago.

The Proud Boys combined macho street politics, nationalism and confrontation with increasingly visible religious ritual. Members prayed together before the January 6 attack on the Capitol, asking for protection and invoking God, country and culture. Former chairman Enrique Tarrio was eventually sentenced to 22 years for seditious conspiracy before Donald Trump pardoned him after returning to the White House.

Then there is Patriot Front, which provides an even better match for the wardrobe department. Hundreds of its members marched through Washington this July in uniform clothing, their faces hidden behind white masks and sunglasses, carrying flags and chanting “Reclaim America”. The group has become known for masked, flashmob-style demonstrations engineered to produce striking images. Patriot Platform appears to understand the same basic truth.

‌



Two hundred men in jeans can look like the queue for a replacement bus service. Put the same men in matching black clothing and balaclavas and suddenly the photographs suggest something considerably grander. The uniform is content. The march is content. The confrontation is content.

View 5 Images Proud Boys supporters in Washington around the January 6, 2021, attack on the US Capitol, when Donald Trump supporters stormed Congress (Image: Amy Harris/REX/Shutterstock)

Apparently nothing screams fearless defender of the nation quite like making absolutely certain nobody can see your face.

Religion is another part of the familiar package. Thomas was jailed for two years following his conviction over an attempted kidnapping in which a man was targeted at knifepoint. After prison, he says he began attending church, and Christianity later became prominent in his activism.

‌



Christianity is founded on forgiveness and redemption. People sincerely find faith in prison and after hitting rock bottom, and nobody else can know what is in Thomas’s heart. But politics has produced enough dramatic conversions to make you wonder why the road to Damascus appears to have such an efficient connecting service from the probation office.

The bigger point is what happens when faith becomes part of the political branding. Immigration stops being an argument about numbers, borders, housing or public services and becomes something more elemental: God, family, homeland, civilisation, good against evil.

America’s Christian-nationalist movements have been mixing those ingredients for years. Britain appears to have finally found the recipe card. And, as ever, we are several seasons behind. The same Americanisation can be seen much higher up British politics, although the organisations and methods are clearly different.

Nigel Farage condemned Patriot Platform’s masked demonstrations, describing the balaclavas as “horrible”, and Reform should not simply be conflated with Thomas’s organisation.

‌



Yet Farage has spent years demonstrating how effectively elements of Donald Trump’s political playbook can be repackaged for Britain: direct communication with supporters, relentless conflict with institutions and the media, insurgent language and an exceptional ability to occupy political oxygen. Temu Trump may be an unkind description, but the joke endures because the resemblance in political marketing is sometimes difficult to miss.

Now even the money is going American. Reform has received £72 million from cryptocurrency billionaires Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne - £36 million apiece, jointly the biggest political donations in British history. Reform says neither man expects favours in return.

Nothing says plucky anti-establishment uprising quite like having £72 million worth of billionaires behind it. But Piddington may tell us more about where the next phase is heading. Because this kind of politics thrives on motion, it needs another town, another row, another crowd, another livestream. Today Piddington. Tomorrow wherever the cameras are pointing.

View 5 Images Patriot Platform leader Daniel “Danny Tommo” Thomas, who has signalled plans to take his movement to Piddington (Image: Getty)

‌



The American playbook is brutally simple: find the flashpoint, flood the scene, turn local anger into national theatre, harvest the pictures and head for the next postcode. That leaves communities such as the Oxfordshire village in danger of becoming little more than film sets in somebody else’s political production.

Residents become extras. Their genuine concerns become props. Their village becomes the next TikTok. America has already seen this show. Britain, apparently, has bought the remake rights. Same grievance. Same God-and-country branding. Same social-media machinery. Just cheaper costumes - and more rain.

News.title: Missing Noah Woods - latest: Last sighting of boy, 3, seen in heartbreaking CCTV
News.content:
Police searching for Noah Woods have released CCTV images of his last known movements before he vanished from a playground in Brantham, Suffolk

Police searching for missing three-year-old Noah Woods have released heartbreaking CCTV footage of his last known movements at a playground before he became separated from a relative.

A massive search operation to find the Suffolk boy has been underway since yesterday, with his desperate father saying he "can't go another night knowing he's out there alone".

Noah was last seen at 2.37pm on Tuesday when he became separated from a relative after visiting Merriam Close playground in Brantham. Police have cordoned off a nearby lake known as Decoy Pond as well as a wooded area, with officers saying it is "out of bounds". Met Police divers are searching the lake.

Hundreds of people flooded into the village early this morning to join the search, with Suffolk Police asking residents in the area to check gardens, sheds and outbuildings.

The force has said it is keeping an "open mind" but that there is "nothing to indicate anything sinister or any element of criminality has taken place".

Noah is described as white, with curly ginger hair. He was last seen wearing a white Bluey T-shirt, shorts and black Vans trainers with a white stripe. He is non-verbal, has partial hearing loss and is currently undergoing an assessment for autism. Because of these vulnerabilities, he will not respond to his name, police said.

News.title: BBC weather forecast says UK's glorious 'mini-heatwave' to last nine September days
News.content:
BBC weather forecast says UK's glorious 'mini-heatwave' to last nine September days

According to the latest BBC Weather data, the UK is set for an extended run of late-summer warmth, with temperatures forecast to reach 22C or higher across nine consecutive days

View 3 Images A beachgoer enjoys a recent sunny day in Merseyside (Image: Colin Lane/Liverpool Echo)

Britons are poised to experience a sustained late-season spell of sunshine.

‌



Temperatures will jump to way above average for the time of year for nine consecutive days later this month, meteorologists understand. The mercury will stay at 22C or above in several regions, according to the most recent BBC Weather projections.

‌



High pressure is expected to secure settled, bright weather across southern areas and the Home Counties from Tuesday September 22. Typically in September, the mercury rarely exceeds 20C across the Southeast of England and mid to late teens in northern areas of the UK.

‌



"Atlantic weather fronts becoming more confined to northern and northwestern areas. As such, plenty of dry and increasingly warm and perhaps rather humid weather will develop," reads the long-range Met Office forecast. BBC graphics also support the understanding the weather is set to be pleasant.

Met Office names 29 areas facing heavy rain on Wednesday - see full list READ MORE :

View 3 Images On Tuesday, London will enjoy a peak temperature of 23C, with a gentle breeze (Image: BBC Weather)

But rain is forecast first, including tonight, and the end of the week is poised to be unsettled for many regions. Downpours are also likely, especially across the Northwest of England, on Friday, forecasters say.

‌



Yet the picture quickly changes and what has been dubbed a "mini-heatwave" is on the horizon. Temperatures will rise swiftly from Tuesday, with the East of England and the Southeast of England to bask in the warmest plumes. However, it will be at least 20C as far north as South Yorkshire, it is understood.

During the hottest spells, most likely to be mid afternoons next week, the mercury could even each 23C in the Southeast of England. Skies will be clear everywhere and winds will be light, and so it may feel even warmer, meteorologists say.

This high pressure will remain for most of the week, and so temperatures will be warmer than the 11.9C and 15.8C, recorded on Tuesday in Lerwick, Scotland and near Carlisle, Cumbria, respectively.

‌



Michelle Keegan just dropped the must-have jacket for autumn in her new Very collection READ MORE :

View 3 Images Sunrise was impressive at Glastonbury Tor, Somerset today (Image: Michelle Cowbourne / SWNS)

But the rain forecast this week is due to be heaviest throughout tonight and into Thursday morning, particularly across northern and western Scotland. Friday's showers will be more widespread though, and strongest during the evening over Lancashire, Cumbria and parts of north Wales.

The weekend will be unsettled too as drizzle is expected on Saturday across southern parts of England, including Somerset and Wiltshire, and south Wales. Sunday, however, is drier for many, leading into the warm spell next week.

Article continues below

The Environment Agency had, until recently, flood alerts in place over concerns for the rain forecast. It had expressed concern for the Tidal River Avon, on the Somerset coast at Porlock Weir and the tidal River Waveney, where it said high tides were expected.

News.title: Wandsworth council tax bills set to rise by 94% with residents paying £958 more
News.content:
Wandsworth council tax bills set to rise by 94% with residents paying £958 more

The maximum amount most councils in England can normally raise bills without a referendum is 5% - but six local authorities have been given permission to increase bills by more than this

View 2 Images Wandsworth has historically had cheap council tax (Image: Alex Robinson Photography via Getty Images)

Wandsworth Council has announced plans to raise council tax by 94% in a move that has been described as “cruel and unnecessary”.

‌



The proposal would see the typical yearly band D council tax bill rise by £958 from April 2027. Wandsworth currently has the lowest council tax, with it costing £1,020 a year for a band D property - in comparison, the average bill across England is £2,392.

‌



The Conservative-run council says the increase is necessary after the Government announced plans to cut its funding. It claims it will lose £84million a year by the end of the next three years under these proposals, which are part of wider measures to redistribute cashflow toward more deprived regions.

‌



Residents told to push bins half a mile as road has too many potholes for lorry READ MORE :

View 2 Images Wandsworth said the increase is needed due to a planned cut in its funding (Image: georgeclerk via Getty Images)

The maximum amount most councils in England can normally raise bills without a referendum is 5%. But the Government has granted six local authorities - Kensington and Chelsea, Westminster, Wandsworth, Hammersmith and Fulham, City of London and Windsor and Maidenhead - permission to increase council tax beyond this cap, following its funding cut announcement.

Wandsworth, Westminster, Richmond and Kensington and Chelsea councils plan on challenging the Government proposals. A final decision on the Wandsworth council tax increase will not be made until early next year.

‌

We also treat our community members to special offers, promotions, and adverts from us and our partners. If you don’t like our community, you can check out any time you like. If you’re curious, you can read our Privacy Notice. NEWSLETTER: Or sign up to the Mirror's Money newsletter here for all the best advice and shopping deals straight to your inbox.

Deputy Leader of Wandsworth Council and Cabinet Member for Finance, Peter Graham, said: “Council tax will need to rise unless Government thinks again. And it must think again.

“We do not want to do this, and we do not take this decision lightly, but the scale of the financial pressure facing Wandsworth means additional income is now needed to protect the services people rely on. Residents should not be left to carry the cost of an unfair funding system.”

Article continues below

Cllr Simon Hogg, Leader of Wandsworth Labour, said: “This increase is cruel and unnecessary and will really hurt hard-pressed local people. Too many local families are just about getting by. This sudden blow will mean no summer holiday, no new school shoes - or more debt. “There’s no financial need for a vast increase this year. The decision is purely political. The Conservatives are whacking it up now so that they can cut taxes before the next election in four years’ time, and bribe you with your own money."

A spokesperson from the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government said: “Local authorities decide the level of council tax they wish to set, but we are clear that in doing so they should put taxpayers first.

“We’ve made over £78billion available for council finances next year, with the majority of money unringfenced so local leaders can decide how best to spend on their local priorities. “And we’re fixing an outdated funding system so funding goes where need is greatest, while protecting councils through the transition and ensuring no area faces a cliff edge.”

News.title: Body found in 11-day search for missing woman, 28, from Nottingham
News.content:
Body found in 11-day search for missing woman, 28, from Nottingham

Holly Whittaker, 28, was last seen in the Mapperley area of Nottingham on September 4

View Image Holly Whittaker (Image: Nottinghamshire Police)

The body of a 28-year-old woman from Nottingham who had been missing for 11 days has been found.

‌



Holly Whittaker was last seen in the Mapperley area of Nottingham on September 4, and police had been searching for her since then.

‌



Officers found the body of a woman near Queen's Road, in Nottingham city centre, on Tuesday afternoon.

‌



The woman has since been formally identified as Ms Whittaker.

Det Ch Insp Claire Gould, of Nottinghamshire Police, said: "Our specially trained officers are supporting Holly's family at this difficult time, following yesterday's tragic development.

Article continues below

"While the circumstances are still being investigated, at this time, we are not treating her death as suspicious.

"We would like to thank everyone who came forward with any information or shared our public appeals since Holly was first reported missing.

"A file will now be prepared for the coroner as our investigations continue."

News.title: Plane crashes in Swiss Alps as police confirm everyone on board is dead
News.content:
Plane crashes in Swiss Alps as police confirm everyone on board is dead

The aircraft crashed near a popular spa and ski resort in Valais, Switzerland, killing all three people on board - the circumstances of the crash are being investigated

View Image Three people have been killed after a plane crashed in Switzerland (Image: Valais Cantonal Police)

Three people have been killed in a plane crash near a popular spa and ski resort in Switzerland.

‌



The light aircraft had taken off from Lugano, a lakeside city in southern Switzerland near the Italian border, and made a stopover in Sion, Valais, before coming down near Luekerbad on Tuesday afternoon, the Valais Cantonal Police said.

‌



Authorities said the plane, which was heading towards Buochs Airport, collided with a mountainside shortly after 4pm in the Fluhalp area.

‌



Three rescue helicopters were deployed to the crash site, while police and fire crews from Luekerbad and Sion Airport also attended.

Bystanders reported heavy smoke in the area before emergency responders arrived and confirmed that all three occupants had died. Work is ongoing to formally identify the victims.

Article continues below

The Swiss Safety Investigation Authority has launched an investigation into the cause of the crash.

News.title: Westminster Cathedral's immersive show - bombs, buried secrets and Hugh Bonneville
News.content:
Westminster Cathedral's immersive show - bombs, buried secrets and Hugh Bonneville

Luminiscence has landed at Westminster Cathedral, giving guests the chance to immerse themselves in its dramatic history, to the soundtrack of live classical music and a choir

View 3 Images Luminiscence has landed at Westminster Cathedral (Image: Luminiscence London)

This is Westminster Cathedral as you've never seen it before.

‌



A new immersive light show has launched at the London landmark, narrated by the star of Paddington and Downton Abbey, Hugh Bonneville. In a drama-packed 50 minute Luminiscence experience, visitors are treated to an inspiring 360 degree light projection concert detailing the turbulent and inspiring history of the building.

‌



With a script written BAFTA and Olivier Award winner Tim Whitnall, set to a beautiful backdrop of live classical music and vocals by the Lux Aeterna choir, the cathedral's roots and progress are brought to life - from a designer's decade-long labour of love to its place as a symbol of hope for a bombed-out city.

‌



View 3 Images The domes of Westminster Cathedral are illuminated by stunning projections in the immersive experience (Image: Luminiscence London)

Renowned for its Neo-Byzantine design of external red and white bric work, the cathedral - formally known as Metropolitan Cathedral of the Most Precious Blood of Our Lord Jesus Christ - was built between 1895 and 1903, after the restoration of Catholicism.

Constructed almost entirely without steel reinforcements, it's long been considered to be a feat of engineering although the interior of the cathedral was left to later generations.

‌



Huge marble columns have since been installed, along with the famous partially-completed mosaics across the ceilings.

Fundraising is underway to finish the work and the show uses projection to help the audience visualise the enchanting splendour that could one day be achieved.

View 3 Images The marble pillars were installed in more recent years (Image: Luminiscence London)

‌



Dazzling lights and climatic music guide guests onwards through the journey of the 50th largest church in the world, which seats some 2,000 people and became a centre of hope during WWII.

While the building escaped the Blitz unscathed, its gardener turned a nearby 1940 German bomb crater into a thriving garden.

The clay soil had absorbed much of the impact, and the hole was filled with soil and transformed into a 'dig for victory' garden, producing 130 pounds of tomatoes and year to help with rationing.

Article continues below

A thought-provoking and profound experience for all the family.

The must-see event runs until October 31, with tickets starting at £31, with children under five free. More information and tickets can be found here.

News.title: Family of missing Noah Woods, 3, 'blown away' as police issue update in Brantham
News.content:
Family of missing Noah Woods, 3, 'blown away' as police issue update in Brantham

The family of missing Noah Woods, who disappeared from a Suffolk village on Tuesday afternoon, are 'blown away' by the support of volunteers helping with the search, police said

Suffolk: CCTV shows last known sighting of missing boy Noah

The family of a missing three-year-old have been "blown away" by the support of hundreds of volunteers who have joined the search for him.

‌



Noah Woods was last seen at Merriam Close Playground in Brantham, Suffolk, on Tuesday afternoon before he ran down a nearby alleyway. He is non-verbal and partially deaf and will not respond to his name being called.

‌



Superintendent Tom Pearse, from Suffolk Police, updated journalists at Brantham Leisure Centre on Wednesday afternoon before speaking to volunteers involved in the search.

‌



He told volunteers: "I give my heartfelt thanks to all of you coming out here today. From what I have seen, it is an unbelievably special community.

View 4 Images Noah Woods went missing from a playground in Brantham, Suffolk, on Tuesday afternoon (Image: Suffolk Police)

"You have demonstrated that by the way you have all come together. I want to pass on the thanks of Noah’s family. They are unbelievably grateful and blown away by your support."

‌



Volunteer Rebecca Lucas, 46, said "everybody’s come together to try and do what they can".

The theatre production company worker from Manningtree, Essex, said: "I’ve got two children, I’ve got a seven-year-old and a three-year-old, and obviously this hits quite close to home with Noah being three.

View 4 Images Noah was with a relative before he went missing (Image: Suffolk Police)

‌



"I think, within the local community, everyone’s really close-knit and it just touches at the heartstrings. Everybody just wants to get involved and see if there’s anything we can do rather than just sit at home."

Ms Lucas attended a briefing at the village hall earlier on Wednesday, where she was given an area to search.

View 4 Images Dozens of volunteers pictured at Brantham Leisure Centre on Wednesday afternoon (Image: Will Colebourne/PA Wire)

‌



She scoured fields and the area around a local church for "anything that could possibly give us a clue", but said they had not found anything yet. She said she would keep helping with the search for "as long as they need us".

Sharon Auton, 60, said she went out to help as soon as she saw news of Noah's disappearance on social media on Tuesday afternoon.

View 4 Images Noah is partially deaf and non-verbal (Image: Suffolk Police)

Article continues below

The foster carer from Brantham said it was "amazing how much the community has got together over this".

Ms Auton said volunteers at the village hall had been split into groups, given maps and sent to search different areas.

She said she wanted to "help find this little boy", adding: "It’s just tragic he’s been lost. I’m hoping he will be found safe and well."

News.title: 'Putney pusher' suspect found dead at home
News.content:
The man suspected of pushing a woman into the path of a bus during a run on Putney Bridge in west London in 2017, has been found dead at his home.

Nicholas Brandram, 44, was under investigation in the so-called "Putney pusher" case, after CCTV went viral showing just how close the woman came to be run over by the 430 bus, in a seemingly unprovoked attack.

He was arrested in June this year on suspicion of attempted grievous bodily harm. Last week, the Metropolitan Police confirmed he had been released under investigation.

The banker was found dead in his home on Tuesday evening. The Met said his death was being treated as "unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious".

News.title: Photos show widespread damage at US sites from Iranian attacks
News.content:
Images showing widespread damage to multiple US sites in the Middle East from Iranian strikes have been obtained by the BBC's US partner CBS.

The photos, provided by active military personnel, show a severed radar jet, flattened trailers and severely damaged buildings.

The undated photos were taken at US bases and sites in Saudi Arabia and Kuwait.

One member of the military, who was not named by CBS, said: "This is major damage to our bases that hasn't been communicated to the American public.

"We're standing there with our eyes closed getting punched in the face."

The White House and US Central Command have been approached for comment.

The photos, which have not been independently verified by the BBC, were published the day after a report from the Pentagon's watchdog confirmed hundreds of buildings and structures at US bases in the Middle East have been damaged and destroyed by Iran.

One of the photos showed a destroyed Boeing E-3 Sentry at Prince Sultan Air Force Base in Saudi Arabia that has been ripped in half, its tail section crumpled into a tangled mess of metal.

News.title: How escalating Saudi oil crisis could drive up prices everywhere
News.content:
Global energy prices have spiked alarmingly again, driven largely in recent days by the escalating conflict between Yemen's Houthis and Saudi Arabia causing chaos for the oil industry.

Petrol and diesel costs have risen rapidly in most countries while the wholesale price of natural gas - used for heating homes and generating electricity - has almost doubled in the UK and Europe since July.

There are growing concerns of another inflationary shock on the world economy, which could cause interest rates to rise, increase mortgage costs and raise the price of almost everything in the shops including food.

So what is behind this latest surge - and what are the implications for the world economy?

News.title: How being music's Mr Nice Guy contributed to biggest crisis of Ed Sheeran's career
News.content:
Singer Ed Sheeran is facing the biggest controversy of his career after a storm over a decision to drop support act Macklemore from his US stadium tour following the rapper's on-stage pro-Palestinian comments.

Sheeran is one of the most successful songwriters of all time. He has sold more than 120 million records and spent more than 1,000 weeks on the US album charts.

Part of his appeal - apart from those insidiously catchy songs - is his everyman persona. He looks and dresses like a fan on the train home from Glastonbury, rather than one of the festival's headliners.

He has carefully cultivated a non-threatening, everyone welcome public image. In 2014, he donated his entire wardrobe to charity shops. The same year, he adopted a one-month-old kitten, saving it from euthanasia, and named it Graham. Today, he runs a charity providing music lessons to under-18s in his home county of Suffolk.

He tries to stay out of politics - usually only getting involved to campaign for issues like copyright protection and ticket touting, or to raise concerns over the impact of Brexit on touring musicians.

But like most artists, he leans left. In 2017, he said he supported then-Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn, despite not endorsing him at the stump.

"People thought that, because I didn't put myself behind him, I wasn't a Corbyn supporter," Sheeran told the Sunday Times. "If you knew me as a person, and listened to my music, you would be able to make a pretty educated guess that he would be the kind of person I really dig."

When it comes to non-musical issues, Sheeran prefers to remain circumspect. His reasoning, he says, is that music should unite. He views his concerts as a "place of safety and sanctuary" built on shared humanity.

This week, that argument has come crumbling down - creating a crisis for his reputation and career.

News.title: Schools in England get extra £500m in bid to avoid teachers' pay strike
News.content:
Schools in England are to get around Â£500 million in extra funding towards the teachers' pay award this school year, reducing the risk of a strike ballot by the largest education union.

Schools had been expected to fund some of the 3.5% teachers pay increase for the current school year out of their existing budgets, which National Education Union (NEU) leaders had strongly objected to.

Daniel Kebede, the General Secretary of the NEU, said the offer of more funding was a "significant" step in negotiations.

In a letter to the union on Wednesday, which has been seen by the BBC, the government said the increase would be funded by savings in employers' contributions to the local government pension scheme.

The letter said the 4.9 percentage point drop in what employers are expected to contribute will deliver "significant savings" on the pay bill for support staff, which will not be clawed back by central government.

The National Education Union said it expected the extra money to be around Â£500m, which schools can now use towards teachers pay this year.

In July, ministers accepted the recommendation of the independent pay review body for teachers and agreed a 3.5% increase from September 2026 would be followed by 3% the following year.

The pay increase had been partly funded by an additional Â£700m for 2026-27 and Â£1.1bn for the following year.

Independent economists at the Institute for Fiscal Studies said that left schools facing a shortfall of around 1% between rising costs and funding this year.

The additional money could potentially bring the uplift for this year into line with next year.

Kebede said schools has been "running on empty" and the funding signalled "a welcome return to reality, and a message of hope for the entire school community".

Paul Whiteman, General Secretary of the National Association of Headteachers, said the decision is "certainly welcome", putting schools in a "better position".

He said his union would look carefully at the detail "to determine whether this means the pay uplift is genuinely fully funded" for schools.

Pepe Di'Iasio, General Secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders, said he was "pleased" at the announcement of additional funding but "the wider pressure on school and college budgets remains intense".

In an indicative ballot by the NEU in April, 90% of teachers who voted said they would be prepared to take industrial action over funding and pay, on a turnout of 48%.

A formal ballot was due to begin on 3 October and close 15 December, raising the prospects of teachers pay strikes early in 2027.

The national executive of the NEU will meet on 24 September to consider whether to call that off following the additional funding on offer from the government.

A spokesperson for Education Secretary Lucy Powell said the government was "confident schools can now meet the costs of the award at a national level".

"The Secretary of State has been clear from day one that supporting teacher recruitment, retention and wellbeing, and rebuilding the relationship with the profession, are among her top priorities."

News.title: Earl Spencer's unreleased book on sister Diana stolen in the Netherlands
News.content:
Copies of Earl Spencer's unreleased book on his sister Diana, Princess of Wales, have been stolen from a truck in the Netherlands.

The BBC understands four copies of the Dutch language edition were taken from a truck while it was en route from the Dutch publisher's printers to their warehouse.

Dutch police said they were aware of the incident and have been approached for comment.

Swan Song: Diana, My Sister is due to be released in the UK and globally on Tuesday, and tells the story of Princess Diana's life from the Earl's perspective.

A source said the truck driver was taking a mandatory break in a car park and was sleeping in his cab at the time the books were stolen.

They added Dutch police are investigating. They did not say where the theft took place.

The Daily Mail, who first reported the theft, external and is serialising the book, said the theft took place earlier this week in the Dutch countryside.

The book's publisher Penguin Michael Joseph - a division of Penguin Random House - and Dutch publisher Overamstel, who have rights to the book in the Netherlands, were approached for comment by the BBC.

News.title: Microsoft says AI rival Anthropic could have 'disastrous impact' on humanity
News.content:
Microsoft's head of AI has warned Anthropic's approach to training its AI model Claude could have a "disastrous impact on the wellbeing of humanity".

Mustafa Suleyman said his rival risked creating something "impossible" to control by treating it like a human - including by telling it it "may be conscious" and was "deserving of independent agency".

"We must not sleepwalk our way into a decision we later come to bitterly regret," he wrote.

The comments are the latest in a series of stark warnings from the AI industry on the possible dangers of the technology. The BBC has contacted Anthropic for comment.

"AIs are not conscious," he wrote. "They do not feel, experience, or suffer. They do not have innate preferences or underlying motivations.

"They are sequence completion engines, internally hollow, designed to follow instructions, and accomplish goals set by humans."

In a lengthy essay, Suleyman praised Anthropic boss Dario Amodei and his team for being "thoughtful, principled, and intellectually honest people" - but nevertheless questioned the company.

He heavily criticised Anthropic for teaching its AI to have human-like qualities, a practice known as anthropomorphising, which he said made it seem as though Claude had its own desires, values and sense of self.

But he argued "consciousness is biological", saying there is "no evidence to suggest that AI is conscious".

As well as calling for a debate on the issue, Suleyman said greater transparency around how AI systems are trained and evaluated was needed.

This, he said, included independent scrutiny of AI behaviour and stronger tools to monitor and control the technology.

Dame Wendy Hall, professor of Computer Science at the University of Southampton, described the comments as "the sort of conversation we need to be having internationally", contrasting it with the "histrionics" from some AI companies which she said only served to "scare everyone".

News.title: Ex-officer jailed over 'toxic' WhatsApp culture
News.content:
An ex-police sergeant who asked to share a female suspect's sex video with "the lads from footy" has been jailed for four years.

Former Cambridgeshire Police officer Paul Street, 41, engaged in "salacious gossip" with former PC Josh Williams after he found intimate pictures and footage on the woman's personal phone.

The Old Bailey heard how Street, of Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire, created a "toxic" WhatsApp culture at work. He was found guilty of two charges of misconduct in a public office.

Judge Mark Lucraft KC said: "The public should expect to be able to trust police officers to act fairly in the execution of their powers to prevent, detect and solve crime."

On Wednesday, the woman told of her "overwhelming sense of shock, violation, anger and humiliation" as Street was sentenced.

The court also heard Street encouraged colleagues in WhatsApp messages to "bully" a teenage detainee.

News.title: Petrol and diesel price rises push UK inflation higher
News.content:
Rises in petrol, diesel and airfares pushed UK inflation up to its highest level in five months in the year to August.

Inflation accelerated to 3.1% from 2.9%, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

The cost of filling up a vehicle soared in August as the conflict in the Middle East continued to disrupt global oil supplies. Petrol prices jumped to their highest for nearly four years, the ONS said, while diesel also rocketed.

Meanwhile, the cost of flying jumped during the key month for summer getaways.

Overall, motor fuel prices rose by 23% compared to August last year.

Oil hit more than $91 a barrel as the US-Israel war with Iran went on. That compares to around $73 just before hostilities began earlier this year.

As a result, average petrol prices have continued to climb and between July and August, they rose by 9.1p to 161.3p per litre.

"This is the highest price recorded since November 2022," said the ONS. At that point, Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine had pushed up global energy costs.

News.title: Village votes to leave UK over asylum housing plan in symbolic referendum
News.content:
Residents of an Oxfordshire village have voted to become independent from the UK in a symbolic referendum held in protest at plans to house more than 1,000 migrants at a former military base.

Villagers in Piddington, near Bicester, voted on Tuesday over Home Office proposals to house up to 1,256 male asylum seekers at nearby MoD Bicester.

The referendum was organised by the parish council and out of 312 votes cast, 285 voted to leave, 26 voted no, and one ballot paper was spoiled.

The culture secretary told BBC Breakfast the government would not reconsider the migrant housing proposal.

Piddington's 350 residents were invited to cast their ballot in a small box outside the village hall.

Delivering the result, parish council vice chair Susannah Parden said: "We are Piddington the village that roars."

Parish council chair Tim McNally added: "This is an example of democracy in operation.

"We went into this village hall as the underdogs - we had a plucky idea. We have given a message to the world."

News.title: Writer and broadcaster Bonnie Greer dies aged 77
News.content:
British-American author and cultural commentator Bonnie Greer has died at the age of 77 after a brief illness, her husband has said.

In a statement delivered with "profound sadness", Greer's widower David Hutchins noted how the acclaimed playwright and critic had made "an enduring contribution to British cultural and public life" with her "intelligence, courage and distinctive voice".

He added: "To me, she was my partner, confidante and inspiration, and I feel profoundly privileged to have shared my life with her."

Hutchins continued: "Those closest to Bonnie will remember her warmth, humour, generosity and extraordinary ability to bring people together."

News.title: Call to raise tax thresholds among union demands ahead of Budget
News.content:
Unions who donate to Labour will meet John Healey on Thursday to press home their demands ahead of next month's Budget.

Unite, the UK's second biggest union, has called for a reversal of the freezing of tax thresholds, that see the lowest paid drawn into paying tax.

The union's leader, Sharon Graham, said she told Andy Burnham that the cut to the winter fuel allowance, carried out under former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer, was a "disgrace", adding: "What to you need to do is winter fuel in reverse - something that says to everyday people I am on your side."

The call is one of a number of policy proposals unions are taking to the chancellor, including increased taxes on tech companies.

Unions say they believe Healey's first budget will define Andy Burnham's direction of travel as prime minister.

Unite took legal action against Sir Keir's government when the winter fuel payment was restricted to the poorest pensioners, and Graham believed this policy - which was not in Labour's manifesto - was politically poisonous.

Burnham said the freezing of tax thresholds had come up on the doorsteps when he was campaigning to return to Westminster as MP for Makerfield.

In her last Budget, then-Chancellor Rachel Reeves froze tax thresholds until 2031. The basic rate of 20% is paid on annual earnings between Â£12,571 and Â£50,270. The higher rate of 40% is paid on earnings between Â£50,271 and Â£125,140.

By not uprating those rates in line with inflation, more lower paid people have paid tax for the first time and more better-off workers, including public service workers such as senior nurses, police officers and teachers, are now paying tax at the higher rate.

Graham said: "We must see things happen immediately. I told him [Burnham] that you have to make working class people believe their best days are in front of them.

"That tax threshold of around Â£12,500 - if that hadn't been frozen for the past few years it would have moved up to over Â£16,000 now. People at the lower end are paying eye-watering amounts of tax."

News.title: Reform defector reveals she voted Remain in Brexit vote and wants Welsh independence
News.content:
A Member of the Senedd who quit Reform to join Plaid Cymru says she would back Welsh independence if a vote were held and has revealed she voted Remain in the 2016 Brexit referendum.

Sarah Cooper-Lesadd, one of 34 Reform MSs elected in May's Senedd election, defected to Plaid on Tuesday.

She told BBC's Walescast that her former party was "completely chaotic" and was "falling apart at the seams".

Her defection - which came on the same day Dan Thomas stepped down as Reform's Welsh leader - means Plaid now has 44 members in Cardiff Bay, and Reform as the largest opposition party has 33 seats.

Thomas quit on Tuesday after he was arrested over the weekend on suspicion of assault and controlling or coercive behaviour. He was bailed pending further enquiries, and denies doing anything wrong.

Cooper-Lesadd said on Wednesday she had approached Plaid Cymru after a "period of deliberation".

"It's been a journey for me since coming to the Senedd, it's come after a period of thinking about it, so it has been a while," she said.

News.title: Judge explains compassionate release of murderer who failed to return to NI jail
News.content:
However, the DUP MLA Trevor Clarke, who sits on the policing board, said the whole process needed looked at.

"I think there's clear evidence that there was an issue in this case and that's now been borne out because this person hasn't come back," he told BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today programme.

"All of the things that the courts have involved themselves in this one, I think, has been wrong.

"A chaperone as opposed to a proper prison guard, this is an individual who cannot even handcuff the person while they're chaperoned, so all of the safeguards that could have been put in place weren't put in place."

Sinn FÃ©in MLA Linda Dillon, who also sits on the policing board, said the decision was down to the individual judge, but it is possible that the prison service had not provided them with sufficient information.

"If the prison service did not give all of the information that allowed them to come to the correct decision... then that is something that has gone wrong within the prison service," she told BBC Radio Ulster's Evening Extra programme.

Dillon added that questions need to be asked regarding why "the court allowed the prisoner to go with a chaperone who was a lay-person rather than prison officers".

On Wednesday, the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) confirmed that Anderson was last seen in the Eastway area of Creggan in Derry.

They also confirmed that they were liaising with An Garda SÃ­ochÃ¡na (Irish police).

News.title: Lucy Letby: Families' solicitor blames hospital bosses for police delay
News.content:
A solicitor representing seven of the families affected by Lucy Letby's crimes has said responsibility for the delay in contacting the police "lies squarely" with hospital executives.

On Tuesday, the Thirlwall Inquiry report revealed bosses at the Countess of Chester Hospital repeatedly failed in their duty of candour to parents, investigators and regulators.

Tamlin Bolton said each of the 1,100 pages of Lady Justice Thirlwall's findings contained "another opportunity where action could have been taken".

In a statement, former hospital executives named in the report said they were reviewing its findings and recommendations, but could not comment further while investigations remained under way.

Lucy Letby, 36, is serving 15 whole-life prison terms for the murder of seven babies and the attempted murder of seven others, including one baby whom she tried to murder twice.

The offences took place between 2015 and 2016, but concerns raised by consultants were not reported to police until May 2017.

News.title: UK in talks about joining global defence bank led by Canada
News.content:
The UK government is in discussions about joining a global investment bank aimed at raising more money for defence spending.

Chancellor John Healey is considering a bid to join the Defence, Security and Resilience Bank (DSRB), not long after his predecessor Rachel Reeves rejected the idea.

Canada has been leading efforts to establish the bank, which supporters say would enable governments to borrow at lower costs to increase military spending.

Treasury officials stressed that no decision has been made. A government spokesperson said it was "fully committed to working alongside our international partners to scale defence industrial capacity."

Before he cancelled commitments due to the death of his father, Prime Minister Andy Burnham had been due to meet Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney in the UK on Wednesday.

Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte is also travelling to the UK for his first meeting with the prime minister.

He is giving a speech in Oxfordshire, where he is expected to say the UK is "serious about security" and praise the country's efforts supporting Ukraine.

He will also say that Nato will "not be intimidated by Russia's campaign of hostile actions.

"Russia wants to stop us helping Ukraine â but their actions will only lead us to do more for Ukraine."

It comes after Nato forces shot down a drone over Lithuania in the latest security scare on the alliance's eastern flank, where tensions remain high amid Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

And on Tuesday Denmark also accused a Russian warship of firing two emergency flares at one of its helicopters while it was tracking the vessel in the Baltic Sea.

The DSRB is a multilateral bank aimed at providing cheaper loans to fund defence projects and has backing from Albania, Bulgaria, Belgium, Greece, Latvia, Luxembourg, Romania, Turkey and Ukraine.

Membership of the bank for the UK and other G7 countries would come with an upfront investment cost of around Â£870m spread over three years.

Paying for the UK's growing defence commitments is one of Healey's biggest headaches as he prepares for the Budget in October and next year's spending review.

The government has so far avoided committing to raising defence spending to 3% of national income by 2030, only repeating the longer term goal of 3.5% by 2035.

A 15-year-old Alaska boy survived about 62 hours stranded atop an overturned fishing boat in the frigid Bering Sea, trying to hold onto his brother and cousin after they drowned, his family says.

Derek Parker Aghnaanga was the lone survivor of a three-person fishing trip that ended when the skiff overturned near St. Lawrence Island. His older brother, Sidney Kulowiyi, 35, and cousin Barton Rookok, 34, died after the boat capsized.

The trio left the Alaska Native village of Savoonga on September 4 to fish for halibut. They were expected to return to St. Lawrence Island by about 3 a.m. on September 6, but never arrived.

Video shows Derek kneeling on top of the overturned skiff as waves crash around him. A U.S. Coast Guard HC-130 Hercules aircraft spotted him around 10:30 a.m. on September 7, after Alaska State Troopers notified the Coast Guard the previous night that the group was overdue. However, the Coast Guard-led search was delayed by dense fog.

Derek spent days exposed to the cold and waves without food or water before the Coast Guard called on the Northwest Explorer, a fishing vessel carrying 13 crew members and NOAA scientists, to help rescue him.

open image in gallery Derek Parker Aghnaanga, 15, was rescued after his fishing boat capsized in the Bering Sea off Alaska, while his older brother and cousin died in the incident ( Reuters )

“Saturday, all the way to Tuesday, that kid was on top of that skiff. I mean, that’s one tough kid,” Adam White, captain of the Northwest Explorer, told Alaska’s News Source.

The crew eventually reached Derek and pulled him aboard the vessel. White said the teenager was visibly suffering from the cold.

“Through the teeth chattering, he had mentioned that his brother was still under the skiff and then he said that in the previous night before our rescue that his cousin had slipped away off the top of the skiff,” White said.

Derek's aunt, Colleen Walker, described the teenager’s ordeal in a GoFundMe campaign set up to help the family with his funeral expenses.

“My nephew tried to hang onto them as long as he could after they drowned,” Walker wrote.

open image in gallery Derek, pictured, and his family members were out fishing for halibut ( GoFundMe )

open image in gallery Derek spent around 62 hours stranded on the boat ( Carlos Alexis Escartin via AP )

Acting as a family spokesperson, Darren Toolie-Noongwook, Derek’s older brother, further told Alaska News Source: “In the middle of the night, waves hitting him, he was kneeling and praying. That’s all he was doing was praying. He believed that he was gonna make it. That’s how he got through it.”

The Coast Guard recovered the bodies of Kulowiyi and Rookok and transported them and Aghnaanga to Nome. Derek is now reunited with his family.

open image in gallery His family said he prayed while sitting alone on the boat, believing he would survive ( Reuters )

The rescue also proved to be an emotional one for the crew, White said.

“When you look into a family member’s eyes ... there’s gratitude, but sorrow at the same time,” White said. “I know I became overwhelmed with it so I had to go hide in my room for a minute.”

US Air Force Secretary Troy Meink this week announced the United States has deployed what he called “on-orbit space control weapons”.

This public statement came as a surprise to many, but not for the reasons you may think. For many years now, China, Russia and the US have accused each other of weaponising space, or of creating an arms race in space. They have all consistently denied doing so. For the US now to declare it has space weapons, it seems like an admission that China and Russia’s accusations are correct.

It’s also worrying, because other countries might feel they have permission to do the same. And this would make space very unsafe, increasing the risk of attacks on satellites, which are crucial for modern militaries, as well as daily life on Earth, as we depend on those same satellites for things like GPS, internet, phones, banking, global shipping and transport.

What is a space control weapon?

The term “space control” may seem odd. But it comes from many years of US policies and military doctrines which all state that the US seeks dominance, superiority and control in space.

In 2025, the US Space Force released its Doctrine Document which stated: “Space control consists of offensive and defensive actions, referred to as counterspace operations.”

open image in gallery US Air Force Secretary Troy Meink this week announced the United States has deployed what he called ‘on-orbit space control weapons’ ( AP Photo/Matt Rourke )

Many countries already have so-called counterspace capabilities: the ability to interfere with each other’s satellites, whether by jamming a communications or GPS signal (which is happening regularly in and around Ukraine), “spoofing” a false GPS signal to confuse militaries about the whereabouts of their adversaries, cyber attacks, or electronic warfare.

None of this is Star Wars, but all of it can be worrying if it escalates.

As for what US space control weapons actually are, and whether they’re any different from existing counterspace capabilities, Meink refused to provide any more details.

There are three possibilities. First, they could be nuclear weapons, or weapons of mass destruction, but this is incredibly unlikely. Under the 1967 Outer Space Treaty it is illegal to place these weapons in orbit around Earth, or in outer space.

Americans and the Soviets both tested nuclear weapons early in the 1960s, and quickly learned their own satellites, as well as those of allies, were impacted immediately and that orbits remained radioactive over time, meaning it wasn’t in their own interests to use these kinds of weapons. It’s also nearly impossible to develop or launch these weapons without it being noticed by other countries’ intelligence-gathering.

Cassandra Steer is Chief Executive Officer, Australasian Centre for Space Governance; Associate Expert, National Security College, Australian National University. This article was first published by The Conversation and is republished under a Creative Commons licence. Read the original article .

Second, the space control weapons could be some other form of physical, or “kinetic” weapons. The Outer Space Treaty doesn’t ban other weapons, so this wouldn’t necessarily be illegal. Conventional explosives don’t work in space, but the Soviets and Americans did test small projectiles from one satellite to another in the 1960s and ‘70s. It would be surprising if this were to be the case now.

On the other hand, in 2022 China demonstrated the ability to grapple a defunct satellite and tug it about 2,000km away from its orbit. This could be used to remove space debris, but it could also be used to remove an active satellite. There is no evidence the US has this capability.

The third possibility is that Meink’s statement was a rebranding of existing counterspace capabilities as “weapons”, to assert power and maybe try and deter Russia and China from interfering with US satellites. We know both China and Russia have space-based jammers used to interrupt satellite signals, and it would make sense that the US has this capability as well, or something similar.

open image in gallery Many countries already have so-called counterspace capabilities: the ability to interfere with each other’s satellites, whether by jamming a communications or GPS signal ( AFP via Getty Images )

If this is the case, which I and other global space security experts estimate to be true, it is posturing. But this is still dangerous. It gives China and Russia plenty of justification to point to the US as an aggressor, and ramp up their own space weapons capabilities.

Destabilising space

This public declaration also plays into the hands of China and Russia, which have been proposing a Treaty on the Prevention of the Placement of Weapons in Outer Space since 2008.

The US and its allies, including Australia, have refused to negotiate the treaty, saying it’s too difficult to know what exactly is a space weapon, and what is being launched.

The Chinese foreign ministry has pointed to Meink’s statement as evidence of the US’ “weaponization of outer space, turning it into a battlefield, as well as an arms race there”. And Russia has called for space to be kept “free of any weapons”.

There has been significant progress in United Nations space arms control discussions over recent years. This statement from the US undermines those efforts.

While some countries still insist the Treaty on the Prevention of the Placement of Weapons in Outer Space is the only solution, there has been some agreement on norms, rules and principles of responsible behaviour in space. In particular, a new norm is emerging against ground-based missiles used as anti-satellite weapons.

Since 1981, every year, the UN General Assembly adopts a resolution on the Prevention of an Arms Race in Outer Space. Sadly, the US has refused to support it since 2023. This week’s declaration fits with this move away from international efforts, which is in line with the current US attitude against international collaboration in general.

Other countries should not shy away from calling out this declaration as escalatory – and should double down on their efforts to prevent an arms race in space when they meet in Geneva this November.

Stocks in London rallied on Wednesday despite news of higher inflation and an expected US rate increase, as oil prices edged lower.

In London, the FTSE 100 index ended up 30.34 points, 0.3%, at 10,688.47. The FTSE 250 advanced 251.46 points, 1.1%, at 24,070.20, and the AIM all-share climbed 5.21 points, 0.7%, to 788.36.

Brent oil was quoted at 104.54 dollars a barrel in London on Wednesday, down from 108.48 dollars late on Tuesday.

Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell, said the oil price fall provided some “much-needed relief” to the market following an intense period that fired up inflation worries.

“The dip in the commodity price might not be enough to steer the Federal Reserve on a different path, though. It is widely expected to raise interest rates today, with the first of potentially two or three hikes over the next six months,” he added.

The US Federal Reserve announces its interest rate call at 7pm with a quarter-point rate increase widely forecast.

Analysts at UBS said: “The decision represents a major policy test for Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh, including his ability to build consensus and manage market expectations around the degree of guidance provided on the interest rate path ahead.”

Ahead of the decision, bond yields eased back from recent highs. The yield on the US 10-year Treasury was quoted at 4.97%, narrowed from 5.01%. The yield on the US 30-year Treasury was quoted at 5.34%, trimmed from 5.37%.

In European equities on Wednesday, the CAC 40 in Paris rose 0.6%, while the DAX 40 in Frankfurt added 0.5%.

In New York, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down slightly at the time of the closing bell in London. The S&P 500 rose 0.5%, and the Nasdaq Composite advanced 0.9%.

Figures in the US showed retail sales increased strongly in August.

The US Census Bureau said retail and food services sales totalled 773.9 billion dollars in August, rising 1.2% from July and 6.0% from a year earlier. The monthly increase beat the FXStreet-cited consensus of 0.8%.

Retail sales had fallen by a revised 0.5% on-month in July, compared with the previously reported 0.6% decline. For the three months from June through August, sales were 6% higher than in the corresponding period a year earlier.

Ksenia Bushmeneva, economist at TD Economics, said retail sales had “roared back to life” in August following a disappointing performance in July.

That said, headwinds are “mounting”, the analyst added, pointing to higher mortgage rates and the squeeze on households from higher energy prices.

“This is likely to lead to some moderation in spending growth as we move into next year,” Ms Bushmeneva said.

In London, investors digested the latest UK consumer price inflation figures from the Office for National Statistics.

The ONS said consumer price inflation accelerated to 3.1% year-on-year in August from 2.9% in July, in line with market expectations cited by FXStreet.

The increase was driven by higher transport costs, particularly motor fuel, as rising oil prices fed through to consumers.

Core CPI, which excludes energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, rose 2.6% annually in August, unchanged from July and also matching market expectations.

Sanjay Raja, Deutsche Bank’s chief UK economist, said: “Bottom line, inflation is on the ascent with an unknown destination. Events in the Middle East continue to add to inflationary pressures.

“For the Bank of England, its job to keep inflation at 2% has become harder. Our own projections point to CPI on course to get close to 4% around the turn of the year. Rates may be restrictive, but the key policy question for the MPC will remain: are they restrictive enough.”

The Bank of England announces its latest interest rate decision at noon on Thursday, with a hold thought to be the most likely decision, albeit with a split vote.

Reflecting on the inflation figures, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said that he was ready to take “difficult decisions” ahead of the government’s coming budget.

While acknowledging that the impact of the Middle East war on inflation was “a challenge”, he said the government “won’t take risks with people’s living standards”.

The pound was quoted at 1.3449 dollars on Wednesday, down from 1.3485 dollars at the same time on Tuesday. Against the euro, sterling fell to 1.1658 euro from 1.1681 euro.

The euro eased to 1.1537 dollars from 1.1545 dollars. Against the yen, the dollar was trading at 155.09 yen, slightly down from 155.12 yen.

On the FTSE 100, Barratt Redrow led the risers, up 12%, after reporting mixed full-year results as the housebuilder looks to weather a tough backdrop for the sector.

The Leicestershire, England-based housebuilder reported better-than-expected profit but trimmed its outlook for financial year 2027.

Citigroup analyst Ephrem Ravi thinks that while lower financial 2027 volume guidance implies some downside risk to consensus earnings estimates, “strong sales momentum, synergy benefits and the sizeable buyback programme should help offset the earnings downside risk”.

Lower bond yields also supported the sector, with Persimmon up 5.8% on the FTSE 100. On the FTSE 250, Bellway, Taylor Wimpey and Vistry rose 7.1%, 5.9% and 5.7% respectively.

Mining stocks rose as metal prices climbed. Fresnillo, Antofagasta and Endeavour Mining advanced 2.2%, 2.7% and 1.6% respectively.

But the weaker oil price saw BP and Shell give back some recent gains, closing down 2.3% and 2.1%.

Gold was quoted at 4,345.07 dollars an ounce on Wednesday, up from 4,285.70 dollars on Tuesday.

The biggest risers on the FTSE 100 were Barratt Redrow, up 32.4p at 308.8p; Persimmon, up 63.5p at 1,162p; Burberry, up 31.4p at 1,009p; SSE, up 68p at 2,401p; and Babcock International Group, up 27.9p at 1,021.5p.

The biggest fallers on the FTSE 100 were St James’s Place, down 28p at 1,085p; BP, down 13.5p at 566.8p; Shell, down 76p at 3,576.5p; Metlen Energy & Metals, down 0.9p at 45.7p; and Compass, down 0.4p at 30.9p.

Thursday’s local corporate calendar has half-year results from retailer Next, and a trading statement from student accommodation provider Unite.

Thursday’s global economic calendar has an interest rate decision in the UK, eurozone CPI data and US initial jobless claims figures.

An Islamic State group member was sentenced Wednesday to 20 years in prison for aiding the terrorist organization that took credit for a suicide bombing that killed 13 U.S. service members and about 160 Afghans at the Kabul airport five years ago during the American military’s chaotic withdrawal from the country.

A federal jury in Virginia had convicted Mohammad Sharifullah in April of providing material support to the IS affiliate known as ISIS-K. But jurors could not agree whether he bore some responsibility for the airport bombing on Aug. 26, 2021.

U.S. troops were conducting an evacuation operation at the airport when a lone suicide bomber detonated an improvised explosive device near an entry point known as Abbey Gate. Sharifullah’s role in the attack was scouting a route to Hamid Karzai International Airport, prosecutors said.

Sharifullah received the maximum sentence for his one-count conviction in an international terrorism case that President Donald Trump heralded last year during a speech to a joint session of Congress.

Sharifullah did not testify at his trial and declined to address the court before U.S. District Judge Anthony Trenga imposed the sentence. The judge said the defendant was a “dedicated terrorist” who expressed no remorse for the “unfathomable” grief and suffering that he had caused.

Trenga heard victim impact statements from several parents of U.S. service members. From a podium only a few feet from where Sharifullah sat, they took turns paying tribute to their children's sacrifices and describing how the attack has shattered their families.

Mark Schmitz of Missouri asked Sharifullah to turn and look at him as he spoke about the life and death of his 20-year-old son, Marine Corps Lance Cpl. Jared Schmitz.

“They may have taken his life, but they'll never take his legacy," Schmitz said. “A bomb killed my son. It did not kill what he stood for.”

Sharifullah requested a 17-year prison sentence, while prosecutors sought 20 years. His lawyers say he was never an ISIS-K leader and has not been convicted of any conduct related to the airport suicide bombing.

"He was brought here because the government believed he participated in the Abbey Gate attack, a theory which it was unable to prove at trial,” defense attorneys wrote.

Prosecutors said in their sentencing memo that “from his teenage years, when he pledged an oath of allegiance to ISIS-K, Sharifullah’s carnage was driven by hate. Hate towards Americans.”

Jurors convicted Sharifullah of providing material support to ISIS-K. They deadlocked on whether any deaths at the airport “resulted from” that conspiracy. Sharifullah could have faced a possible life sentence if the jury had unanimously decided that question.

According to prosecutors, Sharifullah told a journalist that he wanted to “catch and kill the crusaders” from the United States for invading his country after the attacks of Sept. 11, 2001. They said Sharifullah was involved in dozens of other attacks, including a March 2024 assault on a Moscow concert hall that killed roughly 140 people.

Defense lawyers argued that prosecutors failed to present any evidence tying Sharifullah to the Kabul bombing besides his own words during hours of FBI questioning. His team said Sharifullah told FBI agents what he thought they wanted to hear, possibly because he was afraid of being tortured in Pakistani custody before he was brought to the U.S.

A review by U.S. Central Command found that the Abbey Gate bomber was Abdul Rahman al-Logari, an IS member who had been released from an Afghan prison by the Taliban. According to an FBI affidavit. Sharifullah recognized the alleged bomber as an operative he had known while incarcerated.

News.title: ChatGPT boss Sam Altman says ‘the world is right to be afraid’ of AI – but asks people to ‘trust us’
News.content:

The world is “right to be afraid of AI”, says Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI maker ChatGPT.

But he said that people should “trust that we are going to do the right thing because it's the right thing and we feel the magnitude of this”.

Mr Altman and the AI industry generally has come under increased scrutiny in recent days, kickstarted by a warning from a former Anthropic developer that the “people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade”. It has led to new calls for regulation and an increasing recognition among AI executives that it could be sensible to slow down development and focus on the security and safety of the technology.

Now, in a conference in San Francisco, he said that much of the concern was legitimate.

“It doesn't take as much imagination as it used to [...] to imagine how this could go wrong,” he said. “I think the world is right to be afraid of this.

There are “two big challenges” in making AI safe, he said: the danger of a loss-of-control accident or “some other serious thing that could go wrong”, as well as the danger that AI could concentrate power too closely and let specific people exert their worldview.

But he asked that people trust his company to be careful about the technology they are building. “The world should trust that we are going to do the right thing because it's the right thing and we feel the magnitude of this,” he said.

“It’s great for our industry to say we want to come together and we want to be able to coordinate and make sure we have enough time to do this safely,” he said. But he suggested that people get “very scared” because commercial pressures or racing to develop the technology could lead companies or countries to “not do the right thing”, he said.

The speech was Mr Altman’s first public remarks since the post by former Anthropic and OpenAI researcher Jacob Coxon sparked new fear about out-of-control AI. But they echoed a series of tweets that the OpenAI chief executive has posted in response to the growing calls for new safeguards and a slowing of AI development.

“The world deserves confidence that American companies developing increasingly capable AI will act responsibly, especially as the trajectory of progress has steepened,” he said in those posts. “Every frontier lab must deliver on this, and there is no reason any of us should come to work if we cannot.”

He said that the company would “welcome a federal framework that sets consistent safety requirements for frontier AI”. But he warned that companies do not need to work for regulation or government intervention to start building public confidence in AI safeguards, and that AI developers should first start doing what they can themselves to make their systems more secure.

News.content:

Federal workers were paid $9.5 billion not to work during the DOGE-led drive to shrink the government, according to a congressional watchdog.

The Government Accountability Office found paid administrative surged 435 percent from 2023 to 2025, with as much as $6.7 billion of that associated with the administration’s deferred resignation program.

​The DRP, a key feature of the DOGE-led crackdown, involved a January 2025 offer by the Trump administration to around 2 million federal workers.

Employees were given the option to resign while receiving full pay and benefits until September 30 that year. Some 139,963 people took up the offer, data shows.

open image in gallery Elon Musk was the de facto head of DOGE, which oversaw efforts to trim the size of the federal government ( Getty )

​The report, published Tuesday, analyzed payroll data from 76 agencies, representing around 95 percent of the federal workforce.

​Senator Patty Murray, vice-chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, tore into the Trump administration in a statement addressing the report’s findings.

​“After promising to cut waste, Trump instead set billions upon billions in taxpayer dollars on fire to quite literally pay people not to do jobs they loved - from researching cancer cures to taking care of our National Parks, and so much else,” she said.

“Trump spent billions to push out experienced and badly needed experts across government - this was the most expensive way imaginable to make government worse.”

open image in gallery Senator Patty Murray (pictured) accused Trump of setting 'billions upon billions in taxpayer dollars on fire' ( Getty )

The Office of Personnel Management criticized the GAO’s findings in a statement to The Independent.

“The GAO report fails to highlight the difference between a one-time expense ($9.5 billion) to reduce the size of the federal government by 270,000 employees and the $40 billion per year savings in taxpayer dollars that this reduction provides,” a spokesperson said.

“That 400% return on investment is a massive benefit to the taxpayer.”

​Slashing the size of the federal government was one of Trump’s key policies when running for president in 2024, backed by SpaceX CEO Elon Musk.

​When Trump took office, Musk became the de facto head of DOGE - an acronym that stands for Department of Government Efficiency, but shares a name with Musk’s favored meme-based cryptocurrency.

​​The department officially shut down in July, with its de facto leader infamously leaving the Trump administration a year earlier amid rumors of a feud with the president.

The official DOGE website estimates that around $215 billion has been saved overall through its efforts.

Summer signing Omar Marmoush believes Tottenham are on the verge of finding the key to turn around their dismal start to the season.

Roberto De Zerbi’s team have picked up just two points from four Premier League fixtures, with their only goals coming in the Carabao Cup before a 3-1 defeat at Liverpool on Tuesday ended their run.

Encouraging signs were nevertheless evident at Anfield, where Spurs outperformed their hosts across various metrics – shots taken, shots on target, possession, touches in the opposition box – but not in the one that mattered most.

That was partly due to Giorgi Mamardashvili, Liverpool’s backup goalkeeper, who made three fine saves, including a brilliant stop from a deflected Marmoush strike with the score at 2-1 late in the second half.

"He made an unbelievable save and he was one of the best players on the pitch," the on-loan Egypt international, for whom Spurs have an obligation to buy for £60 million at the end of the season, told the club’s website.

open image in gallery Roberto De Zerbi watched his side exit the Carabao Cup on Tuesday ( Getty )

"Everyone can see we reach the goal so many times, we have so much quality on the pitch – and from the people who come off the bench to give us this last push – and when these small details click it will be very good.

"Every game we create more and more chances and I am sure we are very close."

Tottenham’s goalscoring troubles are well documented, with Conor Gallagher’s 69th-minute header marking their first against top-flight opposition since the final day of last season. For a spell it put them in control, but they could not force an equaliser.

"These moments build the mentality and the team together. We are all one big family and we push together," Marmoush added.

"These small glimpses of success give us another push and we have to build this confidence within us without these moments in order to proceed to other games and be very successful.

"All of us in the club – the staff, the fans, the coaching staff, everyone around us – we have to support each other in order to reach our goal because that’s the only way we can reach it."

open image in gallery James Maddison is still not ready to start for Spurs ( Getty )

James Maddison made his third substitute appearance of the season, and while De Zerbi admits he can be the difference-maker, the midfielder is not yet ready to start.

"Maddison is for sure a different player, a special player but he has to be fit, he has to be in the right physical condition because the Premier League intensity is incredible," he said.

De Zerbi did confirm, however, that defender Pedro Porro will be ready to face Aston Villa on Saturday after missing the last two matches with a muscular problem.

“But that is why we cannot say it does not work for anyone. There are players who play every three days with no issues. They are very robust, their performances do not change too much.
