World.title: Famous South African hotel named among the world’s 50 best for 2026
World.content:
Mount Nelson has secured a spot on the prestigious 2026 list of the world’s 50 best hotels. Image: file

South Africa has made its mark on the global luxury travel scene, with one of Cape Town’s most recognisable hotels named among the 50 best hotels in the world for 2026.

Mount Nelson, A Belmond Hotel, took the 34th spot in this year’s #legend ranking, which was unveiled in Paris on 15 September.

The Cape Town landmark was the only South African property to feature in the top 50.



The list covers hotels across 22 destinations and six continents, with Rosewood Hong Kong taking the number one position for a second consecutive year. Asia dominated the ranking, accounting for 18 of the 50 hotels.

But for South Africa, the standout is the famous pink hotel beneath Table Mountain.

Inside Cape Town’s iconic Mount Nelson

Known affectionately as the Pink Lady, Mount Nelson has been part of Cape Town’s hotel scene since 1899.



The hotel sits beneath Table Mountain on nine acres of gardens and has 196 rooms and suites. Its distinctive pink colour was introduced in 1918 and has since become one of the hotel’s defining features.

Today, Mount Nelson combines its historic setting with contemporary luxury, offering several restaurants and bars, a spa, swimming pools and its famous afternoon tea.

Its dining line-up includes Amura by Ángel León, The Red Room by Chefs Warehouse, The Verandah and Planet Bar, among others.



The hotel also places a strong emphasis on South African art, design and local culture, giving guests experiences that extend beyond its accommodation.

What does it cost to stay?

A stay at Mount Nelson comes with a luxury-hotel price tag, although the exact rate depends on the room, dates and season.

The hotel currently offers everything from standard rooms at around R20 000 per night to large signature suites at around R47 000-R80 000 per night. (Prices correct at time of publishing)



For South African travellers, the hotel also has a South African Residents Promotion, which includes accommodation and daily breakfast, although rates vary according to availability and booking dates.

For those wanting a taste of the Mount Nelson experience without booking a room, the hotel also offers its famous afternoon tea, which costs R650 per adult and R350 per child under 12, while a pool cabana costs R6 000 per day for resident guests.

Mount Nelson joins the world’s best

The 2026 list placed Mount Nelson at number 34, putting the Cape Town hotel alongside some of the world’s best-known luxury properties.



The top five were:

Rosewood Hong Kong – Hong Kong Capella Bangkok – Bangkok Four Seasons Bangkok at Chao Phraya River – Bangkok Atlantis The Royal – Dubai Passalacqua – Lake Como

Other notable hotels in the top 50 included Claridge’s in London, Hôtel de Crillon in Paris, Raffles Singapore, The Taj Mahal Palace in Mumbai and The Peninsula Hong Kong.

World.title: Eskom to implement 13-hour power outage in Gauteng on Thursday
World.content:
Due to planned maintenance, Eskom has scheduled a 13-hour power outage that will affect some areas in parts of Ga-Rankuwa in Tshwane, Gauteng.

The maintenance is scheduled for Thursday, 17 September, from 06:00 to 19:00.

ESKOM SCHEDULES 13-HOUR POWER OUTAGE

Eskom stated that there will be an electricity supply disruption in Ga-Rankuwa, Tshwane due to maintenance that will be conducted on the distribution network.



“The power outage will affect customers in Kgabalatsane and Michas View on Thursday, 17 September, from 09:00 – 19:00. The interruption of electricity is necessary to perform essential maintenance on our distribution power lines,” the power utility said.

“Eskom in Gauteng conducts planned maintenance on the distribution electricity network across the province as part of its maintenance plan. It is essential for maintenance to be conducted to service the infrastructure to ensure the safety, reliability, and efficiency of the electricity supply,” Eskom added.

AFFECTED RESIDENTS URGED TO TREAT ELECTRICAL APPLIANCES AS LIVE

In the interest of safety, Eskom said customers should treat all electrical appliances as live at all times during the power outage.



“Eskom apologises for any inconvenience that may be caused by this maintenance. Should circumstances beyond the control of Eskom arise, the planned electricity maintenance may not proceed as communicated,” the power utility added.

World.title: Who was Owen Ndlovu? Former SABC presenter found dead
World.content:
Former SABC presenter Owen Ndlovu was found dead on Wednesday 16 September, days after being hijacked and kidnapped in Katlehong, on Gauteng’s East Rand.

OWEN NDLOVU’S BODY FOUND

Police spokesperson Colonel Dimakatso Nevhuhulwi confirmed that Ndlovu was fetching his wife from a church service in Katlehong, when three approached their vehicle. One, who was allegedly armed with a firearm pushed her aside and forced Ndlovu into the back seat of his Ford Raptor bakkie before driving off.

His body was discovered the following morning by residents of Thokoza in Ekurhuleni having sustained gunshot wounds. The hijacked bakkie was later found abandoned in Walkerville. Police have launched a manhunt for the three suspects. A postmortem is expected to formally confirm the cause of death.



“According to the residents who found him, Owen had sustained gunshot wounds. His bag was also found a few metres from where his body was discovered,” said family spokesperson Eugene Mthethwa.

“At this stage, the family is awaiting further information from the relevant authorities regarding the circumstances surrounding Owen’s death,” said Mthethwa.

WHO WAS OWEN NDLOVU?

World.title: DA offers to add R500K to reward in Ekurhuleni deaths probe
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - The Democratic Alliance (DA) has offered to add an additional R500 000 to the cash reward for information that could assist investigation into the deaths of multiple women in Ekurhuleni.

This amount follows a R400 000 cash reward which was announced by Acting National Police Commissioner, Puleng Dimpane, on Tuesday night.

This then brings the total cash reward to R900 000.

READ | R400k reward offered in Ekurhuleni women's deaths probe

In a statement on Wednesday, the DA said their intention is to add to the “efforts of law enforcement”.

“The DA is adding an extra reason for all relevant information to be handed over now, to address this crisis quickly. Ekurhuleni cannot wait. Women cannot wait. Justice cannot wait,” the party said.

On Tuesday, Acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia reflected on the state's cash reward in place as one of other measures being implemented as investigations into the matter continue.

Other measures include the establishment of a high-level multidisciplinary team to lead the investigation.

There will also be an increased police presence through Operation Shanela in Kempton Park and surrounding areas.

World.title: South Africa pushes back on US visa curbs
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - South Africa on Wednesday hit back at new US visa restrictions over its racial equity policies, accusing the Trump administration of distorting its laws and further straining ties between Washington and one of Africa's most influential powers.

The dispute is the latest front in a broader clash over race, trade and diplomacy that has seen Washington cut aid, impose tariffs, expel South Africa's ambassador and boycott a G20 summit in Johannesburg, all against the unresolved legacy of white minority rule.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the new visa restrictions would target those who promote "race-based discrimination, incite violence, or enable land confiscation without compensation in South Africa".

International Relations Minister Ronald Lamola said Pretoria viewed the move "with concern" and that Washington was echoing narratives promoted by fringe groups opposed to South Africa's post-apartheid reforms.

"We reiterate that healing the divisions of the past and establishing a society based on democratic values, social justice and fundamental human rights is a constitutional imperative," Lamola said in a statement.

READ: US imposes visa curbs on SA over 'race-based discrimination'

The United States did not immediately name any individuals targeted by the restrictions but warned of further "severe" action.

"This visa restriction policy is only the first step in a series of escalatory measures that will show America's firm resolve in this matter," US ambassador to South Africa, Brent Bozell, said.

- 'Hypocrisy' -

President Donald Trump has criticised South Africa's land reform and employment equity laws, which were introduced after the end of apartheid to address racial disparities that remain among the world's widest.

Trump has portrayed the measures as discriminatory against Afrikaners, the white minority descended largely from Dutch settlers, a claim Pretoria rejects.

In 2025, he berated President Cyril Ramaphosa in the Oval Office over discredited claims of a "white genocide" in South Africa.

While the US president has broadly cracked down on immigration, his administration has offered refugee status to thousands of white South Africans it says face persecution.

Lamola rejected suggestions that the government was targeting any racial group, saying crime remained a national challenge affecting all South Africans.

READ: 'Broader attack': Analyst warns of escalating US pressure on South Africa

The opposition uMkhonto we Sizwe (MK) party, led by former president Jacob Zuma, also condemned the visa restrictions, calling them an affront to South Africa's sovereignty.

"The hypocrisy of Washington's position is breathtaking. It lectures South Africa, while arming Israel amid the reported killing of more than 73,000 Palestinians in Gaza," it said in a statement.

Despite the tensions, Pretoria and Washington have remained engaged in efforts to thaw relations.

"The discussions have highlighted the need for any resolution to consider South Africa's unique circumstances and to respect its democracy, constitution, sovereignty, and the will of its people," Lamola said.

South Africa is the United States' largest trading partner on the African continent with more than 500 US businesses and 30,000 US citizens based in the country.

South Africa said last month it would offer a "generous" new trade deal to the United States as it seeks to avoid hefty tariffs that threaten job losses on top of a dire unemployment crisis.

World.title: The endless cycle: Women die, outrage follows, nothing changes
World.content:
South Africa repeatedly finds itself trapped in the same devastating cycle.

A woman is abused, sexually assaulted or murdered.

Her story captures national attention, and the country erupts in outrage.

Social media fills with calls for justice, politicians issue statements condemning the violence, strategies are debated, and the government vows to do more.

Then, slowly, the noise dies down. The speeches become yesterday’s news, and the urgency from those in power appears to fade with it.

That's until another woman becomes the next headline.

This raises a difficult question.

At what point will the government move beyond statements, speeches, and promises, and treat gender-based violence (GBV) as the national crisis it truly is?

South Africa has spoken about GBV for years.

Strategies, policies, and laws are in place to protect women and hold perpetrators accountable.

Yet, women continue to be raped, assaulted, and murdered.

A total of 569 women were killed between April and June alone, a stark reminder that these are not isolated tragedies, but part of a persistent, systemic crisis.

The question is therefore no longer whether the government recognizes GBV as a problem. It does.

The real question is: What it is actually doing to stop the next woman from becoming a statistic?

On the afternoon of Wednesday, 9 September, 38-year-old Elizabeth "Tsontso" Moselakgomo went out for a routine afternoon run in Kempton Park.

She never came home. As hours turned into days, her friends and fellow runners took to social media, desperately appealing to the public for help.

They shared her photographs and urged anyone with information about her whereabouts to come forward.

Then came the devastating news that several women's bodies had been discovered in the area.

For women across South Africa, the weekend felt unbearably heavy. As the country waited for answers, prayers were shared, and loved ones held onto the fleeting hope that Moselakgomo would return home safely to her eight-year-old daughter.

The nation waited anxiously for the identification results, with every update carrying the weight of a country holding its collective breath.

When Moselakgomo was positively identified as one of the deceased, that collective hope collapsed into profound grief, all devastated by the reality of a woman who had simply gone out for a run and never returned.

For her family, the agonizing search was over, but a lifetime of pain had just begun.

Once again, South Africa is left confronting the terrifying reality faced by women who leave their homes and do not make it back.

Women should not have to become national headlines before their safety becomes a priority.

We've heard the speeches, the promises and the strategies.

What we desperately need now is urgency, strict implementation, and lasting change.

The ultimate measure of the government’s response to gender-based violence cannot simply be how strongly it condemns the latest tragedy.

It must be whether its actions successfully prevent the next one.

World.title: Gauteng requests army’s help to fight crime
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Gauteng has requested assistance of the South African National Defence Force’s (SANDF) in the fight against crime in the province.

The request follows the discovery of the bodies of eight women in the Ekurhuleni area over the past two months.

Speaking during an extensive media briefing on the state of governance in the province, Premier Panyaza Lesufi said the killings in Ekurhuleni highlighted a disturbing trend.

“We have agreed that we have to bring every resource that we have to find the perpetrators because, if we can’t, we will continue to have this anxiety and fear, and people will not believe that the system can protect [them],” Lesufi said.

An emergency meeting with acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia on Tuesday evening resolved that Kempton Park and surrounding areas should be placed under lockdown.

“Every resource that we have must be deployed there until we’ve got a resolution [on] why we have so many bodies in that region. If we leave it unattended, our credibility as the state will be challenged,” Lesufi said.

Lesufi said the province had mandated Cachalia to engage the relevant ministry to request the SANDF’s assistance.

“They are already in Gauteng; we just have to redefine the roles. We just need an additional resource. The minister is engaging the relevant minister and the president on this one,” he said.

World.title: SA Visa restrictions suspicious ahead of US midterm elections - Analyst
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - It is intriguing that the US visa ban announcement on South Africa comes two months before the country's midterm elections.

This is according International Relations Expert Brooks Spector. Even more intriguing, he said, is Afrikaner groups like Lex Libertas and their presentations in Washington DC.

"The Republican Party is in some difficulties," he said.

On Tuesday, the US announced new visa restrictions targeting certain foreign nationals linked to what Washington describes as race-based discrimination, incitement of violence and uncompensated land seizures in South Africa.

The Trump administration has again raised allegations of government-sponsored discrimination against Afrikaners and concerns over land expropriation in South Africa.

World.title: In hydropowered Bhutan, solar starts to rise
World.content:
THIMPHU - Engineer Rinzin Galley stands on a platform overlooking a former military shooting range on the edge of Bhutan's capital Thimphu, now home to a gleaming field of solar panels.

With abundant waterways, Bhutan has long relied on hydroelectric power to meet its electricity needs and stay carbon negative -- absorbing more planet-warming gases than it emits.

But demand is growing, and in winter, when rivers run low before the mountain melt arrives, Bhutan already relies on imported Indian electricity.

Climate change is also threatening the future of the glaciers that feed those rivers, adding impetus to a push for energy diversification.

"Solar projects are booming," said Rinzin, senior engineer at Norion Renewable Energy.

The company's biggest project to date is the Dechencholing solar farm on former military land, with an installed capacity of 4.45 megawatts (MW).

Dechencholing is one of several solar fields developed in recent years, including the country's first mega project -- Sephu, with over 22 MW capacity.

That is relatively modest, especially compared to the vast solar fields installed in neighbouring China.

But it represents a new direction for Bhutan, where hydropower exports account for up to 15 percent of GDP, according to the World Bank.

World.title: Helen Mirren delves into Patricia Highsmith's mind in 'A Talent for Murder'
World.content:
TORONTO - Helen Mirren makes no secret of her admiration for writers, something reflected in her portrayal of American author Patricia Highsmith in "A Talent for Murder," the thriller that premiered at the Toronto Film Festival.

"It was a fascinating journey to go into her psychology," the 81-year-old British Oscar winner commented this week at a roundtable with journalists.

In "A Talent for Murder," Mirren embodies Highsmith, the author of the Tom Ripley novels, who moved in the 1980s to a small town in Switzerland, where she led an increasingly secluded life.

Directed by Anton Corbijn, the film presents a psychological duel between the renowned writer and her agent, Edward Ridgeway (Alden Ehrenreich), who tries to convince her to write a new Tom Ripley novel.

"Playing Highsmith was intense," Mirren told AFP.

Although there wasn't much audiovisual material available, the actor found clues to portray the reclusive writer in interviews and videos.

In that process, Mirren discovered she had nothing in common with her character.

"I've gone in the opposite direction in my attitude to life. She became very embittered, very private, isolated," Mirren said of Highsmith. "She was not a very nice person at the end of her life at all."

Likewise, the idea that anyone is capable of committing a crime is inconceivable to Mirren.

"I've never thought of killing a person. I don't think Patricia Highsmith is right about that," she said.

And the film doesn't hide that side of her personality.

"One wants to pay respect to her genius and her brilliance," Mirren said. "But I think it would do her a disservice to try and smooth over the edges that she very much had."

World.title: China warns against space 'battlefield' after US says weapons deployed
World.content:
BEIJING - China warned against turning outer space into a "battlefield" and Russia said it must be "free from any weapon" after the United States confirmed for the first time that it has arms deployed in orbit above the Earth.

Analysts said that the revelation by Washington confirmed an open secret but the timing of the announcement risked exacerbating tensions with Beijing and the risk of a weapons race in space.

The announcement marked a new stage in the major powers' rush for military space capabilities, driven by rapid technological advancements but lacking a comprehensive legal framework.

"The US has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action," a US Space Force spokesperson said in a statement that did not provide specifics on the weapons.

China's foreign ministry opposed the move, warning against the "weaponisation of outer space, turning it into a battlefield, as well as an arms race there".

"We urge the US side to stop expanding its military capabilities and preparing for war in outer space," ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun told a news briefing.

Russia called Tuesday for space to be kept "free of any weapons".

"We are counting on broad international consolidation to continue working toward the complete demilitarisation of space," said Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov.

- What are the US capabilities? -

The US statement did not provide concrete details about what weapons are deployed in space and how many.

"Space control encapsulates the mission areas required to contest and control the space domain -- employing kinetic and non-kinetic means to affect adversary capabilities," the statement said.

"These capabilities can be employed for offensive and defensive purposes," it added.

Non-kinetic means could include lasers to blind satellites, or even electromagnetic or cyber jamming of their data links.

- Why does the US want weapons in space? -

For Washington, both Russia and China -- its two main geopolitical rivals -- pose potential threats to US interests in space.

China "develops and operates space and counterspace capabilities as part of a military modernisation strategy," according to the US Space Force.

Russia, meanwhile, "views space as a warfighting domain and believes space supremacy will be a decisive factor in future conflicts", it said.

The militarisation of space is as old as the space race itself -- as soon as the USSR's Sputnik was launched into orbit as the first probe in space in 1957, Washington and Moscow began exploring ways to both arm and destroy satellites.

India in March 2019 said it had destroyed a low-orbiting satellite, following in the footsteps of Russia, China and the US, in a missile test that proved the nation was among the world's most advanced space powers.

- How might China react? -

Song Zhongping, an independent military commentator based in Hong Kong and former Chinese army instructor, told AFP the announcement was "no surprise at all" as the fact that the US possesses such weapons "has long been an open secret".

"The only difference is that the US used to keep it ambiguous, whereas now it has gone public, which shows that Washington is no longer trying to hide it," he added.

"China will not stand by and do nothing", he warned, noting Beijing already has its own space station in orbit.

"Whether China deploys weapons in space will depend entirely on whether the United States moves in that direction," he said.

The Wall Street Journal said Beijing supplied Iran with satellite imagery that enabled Tehran to precisely target military facilities and kill US service members in Jordan in July -- a claim China has denied.

- Can weapons in outer space be regulated? -

The biggest worry was once about nuclear weapons in space, but the superpowers and other countries signed the Outer Space Treaty in 1967, banning weapons of mass destruction in orbit.

Since then, Russia, the United States, China and India have explored ways to fight in space outside of that treaty, including by targeting rivals' satellites, which are key for military communications, surveillance and navigation.

"There is a regulatory vacuum because Article 4 of the 1967 treaty only forbids weapons of mass destruction and nuclear weapons in orbit," said space law expert Laetitia Cesari.

She said the topic would likely be on the agenda at the next UN disarmament meeting in November.

"Moscow and Beijing have been wanting to work for about twenty years on a treaty to prevent the placement of weapons in space," while "Western states are trying instead to work on the notion of responsible behaviour," Cesari said.

The US announcement "will likely give impetus to the restrictive approach that Moscow and Beijing are pushing for," she added.

World.title: Farmer's widow and brother to face murder charges
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Michael Maina Karembesha and Mary Muthoni before Kitale Law Courts on September 16, 2026. [Martin Ndiema, Standard]

The widow and brother of the late prominent farmer Joseph Njenga Njuguna from Chepchoina in Trans Nzoia County will face murder charges at the High Court in Kitale.

Kitale Magistrate Wilkister Magwi Ghati ordered the deceased’s widow, Mary Muthoni and his brother, Michael Maina Karembesha, to be held at Endebess Police Station until they enter their pleas on Thursday.

This decision came after the Directorate of Criminal Investigations (DCI) in Endebess requested more time to conclude investigation before formally charging the suspects.

On Wednesday, Ghati said that the court had reviewed a letter dated September 16, 2026, along with the prosecution's arguments.

“The first suspect, Muthoni, the wife of the deceased, and the third suspect, Maina, the deceased's brother, will be held at Endebess Police Station to take their plea on September 17, 2026, before the High Court,” the magistrate said.

The magistrate also ordered the release of the second suspect from custody who will serve as the prosecution witness.

The farmer’s security guard Joseph Mboche will stand as the prosecution witness.

The prosecution informed the court that the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions (ODPP) had completed investigations and found sufficient evidence to charge Muthoni and Maina with murder, in violation of Sections 203 and 204 of the Penal Code.

However, they indicated that there was not enough evidence to charge Joseph Mwangi, and another security guard, Kefa Kipsami.

The prosecution requested the court to release the two, who would serve as the prosecution witnesses in the case.

Njuguna, 68, was discovered dead in his home at Kiptugut Farm in Kimase, Chepchoina, three weeks ago.

Muthoni, was said to have been kidnapped during the incident and was later found in Kitale town.

World.title: Muthaiga Golf Club restores access after KFS standoff
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Muthaiga Golf Club has restored access to a section of its course that was temporarily taken over by the Kenya Forest Service (KFS), hours after the agency moved into the area, claiming it forms part of Karura Forest.

The disruption affected the Front Nine, covering Holes Two to Nine, before the club’s board intervened to restore normal operations.

In a statement issued Tuesday, Muthaiga Golf Club Chairman Dennis Mwirigi said the board had taken the necessary steps to facilitate the resumption of activities after the temporary disruption.

“We are pleased to confirm that access to the affected part of the course has been restored and members may proceed with their scheduled activities as usual,” Mwirigi said.

He said the board remained committed to protecting the club’s interests, assets and members while addressing the matter through the appropriate channels.

The development follows an earlier communication to members informing them that KFS had taken over access to the affected section, claiming it was part of Karura Forest.

The club had initially said the Front Nine would not be accessible until further notice as it sought to resolve the matter. The driving range and parking areas were not affected.

The incident sparked criticism over the manner in which KFS handled the dispute, with Prof Karanja, Chairperson of Friends of Karura Forest, urging the agency to pursue dialogue and legal channels.

Prof Karanja said KFS should have first engaged the club’s management and clearly explained its claim over the disputed land instead of deploying dogs, guns and heavy security.

“If they don't agree that it was your land, go to court. The court will determine,” he said.

He questioned whether KFS had adequately demonstrated that the disputed section was forest land or explained how it was allegedly acquired by Muthaiga Golf Club.

“They should have come publicly and said, look, Muthaiga, that area and that area belong to the forest,” Prof Karanja said.

He said KFS should identify the specific portion of land it claims belongs to the forest and explain the basis of its claim before taking further action.

Prof Karanja argued that the dispute should be resolved through established legal procedures rather than force. “Trees are not protected by guns,” he said.

He described the deployment of armed personnel as the wrong way of resolving a land dispute and called for engagement between KFS and the golf club.

Prof Karanja also warned that actions by government agencies could have wider implications for the administration of President William Ruto, saying confrontational conduct could lead members of the public to associate such actions directly with the government.

“When government departments behave like this, everybody now starts thinking, oh, it's Ruto's whatever,” he said.

He further recalled a previous dispute involving Friends of Karura Forest, where he said armed personnel were deployed and the group removed from an area before senior government officials intervened.

According to Prof Karanja, officials from the Treasury and forestry departments eventually intervened and encouraged dialogue to resolve the matter.

He urged KFS to adopt a similar approach in the Muthaiga dispute, saying the agency and the club should present their respective claims and seek a court determination if they cannot agree.

For now, the restoration of access means members can resume their scheduled activities, while the underlying dispute over the contested section remains subject to further engagement between KFS and the club.

World.title: Juja couple's surprise blessing of five babies
World.content:
Mercy Kanini, 28, from Juja, Kiambu County, gave birth to five children at Thika Level Five Hospital. [Gitau Wanyoike, Standard]

A couple from Juja, Kiambu County, is celebrating the unexpected arrival of five babies after scans during pregnancy showed they were expecting quadruplets.

Mercy Kanini, 28, delivered four girls and a boy through normal delivery at Thika Level Five Hospital, in a rare case believed to be among only a handful of quintuplet births recorded in Kenya.

World.title: Police to restrict access to CBD during Linda Mwananchi Nairobi rally
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Linda Mwananchi officials during a rally. [Courtesy]

Organisers of the Linda Mwananchi rally and their supporters will not be allowed to access Nairobi’s Central Business District (CBD), Nairobi Regional Police Commander Issa Mohamud has warned.

According to Mohamud, police had received notification of the planned rally, which is scheduled to take place at Jacaranda Grounds on Sunday, through Embakasi East MP Babu Owino.

However, he warned that the CBD would remain off-limits, saying police would not allow Nairobi to become a battleground for political supremacy.

“The National Police Service respects the constitutional right of every Kenyan to assemble, demonstrate, express political views, and participate in public affairs, but that right must be exercised peacefully, lawfully, and with respect to the rights and safety of other Kenyans,” Mohamud stated.

According to Mohamud, they had received a tip that some individuals were planning to mobilise goons to disrupt the rally, prompting the directive to keep the CBD out of bounds.

“We have received some information, some credible information, that some individuals may seek to mobilise groups of unruly youths and goons to outnumber and intimidate and confront rival groups.”

“Therefore, I make a direct appeal to all political leaders, organisers or influencers to restrain their supporters and control their crowds. No political objective is worth the blood of a Kenyan,” he added.

Mohamud assured the organisers and those planning to attend the rally that police would provide security throughout the event and facilitate all lawful activities.

The Linda Mwananchi movement is set to hold its Nairobi rally on Sunday, September 13. The procession will start at All Saints Cathedral before proceeding to Jacaranda Grounds.

World.title: ODM vows not to interfere with Linda Mwananchi rally in Nairobi
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Linda Mwananchi leaders during a rally in Western Kenya. [Linda Mwananchi, X]

The Orange Democratic Movement (ODM) has said it will not disrupt the planned Linda Mwananchi rally scheduled for Sunday at Jacaranda Grounds.

In a statement on Friday, September 11, ODM Nairobi Chairman George Aladwa said the party had no business interfering with the rally, noting that Linda Mwananchi had a right to speak to Nairobi residents.

“I want to make it clear that nobody in ODM has any intention of disrupting or interfering with the Linda Mwananchi rally,” Aladwa stated.

He added: “We believe that political competition should be about ideas, policies and the ability to convince Kenyans, rather than confrontations between supporters of different political formations.”

Aladwa said ODM’s opponents had a right to tell Nairobi residents what they stood for and what they intended to offer Kenyans.

“The people are intelligent enough to listen to different political messages and make their own decisions,” Aladwa said.

At the same time, Aladwa said ODM was engaged in an extensive programme to market and strengthen the party across Nairobi as it prepared for activities to commemorate the anniversary of the death of its former party leader, the late Raila Amolo Odinga.

The chairman lauded Odinga for his contribution to Kenya’s democracy, the struggle for constitutional reforms and the political transformation of the country, saying his contribution could not be erased.

“His legacy remains an important part of ODM and Kenya’s political history. As we approach the 2027 General Election, our responsibility is to ensure that ODM remains strong, organised and firmly rooted across Nairobi,” the chairman stated.

“We will continue engaging residents in all constituencies and wards and explaining the party’s agenda to the people. I appeal to ODM supporters to remain calm and focused. Do not allow yourselves to be provoked into unnecessary political confrontations,” he added.

World.title: Ndindi Nyoro tells Ruto to keep off Tata Chemicals
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

PPK leader Ndindi Nyoro addresses a rally at Nambale market in Busia on August 30, 2026. [Benjamin Sakwa, Standard]

Kiharu MP Ndindi Nyoro has cautioned President William Ruto against meddling in the affairs of Tata Chemicals, Africa’s largest soda ash plant in Lake Magadi, Kajiado County.

Nyoro, who is the Peoples’ Party of Kenya leader, has accused President Ruto of an alleged plot to take control of Tata Chemicals through a shareholding scheme.

He said Ruto’s directive on Tata Chemicals closure raises concerns over the future of multinational firms and their operations in the country.

Speaking during a tour of Wote, Makueni County, on Thursday, Nyoro termed the Head of State’s move selfish, saying even if he had since softened his stance on the firm, it remains wanting for investors.

“His utterances were and remain wanting for external and internal investors. We don’t want investors to work in a bad political environment. Even if he seems to have made a U-turn on the matter, we are aware he has been pushing to be a shareholder in the company. We don’t want investors to be interfered with politically because we must create an environment where our people have access to job opportunities. It is almost reaching a catastrophic level in terms of lack of jobs for our people,” he said

The PPK leader warned that the country is in a bad economic state with a Sh13.5 trillion debt that is projected to grow further by next year.

“When Ruto exits next year the debt will be more than Sh15 trillion. The next president, who will be coming from the opposition, will have hard times in running this country. For every Sh100 that will be collected as tax from 2028, Sh91 will be used to repay government debts. We should not have time now to fight as opposition and also as Kenyans. We must hold hands and send the president back home because of his failures,” Nyoro said.

The MP urged opposition leaders to put aside their political differences and unite behind a single presidential candidate ahead of the 2027 General Election, saying that a united opposition would have a better chance of defeating President Ruto.

“If the opposition wants to defeat President Ruto, they must come together and present one presidential candidate. I am ready to talk to all the opposition principals,” Nyoro said.

Nyoro also outlined a raft of proposals he says could help revive Kenya’s economy and ease the financial burden on ordinary citizens.

Among his proposals is the use of the National Social Security Fund (NSSF) to strengthen the health sector. He argued that Kenyans should be able to access quality healthcare without being forced to bear the full cost of medical services.

Nyoro further proposed changes to the way education is financed, suggesting that bursaries currently administered through the National Government Constituencies Development Fund (NG-CDF) and county governments be channelled towards financing free primary and secondary education.

He said such an approach would create a more uniform education financing system and ensure that children from poor households are not disadvantaged because of their parents' inability to meet school-related expenses.

Nyoro's proposals come amid growing debate over the country's economic direction, the cost of living, access to healthcare and the financing of education.

World.title: Sisi and Bin Salman – Our understanding is absolute, and our goals are the same
World.content:
A meeting on Tuesday between President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi and Prince Mohammed bin Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud—Crown Prince and Prime Minister of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia—resulted in a consensus that relations between Egypt and Saudi Arabia must serve as an example for the rest of the Arab world, and that the security of Saudi Arabia and the Gulf states is integral to Egypt’s national security.

Egypt also affirmed its unequivocal rejection of any aggression or threats targeting Saudi Arabia’s sovereignty, stability, and territorial integrity, or freedom of navigation in international maritime corridors.

Both sides emphasized that current circumstances necessitate greater solidarity between both nations, noting their shared interests and objectives as well as their absolute mutual understanding.

They further highlighted that the Crown Prince’s visit underscores the solidarity and deep fraternal bonds uniting Egypt, the Kingdom, and all Gulf states.

The meeting comes as Sisi receives Prince Mohammed bin Salman during the Saudi Crown Prince’s working visit to Egypt.

Both leaders agreed on the need to intensify efforts to devise and implement practical measures for enhancing bilateral cooperation and removing any obstacles hindering the growth of trade and investment.

The aim is to elevate relations to a level commensurate with the historical ties and strategic neighborly relationship between Egypt and Saudi Arabia.

The Spokesperson for the Egyptian Presidency, Mohamed al-Shennawy said that the discussions addressed regional developments and current challenges, with the President reaffirming Egypt’s steadfast position of supporting the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and all Arab nations during this crisis.

Addressing regional challenges

The talks tackled regional developments and current challenges.

President Sisi reiterated Egypt’s unwavering position in supporting Saudi Arabia and all Arab countries in confronting the prevailing regional circumstances.

Both sides reaffirmed the need to intensify coordination and communication between the two countries.

The Crown Prince appreciated Egypt’s various positions, under the leadership of President Sisi, in support of regional stability and peace efforts, valuing Egypt’s solidarity and support for the kingdom in confronting the recent geopolitical challenges.

The two sides also underscored the joint Egyptian-Saudi stance in support of ensuring freedom and security of maritime navigation in the Straits of Hormuz, Bab al-Mandeb, and the Red Sea.

President Sisi stressed Egypt’s support for the measures taken by the kingdom to safeguard its security and stability, as well as for efforts to reach a comprehensive and sustainable political solution to the Yemen crisis.

The two leaders affirmed the unity of Egyptian and Saudi positions on the Palestinian cause and the need to achieve a just and comprehensive settlement based on the two-state solution and the relevant resolutions of international legitimacy.

And both sides stressed the need to implement the obligations of the second phase of the US President’s peace plan and UN Security Council Resolution 2803, while ensuring the delivery of sufficient quantities of humanitarian aid to the Gaza Strip and putting an end to Israeli violations in Gaza, the West Bank, and East Jerusalem.

The President and the Crown Prince further reaffirmed Egypt and Saudi Arabia’s continued support for the security and stability of Sudan, the need to preserve the exclusivity of its national institutions, and the rejection of equating the Sudanese Armed Forces with any militias or other illegitimate parallel entities.

They stressed that any threat to Sudan’s unity and territorial integrity poses a danger to the collective security of Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and all countries of the region.

The meeting also witnessed an affirmation of shared Egyptian-Saudi positions in support of the sovereignty and stability of all Arab countries.

President Sisi and the Crown Prince concurred on maintaining direct consultations and coordination in the coming period on various bilateral issues and regional developments.

World.title: Why Trump’s diesel woes are playing right into Moscow’s hands
World.content:
Faced with record diesel prices and less than two months to go until the midterm elections, Donald Trump has reverted to a default setting in his turbulent and abortive campaign to end the Ukraine war: blaming the victim. His timing could not be worse for Ukraine, or more beneficial to Russia.

“Mr. Zelensky has to do one thing: He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia,” the US president told reporters Sunday, referring to his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky. “It’s hurting the world.”

Trump’s attitude is at best inconsistent, coming less than a year after sources told CNN the US had increased intelligence-sharing with Ukraine so it could hit Russian energy sites (back when oil prices were low), and barely a week after he claimed gas prices would come down when the Iran war ends (without mentioning the Ukraine war).

It’s also incorrect, according to analysts, to claim that if Ukraine stopped attacking Russian refineries, the price problem would be solved. Andy Lipow, from Texas-based Lipow Oil Associates, estimates that Russia’s decision to ban exports in response to Ukrainian attacks has taken 800,000 barrels per day of diesel off the market. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz, meanwhile, has affected 1.2 million barrels a day.

At worst, this is another betrayal of Kyiv, which, faced with a critical lack of air defenses, is playing one of the few cards it has left — hitting Russia’s military machine and the energy resources that power it on Russian soil. The betrayal is all the more painful, coming amid almost constant Russian drone and missile attacks and ahead of a winter that Moscow openly plans to weaponize.

On Monday, Trump claimed on Truth Social that both Russia and Ukraine had agreed to halt attacks on each other’s energy sites (spoiler: they hadn’t). What followed in the Kremlin’s response was a master class in truth-twisting, as it extracted every last drop of PR gold.

Ukrainian law enforcement officers stand among the debris of a destroyed petrol station, following an air attack earlier this month. AFP/Getty Images

First, simple tactics. In a comment likely designed to placate Trump, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov called the proposal “a very good idea,” adding: “We are in contact with the American side.” He also offered up the usual fiction designed to make Ukraine look bad: “We always favor peaceful solutions.”

Then, a more delicate maneuver: how to continue painting Ukraine as the aggressor without letting slip the facade that the refinery strikes are not actually that bad for Russia.

“While such a truce would allow us to fully saturate our domestic market… it is currently nearing full saturation,” Peskov claimed. “The issue is not production; it is about ensuring unhindered access for these petroleum products to global markets.” That allowed him to deflect from refineries to a recent surge in Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil tankers. No mention of Russia’s attacks on commercial shipping and Ukrainian ports.

And then the final salvo from Peskov: “The second necessary step is, of course, to lift the sanctions. Only then will the world be adequately supplied with these petroleum products.”

The Kremlin may see an opening here. The US temporarily lifted some sanctions on Russia earlier this year as the Iran war threatened oil supplies. It could also be an attempt to avert the opposite outcome. This week, the Trump administration slapped sanctions on one of Russia’s biggest banks over its ties to Iran, at the same time as the US House moved closer to a vote on a sweeping Russian sanctions bill co-authored by Sen. Lindsey Graham before his death in July.

For Zelensky, this must feel like whiplash. It was just over a week ago that Trump’s foreign policy envoys hugged him, cameras flashing, in the middle of Kyiv on their long-promised first trip to Ukraine, offering up hope of new momentum for diplomacy. The warning signs were there. They had gone to Russia first. Trump followed up with a call to Putin, but not Zelensky. And while Patriot interceptor supplies are still on the table, Trump remarked this week they were considering “a less sophisticated version” for Kyiv.

Even if you strip out Trump’s apparent personal preference for Putin and the factual inconsistencies in his decision to blame Ukraine for diesel prices, we’re back to the central debate that has shaped this conflict from the start. How to punish Russia, a systemically important oil producer, without punishing yourself in the process? And will any resolve to do so go out the window when oil prices rise?

World.title: Acts abandon Ed Sheeran tour after Macklemore barred over ‘Free Palestine’ comments
World.content:
Ed Sheeran’s international tour has been thrown into crisis, with one opening act, the rapper Macklemore, dropped from the tour’s US dates for his onstage support of Palestine, and all of the British singer’s other openers quitting to protest the removal.

On Monday, Robert Kraft, the billionaire owner of the New England Patriots, said he would bar Macklemore from performing at Gillette Stadium in Massachusetts this month. Macklemore, who made pro-Palestinian remarks during shows in New Jersey, said he had been removed from the rest of Sheeran’s American tour as well.

“Artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed,” Finneas wrote on Instagram , dropping out of the tour. “I stand with Palestine and its people.” Jordan Strauss/Invision/AP

On Tuesday, Finneas, a producer who is also Billie Eilish’s brother, the Irish singer-songwriter Aaron Rowe, the Irish band Beoga and the Danish band Lukas Graham all withdrew from their opening slots on the tour, expressing support for both Macklemore and the Palestinian people.

Macklemore, a rapper best known for 2012’s “Thrift Shop,” has publicly advocated for Palestinian rights since Israel began its years-long bombing campaign in Gaza after the October 7 attacks. Opening for Sheeran earlier this month at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey, the rapper wore a black-and-white keffiyeh tied around his neck.

“A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place, was so I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very near and dear to my heart: Free Palestine,” he said, according to video of the event. He added that “to all of my Jewish brothers and sisters, criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide in no way is a criticism of you.”

Macklemore has regularly performed at pro-Palestinian rallies since 2023. In 2024, he released “Hind’s Hall,” named after the building taken over by Columbia student protesters, who renamed it in honor of Hind Rajab, a 5-year-old Palestinian girl killed by Israeli soldiers in Gaza.

His comments at Sheeran’s show prompted criticism from the singer Pink and a petition against his appearances. On Monday, Macklemore announced on Instagram he’d been dropped from Sheeran’s remaining US tour dates.

Macklemore has pointed the blame squarely at Kraft, who owns Gillette Stadium, where Sheeran and Macklemore were scheduled to perform later this month. Kraft, Macklemore said, had “rallied some of the other stadium owners” and given Sheeran an ultimatum: “if Macklemore stays on the tour, you will not be allowed to play in our venues.”

Kraft, an advocate for Israel who withdrew funding for Columbia University to rebuke the school for its handling of protests against the war in Gaza, confirmed that he chose to cancel Macklemore’s performances at Gillette Stadium. He didn’t address Macklemore’s claims that he had “rallied” other stadium owners, and did not respond to requests for more information.

Ed Sheeran, one of the world’s best-selling and most-streamed artists, defended his silence around “the conflict between Israel and Palestine.” Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for iHeartRadio

“Based on Macklemore’s recent actions, material shared from the stage during Ed Sheeran’s shows in New Jersey, and a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery that we believe has been deeply offensive and hurtful to the Jewish community, we determined that his participation in the September 25th and 26th concerts at Gillette Stadium would cross that line,” Kraft said in a statement.

“This decision is not about diminishing the suffering of innocent Palestinians or denying anyone the right to advocate on their behalf,” he went on. “Too many lives have been lost and there has been too much suffering, but only sharing selective information and ignoring the actions of Hamas is not honest and only advances more divisiveness and hate.”

Sheeran placed the blame on the concert promoter, who he said forced his hand. “After Macklemore’s performances at my New Jersey shows, venues on my upcoming tour dates communicated that they would pull the shows if he was still supporting,” he said on Instagram Tuesday. “Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter’s decision, it was not mine.” The promoter didn’t respond to a request for comment.

Chilling effect

Legally, under the First Amendment, Kraft and other people who privately own stadiums have the right to choose who performs at their venues, said Lee Rowland, the executive director of the National Coalition Against Censorship. But “that doesn’t mean that that’s healthy for our democracy or good for free expression,” Rowland said.

Rowland said the cancellation of Macklemore’s tour dates “illustrates the immense power that money has over our public discourse.”

Macklemore was scheduled to open for Sheeran at seven more stadiums in the US. Several of those are publicly owned. The remaining venues did not respond to requests for comment.

Among them is AT&T Stadium, which is owned by the city of Arlington, Texas. AT&T Stadium is scheduled to host a sold-out show later this year by Ye, who made a spate of antisemitic comments that he now attributes to a brain injury and untreated bipolar disorder, and who is selling out shows in the US.

In 2014, Macklemore publicly apologized for performing while wearing a hooked false nose, wig and fake beard, which he called a “random costume” but which observers widely read as an antisemitic caricature. Kraft did not respond to a question about whether he was referring to that incident or to something else when he accused Macklemore of past antisemitism.

The Macklemore cancellation will likely have a chilling effect on other artists, Rowland said.

“We are undoubtedly going to see widespread self-censorship, so that artists ensure their content is uncontroversial and anodyne enough not to offend a promoter or a stadium owner that would then deprive the audience of their performance.”

In his statement, Sheeran, one of the world’s best-selling and most-streamed artists, said he was “not complicit” and defended his silence around “the conflict between Israel and Palestine.”

“I have my personal views on this devastating conflict,” he said. “Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn’t mean I don’t have them, and it doesn’t mean I don’t care.”

The children’s entertainer and advocate Ms. Rachel, who has been a leading humanitarian critic of the war in Gaza, called Sheeran out for his public neutrality, writing on Instagram, “Ed Sheeran is making a political statement to his fans when he does a concert to support Ukraine, but considers Palestine too dangerous and political.”

Beyond his fellow tour members quitting in protest, Macklemore received nods of support from Reps. Ilhan Omar and Pramila Jayapal and the musicians Zara Larsson and PinkPantheress.

In his statement, Macklemore sought to refocus attention on Gaza, where more than 70,000 people — many of them women and children — have been killed.

Sheeran “told me that the words ‘Free Palestine’ and the image of the Palestinian flag were hurtful to a lot of people he spoke with,” Macklemore said.

“I told him that if those words were more offensive than tens of thousands of Palestinian children being killed by Israel, then there was a fundamental disconnect between where those people stood and where I stood.”

World.title: El Niño just leveled up to super status. Here’s what that means for the weather
World.content:
An already-strong El Niño just turned super as the phenomenon crosses into unprecedented territory.

The natural climate cycle has been strengthening at a breakneck pace since it was first declared in June and is stronger now than it’s ever been on this date. And isn’t done bulking up yet.

Forecasters have thought for months that El Niño would become very strong or “super” by this fall. The key measure of its strength has now crossed that threshold and will continue to soar higher.

As a refresher: El Niño is characterized by warmer–than–average water temperatures along the equator in the Pacific Ocean. The warmer water triggers corresponding shifts in the atmosphere that have a domino effect on weather patterns around the globe.

An active Pacific hurricane season that’s churned out multiple threats for Hawaii, a hurricane-less Atlantic hurricane season to date and Indonesia’s overwhelming wildfires are just a few effects of this very strong El Niño.

The stronger an El Niño is, the more likely it is to influence these types of weather patterns — but it doesn’t guarantee more extreme impacts.

Turning super

To capture El Niño’s strength, National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration forecasters measure how far above normal sea surface temperatures are in a specific region of the Pacific, using a metric called the Niño 3.4 Relative Oceanic Niño Index, or RONI.

The latest weekly RONI value just hit 2.0 degrees Celsius, 3.6 degrees Fahrenheit, above average. This is the threshold for “very strong,” the highest official category set by forecasters. That’s also when El Niño gains its unofficial “super” moniker.

These weekly values from NOAA capture a reliable snapshot of El Niño’s strength in real-time, which is crucial because of just how fast the event is gaining ground.

This time a year ago, a weak La Niña — El Niño’s cool counterpart — was in place, and only a handful of other years have had such a rapid flip to a potent El Niño, including the strongest ever event from 1982 to 1983.

Even so, using the weekly values is a slight departure from the norm.

NOAA’s most widely recognized strength metric is a three-month rolling average RONI. The rolling average’s purpose is to smooth out choppy short-term changes in data in favor of capturing a cleaner long-term average; that value updates once a month.

This is how a climate record that dates back decades is built, but the delayed data means it’ll take weeks for that reading to truly capture how super-sized El Niño is right now.

Breaking new ground

This isn’t a normal event: In addition to being the strongest El Niño on record on this date, it’s ultimately likely to become stronger than any event before it.

By the end of the year, El Niño has a 75 percent chance of peaking as the strongest event since records began in 1950, according to NOAA’s latest forecast issued last week.

This year’s El Niño is also happening in a much hotter world than previous record-setting events due to climate change. One look at sea surface temperatures from this year compared to past record events shows just how much fossil fuel pollution has rewritten the rules.

Climate change has literally changed the metric used to monitor El Niño. This event is the first to be captured by NOAA’s aforementioned RONI, which was first implemented in February.

The old metric took sea surface temperatures at face value, but RONI subtracts out how much warmer the Pacific Ocean is because of climate change to get the “true” strength of El Niño.

Even so, this El Niño continues to clear hurdles in its pursuit of record-breaking strength later this fall or early this winter.

Past, present and still to come

Winter is when El Niño is forecast to hit its peak strength and is also typically when its influence on global weather is most pronounced, but it’s already left many calling cards behind this summer as it strengthened rapidly.

It was, and continues to be, a major factor in both the Atlantic and Pacific hurricane seasons. In the Atlantic, it’s taken storm-killing wind shear to extreme levels and kept it there, even at what should be the busiest time of the season. That’s created a record-long wait for the season’s first hurricane.

El Niño has prevented that same type of wind shear over the exceptionally warm Pacific and activity exploded. Sixteen storms, including two Category 5 hurricanes, have formed and thrived in the eastern and central parts of the ocean so far, with Hawaii alone facing three tropical systems in less than a month.

Fourteen of those storms originated in the East Pacific, which, with two and a half months of the season still to come, will likely blow past its average seasonal storm total of 15.

Elsewhere, Indonesia is battling widespread wildfires and conditions could deteriorate further: El Niño years make the country drier than usual, which leaves plenty of tinder-dry vegetation for blazes to consume and limited rainfall to help fire crews tamp down ongoing activity.

El Niño also raises global average air temperatures above levels already being increased by climate change and was a factor in making this summer such a scorcher around the globe. This August was Earth’s hottest on record and could mark the start of a record-breaking warm stretch that would likely culminate in a record-hot 2027 — and possibly 2026 — globally.

It’s clear El Niño is already a major player, but it will hit its full stride in the months ahead, right on time to dictate winter weather across the US.

World.title: One word that explains Trump’s AI denialism
World.content:
Washington’s biggest question this week: Why is President Donald Trump so furiously against an AI slowdown in the wake of apocalyptic warnings from some top industry executives?

The clue is in one word — “hoax” — that he’s using to ridicule fears that computerized agents could one day seek to destroy humanity.

When Trump reaches for the H-word, two things are usually happening: He’s facing a controversy threatening his political or personal priorities, and he’s lost control of the politics.

Trump has long dismissed climate change as a “hoax.” So it was a tell that he went on social media to specifically draw an analogy between a planet that is warming despite his denials and the calls for AI controls expressed by leaders in the industry.

By changing reality, Trump frees himself from an obligation to act. In energy policy, that means “drill, baby, drill.” His administration has slashed regulation, pleasing oil industry donors. His rants against wind farms suggest he hankers for a 20th-century economy running on carbon.

The Jeffrey Epstein saga is a “Democratic hoax,” according to Trump. Searing testimonies from the accused sex offender’s victims make this a ridiculous charge. But Trump wants to end the storm over his onetime friend that periodically trips up his administration.

Epstein survivors Lisa-Jena and Dani Hannah Bensky listen as Roza testifies about her experience during a House Oversight Committee hearing with advocates and survivors of Jeffrey Epstein’s sexual abuse, at West Palm Beach City Hall in West Palm Beach Florida, on May 12. Joe Raedle/Getty Images

The same is true of another supposed “hoax”: the investigations into the Capitol riot on January 6, 2021. The outrage was the culmination of another event Trump wants America to forget: his bid to overturn the 2020 election. The hoax routine worked — it got him back to the White House to wield expansive executive power.

The president seems to hope that by simply branding fears of runaway AI as a hoax, he can make them go away.

But why?

Trump is no ordinary president

One of a president’s jobs is to counsel a fearful nation, to examine and explain threats, and to advise whether a national effort must be summoned. “The only thing we have to fear is fear itself,” Franklin Roosevelt said at the start of a presidency deep in the Great Depression.

Every commander in chief followed suit in the Cold War. And George W. Bush corralled the country after 9/11, almost exactly 25 years ago.

That’s not Trump’s way.

But even as a political matter, Trump might be advised to take the AI freakout seriously. Americans are worried — not necessarily about extinction, but that the new technology will take their jobs. And by rejecting voter concerns about data centers, the president is leaping onto the wrong side of yet another issue as the GOP braces for tough midterm elections.

Demonstrators against AI hold signs during a protest outside the G20 Innovation Ministerial in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, on Septeber 2. Cornell Watson/Bloomberg/Getty Images

But the president’s blasé attitude to AI may be traced to a host of political, economic and personality traits that have unleashed turmoil across his two presidencies and that will shape his legacy.

One reason may be economic.

Any signal that AI development may slow would almost certainly trigger a reaction on the markets. As his Iran war sticks Americans with high gas prices and record diesel costs, Trump can’t afford any Wall Street turbulence that would hurt 401k accounts and check GDP growth.

He’s also showing philosophical objections to a slowdown. His presidency has been about unleashing business to make money, not dialing it back.

Former White House AI czar David Sacks argued over the weekend that by expressing concerns about AI’s destructive potential, industry titans were trying to pressure politicians and the public into creating their own “preferred” regulatory system.

Trump is taking a similar approach. “When, in the History of Business, did anyone see the Leaders of an Industry call for Regulation that, if strongly implemented, will drive them into oblivion and bankruptcy?” the president wrote Monday.

Trump’s governing style isn’t a good fit for this deeply complex issue. He said this week that he’s an AI user, but whether that goes beyond posting wild memes depicting himself as various superheroes is unclear. And he gets his news from the traveling printer of his aide Natalie Harp.

At the same time, there’s a possibility that’s often overlooked in the riotous Washington of the second Trump era: What if the president is going against the tide because he’s right about a few things?

This would not be the first time that a new technology has triggered warnings of doom that don’t play out. And some skeptics doubt alarmist talk from AI chiefs is genuine, suspecting that they are obliquely talking up the potential of their technology ahead of initial public offerings in the coming months.

And Trump has a serious point that even if the US slows AI development, China probably won’t, which would give it a superpower advantage.

Plenty of Democrats feel the same way, including President Joe Biden’s former national security adviser Jake Sullivan, who wrote in Foreign Affairs earlier this year that Washington “must up its game” in integrating AI across the military, warning that the US would lose leverage if it failed.

‘Hoax buster’

But Trump’s vision of his own power and place in history also explain his behavior.

He posted on Monday that America would be fine because it had a “STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT.” This might placate some supporters — but even if it’s true, it’s hardly a viable position. AI will be a generational issue long after he’s left office, and Trump, as the incumbent president, has a responsibility to set an early course.

President Donald Trump sits between OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis during a working lunch with G7 leaders, G7 outreach partners and global tech CEOs, during the G7 Summit in Evian-les-Bains, France, on June 17. Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters

Trump critics might wonder whether his views are shaped by personal considerations, including his ownership of stocks exposed to AI, as disclosed in a recent financial filing. The White House insists his accounts are independently managed by third-party institutions. But ethical questions raised by administration officials regulating industries in which their personal wealth is deeply invested has been a constant shadow over the president’s second term.

Trump’s resistance to unpleasant truths is also at work.

He’s never presented his presidency as a vehicle for confronting far-off threats or to tackle complex problems. He’s used it to enact revenge against his enemies, to troll his political foes, to boost his own fame and to invade the psyches of billions of people across the globe.

Trump would never issue the kind of dialectical statement that his first predecessor, President Barack Obama, released on Tuesday. The 44th president said he’d been agonizing over AI for a decade and that it was time for top US leaders to convene a national conversation.

“Whether this technology results in amazing breakthroughs in medicine, energy and education or unleashes huge economic disruptions, greater inequality, and potential catastrophe will depend on the choices that we make right now – choices that should be made not just by the companies involved, but by all of us,” Obama wrote.

Some Americans might have hoped from similar from Trump. But he’s a rebel and a backlash president. His anti-establishment credentials depend on being an outsider, not a unifier.

And Obama’s path ultimately points to a US-led international coalition. Trump hates multinational altruism. “America First” is about doubling down on US power, not watering it down.

If Trump refuses to lead, will Congress step in?

The US Capitol is seen past antennas and satellites atop the FBI Washington Field Office, on February 10. Al Drago/Getty Images

There’s no time for serious action before the midterms. But if AI explodes as a top campaign theme, it’s likely to drive the legislative agenda of whoever controls the House and Senate next year. And if Republicans suffer a wipeout because of Trump’s refusal to listen to voters, they may have an incentive to break with the president.

But they will be on their own.

“I am the Hoax Buster, and I’m right now breaking another Hoax — That AI is going to take over, consume, and destroy the World, and that Robots will be marching into our Cities, and getting rid of us all!” Trump wrote on Truth Social on Monday.

World.title: Official dismissed, 3 suspects apprehended for tree felling in Kafr al-Sheikh and Gharbiya
World.content:
Minister of Local Development and Environment Manal Awad on Tuesday ruled to dismiss al-Sayed Hamza—the head of the Desouk Center and City in Kafr el-Sheikh Governorate—from his post.

This decision followed the discovery that several trees had been cut down near the Edfina Barrages in the city.

Awad also moved to refer the entire incident to the competent investigative authorities and coordinate with the Minister of Water Resources and Irrigation to ensure those involved face investigation.

Images spread online showed workers cutting down mature trees in the vicinity of the Edfina Barrages in Metoubes and loading them onto a pickup truck, presumably to sell them.

In response, Hamza—following the decision to remove him from office—asserted that the Edfina Barrages fall under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Irrigation, not the city council.

He said, “I have no authority over the barrages; I cannot even remove a single nail from the site without consulting them.”

Regarding the incident, he explained: “The events took place starting September 1st; a pruning committee from the Irrigation Directorate cut down 53 trees between September 1-8—within the Barrages area—loaded them onto their own vehicles, and transported them to the Directorate’s warehouses. This occurred prior to the Cabinet’s decision banning the felling of trees.”

He continued, noting that “the incident recently came to light after citizens circulated photos and complaints on social media.”

Arrests made

Security forces from the Gharbiya Security Directorate also apprehended three individuals accused of cutting down a massive tree near the al-Mahalla Industrial School—located in the First District of al-Mahalla al-Kubra—and making off with it, following a report filed by the district administration.

The Director of Gharbiya Security formed an investigative team to solve the case, apprehend the perpetrators, and review surveillance camera footage from the area.

It was revealed that three individuals—a timber merchant, a retired local government employee, and a residential building watchman— committed the act.

They had conspired to cut down the massive tree and sell its wood for profit.

Detectives successfully apprehended the suspects, initiated legal proceedings, and referred them to the investigative authorities.

The Ministry of Agriculture also denied that trees were being cut down at the Fish Garden in Zamalek, asserting that all trees and plants there are in good condition, with the exception of a single tree that had fallen due to the natural end of its lifespan.

Edited translation from Al-Masry Al-Youm

World.title: A real mummy’s curse? The health risks associated with the trade of human remains
World.content:
“The mummy’s curse” might have some basis in reality after all, after a recent academic study warned of genuine health risks associated with the murky trade in mummified human remains—a practice increasingly spreading across social media, e-commerce platforms, and auction houses.

The study, titled “The real mummy’s curse: Health risks associated with the sale and trade of mummified remains,” was published in the International Journal of Cultural Property by Cambridge University Press.

It was co-authored by researchers specializing in bioarchaeology and the preservation of human remains.

According to The Guardian, scientists analyzed 128 s and posts offering mummified human remains for sale on Meta-owned platforms, e-commerce sites, online stores, and auction houses.

They reached conclusions they described as “grim,” particularly given the appearance of remains showing clear signs of deterioration, all without adequate warnings or guidelines regarding how to handle them.

Hands and feet were among the most common mummified body parts offered for sale, followed closely by heads.

Human heads—whether intact or partial—and skulls retaining soft tissue or hair accounted for approximately 51.6 percent of the sample studied by researchers.

Deadly spores, heavy metals

The danger of this trade is compounded by the nature of the substances used in ancient mummification processes.

Human tissues were sometimes preserved using chemicals and heavy metals—such as arsenic, mercury, and lead—which can pose health risks if handled without proper protective measures.

However, the risk is not limited to chemicals alone; mummified remains can harbor dormant microorganisms even centuries after the tissue has dried out.

When remains are disturbed or touched, fungal spores can become airborne, making inhalation a potential health risk.

The study cites an incident from the 1970s which killed 10 out of 12 conservationists who opened the tomb of King Casimir IV in Kraków, Poland; it is believed that inhaling Aspergillus fungal spores was the cause.

The study also links the Aspergillus fungus to the 1923 death of Lord Carnarvon, a key financier of the discovery of Tutankhamun’s tomb in the Valley of the Kings.

His death subsequently became one of the stories fueling the legend of “the mummy’s curse” which holds that opening ancient tombs can bring about illness or death.

However, researchers emphasize that these dangers stem from biological and chemical hazards that can be scientifically explained.

Improper storage

A professor of human bioarchaeology at Staffordshire University, Kirsty Squires, stated that some individuals involved in the trade of mummified remains do not appear to grasp the extent of the risks.

She noted that images posted online show severely deteriorated remains kept in open areas within homes—sometimes without protective cases or proper storage conditions.

The issue extends beyond buyers and sellers; human remains can be transported via postal and shipping services, exposing warehouse workers, drivers, logistics personnel, and customs officials to potential risks—particularly as they may handle these shipments without knowing their contents or wearing appropriate protective gear.

Ultimately, the study reveals that the obsession with mummies and ancient human remains has devolved into a trade fraught with genuine risks.

This necessitates the implementation of stricter regulations for handling such materials to protect not only the collectors but also anyone who might touch or transport them without being aware of their nature.

World.title: Egypt, Japan explore cooperation opportunities to enhance teacher training programs
World.content:
Minister of Education and Technical Education Mohamed Abdel Latif reviewed with Japanese Ambassador to Egypt Iwai Fumio ways to promote bilateral cooperation in the education sector.

During a meeting with the Japanese diplomat on Tuesday, the minister discussed cooperation for expanding joint initiatives, highlighting the successful model of the Egyptian-Japanese schools.

Abdel Latif highlighted the ministry’s strategy to integrate Japanese educational expertise, notably the Tokkatsu activities, which aim to foster students’ social skills, teamwork and personal responsibility.

He said Japan is a key partner in this strategy due to its well-established expertise and integrated approach to developing the educational process, in line with Egypt’s priorities and future goals.

The two sides also explored opportunities to enhance teacher training programs, facilitate the exchange of educational practices, and adopt innovative student activities tailored to meet labor market demands and national development goals.

Meanwhile, Fumio reaffirmed his country’s commitment to supporting Egypt’s educational development and ongoing partnership.

A great host senior officials from the ministry and the Japanese embassy in Cairo attended the meeting.
