World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - September 16, 2026
World.content:
press review

U.S. Imposes Visa Restrictions Over South Africa

The United States has announced visa restrictions against people it accuses of discriminating against South Africa's white minority. This has further escalated tensions between Washington and Pretoria. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the restrictions would target people involved in what the US describes as race-based discrimination, inciting violence or enabling land confiscation without compensation. No individuals were named. South Africa has repeatedly rejected US claims of discrimination and white persecution, saying its land reform policies are aimed at addressing inequalities created under apartheid and do not allow arbitrary seizure of property. The US embassy in Pretoria said the visa measures were the first in a series of possible escalatory steps. South Africa has sought to ease tensions through diplomatic engagement.

DR Congo Protests Tshisekedi Constitutional Plans



Police in the Democratic Republic of Congo used tear gas and arrested protesters as demonstrations were held in several cities against President Felix Tshisekedi's plans to change the constitution. Opposition parties have united under the C64 coalition to oppose the proposed changes, which they say could allow Tshisekedi to seek a third term. Clashes broke out between opposition and pro-government supporters in Kinshasa, while police dispersed demonstrations that had been banned by local authorities. Protests were also reported in Lubumbashi and Mbandaka, where activists defied bans and were dispersed by security forces. Opposition figures accused authorities of making arbitrary arrests, while police said they were maintaining public order. The constitutional changes come as the country continues to face conflict in the east, including fighting involving the Rwanda-backed M23 armed group. The opposition has also rejected Tshisekedi's offer of national dialogue, accusing him of using it to strengthen his position.

South African President Vows Justice As More Women's Bodies Found in Kempton Park

South African police are investigating the deaths of eight women whose bodies have been found at different locations in Ekurhuleni, east of Johannesburg, since July. Several of the women were found naked or partially clothed, with some showing signs of possible sexual violence, raising concerns that the cases could be connected. Police have not confirmed that a serial killer is responsible but are investigating whether one person or a group may be behind the deaths. One suspect remains in custody following the discovery of the first body. The latest deaths have prompted warnings for women in the area to avoid walking or jogging alone, particularly in isolated locations. President Cyril Ramaphosa has ordered police to prioritise the investigations, while Acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia said the deaths must not be in vain. The killings have intensified concerns over South Africa's persistent gender-based violence, with authorities yet to establish whether the cases are linked.

Algeria Faces Pressure Over Death Penalty Expansion

Amnesty International is urging Algeria to abandon plans to expand the use of the death penalty following deadly wildfires that devastated parts of the country. President Abdelmadjid Tebboune has ordered changes to the Penal Code to allow the death penalty for people convicted of deliberately starting or instigating fires, and has indicated that it could also be extended to child abduction and abuse. Algeria has not executed since 1993, although courts continue to impose death sentences. Amnesty said that the wildfire response should focus on prevention, emergency preparedness and independent investigations into all factors that contributed to the deaths, rather than expanding capital punishment. The organisation also raised concerns over the use of terrorism-related charges carrying the death penalty against people accused of involvement in the fires. It said Algeria should ensure fair trials and accountability while taking into account the role of climate change and weaknesses in disaster preparedness.

Boko Haram Rejects Nigeria Ceasefire Claims in New Video

Boko Haram has denied reports that it reached a ceasefire agreement with the Nigerian government, dismissing the claims as false. In a video, the group's Sharia judge, Mallam Abdulrahman, said its leadership had not agreed to any truce, although he acknowledged that reconciliation was possible under Islamic principles. He accused the Nigerian government of misleading the public and urged fighters not to be discouraged by reports of a ceasefire. The denial follows reports that the government had secretly reached an agreement with a faction led by Bakura Doro, allegedly linked to negotiations for the release of more than 300 civilians abducted in Borno State in March. The reports claimed the agreement had been in place since June and involved a ransom payment, which the government has denied. Nigerian officials have not confirmed the existence of a ceasefire, with the presidency directing questions to the National Security Adviser or Defence Ministry.

Close 

WHO Reports Active Mpox Transmission in 11 African Nations

The World Health Organization said that 11 African countries recorded active mpox transmission during the six weeks to 16 August 2026, reporting 1,153 confirmed cases and seven deaths. Madagascar recorded the highest number with 785 cases, followed by Angola with 184, Kenya with 94, the Democratic Republic of Congo with 41 and Cameroon with 28. WHO said weekly confirmed cases have remained relatively stable at around 200. However, reporting delays and reduced surveillance mean the figures could be underestimated. The figures form part of a wider outbreak that has affected 35 African countries since January 2025. More than 52,000 confirmed cases and 238 deaths were recorded on the continent by 16 August 2026. Madagascar remains the main concern, with WHO describing its outbreak as the largest globally and in Africa since December 2025. Despite Africa CDC ending its continental public health emergency declaration in January, WHO said mpox remains a significant health concern and has extended its standing recommendations through August 2027.

World.title: South Africa: U.S. Imposes Visa Restrictions on South Africa, Citing Race-Based Discrimination
World.content:
The United States has announced visa restrictions against people it accuses of discriminating against South Africa's white minority.

This has further escalated tensions between Washington and Pretoria.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the restrictions would target people involved in what the US describes as race-based discrimination, inciting violence or enabling land confiscation without compensation. No individuals were named.

South Africa has repeatedly rejected US claims of discrimination and white persecution, saying its land reform policies are aimed at addressing inequalities created under apartheid and do not allow arbitrary seizure of property.

The US embassy in Pretoria said the visa measures were the first in a series of possible escalatory steps. South Africa has sought to ease tensions through diplomatic engagement.

World.title: Congo-Kinshasa: DR Congo Protests Tshisekedi Constitutional Plans
World.content:
Police in the Democratic Republic of Congo used tear gas and arrested protesters as demonstrations were held in several cities against President Felix Tshisekedi's plans to change the constitution.

Opposition parties have united under the C64 coalition to oppose the proposed changes, which they say could allow Tshisekedi to seek a third term.

Clashes broke out between opposition and pro-government supporters in Kinshasa, while police dispersed demonstrations that had been banned by local authorities. Protests were also reported in Lubumbashi and Mbandaka, where activists defied bans and were dispersed by security forces.

Opposition figures accused authorities of making arbitrary arrests, while police said they were maintaining public order.

The constitutional changes come as the country continues to face conflict in the east, including fighting involving the Rwanda-backed M23 armed group.

The opposition has also rejected Tshisekedi's offer of national dialogue, accusing him of using it to strengthen his position.

World.title: South Africa: Suspect Sought as Police Probe Ekurhuleni Murders - South African News Briefs - September 16, 2026
World.content:
press review

Police Pursue Person of Interest in Ekurhuleni Murders

Police said that they are pursuing a person of interest in connection with the deaths of eight women in Ekurhuleni, reports EWN. Police have not disclosed the individual's identity or gender, and they have not confirmed which cases the person may be linked to. The women have been found since July, with several discovered half-naked and bruised. The expert will testify about the processes used to assess the integrity and suitability of people appointed to law enforcement positions. The evidence could shed light on whether existing vetting systems effectively identify candidates suitable for senior roles, amid testimony on the conduct and integrity of senior law enforcement officials.

SASSA Grant System Faces Scrutiny Over Bank Checks

The South African Social Security Agency's automated verification system for the R370 Social Relief of Distress grant is reportedly causing problems for some applicants because bank transactions can be interpreted as income, according to Wits University legal expert Busisiwe Kamolane-Kgadima. The system checks applicants’ information against government and banking records to determine whether they exceed the income threshold. She said such checks are necessary to prevent people from receiving benefits they do not qualify for. She raised concerns about the heavy reliance on an automated process, which may not account for the nature or source of individual bank transactions.

World.title: Rwanda: Rwanda Eyes Nuclear Tech to Improve Agriculture
World.content:
The governement is exploring the use of nuclear and isotopic techniques to improve agricultural productivity, food safety and resilience to climate change, Minister of State for Infrastructure Armand Zingiro has said.

He was speaking during the 70th Regular Session of the IAEA General Conference in Vienna, Austria, which is taking place from September 14 to 18.

ALSO READ: Inside Rwanda's nuclear development ambitions

"In agriculture and food security, Rwanda recognises the significant potential of nuclear and isotopic techniques to improve agricultural productivity, food safety, nutrition and climate resilience," said Zingiro, who led the Rwandan delegation attending the conference.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Nuclear technology is used in agriculture primarily through radiation and isotope techniques to improve crop yields, control pests, manage natural resources, and ensure food safety.

"Rwanda has therefore expressed its interest in participating in the Atoms4Food initiative, jointly supported by the IAEA and the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations."

The initiative supports countries in using nuclear and other technologies to improve agricultural and livestock productivity, manage natural resources, reduce food losses, improve food safety and nutrition, and strengthen resilience to climate change.

Zingiro said Rwanda plans to work with the IAEA and FAO to assess its national priorities and capacities and develop a programme tailored to the country's needs.

He said the cooperation would support the country's efforts to strengthen food security, improve agricultural productivity and food safety, reduce post-harvest losses and build climate-resilient food systems.

ALSO READ: Nuclear energy: Why Rwanda is opting for small modular reactors

The interest in agricultural applications comes as Rwanda continues to develop its wider nuclear science and technology programme, including plans for nuclear power and a research reactor.

In March, Rwanda hosted an IAEA Integrated Nuclear Infrastructure Review (INIR) mission, which assessed the country's progress in developing the infrastructure needed for the safe, secure and sustainable introduction of nuclear power.

The review provided recommendations for the next stage of the programme, including finalising a comprehensive report to support national decision-making on the introduction of nuclear power, completing the review of national legislation, and further developing and adopting policies and strategies for the nuclear power programme.

"Following the INIR mission, Rwanda has already developed an Integrated Work Plan for the implementation of the INIR recommendations, which provides a coordinated framework for addressing the identified areas and strengthening Rwanda's readiness in line with the IAEA Milestones Approach," Zingiro said.

Close 

He said the government would continue working with the IAEA to implement and monitor the work plan.

Alongside the nuclear power programme, Rwanda is preparing to develop a research reactor as part of the planned Centre for Nuclear Science and Technology.

The country hosted an IAEA Integrated Nuclear Infrastructure Review for Research Reactors (INIR-RR) mission in July to assess its preparedness for developing the facility.

The mission provided recommendations on the institutional, technical and human capacity needed to support the project.

He said Rwanda was also focused on developing the human and institutional capacity needed to sustain its nuclear programme through specialised training, education, knowledge management and international partnerships.

The government is pursuing nuclear applications in other sectors, including healthcare, where it is working to strengthen cancer diagnosis and treatment through radiopharmaceutical production and Positron emission tomography (PET) imaging.

"Rwanda further reaffirms its commitment to nuclear safety, nuclear security, safeguards and radiation protection as fundamental pillars of its national nuclear programme," he said.

The government, he added, would continue working with the IAEA and other partners to ensure that nuclear activities are carried out in line with international obligations and standards.

World.title: Mali: One Man's Quest to End Female Genital Mutilation (FGM) in Mali
World.content:
Sidi Haidara leads a community dialogue in Mopti, Mali, where families, young people and local leaders discuss girls' rights and ways to end female genital mutilation.

United Nations — After years of defending FGM as a cultural practice, Sidi Haidara came to a realization: No tradition should come at the expense of a girl's health, rights, or future.

In Mali, an estimated nine out of ten women and girls have undergone female genital mutilation (FGM). And for years, Sidi Haidara, a father and recognized leader in his community, believed the practice was simply part of life.

Like many people in his community in central Mali, he saw it as a tradition passed down through generations - one that should be preserved.

Today, he walks from village to village with a very different message: No tradition should come at the expense of a girl's health, rights, or future.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

His story goes beyond one man's personal transformation. Across parts of West and Central Africa, FGM remains deeply rooted - with Mali having one of the highest rates in the region and no laws that specifically criminalize the practice. Even recently, some men in Mali have launched an all-male pro-FGM campaign on the grounds of protecting tradition.

In places where social norms are deeply entrenched, change often begins with trusted voices from within the community - voices like Haidara's.

After spending years defending female genital mutilation, Sidi Haidara now leads community dialogues in Mopti, Mali, encouraging families to protect girls' rights and abandon the practice. Credit: UN Women/Dieneba Deme

How UN Women and partners are shifting mindsets and empowering new anti-FGM advocates in Mali

"I used to believe that this practice was part of our traditions and needed to be preserved", says Haidara.

Nothing suggested that he would one day become one of the people advocating for its abandonment.

His perspective began to change after taking part in training sessions, workshops, and community dialogues organized through the Men and Boys as Agents of Change project, implemented by UN Women with financial support from the Government of Germany.

As he listened to different experiences and learned about the consequences of FGM, he began questioning his beliefs - beliefs he had never challenged before. He also came to understand that lasting change cannot simply be imposed - it grows through dialogue, trust, and community ownership.

"UN Women's trainings - with the support of Germany - transformed my understanding of female genital mutilation. I learned about the physical, psychological, and social consequences that this practice imposes on girls."

How to end FGM in Mali: Begin with listening, questioning, and conversing

"Today, I regularly organize awareness-raising sessions with families, religious leaders, young people, and women", he explains.

Rather than telling people what to think, he encourages conversations about what it means to protect girls and challenges long-held beliefs through dialogue.

Little by little, those conversations are making a difference. "I can see change: more parents are asking questions, several families are abandoning female genital mutilation, and discussions about protecting girls have become more open."

"I am convinced that protecting girls today means investing in the future of our entire community."

People can change - and so can social norms

Haidara's journey is part of a broader movement taking place across the regions of Mopti and Gao in Mali.

With support from the Government of Germany, UN Women works alongside religious and traditional leaders, women, young people, and men like Haidara who are committed to community-driven initiatives that prevent violence against women and girls and challenge harmful social norms.

To date, 50 community initiatives have been implemented across the two regions, while eight community-dialogue platforms provide spaces for people to discuss girls' rights, their protection, and ways to prevent gender-based violence.

Close 

For Haidara, abandoning a harmful practice is about more than leaving a tradition behind. It is about giving girls the opportunity to grow up safely, stay in school, and shape their own futures.

His journey shows that some of the most meaningful changes happen when those who once upheld harmful social norms become the people helping to transform them.

Haidara knows traditions do not change overnight. But every conversation creates an opportunity for reflection. Every family that chooses to protect its daughters helps write a different future from the one that generations before them inherited.

In Mopti and Gao, these conversations are showing that lasting change does not necessarily begin with a new law or policy. More often, it begins when communities themselves decide to imagine a different future for their girls.

Source: UNFPA

IPS UN Bureau

World.title: Congo-Kinshasa: Ebola Outbreak Slows in Parts of DR Congo but Crisis Remains Severe
World.content:
Ebola infections are slowing in parts of eastern Democratic Republic of Congo four months into the outbreak, but cases are climbing fast in North Kivu and the World Health Organization (WHO) says it is too early to declare that the epidemic has peaked.

Since the outbreak was officially declared on 15 May, 7,258 cases have been confirmed, including 3,510 deaths, while 1,726 people have recovered. The virus has now reached seven provinces.

Congolese Health Minister Samuel Kamba said on Saturday that the epidemic had passed its peak, pointing to a gradual slowdown in transmission since mid-August. Daily infections have fallen from around 120 new cases to nearly 80.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

There are also signs of improvement in Ituri province, the epicentre of the outbreak, which accounts for 78 percent of confirmed cases. Three health zones - Adja, Kambala and Mahagi - have gone 41 days without recording a new case, health officials at the African Union said.

But the WHO has stopped short of declaring that the outbreak has peaked, warning that improvements in some areas mask sharply different trends elsewhere.

Ebola deaths in DR Congo top 3,000 as WHO says vaccine trials imminent

Progress but no peak yet

"Trends at the national level do not reflect trends at the provincial or local level," Olivier le Polain, head of the WHO's epidemiology and analysis unit, told reporters in Geneva.

Asked on Tuesday whether the outbreak had reached a turning point, le Polain remained cautious.

"It's too early to confidently say we have passed a peak."

Ebola is spreading at an "exponential" rate in North Kivu, particularly in the city of Butembo, the WHO said. The province accounted for around 45 percent of all cases reported last week.

South Ubangi became the seventh province affected after a case was detected there last week, far from the epicentre.

The new case shows the risk of the epidemic spreading to other parts of the country as large numbers of people move around, the WHO said.

Another 5,000 health workers are needed to tackle the epidemic, the organisation estimated last week.

Several treatments and vaccines are being tested against the Bundibugyo Ebola virus behind the current outbreak, for which no approved vaccine or treatment currently exists.

DRC school year begins amid Ebola, strikes and conflict

A months-long fight

Efforts to curb Ebola in eastern DR Congo are beginning to show results, UN officials said on Tuesday, but they stressed that the epidemic remains severe and will take months to bring under control.

"It remains a deadly and a massive epidemic," UN special Ebola coordinator Julien Harneis told reporters in Geneva.

Close 

"There are some areas of progress, but nonetheless, in other areas, we continue to see growth in cases."

(with newswires)

World.title: South Africa: Ekurhuleni Under Lockdown - Police Launch Manhunt in Kempton Park After Eighth Murder Victim Found
World.content:
The bodies of eight women have been discovered in Ekurhuleni between July and September, prompting an intensive police investigation. Authorities are urging the public to come forward with useful information and avoid speculation.

The SA Police Service (SAPS) is planning to "lock down" Kempton Park and surrounding locales in the coming weeks as an assembled specialist team works to find the killer or killers of eight women whose bodies have recently been discovered in the area.

Speaking to the media on Tuesday night, acting Police Minister Professor Firoz Cachalia gave a briefing on the investigation hours after another woman's body was discovered behind Club 69 in KwaThema, Springs, Ekurhuleni. The body was that of an unidentified woman in her thirties, found naked and in a state of decomposition.

High-level response

Cachalia said a multidisciplinary team with the necessary expertise had been assembled to investigate the killings.

"The team is in place, and I can give you the assurance, based on past experience, that when it comes to such situations, the South African Police Service has the experience, the high-level expertise, to investigate cases of this kind.

"I also give you the assurance that the political leadership has a responsibility, which we will shoulder, to work with our law enforcement agencies, to ensure that the investigation continues until we get clarity, a result that the families deserve and our people expect," said Cachalia....

World.title: $60 sourdough bread loaf sparks outrage online: 'Would never pay that much'
World.content:

Rye, the first United States location of Austrian bakery Martin Auer, recently opened in New York City — and its $60 loaf of rye sourdough is drawing attention.

The new concept on Lafayette Street focuses on one thing: bread.

Its 100% rye sourdough is made with "organic Austrian rye flour, water, salt and a lot of time during the process, because it takes a long time to make the bread," co-owner Tim Auer told Fox News Digital.

COSTCO SHOPPERS DIVIDED OVER NEW 'SOURDOUGH' BREAD AS CRITICS SAY IT'S NOT THE REAL THING

The bakery uses a sourdough culture that Auer said has been in his family for more than 50 years and was brought to New York from Austria.

Preparing the sourdough takes about a day, he said. The dough is then mixed, rested, shaped and fermented again before spending about 70 minutes in the oven. After baking, the dense rye loaf needs to rest for at least eight hours before it can be properly sliced.

Each full loaf weighs about 3.3 pounds and sells for $60.

The $60 price reflects the ingredients and work behind each loaf, as well as the cost of operating in New York, Auer said.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"The price of the bread is the result of all the efforts and costs that went into this project but also every single loaf," Auer said.

"It's obviously all handmade here on Lafayette Street in one of the most expensive cities in the world, using only the best ingredients, meaning the best rye flour that we import from Austria. And we wanted to give the craft and the bread the stage we think it deserves. And with all these efforts, that's the price."

Customers don't have to spend $60 to try it. A half loaf sells for $30 and a quarter loaf for $15, and Rye also sells the bread by the slice.

Still, the price has generated criticism on social media.

World.title: Shota Imanaga's home run struggles and Wrigley wind make over 7.5 the play for Braves-Cubs
World.content:
This late in the season, there are a few types of series: one that doesn't matter at all because neither team will make the postseason. Another is between one team that is still battling for the postseason.

Then there are those between two teams trying to make the playoffs or solidify their position. And, finally, there is one between two teams that are essentially locked into making the postseason, but maybe not the exact spot. That's what we have tonight between the Atlanta Braves and the Chicago Cubs, perhaps a preview of a playoff series.

The Braves are one of the more consistent teams in baseball this season. They've been one of the best teams in the sport all year, and since opening day, they've positioned themselves as the division leader. I believe they may have lost it for a stretch when the Philadelphia Phillies were hot, but the point remains that this is one of the more complete and best teams in baseball. However, they do have a weakness: road games. They are above .500 on the road, but being 26 games above .500 overall, the majority of that is their home record.

There really isn't a question about whether the Braves will make the postseason; they just need to lock up the division, and they currently have a 5.5-game lead. Looking to push that division lead further is today's starter, JR Ritchie. For the season, Ritchie is 1-2 with a 4.50 ERA and a 1.43 WHIP. He really doesn't have significantly different home and road splits. However, he does have a 5.13 ERA in night games compared to 3.06 on the road. Ritchie has pitched better lately, but doesn't go too deep into games. The Cubs haven't seen much of him and are hitting just .167 against Ritchie.

The Cubs have also held strong with their position for much of the season. They've never really been able to overtake the Brewers in the NL Central, but they've been in control of the first Wild Card spot for much of the year. If you gave the Cubs a better rotation, they probably would be the World Series favorite, or at least up there with the Dodgers. The offense has carried this team for much of the year, specifically Pete Crow-Armstrong.

The records offer a glimpse into internal FBI discussions surrounding two politically charged matters and prompted Grassley to accuse bureau personnel of political bias, saying the exchanges showed the "Deep State" working against Trump. The documents were released as part of a broader batch involving Crossfire Hurricane and other FBI matters.

"The previous Democrat administrations under Obama and Biden conducted secret, insidious and downright evil operations that almost took down our government," Grassley said during an Oversight hearing with FBI Director Kash Patel. "That's arguably worse than Watergate."

Crossfire Hurricane was the FBI's 2016 counterintelligence investigation into whether members of Donald Trump's presidential campaign coordinated with Russia's election interference, though Special Counsel Robert Mueller's investigation did not establish a criminal conspiracy between the campaign and the Russian government.

DAN BONGINO REVEALS HE FOUND 'MOTHER LODE' OF SECRET RUSSIAGATE FILES INSIDE FBI BURN BAGS

Over the past decade, the Senate Judiciary Committee, at the direction of Grassley, has released several rounds of documents from a few FBI operations such as Operation Arctic Frost and Round River, alleging that the Justice Department was being weaponized against Trump and Republicans.

"The overall sustained efforts by the Deep State in the dark corners of the bureaucracy is worse than anything Trump has been accused of. At least he’s upfront and open so people can judge," Grassley said.

At the center of the Senate Judiciary Committee's most recent document release are three former FBI agents: Gounaud, Walter Giardina, who was fired by Patel in August over accusations of political weaponization, and Timothy Thibault.

Gounaud, who left the bureau in February, according to his LinkedIn, sent an email in February 2025 seeking to begin a criminal investigation of Musk. At the time, Musk was a special government employee overseeing DOGE. Gounaud's complaint centered on Musk announcing on X his plan to have all government employees share five things they worked on that day.

"Musk used a non government system (twitter) to relate information that allegedly was for official purposes. In doing so, because he is monetized (he is a majority owner of twitter) he likely generated income for himself based on Twitter's monetization model and/or advertising revenues," Gounaud wrote. "His use of twitter in this and other instances is conceptually similar to Hillary Clinton's misuse of a private email server for government business."

Grassley later criticized the former FBI agent in a post on X.

JACK SMITH'S SENATE PHONE RECORDS PROBE TURNS TO VERIZON'S HANDLING OF SUBPOENAS

"Here is an email I released 2day showing an FBI agent who was ready2 open a CRIMINAL CASE all bc Elon Musk asked govt bureaucrats 2 report 5 things they did in a wk," Grassley wrote. "Compare that 2 Iowans who work frm sunup to sundown EVERY DAY Washington rlly is an island surrounded by reality."

The document dump also shows that Giardina emailed at least seven times over the course of four weeks beginning in January 2017 asking to be assigned to Crossfire Hurricane. The findings of the investigation were handed off to special counsel Robert Mueller a few months later in May.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

The emails show that Giardina was in correspondence with Thibault, who Grassley had accused of violating the Hatch Act. The allegation, which was investigated and dismissed by the U.S. Office of Special Counsel (OSC), stemmed from Thibault resharing a post on then Twitter by the Lincoln Project, which called Trump a "psychologically broken, embittered, and deeply unhappy man."

Thibault is included in several emails sent by Giardina to former Supervising Agent Joe Pientka.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Based on the records known to date, that case didn’t advance," Grassley said. "His efforts, as well as the case he tried to open on Senator Sinema, undercut public statements by former FBI officials that agents don’t get to pick their cases."

Fox News Digital reached out to the FBI for comment.

World.title: 5 states could be the biggest losers in Trump's trade war with Canada, expert warns
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Americans' pocketbooks could take yet another hit ahead of the November election as President Donald Trump escalates his trade war with Canada — with five key battleground states likely facing the most fallout.

Billions of dollars in U.S. exports are exposed to the northern neighbor's retaliatory tariffs that target American goods across a range of industries. The outcome? Costs are expected to continue rising for U.S. businesses and consumers in the weeks leading to the must-win midterms.

Affordability remains a prominent issue for voters, while tariffs remain a cornerstone of Trump's economic agenda. He claims the strategy will result in more domestic manufacturing and pressure trade partners into agreements that are more beneficial for American industries and consumers. But the result so far has been an increase in prices for the average American family.

"American manufacturers or American businesses who rely on Canadian inputs are going to start to feel the pain right in the lead up to going to the ballot box," David Clement, policy director of the free market nonprofit Consumer Choice Center, told Fox News Digital.

TRUMP JUST EXPANDED HIS TARIFF PLAYBOOK WITH A POWERFUL TRADE WEAPON NO PRESIDENT HAS EVER USED

Clement identified Ohio, Illinois, Michigan, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin as among the states most exposed to negative fallout, based on their current trade with Canada and the goods targeted by the tariffs.

"Ohio is by far the most vulnerable state in terms of exposure from the Canadian retaliatory tariffs," Clement said, estimating roughly $2.3 billion in exports to Canada are exposed.

He pointed to machinery, transportation products, minerals and metals as major sources of that vulnerability.

In Michigan, the impact is particularly evident in the auto industry, where supply chains are deeply intertwined with neighboring Ontario.

"Most Americans don’t know that a single component on a U.S.-assembled vehicle can cross the border upwards of eight times before it’s actually completed," Clement said.

"When you are tariffing automotive parts going across the border each way," he added, "it really gums up the very intertwined supply chain for cars between Michigan and Ontario."

A FRESH MIDTERM HEADACHE FOR THE GOP JUST HIT A NATIONAL RECORD

Those costs can eventually make their way to consumers, Clement argued.

Pennsylvania also faces significant exposure. Clement said about 25% of the state's exports go to Canada, much of it machinery and equipment, putting just under $1.8 billion in exports at risk.

What the trade fight means politically is less certain. Clement argued that even a change in congressional control after November would not necessarily bring the tariffs to an end.

A POPULAR COCKTAIL HAS A TRUMP TRADE PROBLEM YOU PROBABLY DIDN’T KNOW ABOUT

"The idea that Canadian retaliatory tariffs are going to swing the midterms in the Democrats’ favor and then all of a sudden create an end to the trade war is a fantasy," Clement said.

He cited the legislative hurdles to reversing presidential trade policy and noted that the Biden administration kept a number of tariffs imposed during Trump's first term.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Still, Clement argued the timing could matter, with Canada's retaliatory tariffs already in place as the midterms approach.

"Cost of living, cost of goods, cost of doing business is such an important factor for Americans who are going to be casting a ballot," he said.

World.title: House to leave early, punting Hegseth impeachment vote until after November elections
World.content:
House lawmakers will leave Washington on Wednesday night for the last time before the November midterm elections, after GOP leaders said they were canceling votes set for Thursday.

The change in schedule means that the House won’t vote on Republican Rep. Thomas Massie’s resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth until after Election Day.

GOP leaders insisted their decision had nothing to do with Massie’s impeachment efforts. But they were eager to avoid a difficult vote for many of their vulnerable Republican members who have been uneasy with Hegseth’s leadership during the unpopular six-month war with Iran.

The House will have to deal with a measure to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth after the elections. Mehmet Eser / Anadolu via Getty Images

Massie’s resolution was filed as privileged, so the House must take it up soon after it returns to Washington.

Talking to reporters, House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., who is overseeing a razor-thin GOP majority, said he wanted his members to return home and get back on the campaign trail.

“It’s time for our members to go home to their districts and make their case to the American people. To go and explain all the great things we’ve done. You’ve seen the record. You’ve seen what we’ve delivered ... the largest middle- and working-class tax cut in U.S. history. We have the violent crime rate at a 126-year low,” Johnson said.

It’s “an extraordinary record of achievement,” he added, “and so I’m excited for my Republican colleagues to go home and talk to the American people, work in their districts, and explain to them not only serving their constituents but explaining to them all the great things we’ve done for them and all the things we’re going to do in the days ahead.”

World.title: Saudi Arabia accuses Houthis of attacking Mecca, warns holy city is a ‘red line’
World.content:
Saudi Arabia has accused the Iran-backed Houthi rebels of attempting to attack Islam’s holiest city, declaring Mecca a “red line” in the escalating conflict.

The kingdom’s claim drew condemnation from across the Middle East, but no immediate sign of military support as fears grew of a return to all-out war between the key U.S. ally and the Yemeni rebels.

The Houthis swiftly denied targeting Mecca, saying their operations had targeted Saudi oil facilities and military bases, “far removed” from the sacred site of the birthplace of the Prophet Muhammad. They accused Saudi Arabia of spreading “fabrications and lies.”

The Houthis’ rapid ground advance in Yemen and aerial attacks on Saudi Arabia have shut down a crucial oil pipeline, threatened energy supplies through a second major shipping route and left the kingdom struggling to respond.

The mounting hostilities have threatened to open a second front in the Iran war, with oil and gas prices rising. President Donald Trump has so far offered no sign of any U.S. plans to intervene in this new theater.

The United States on Wednesday upgraded its travel advisory to Saudi Arabia to Level 3 amid the escalating conflict, warning Americans to “reconsider travel” to the kingdom and banning government employees from travel near the Yemen border.

Saudi military spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki said Wednesday that the country’s air defense forces had intercepted the drone south of Mecca just before 7 p.m. local time Tuesday (12 p.m. ET), according to a statement.

He emphasized that the security of the holy city and of pilgrims was a “red line,” warning there would be no hesitation to take “necessary and deterrent measures” against the Houthis, the statement said.

Mecca is known as the birthplace of the Prophet Muhammad, with millions of Muslims from around the world making the pilgrimage to the holy city each year.

“While the Houthis and Saudi Arabia trade barbs over whether the target was Mecca or not,” said Adam Baron, a fellow at New America, a think tank based in Washington, D.C., who follows Yemen and the wider Gulf region, “what is clear is you’re seeing a real demonstration of the Houthis’ continued strategic depth.”

He added: “The fact that they were able to strike this deep in Saudi Arabia is really a signal toward their capacity, if not future intentions.”

The Iran-backed rebels have ramped up attacks on cities across the kingdom after also capturing a key Red Sea port city and island in their bid to gain control of the crucial Bab el Mandeb strait.

Oil prices have soared over fears that the Houthis could shut down the waterway, which has been a crucial transit route for Saudi Arabian oil exports with the Strait of Hormuz largely closed by Iran since the U.S. and Israel launched their war in late February.

The international benchmark, Brent crude, was at around $108 per barrel early Wednesday. The nationwide average cost of diesel fuel hit another all-time high of $6.31.

Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif condemned the alleged Mecca attack as a “dastardly and heinous” act.

Sharif, who recently agreed a joint defense agreement with Saudi Arabia, did not directly mention the Houthis in his statement, but reiterated Pakistan’s general support for the kingdom.

The U.S. conducted a deadly bombing campaign against the Houthis last year, but has shown little appetite for another.

Trump said over the weekend that the Houthis had called his administration and said they “don’t want to fight with us.” Speaking with reporters during a visit to Dublin on Saturday, he said he also spoke with Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and maintained that everything would “work out fine and dandy” in the region.

The Houthis and the opposing coalition backing the internationally-supported Yemeni government have been fighting a civil war since 2014, with no clear resolution despite a truce agreed years ago.

The United Nations Security Council met Tuesday in an emergency session to discuss the rising violence in Yemen, the region’s poorest country, with member countries urging de-escalation.

The U.N. warned that the ongoing clashes between Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces and Houthi rebels have displaced at least 125,000 people since the start of September.

World.title: Supreme Court pushes back against Trump and GOP ahead of the midterm elections
World.content:
WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court in the last week has delivered major blows to President Donald Trump and his fellow Republicans that suggest the justices will not be receptive to last-minute efforts to change election rules heading into the midterms.

With control of Congress at stake, the court on Monday night blocked Trump’s plan to exert federal control over mail-in ballots via a Postal Service regulation.

The decision came after the court twice last week ruled against Republicans by declining to revive a new congressional map in Missouri that would have eliminated one of two Democratic-held districts.

While the court has a 6-3 conservative majority that often rules for Republican priorities, there are limits to how receptive some justices are to more extreme requests, election law experts told NBC News. That’s especially true for cases that could disrupt voters when an election is close or already underway.

Justin Levitt, an NBC News contributor and election law expert at Loyola Law School in Los Angeles, said the recent decisions show “there aren’t five votes for abject chaos.”

“I think the court is going to pay very close attention to any extraordinary actions that destabilize the electoral process,” said Bob Bauer, who served as White House counsel under President Barack Obama. “There’s a signal here that this sort of late intervention is going to receive scrutiny.”

On the left, the Supreme Court has been viewed with particular distrust and alarm as it relates to election issues following a major ruling in the spring that further weakened the landmark Voting Rights Act.

In the aftermath, the court quickly allowed Republican states to draw new congressional maps that eliminated majority-Black, Democratic-held seats.

But now it is Trump who appears angered and frustrated by the court’s actions.

“It is a big loss for Republicans, and America itself, and makes cheating by the Radical Left ‘Dumocrats,’ on Mail-In Ballots, a much easier thing to do — And now they have an open field to do so!” he said in a Truth Social post on Tuesday, repeating his unfounded claims about widespread election fraud.

With some states already sending out ballots for the midterm elections, timing was an issue for Republicans in both cases.

The Missouri Supreme Court faulted Republican Secretary of State Denny Hoskins for delaying a decision on whether the new map could be challenged, ultimately finding him in contempt for defying its ruling in favor of plaintiffs.

As for the Postal Service, it pushed through the new regulation despite concerns raised by election officials that they would be unable to implement it in time.

“In both instances, the court said we’re not going to countenance that,” said Travis Crum, an NBC News contributor and law professor at Washington University in St. Louis. “I do think that the Missouri case is going to send the message that dragging your feet like this is not going to be rewarded by the Supreme Court.”

There are limits to how receptive the Supreme Court is to more extreme election requests, experts said. Matt Nighswander / NBC News file

As the November elections loom, efforts to make late changes to the rules, including any new proposals from the Trump administration relating to mail-in ballots, are likely to meet with a similarly frosty reception from the justices, experts said. They cautioned, though, that it is too early to say what new litigation could arise ahead of or after Election Day.

Among the concerns that have been raised by some election officials are that the Trump administration could post federal immigration agents near polling places, although officials have said they have no current plans to do so.

As he has done previously, Trump might also complain about mail-in ballots being counted after in-person votes, claiming voter fraud because the outcome might appear to change, even though it is customary for various jurisdictions to continue counting ballots after Election Day under state law.

States with competitive elections, especially those that could determine control of the Senate, could be a particular focus for any Election Day or post-election litigation. These include Texas and Georgia, two states under Republican control with competitive races. Alaska, where votes often take a long time to count, is another state that could attract litigation, with Democrats hoping to win the Senate race there.

One fear among election administrators is that the federal government could try to seize ballots and other voting records over claims of election fraud similar to those Trump and his allies raised, and courts rejected, following the 2020 presidential election. In January, the FBI searched an election office in Georgia, seizing 2020 election ballots.

But as the Supreme Court has shown in other cases, the conservative majority follows its own agenda, not Trump’s, and has delivered him major defeats this year on his sweeping tariffs and plan to roll back birthright citizenship.

“This court is radically conservative,” Levitt said, “but not actually in the tank for Trump’s particular version of personalist chaos.”

World.title: Apple’s record night and Colbert’s Emmys wins highlight TV in transition
World.content:
Some of the biggest laughs of the night came from the mini-monologue John Mulaney delivered as he presented the category of outstanding lead actor in a drama. “This award is for the guys, just men being men,” Mulaney said. “Finally, something for the fellas.” The award itself wasn’t a surprise — front-runner Noah Wyle of “The Pitt” took it home. But Mulaney’s bit, including a joke that earned a bleep from NBC censors, had the audience in the room roaring and people at home wondering how long until he finally hosts a major awards show. (Mulaney did host the Film Academy’s Governors Awards in 2024, but that show isn’t televised.)

The era of Apple

New Apple CEO John Ternus attended the Emmys, and he had lots to celebrate besides the $2,000 foldable iPhone he showed off on the red carpet. For the first time since it launched in 2019, Apple TV collected more Emmys than any other outlet.

Including its wins at last weekend’s two Emmy nights, Apple took home 28 trophies total this year, with a record 14 for freshman comedy “Widow’s Bay” and six for “Pluribus.” HBO came in second with 21, with “DTF St. Louis” collecting seven and “The Pitt” six. Netflix followed in third with 16, winning three each for “Love on the Spectrum” and “Beef.”

Matthew Rhys accepts the award for lead actor in a comedy series for Apple TV's "Widow's Bay." Patrick T. Fallon / AFP via Getty Images

Quiet reflection over fiery politics

If you were betting on Colbert to riff on President Donald Trump and the Federal Communications Commission or open up about the events leading up to his late-night program’s cancellation, you were out of luck. He kept his acceptance speech focused squarely on his gratitude for his 11-year run at CBS, his writing staff and his wife.

In general, the Emmys were light on topical humor or references to current events such as the Iran war, AI or the looming Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger.

Sally Field did sneak in a subtle line that some interpreted as an anti-merger dig as she accepted an Emmy for her performance in the Netflix movie “Remarkably Bright Creatures.” “We’re the arts,” Field said. “We matter. Our voices matter. Our diversity, our unique storytelling matters. We can’t let those voices be silenced or compromised or merged.”

Instead of fiery political commentary, this year’s ceremony leaned more reflective, with earnest meditations from Hargitay and “Pluribus” creator Vince Gilligan on TV’s power to unite a divided country.

The winner of one of the night’s marquee categories trained his attention on TV’s important role in troubled times. “Yes, we are entertainers. We make you laugh, we make you cry, occasionally we make you look away in disgust,” R. Scott Gemmill, the creator of “The Pitt,” said in his acceptance speech for best drama series. “But when I look around this room, I see something more important than the awards and the ratings. I see a whole community that is still trying to do the right thing.”

Serious notes

In a year filled with losses in the entertainment industry, the telecast included sorrowful tributes to the late Rob Reiner, Catherine O’Hara and sitcom giant James Burrows. Reba McEntire sang Dolly Parton’s “Appalachian Memories” just a few weeks after Parton’s death, and Noah Kahan performed “Bridge Over Troubled Water” during the In Memoriam montage.

But the longest ovation of the night came for a performer who has defied the odds to remain in the business: Michael J. Fox, accepting the Bob Hope Humanitarian Award from his wheelchair. Fox shared that he kept his Parkinson’s diagnosis secret for a long time and wondered whether audiences would still laugh at his jokes if they knew he was sick. Ultimately, he said, “I understood that accepting Parkinson’s didn’t mean I had to surrender to it.”

Julianna Margulies presents Michael J. Fox with the Bob Hope Humanitarian Award. Robert Gauthier / Los Angeles Times via Getty Images

The two Emmys personas

For years, Jack Nicholson appeared in the front row at the Oscars, the picture of cool detachment and old Hollywood charm. “Shrinking” nominee Harrison Ford seems to be stepping into that role at the Emmys as the guy everyone else seems to want to get next to, who really himself just wants to get home.

Harrison Ford shares a laugh with Jason Segel. Jordan Strauss / Invision for the Television Academy / AP

In contrast Monday night was enthusiastic “Widow’s Bay” creator Katie Dippold, who didn’t even try to contain her glee at her show’s many awards. During her acceptance speech for writing, Dippold declared: “I promise all of you that no one will ever step foot in my home without seeing this thing [her Emmy]. I’m sorry, this is going to become my entire personality now.”

World.title: Coast Guard, FBI boarded Texas-bound oil tanker to investigate cyberattack
World.content:
Coast Guard personnel and FBI agents boarded a Texas-bound commercial oil tanker in the Atlantic last month after determining the ship's network may have been compromised by a foreign actor, the Coast Guard said Tuesday. Iranian state media claimed that hackers obtained control over propulsion, navigation and cargo systems and lost communications for 30 hours.

The Coast Guard did not disclose the name of the ship, but Iranian reports identified it as the VL Prosperity, a massive 333-meter supertanker capable of carrying roughly 2.3 million barrels of oil. Public vessel data shows the Liberian-flagged very large crude carrier was bound for Galveston, Texas. South Korea-based HMM Ocean Service Co., Ltd., which manages the VL Prosperity, confirmed the Coast Guard had boarded the vessel.

On Aug. 20, Iran's Mehr News Agency reported that VL Prosperity had been attacked and had lost communications on Aug. 7 while sailing from Egypt's Sidi Kerir terminal toward the U.S. Citing an unnamed crew member, Mehr's report alleged that the attackers penetrated engine-room systems, reduced engine cooling flow, increased engine speed and interfered with fuel and lubricating-oil systems.

August 2026: U.S. Coast Guard teams board oil tanker. Provided by U.S. Coast Guard

According to the Coast Guard, a specialized team of its law enforcement personnel, a vessel inspector, Coast Guard Cyber Protection Team members and FBI Cyber Action Team operators boarded the ship on Aug. 21. The team examined both the vessel's operational technology and information-technology systems and worked with the crew and the ship's corporate operators to eradicate the threat. On Tuesday, the Coast Guard said there were currently "no reports of operational disruptions, vessel instability, physical danger to crews, or environmental impacts."

August 2026: U.S. Coast Guard teams board oil tanker in Atlantic Ocean. Provided by U.S. Coast Guard

Unconfirmed reports of the attack first surfaced publicly after the ship passed through the Strait of Gibraltar, between Spain and Morocco.

The risk of penetrating a commercial oil tanker's system goes beyond stolen data or disabled communications. Modern tankers use interconnected operational technology, or OT, to control the vessels — with propulsion, navigation and cargo systems all internet-connected. Though it's unlikely, if a hostile state can reach and even hijack those systems remotely, an attacker could theoretically manipulate a vessel's movement or critical machinery, potentially turning a massive oil tanker into a weapon against a port.

The U.S. has not provided details on the extent of the possible breach, only confirming there were indications the vessel's network had been compromised. HMM stated that it "has rigorous cyber protocols in place to ensure the safety and security of vessels under our care."

The U.S. has also so far not attributed the possible cyber attack to a specific actor. After Mehr's report, Iranian state media amplified the story in the weeks following the breach, suggesting that the regime was opening a new cyber front in the war with the U.S. Four days after Mehr's report, Iran's Tasnim News Agency published an article with the headline "No American Vessel Is Safe Anymore: Will Cannons Give Way to Codes?"

World.title: Is the U.S. and China's mutual distrust the biggest risk as AI evolves?
World.content:
As fears grow that the race for AI supremacy could be hurtling us all toward a grim fate not unlike the apocalyptic plot line of the Terminator movies, analysts tell CBS News that mutual distrust between the U.S. and China, as much as the technology itself, could lead humanity "off a cliff."

The long-term fear among experts like the Anthropic researcher whose dire prediction stole headlines a week ago, is that superintelligence — a theoretical AI agent smarter than any person — could start to see humans as rivals for essential resources, endangering our survival.

The bosses of major U.S. AI firms OpenAI and Anthropic have now called for a slowing of AI development, to "pace the frontier."

China, the other major hub of work to push that frontier alongside Silicon Valley, has had its own warnings. A team of U.S. researchers last week used AI to expose a flaw in China's "app for everything" WeChat, which is used by more than 800 million people in the country.

Many Chinese firms agree with the growing consensus that AI must be regulated, according to Leia Wang, non-resident scholar at the Carnegie Endowment for Peace, who mentioned the Artificial Intelligence Laboratory in Shanghai as an example of a "highly reputable body" working on AI safety.

Yi Zeng, the dean of the Beijing Institute of AI Safety and Governance, wrote in a research paper shared with CBS News that "the catastrophic risks posed by AI, and the hidden danger of human extinction, are growing by the day."

Britain's King Charles III is to convene a meeting in Scotland on Thursday of industry leaders to discuss "whether a shared set of principles can be developed" to guide the future development and use of AI.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, whose firm is among those attending the conference, said in April that it was essential that U.S. and Chinese researchers "are actually talking."

This bilateral coordination by industry leaders "is glaringly missing because of our current attitude about China as an adversary," he said.

Distrust, and "Chinese killer robots"

A group of Democratic U.S. lawmakers have called on House Speaker Mike Johnson to delay the upcoming recess to get legislation passed on AI safeguards.

Johnson said Sunday, however, that rushing regulations into law would mean the U.S. "will lose the race to China, and that is a threat to every single American."

Republican Senator Ted Cruz said last week that "if there are gonna be killer robots, I'd rather they be American killer robots than Chinese killer robots."

On Monday, President Trump dismissed warnings of an AI threat as a "sick conspiracy," adding in his Truth Social post that "the only one that is happy about it is China. WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS!"

"It's not that the U.S. government doesn't think AI is risky," Wang told CBS News, but that when it comes to U.S. leaders' "China-facing AI thoughts, the number one concern is technological competition."

China's leaders have made some overtures toward collaboration on AI safety.

In June, President Xi Jinping explicitly warned of the dangers of a "loss of control" of the technology. A month later he said countries must work together to "ensure that AI is always under human control."

But like many senior U.S. officials, China's government has rejected calls to slow the pace of development, viewing the concept as an effort by the U.S. "to assert its technological dominance," said Wang.

After Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said the U.S. and its global partners should collaborate "to keep democracies' AI lead over autocracies as large as possible, to give us the breathing room we need in order to pace effectively," China's Foreign Ministry said Monday that "narratives of threat … serve only to disrupt the process of global AI governance."

Competition and mutual suspicion between the world's two biggest economies may come as little surprise, but Wang told CBS News that reducing the "AI safety conversation into a technological competition conversation" was "the most unhelpful framing," given the risks involved.

In a February essay entitled "Who will save the world from a U.S.-China AI arms race?," National University of Singapore lecturer Alex Capri, an expert in trade and technology, wrote that the two countries "face a prisoner's dilemma … both would be safer with restraint, yet each accelerates development to avoid falling victim to the other."

Ways forward

"A coordinated slowdown or grand international agreement might not be the right frame to engage Chinese firms and the government," Kwan Yee Ng, Head of International Governance at Concordia AI, an AI safety consultancy based in Beijing, told CBS News.

She added, however, that "there are many things the two countries can work on."

That "low-hanging fruit," according to Ng, includes sharing cybersecurity best practices, coordinating to avoid any misuse of AI by terrorist groups or agents seeking to cause economic turmoil, and opening up low-level government talks to share granular technical information.

Matt Sheehan, a colleague and fellow researcher of Wang's at the Carnegie Endowment, argues that another approach is "AI safety in parallel," which would see the two countries "move forward on parallel tracks, each advancing the technology and also acting to reduce the risks because they believe it is essential to their own national security — regardless of what the other does."

An existential moment

China's government said after a May meeting in Beijing between Mr. Trump and Xi that the leaders had "agreed to hold dialogue between the two governments" on AI.

President Trump acknowledged discussing the notion of "guardrails" on AI development with Xi, but in an analysis of the summit, the Center for Strategic and International Studies said "there was little indication of meaningful progress on the core disputes," and it noted that the White House did not confirm any new dialogue with Beijing on the topic.

Mr. Trump is due to meet with Xi again in Washington on Sept. 24, and they are expected to discuss AI security.

President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping tour Zhongnanhai Garden on May 15, 2026, in Beijing, China. Evan Vucci-Pool/Getty/China Pool

The hope among many analysts, however faint, is that the growing urgency of concern over unbridled AI advancement, despite Mr. Trump's rejection of the worries, will push the leaders to back coordination on some level.

"It's like, here's the big concern over here," said Wang, referring to the existential AI fears, "and then they're fighting about this thing — and it's gonna drive us off a cliff."

"The choices our generation makes will determine whether and how human civilization survives and develops," added Zeng.

World.title: Amazon raises starting pay to $20 an hour and adds Whole Foods perks
World.content:
Amazon will increase the minimum starting pay for full-time operations workers to $20 an hour and add grocery discounts for all U.S. workers, the e-commerce giant announced Wednesday.

The new hourly wage represents a $1 increase from its current starting level. With the bump, Amazon said average pay will now be $24 an hour for Amazon workers.

Operations workers at Amazon handle logistics, transportation and other work at its fulfillment centers.

Amazon also announced a series of new employee perks on Wednesday. Beginning Oct. 1, all U.S. employees will get 10% off eligible fresh groceries on Amazon.com and the Whole Foods website, and a 20% discount in-store at Whole Foods locations.

The Seattle-based company also said it is offering employee memberships with First Tech Federal Credit Union, which provides banking services, starting in late 2026. First Tech partners with major tech companies, including Intel and Microsoft.

Qualified employees, their spouses and their children will qualify for First Tech membership for life, meaning they can access it even after they leave the company, Amazon said in its release.

The new perks add to existing benefits such as free Prime memberships and healthcare insurance for eligible employees.

Amazon employs roughly 1.5 million workers total, according to FactSet. On its website, the company claims it has "created more jobs across America in the last decade than any other company."

World.title: Obamas' dog Sunny dies: "A cherished member of our family"
World.content:
Washington — Former President Barack Obama announced Wednesday that the family's dog, Sunny, had died, calling the 13-year-old Portuguese water dog a "cherished member of our family."

In a social media post, Obama wrote "we will miss her terribly."

"As far as our family was concerned, she was pretty much perfect," Obama wrote. The post was reshared by his wife, former first lady Michelle Obama, and had been viewed on X over 2 million times within three hours of being shared. They also shared a Facebook post with several photos, including one with the pope, which had hundreds of thousands of reactions.

The Obama family adopted Sunny as a puppy during his second term in 2013. On Wednesday, Obama wrote that the whole household, including their first dog, Bo, "immediately fell in love" with her, adding that for the next 13 years, "she would be by our side – always loyal, always sweet, always ready for adventure, still fiery and gorgeous till the very end of her days. "

Obama also described the contrast between his two dogs' personalities. Bo could usually be won over with a treat, he wrote, whereas Sunny "was more interested in having us run around with her, roll on the floor with her, or have her belly rubbed for as long as we were willing."

Sunny's best qualities. Both of the Obamas' dogs were famous for running around the White House lawn, and the former president Obama also described Sunny in his memorial post as "athletic and full of boundless energy." He also wrote about her quirks, such as how the Portuguese water dog had an ironic hatred for getting wet. "As far as our family was concerned, she was pretty much perfect," he wrote.

Obama's daughters Sasha and Malia, who were 12 and 14 when Sunny joined the family, also were close with Sunny, Obama said. "She (Sunny) loved the girls, even if they were pestering her when she was napping," Obama wrote. Sunny was also a great addition to the White House staff, Obama said. "She loved our team, and would often follow them around, helping them on the job."

Sunny's death comes more than five years after the Obamas lost Bo, who the family said died of cancer in 2021 at the age of 12. The Obamas adopted Bo in 2009, fulfilling a campaign promise to Malia and Sasha. Bo had been with the Obamas since shortly after Barack Obama's first inauguration in 2009. Sunny joined the family a few years later as a companion for Bo, and the pair were soon after dubbed "the first dogs" by the press.

World.title: 3 dead after NBC Los Angeles news helicopter crashes in Chatsworth
World.content:
Three people were killed when an NBC Los Angeles helicopter crashed in the San Fernando Valley on Tuesday night near the scene of a deadly Metro bus crash in Chatsworth.

The crash happened just before 7 p.m. between two commercial buildings at a storage facility in the 9100 block of N. Mason Avenue, according to Los Angeles firefighters. The aircraft appeared to have landed on top of two shipping containers and several vehicles that were parked in the area.

Around 9 p.m., NBCLA confirmed that the helicopter belonged to their station. NBCLA later identified the two victims on board the helicopter as aerial news reporter Eliana Moreno and pilot George Marciniw.

"We are deeply saddened to share that a helicopter providing aerial news coverage for NBC4 and Telemundo 52 was involved in a fatal accident in Los Angeles on Tuesday evening," said a statement from NBCLA and Telemundo 52. "We extend our heartfelt condolences to the families, friends and colleagues of those who lost their lives."

LAFD Captain Branden Silverman said a third victim was pronounced dead at the scene of the crash. Officials believe they were outside of the helicopter when it crashed.

The Los Angeles County Medical Examiner has identified the person as 29-year-old Edy Guitierrez Mejia.

Circumstances surrounding the incident remain unclear, but aerial footage showed Los Angeles firefighters working to fight the flames from a large fire that broke out after the crash and spread to the nearby vehicles.

Two other victims were taken to a local hospital in unknown condition, LAFD Captain Rico Gross said during a news conference late Tuesday night. The nature of their injuries was not immediately noted.

The National Transportation Safety Board and the Federal Aviation Administration confirmed that they will be investigating the helicopter crash. The FAA said the NTSB will lead the investigation. Both are expected to be at the scene on Wednesday. Los Angeles police are also investigating the crash.

Mayor Bass and Gov. Newsom speak on tragic day

Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass and other city leaders spoke during the news conference.

"This is a very, very tragic day in Los Angeles," Bass said while speaking during a news conference. "We lost five Angelenos today, and my hearts certainly go out to the families and friends to all of those that we lost. ... This is a heartbreaking night for our city, and my thoughts and prayers are with first and foremost with the families and loved ones that we lost today."

Supervisor Lindsey Horvath called on Angelenos to support one another during such difficult times.

"Tonight is a time to care for the people who are hurting, to support our first responders and to stand together as a community," Horvath said. "Chatsworth has experienced an incredibly difficult day. To everyone grieving, recovering or processing what they experienced today, we are here for you and we stand with you."

California Gov. Gavin Newsom also shared a message on Facebook late Tuesday.

"Our hearts are with the victims and families of tonight's devastating Metro bus and helicopter crashes in Chatsworth, and with the entire NBC4 family. Thank you to the first responders working tirelessly tonight," Newsom's post said.

CBS LA anchors and reporters also spoke on the tragedy impacting the tight-knit news community in Los Angeles after the helicopter's affiliation was confirmed.

"It was a double tragedy," said CBS LA's Desmond Shaw. "I don't want the poor people that were caught in the bus crash today - I don't want them to be forgotten either ... I obviously just have to give my heartfelt condolences to NBC and the family members of the crew on board."

"Our hearts go out to all of them. This is when we all come together for something like this, even if you've never met the person," CBS LA anchor Pat Harvey said. "I want to say that we have each other's backs."

"That helicopter community is a small group of people, and it's just devastating to know that this has happened to one of those people, to our friends and our colleagues at NBC4," CBS LA assignment editor Mike Rogers said. "Our hearts are shattered with you."

NBCLA mourns loss of colleagues

NBCLA and Telemundo 52 are mourning the loss of two of their colleagues, Moreno and Marciniw.

The station reported that Moreno was born in Orange County and was a 2010 graduate of Chapman University. She studied broadcast journalism and political science. NBCLA added that she joined the Angel City Air helicopter team in September 2010.

Moreno worked across other Southern California news outlets, including CBS LA.

Marciniw also grew up in Southern California and graduated from Burbank High School in 1974.

Moreno and Marciniw began flying together in 2023.

CBS LA's Mark Liu said he previously worked with Moreno when she was beginning her career as a news helicopter reporter.

"I had the opportunity to work with her when I was an assignment manager when I was in the newsroom back then," Liu said. "What I remember about her is that she was so enthusiastic and so excited for this job. She described it as one of the greatest jobs in television news."

CBS LA reporter Rick Montanez also previously worked with Moreno. He described her as passionate and dedicated to covering news.

"I worked with her on a lot of breaking news during my years I spent in the NBC newsroom covering wildfires, covering breaking news across Southern California," Montanez said. "You could just feel the passion in her for this, this calling."
