World.title: Polls show Argentine distrust of Milei's shift on the Falklands
World.content:
Polls show Argentine distrust of Milei's shift on the Falklands

14th Monday, September 2026 - 22:06 UTC Full article

Photo: Nicolás Aguilera/AFP

Two private Argentine pollsters released findings this week pointing to an adverse reception of President Javier Milei's shift on the Falklands, even though the sovereignty claim commands broad consensus in Argentine society.

The consultancy Analogías, which surveyed views of the national government between September 5 and 8, reported that 61% of respondents expressed distrust of the president's new position: 49.8% said they did not believe him at all and 11.2% believed him little. The firm did not publish technical details such as sample size or margin of error.

Monitor Digital, which analyzed 89,900 mentions of the government on social media, ranked the Islands as the second axis of the official digital conversation, clustered around terms such as sovereignty, measures, the United Kingdom and the United States. Its director, Diego Corbalán, told Perfil the volume did not translate into support: “In some way the government managed to place the issue, but it is not clear that all of it works to its benefit.”

The same study played down the reach of the matter beyond political circles. Across nearly a thousand Google trends recorded in the week after the September 3 televised address, the cluster associated with the Islands appeared only at 27th place, with some 50,000 searches, and the foreign policy category accounted for 0.8% of the total, far below sports and entertainment.

The sequence began with that address, in which Milei asserted sovereignty over the archipelago and announced measures against oil development. The following day the government confirmed sanctions against individuals and companies linked to that activity, and this week it is preparing to send Congress a National Sovereignty Defense bill.

The announcements followed the World Cup episode in July, when National Security Minister Alejandra Monteoliva endorsed a ban on flags and shirts referring to the Islands during the semifinal between Argentina and England. The players themselves defied the measure by displaying a banner at the end of the match, and the episode led to the suspension of debate on the land ownership bill in the Senate.

On Sunday the government distributed to the press an institutional video by Santiago Oria, director of audiovisual production at the Presidency, combining statements by Milei, remarks by U.S. President Donald Trump on a possible review of Washington's neutral position, and footage of the match against England, set to terrace music. Milei and La Libertad Avanza figures shared the piece.

Corbalán criticized the strategy in political terms: in adopting it, he said, the libertarians “embrace the whole Kirchnerist populist mode,” which he described as chauvinism.

Islanders confirmed their status as a British Overseas Territory in the 2013 referendum, with 99.8% of the vote.

World.title: Is Mexico’s soccer league a monopoly? Antitrust officials are looking to find out
World.content:
The National Antitrust Commission (CNA) has unilaterally opened an investigation into Liga MX, Mexico’s top professional soccer league and a massive cultural touchstone that captures the country’s passion for the sport.

An internal CNA document says the investigation aims to identify “the possible commission of relative monopolistic practices in the market of ‘affiliation, organization and access’ to professional federated football competitions in Mexico, as well as similar or related services.”

⚽ ¿Cómo investigamos el funcionamiento de un mercado?

José Manuel Haro Zepeda, titular de nuestra Autoridad Investigadora, explicó en @MVSNoticias las herramientas con las que contamos para analizar la organización y acceso a competiciones de fútbol profesional en México. pic.twitter.com/r2qgofrR9M — Comisión Nacional Antimonopolio (@AntimonopolioMX) September 15, 2026

In short, the CNA wants to know if a small group is violating the Federal Law of Economic Competition by unfairly controlling who can join, who can compete and how tournaments are organized, to the exclusion of other interested parties.

“After analyzing the events that occurred in recent months, the Investigating Authority determined that it has sufficient evidence to formally open an investigation on its own initiative for possible monopolistic practices in the professional soccer market in Mexico,” the CNA said in a public report.

The recent events referred to are likely related to a Liga MX decision in July to scrap promotion/relegation between the top-flight Mexican soccer league and the second-tier Liga Expansión. Liga MX also announced the end to payouts to the second-tier sides.

Promotion and relegation were scrapped in 2020 to insulate the clubs from the financial impacts of lost revenue during the enforced lockdown ordered due to the Covid-19 pandemic.

Liga Expansión officials fiercely disputed the decision, even filing a suit with the Court of Arbitration for Sport, which ruled that the 2026-27 campaign was the earliest point at which promotion/relegation ought to be reinstituted.

Critics have also identified the league’s policy regarding possession of television broadcasting rights by teams as a monopolistic practice.

The commission has sought to make clear that there are no defendants identified as yet and it hasn’t been determined exactly who will be investigated. Instead, the probe will simply review whether competition law is being followed.

The investigation can last up to 120 business days, but can be extended up to three times longer if necessary. During that time, the CNA can request documents, visit offices, summon people to testify and conduct inspections.

If guilt is determined, the Liga MX and its member teams could face a penalty of up to 10% of their annual income and would be required to correct any monopolistic practices detected.

With reports from ESPN, El Economista, El Universal and SportCa

World.title: Should you be worried about the presence of brain-eating amoeba in Yucatán water bodies?
World.content:
A man died of Primary Amoebic Meningoencephalitis (PAM) in a Mérida hospital last week, most likely from contact with the brain-eating amoeba Naegleria fowleri, the Yucatán Health Services (SSY) reported on Monday.

The SSY confirmed the presence of N. fowleri in an artificial lake at the La Isla shopping center in Mérida, where the 34-year-old man worked as a water sports instructor.

FAMILIARES DESPIDEN A CARLOS, INSTRUCTOR QUE F4LL3C10 POR AMEBA COME CEREBROS#Video | Familiares y amigos despidieron con tristeza a Carlos, el joven instructor de wakeboard de 33 años que perdió la v1d4 tras contraer una agresiva infección por la ameba ‘Naegleria fowleri’ en… pic.twitter.com/f57zIqs8Ly — Yucatán Ahora (@yucatanahora) September 15, 2026

“It is a serious and extremely rare disease; this is the first case registered in Yucatán,” the SSY said in a statement.

The microorganism is most commonly found in stagnant, warm waters between 35°C and 46°C. It enters the body when contaminated water is forcefully inhaled through the nose, although it can also occur while swimming, diving or submerging one’s head in lakes, rivers or poorly chlorinated swimming pools.

PAM is not transmitted from person to person and is not acquired by drinking contaminated water, the SSY emphasized.

People living in the Yucatán capital have expressed concern about the water quality in nearby cenotes, where swimming is common. However, experts suggest that natural freshwater bodies are cooler, at between 24°C and 26°C, making the presence of N. fowleri far less likely.

The development of microorganisms in pools can be avoided through chlorination and pH management, and in larger water bodies through adequate water movement, which promotes aeration. Regular cleaning and maintenance can also help avoid the accumulation of sediment, organic matter, algae and biofilms in stagnant water, conditions that attract N. fowleri.

The first symptoms of PAM are usually severe headache, fever, nausea and vomiting. According to initial reports, the victim presented with severe symptoms of central nervous system infection and was taken to a hospital in the city, where he died.

Health authorities ordered the temporary closure of the water feature at La Isla while samples were tested at the Hidalgo State Public Health Laboratory, which confirmed the presence of N. fowleri. Meanwhile, cleaning efforts and technical inspections were carried out at the site.

Epidemiological investigators are conducting interviews to locate other individuals who may have come into contact with the water.

The SSY said it plans to investigate the companies responsible for water quality and lake maintenance for their compliance with Mexican rules and regulations.

“Anyone who has violated health regulations will be sanctioned,” the SSY stressed.

According to the SSY statement, once the responsible company demonstrates through laboratory tests that the lake water is suitable for recreational use in accordance with legal standards, a new verification and sampling of the water will be conducted and a decision will be made on whether to lift the temporary closure.

With reports from Reportur, La Jornada and Diario de Yucatán

World.title: 139 US troops cleared to enter Mexico for joint training in Chihuahua
World.content:
More than 100 U.S. soldiers will travel to Mexico this month to participate in joint training exercises with Mexican military personnel in the northern state of Chihuahua.

The federal Senate on Monday granted President Claudia Sheinbaum the authority to allow the entry into Mexico of 139 U.S. Army troops, who are scheduled to land at the Santa Gertrudis Air Force Base south of Chihuahua city this Sunday.

The granting of that authority comes amid security-related tension in the Mexico-U.S. relationship.

Among the causes of that tension are the CIA’s alleged participation in a drug lab raid in Chihuahua in April without the knowledge or authorization of the Mexican government; U.S. prosecutors’ drug-trafficking accusations against Sinaloa Gov. Rubén Rocha Moya and other current and former officials; and suggestions from Trump administration officials that the U.S. could take unilateral action against Mexican drug cartels on Mexican soil.

While each of those developments has drawn the ire of Sheinbaum, the president remains committed to cooperating with the Trump administration on security on the proviso that Mexican sovereignty and territorial integrity are respected. One example of that cooperation is a joint anti-drone operation that is currently taking place on the border between Tijuana and San Diego.

U.S. soldiers have previously traveled to Mexico to undertake joint training exercises with Mexican personnel. However, the U.S. contingent set to arrive in Chihuahua on Sunday is larger than previous ones that have come to Mexico.

Here’s everything you need to know about the upcoming military collaboration on Mexican soil.

Where will the joint training exercises take place?

The joint training exercises will take place at the Centro Nacional de Adiestramiento (National Training Center), located in Santa Gertrudis in the municipality of Saucillo, Chihuahua. The CNA is the Mexican military’s largest training facility.

Among the simulated combat exercises U.S. and Mexican military personnel will conduct are the destruction of sniper positions; the seizure of an airfield; an air assault; the destruction of a fuel-supply point; and the capture and extraction of a target using live fire.

The U.S. soldiers will stay at the CNA during their time in Mexico.

What is the objective of the training exercises?

The Senate said in a statement that the aim of the joint training exercises is to “strengthen operational capabilities between the United States and Mexican Armed Forces through the planning and execution of military operations under the principles of respect, sovereignty and territorial integrity; shared responsibility; mutual trust; and collaboration without subordination.

The Senate said that the joint training “will not only have a positive impact on strengthening individual and collective preparedness, but will also contribute to the improvement of bilateral military cooperation mechanisms.”

How long will the US soldiers remain in Mexico?

The U.S. troops will arrive in Chihuahua on a U.S. Air Force plane on Sept. 20 and return to the United States on Sept. 30. Therefore, the soldiers will be in Mexico for a total of 11 days.

The Senate noted that the U.S. troops will enter Mexico “with weapons.”

Which division of the US army to the soldiers belong to?

The 139 soldiers coming to Mexico belong to the 101st Airborne Division of the U.S. Army. The division, known as the “Screaming Eagles,” is the only air assault division of the United States Army. It is based at Fort Campbell, Kentucky.

With reports from La Silla Rota, El Economista and El Financiero

World.title: Tehran’s Azadi Tower bears Mexican flag in first-ever Independence Day tribute
World.content:
For the first time, Iran lit one of its most recognizable landmarks in the green, white and red of the Mexican flag, turning Tehran’s Azadi Tower into a striking Independence Day tribute Tuesday night.

The Azadi Tower illumination marked the 216th anniversary of the Grito de Dolores — the 1810 call by priest Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla that launched Mexico’s war for independence from Spain.

La emblemática Torre Azadi, símbolo de Teherán, se iluminó con los colores de la bandera mexicana para conmemorar el 216° aniversario de la Independencia de México. La Embajada de Irán en México destacó el acto como un gesto de amistad entre ambos pueblos. Más en La Jornada:… pic.twitter.com/tfgRRj5ddy — La Jornada (@lajornadaonline) September 15, 2026

“Today, Mexico is not in Mexico. It is in the heart of Iran,” the Iranian Embassy in Mexico posted Sept. 15 with a video of the glowing monument.

The display marked the first time Iran has illuminated a monument in honor of Mexico, according to the newspaper El Universal.

Those colors, however, are not inherently unusual at Azadi Tower, since green, white and red are also Iran’s national colors. For example, on Feb. 10, 2024, it was lit up in that way for the 45th anniversary of the 1979 Islamic Revolution.

Speaking to HispanTV from Tehran, Mexican Ambassador Guillermo Puente Ordorica called the lighting “a great gesture of friendship” that Mexicans will cherish.

Built in 1971, the 45-meter Azadi Tower was originally called Shahyad Tower, then renamed Azadi (Persian for “freedom”) after the 1979 revolution. The tower and its surrounding square are often the site of major public gatherings.

Beyond Iran, Mexican communities and diplomats marked Día de la Independencia across several continents.

In New York, Mayor Zohran Mamdani was grand marshal Sunday at a Mexican Independence Day parade in Brooklyn, wearing a tricolor sash and carrying a Mexican flag. He said he was proud to be the first New York City mayor to march in the parade with “a community that has fostered cultural pride for generations.”

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Mayor Zohran Kwame Mamdani (@nycmayor)

Mamdani’s remarks came just days after U.S. Vice President JD Vance criticized a protester carrying a Mexican flag at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas, calling him an “idiot” and telling him, “If you love Mexico so much, get your ass over there. I’ll buy you the plane ticket.”

Elsewhere, Mexico’s ambassador to the United Kingdom, Alejandro Gertz Manero, led a Grito ceremony in London, where festivities included music, food, dance and other traditions.

In Madrid, the Mexican Embassy hosted a public Grito in Chamberí Square, followed by folk ballet, mariachi and a circus performance.

Mexican celebrations were also reported in Krakow, Rome, Vienna, Beijing, Seoul, Barcelona, Budapest and Kansas City.

With reports from El Universal, La Jornada and Madrid Gazette

World.title: New US-Mexico water agreement means reduced allotments but a heathier Colorado River
World.content:
A long-running dispute between Mexico and the United States over Colorado River water-sharing has been resolved — at least for the next two years — with Mexico getting significantly less water as a result.

The U.S. is also receiving less water as part of a joint effort to mitigate ongoing drought conditions and low reservoir levels in the Colorado River basin.

In fact, under the new agreement, formally called Minute 334 and finalized by the International Boundary and Water Commission (IBWC) on Sept. 2, Mexico’s 16.7% (250,000 acre-feet) annual reduction of its previous typical water allocation is equivalent to water-use reductions imposed on U.S. Lower Basin states (Arizona, California and Nevada).

The agreement also implements a strategy to manage the salinity of Colorado River water as it reaches Mexico. Consultations regarding possible further cuts are contemplated for 2028 if conditions worsen.

Minute 334 was signed by Mexican IBWC Commissioner Adriana Reséndez and her U.S. counterpart, Chad McIntosh, with the participation of Mexican IBWC Secretary Manuel Morales. The U.S. Department of the Interior confirmed the approval of both governments.

“This Minute makes sure water is shared fairly among our users and protects the health of the Colorado River during these difficult times,” McIntosh said in a news release. “Both countries deserve a lot of credit for agreeing to these water reductions and other measures.”

Reséndez insisted on proportionality between the two countries, defending Mexico’s position even as it has struggled to meet its obligations in the original 1944 treaty.

When the most recent five-year cycle of that treaty came to an end on Oct. 24 last year, Mexico still owed 865,136 acre-feet of water, though the terms of the treaty grant Mexico five years to catch up.

The reduction agreed to in Minute 334 is equivalent to one-sixth of Mexico’s annual allocation established in the treaty, about 1.85 billion cubic meters.

The two nations also agreed to cooperate on managing the Colorado River Delta in Mexico, which has been transformed from a lush 2-million-acre wetland into a mostly dry salt flat due to decades of intensive upstream dam construction and water diversions.

With reports from El Universal, WaterWorld and The Colorado Sun

World.title: MND Local: WTA Tennis, an international film fest and more events in Guadalajara
World.content:
Late September in Guadalajara brings an action-packed calendar. Upcoming events include a World Migrant Day celebration benefiting a local nonprofit organization, an international film festival and the 2026 Guadalajara Open, an important stop on the Women’s Tennis Association (WTA) professional tour.

Top female tennis players to compete at the Guadalajara Open this week

Following hard on the heels of the U.S. Open in New York City, Zapopan welcomes a select group of the WTA’s brightest stars to the Guadalajara Open this week.

The annual event, played at the Panamerican Tennis Center in Parque Metropolitano, attracts a diverse group of top female tennis players from around the globe. The field will compete in singles and doubles for a US $1.2 million purse and a top singles prize of US $185,500.

Confirmed players for this year’s event include world number 11 Marta Kostyuk of Ukraine and world number 14 and defending champion Iva Jovic of the United States.

Kostyuk returns to Mexico as one of the hottest players on the WTA tour during the 2026 season, having reached the semifinals of Wimbledon and Roland Garros, in addition to claiming two titles on clay last spring. She last competed at the Guadalajara Open in 2023, where she reached the second round.

Latin American tennis will also be well represented, with Colombian veteran Camila Osorio and Mexican No. 1 Renata Zarazúa scheduled to compete.

For details, visit the tournament website.

Dates: Sept. 13-19, 2026.

Sept. 13-19, 2026. Location: Centro Panamericano de Tenis, Zapopan, Jalisco.

Centro Panamericano de Tenis, Zapopan, Jalisco. Cost: Individual tickets start at 866 pesos, not including fees. Tournament packages are available on Boletomovil.

Aeroméxico to launch nonstop service from Guadalajara to Paris in 2027

Savoring the perfect pain au chocolat is about to get a little easier for Francophile Tapatíos. Starting April 13, 2027, the city will have its second direct European flight route, as Aeroméxico launches nonstop service between Guadalajara’s Miguel Hidalgo International Airport (GDL) and Paris-Charles de Gaulle (CDG).

The route will run three times per week on Tuesdays, Fridays and Sundays, departing Guadalajara at 1:55 p.m. and arriving in Paris at 9:25 a.m. the following day. Return flights will operate on Mondays, Wednesdays and Saturdays, departing Paris at 11:40 a.m. and arriving in Guadalajara at 4:10 p.m. the same day.

“Adding Guadalajara–Paris … strengthens our network, offers customers more travel options and further consolidates our position as the leading airline between Mexico and Europe,” Giancarlo Mulinelli, senior vice president of global sales at Aeroméxico, told Aviacionline last week.

Celebrate World Migrant Day with the Rhizome Center

Later this month, Guadalajara residents will have the opportunity to celebrate World Migrant Day at a community celebration featuring local food, culture and a social cause.

Hosted by The Rhizome Center, this year’s festival, “Many Journeys. One Community,” is both a fundraiser and an opportunity to raise awareness about the organization’s work. During the event, guests can sample food from 15 migrant kitchens, enjoy live French, Cuban and Syrian music, listen to storytelling, and meet artists sharing their craft and culture.

The Rhizome Center was founded in 2018 during President Donald Trump’s first term, with a mission to provide direct support to deportees and refugees sent to Mexico.

Since his return to office, the need has grown. Many deportees arrive with no resources or documentation to regularize their status in Mexico. Filling that void, the organization provides legal aid, crisis assistance, counseling and other services.

Run by executive director and founder Tran Dang, The Rhizome Center derived its name from plant rhizomes — the underground roots that provide essential nutrients — symbolizing humanity’s resilience and interconnectedness across borders.

For more information about The Rhizome Center for Migrants and details on how to support the cause, visit the group’s Instagram account. Donations are accepted via PayPal and Zelle.

Date: Saturday, Sept. 27, from 3 p.m. to 7 p.m.

Saturday, Sept. 27, from 3 p.m. to 7 p.m. Location: Casa Zuno, Avenida Unión 2226, Colonia Americana, Guadalajara.

Casa Zuno, Avenida Unión 2226, Colonia Americana, Guadalajara. Cost: General admission is 375 pesos. VIP tickets are 500 pesos per person and guarantee a seat.

The MUBI film fest lands in Guadalajara next weekend

View this post on Instagram A post shared by MUBI México (@mubimexico)

Global distributor, producer and streaming service MUBI recently added film festivals to its portfolio and announced a Guadalajara edition from Sept. 18-20. The festival will screen independent feature films and shorts, alongside filmmaker Q&As, workshops, installations and DJ sets.

Anticipated films on the schedule include:

“Her Private Hell” by Nicolas Winding Refn

“Pulp: What Do You Do for an Encore?” by Garth Jennings

“Hope: The First Impact” by Na Hong-jin

“Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma” by Jane Schoenbrun

“Rose” by Markus Schleinzer

For moviegoers seeking nostalgia, Ridley Scott’s 1991 feminist classic “Thelma & Louise,” starring Susan Sarandon, Geena Davis and Brad Pitt, is also on the schedule.

For full program details, visit Mubi Mexico’s website. In addition to Guadalajara, MUBI Fest 2026 made stops in Mexico City, São Paulo, Bogotá and Buenos Aires this year.

Dates: Sept. 18-20.

Sept. 18-20. Location: FICG Cineteca, Av. Perif. Pte. Manuel Gómez Morin 1695, Rinconada de la Azalea, Belenes Norte, Zapopan.

FICG Cineteca, Av. Perif. Pte. Manuel Gómez Morin 1695, Rinconada de la Azalea, Belenes Norte, Zapopan. Cost: Tickets available on the MUBI website.

MND writer Dawn Stoner is reporting from Guadalajara.

World.title: Mexico City-area airports to halt takeoffs and landings for 4 hours tomorrow
World.content:
Takeoffs and landings at the Mexico City International Airport (AICM) will be suspended for four hours on Wednesday, Sept. 16, to ensure that military aircraft can operate safely in the capital’s airspace while the annual Independence Day parade takes place below.

The Mexican Navy, which operates the AICM, announced the suspension in a statement.

El AICM suspenderá operaciones aéreas por desfile del 16 de septiembre. ➡️ https://t.co/T6iEPTFtOa @aeropuertos_GAM pic.twitter.com/wJK8Khf3YB — Aeropuerto Internacional Benito Juárez CDMX (@AICM_mx) September 14, 2026

“To ensure the safety of the military air maneuvers that will be carried out to commemorate the 216th anniversary of the start of Mexico’s independence, and as directed by the aviation authority, the Mexico City Benito Juárez International Airport (AICM) will suspend aircraft takeoffs and landings on September 16 from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m.,” the navy said.

“According to NOTAMs [Notices to Airmen] A8260/26 and B1724/26, … issued by the Federal Civil Aviation Agency (AFAC) and disseminated through the Mexican Airspace Navigation Services (SENEAM), the airport will be closed to all types of flights during the specified hours.”

The Felipe Ángeles International Airport (AIFA) in México state will also suspend takeoffs and landings between 10 a.m. and 2 p.m. Wednesday. Military aircraft that will conduct flyovers as part of the Independence Day festivities will take off from the Santa Lucía Air Force Base, which adjoins AIFA.

The navy advised air passengers who have a flight scheduled for Wednesday to ask their airlines about the status of their flights as “this event will result in some adjustments to scheduled times.”

The Independence Day parade is scheduled to begin at 10 a.m. Wednesday with a flyover of nearly 100 Air Force and National Guard airplanes and helicopters above the Zócalo, Mexico City’s central square — including F-5 fighters performing a fleur-de-lis maneuver.

The ground procession will start near the Zócalo, pass the Palacio de Bellas Artes (Palace of Fine Arts), continue along Juárez Avenue and Paseo de la Reforma, and end at the Campo Marte military complex near Chapultepec Park.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Following a higher soda tax, is a salty foods tax coming next?
World.content:
Lawmakers from Mexico’s ruling party Morena, the Workers’ Party (PT) and the Green Party (PVEM) have submitted a congressional proposal to apply a Special Tax on Production and Services (IEPS) to certain processed foods with excessive sodium content, such as cured meats, instant soups, sauces and dressings.

The initiative seeks to expand a tax strategy that has been applied since the 1980s to products considered harmful to health, such as sugary drinks, tobacco and high-calorie foods.

The bill’s proponents estimate that a tax on products with high sodium levels could generate approximately 12 billion pesos (US $116.6 million) in additional federal revenue, while helping reduce the prevalence of diseases associated with excessive salt consumption.

The focus would be on processed products exceeding technical criteria for sodium content, particularly front-of-package warning labels under NOM-051, which indicate “Excess Sodium.” This means that the potential measure would not penalize the domestic use of salt, nor would it, in principle, indiscriminately cover all salty foods.

The initiative follows growing concerns regarding average sodium intake in Mexico.

According to the NGO El Poder del Consumidor (The Power of the Consumer), the Mexican adult population consumes an average of 3.3 grams of sodium per day, far exceeding the World Health Organization (WHO) recommendation, which advises against exceeding 2 grams daily. Excess sodium consumption is related to cardiovascular diseases – the leading cause of death in Mexico – and hypertension.

Meeting the WHO’s target of a 30% reduction in sodium intake by 2030 could save an estimated 7 million lives globally and annually prevent approximately 5% of deaths in Mexico from cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease and stomach cancer.

Dr. Jorge Vargas, a researcher at El Poder del Consumidor, told the news outlet Infobae that “the fact that Mexico is finally considering a sodium tax is positive news,” but cautioned that the technical design would be a decisive factor in determining whether the tax alters consumption habits and drives companies to reduce the salt content of their products. He also urged lawmakers to review the results observed in other countries before voting on the initiative.

The proposal follows a recent IEPS increase targeting domestic sugar consumption, which, according to the government’s 2027 budget proposal, is forecast to bring in over 76.92 billion pesos ($4.5 billion) next year from soft drinks alone.

With reports from El Universal and El Financiero

World.title: AySA Privatization Narrows to Two Bidders Amid Lawsuit
World.content:
ARGENTINA · PRIVATISATION

Key Facts — What happened Argentina opened AySA’s technical bids on 15 September; only two consortiums qualified out of 17 offers.

— The bidders Rowing S.A. with Arcos, Transclor and PHX face Grupo Roggio’s Roggio ROAS S.A.U.

— What’s for sale The state’s 90% of AySA, which supplies water to about 14 million people.

— The investment ask The winner must commit close to US$2 billion in the first five years.

— The legal fight A La Plata appeals court has barred any change to AySA’s water-access duties for now.

— The catch Officials say that injunction blocks a future ownership change, not the bidding process itself.

AySA’s General San Martín treatment plant in Palermo, Buenos Aires. Two consortiums are now competing to take over the utility. (Photo, internet reproduction)

Argentina’s biggest privatization this year has cleared its first real hurdle. Seventeen offers came in for AySA, and only two survived technical review.

The government opened technical bids for AySA, the state water utility, on Tuesday. Two local consortiums qualified to move forward, while a court fight over the sale continues in the background.

What Is Being Sold

AySA supplies drinking water and sewage service to Buenos Aires and 26 surrounding municipalities. Roughly 14 million people across Greater Buenos Aires depend on it every day.

The government is selling 90% of the company’s shares to a single strategic operator. Employees keep the remaining 10% through Argentina’s existing shared-ownership scheme.

Officials have set no minimum reserve price for the sale itself. Instead, the winner is chosen through investment commitments and operating terms laid out in the tender.

Who Is Left Standing

Seventeen offers were submitted before Tuesday’s deadline, a striking number for an asset this large. Only two of the seventeen consortiums passed the technical evaluation stage.

One is led by Rowing S.A. alongside Arcos, Transclor and PHX. Transclor is headed by businessman Mauricio Filiberti, who has been named in earlier reporting on the sale.

The other is Roggio ROAS S.A.U., tied to the Córdoba-based construction group Grupo Roggio. Both groups now move to the next phase, where compliance is verified in detail.

What the Winner Must Promise

Economy Minister Luis Caputo has said the winning bidder must commit more than US$2 billion over the first five years. Reported figures for the full concession run even higher, into the tens of billions over three decades.

The government expects the sale itself to raise somewhere around US$500 million. That figure covers only the transfer of shares, not the investment pledges that come with them.

The Court Fight in the Background

A panel of the La Plata appeals court upheld an injunction just a week before Tuesday’s bid opening. It bars AySA from modifying, limiting or suspending its water-access obligations while a review continues.

The Buenos Aires provincial ombudsman’s office had requested the measure. Judges Pablo Muñoz, Gerónimo Arias and María Ventura Martínez signed the ruling.

Guido Lorenzino, the provincial ombudsman, argues the sale’s terms would leave a private buyer with no obligation to guarantee water access. He says environmental liabilities would instead fall on the province and its municipalities.

Government lawyers see it differently, arguing the injunction protects service obligations rather than blocking the tender. No violation occurs, they say, until ownership actually changes hands.

A Long Road Already Traveled

Argentina first launched this tender back in May, aiming for a strategic operator to take AySA’s controlling stake. A La Plata court briefly suspended the process in June, pending an audit of environmental liabilities.

The bid deadline itself moved twice, first to 27 August and then to 15 September, as the ministry sought wider participation. Tuesday’s opening was, in that sense, a deadline that finally held.

What Changes for Customers and Workers

AySA currently employs 5,890 people, down from 7,700 a few years earlier. The tender itself sets no requirement to keep that same headcount.

Existing labor agreements still apply, since AySA continues operating as the same legal entity. Any changes to staffing are expected to come through technology upgrades, not sudden layoffs.

Water rates will not be frozen, nor will they face one sweeping revision right away. Two separate mechanisms adjust costs and reward service quality until a full tariff review in 2032.

Water and sewage bills already make up just 2.2% of an average salary in Argentina. That is reportedly the lowest such share anywhere in Latin America.

The privatization contract sets steadily rising coverage targets all the way through 2056. Water coverage should reach 90% and sewage coverage 75%, up from about 75% and 64% today.

What Happens Next

Both consortiums now enter a compliance-verification phase before economic offers are opened. Only after that stage will the government know what either group is actually willing to pay.

The ombudsman’s court fight is still unresolved and could yet complicate a final transfer. For now, the tender itself keeps moving forward on schedule.

More: Argentina news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many offers did AySA’s tender receive?

Seventeen offers were submitted, though only two consortiums passed the technical evaluation stage.

Which two groups are still competing?

Rowing S.A. with Arcos, Transclor and PHX, and separately Grupo Roggio’s Roggio ROAS S.A.U.

How much must the winner invest?

Officials have cited more than US$2 billion in required investment over the concession’s first five years.

Does the court injunction stop the sale?

No, government lawyers say it protects service obligations only, and does not halt the bidding itself.

How much does Argentina expect to raise?

Roughly US$500 million from the share sale alone, separate from the investment commitments required.

Sources: Infobae, La Nación, iProfesional, Dolarhoy, Perfil.

World.title: Transener Buyers Recover Millions Paid in Privatization
World.content:
ARGENTINA · ENERGY

Key Facts — What happened Transener’s board approved a 253.536 billion peso dividend on 1 September (about US$165.7 million).

— Who benefits The consortium that bought into the company weeks earlier collects part of that payout.

— The numbers Edison Energía and Genneia together take roughly US$44.5 million; Pampa Energía takes about US$44.7 million.

— The purchase Edison Energía and Genneia paid US$356.17 million in April for the state’s 50% of Citelec, Transener’s controlling holding company.

— The strategy The state delayed this dividend for months, specifically to help raise its own sale price.

— The catch The cash paid out came from reserves Transener built up while still under state control.

A Transener transmission facility in Córdoba province. The company’s new private owners have already collected dividends from cash built up under state control. (Photo, internet reproduction)

Argentina sold its stake in Transener five months ago for US$356 million. Its new owners have already collected tens of millions of dollars back in dividends.

Transener’s board approved a dividend payout worth 253.536 billion pesos on 1 September. At the official exchange rate of 1,530 pesos per dollar on 15 September, that works out to roughly US$165.7 million.

How the Payout Works

Transener is Argentina’s largest electricity transmission company, carrying most of the country’s high-voltage power. It is controlled by Citelec, a holding company that owns 52.65% of Transener’s shares.

Citelec itself receives roughly US$89 million of the new dividend, in proportion to its stake. That money is then split again among Citelec’s own shareholders.

The remaining 47.35% of the payout goes to other Transener shareholders directly. That includes ANSES’s pension reserve fund, which owns 19% of the company, plus investors on the Buenos Aires exchange.

Who Gets What

Pampa Energía has long held half of Citelec and keeps that stake today. Its share of the new dividend comes to about US$44.7 million.

The other half of Citelec changed hands in April, when the state sold its portion to two buyers. Edison Energía and Genneia together collect roughly US$44.5 million from this same payout.

Edison Energía is controlled by brothers Juan and Patricio Neuss, alongside partners in the Inverlat investment group. Genneia is the renewable energy company chaired by Jorge Brito.

Why the State Waited

Transener had built up large cash reserves while still under state control, and could have distributed them earlier in 2026. Enarsa president Tristan Socas argued against that, according to officials involved.

His reasoning was straightforward. Bidders who knew about a coming dividend might lower what they offered for the state’s stake.

Holding the cash inside the company, instead, made that stake look more attractive to buyers. It also let the state capture more of that value through the sale price itself.

In April, while the state still held its shares, Transener’s shareholders set aside 522.590 billion pesos for future dividends. That reserve, worth roughly US$341.6 million at Tuesday’s exchange rate, went on to fund September’s payout.

The Backstory: A Contested Sale

Edison Energía and Genneia won the state’s 50% of Citelec in a competitive bid on 28 April. Their US$356.17 million offer beat Central Puerto’s US$301 million and Edenor’s US$230 million.

The sale closed formally in May, transferring day-to-day control of Transener to its new private shareholders. Barely three months later, the company approved the dividend now drawing scrutiny.

A Lawmaker Cries Foul

Buenos Aires provincial deputy Ricardo Lissalde, of the Fuerza Patria bloc, has filed a bill seeking to reject the privatization outright. He argues public reserves effectively helped finance the buyers’ own purchase.

Lissalde called the outcome “an inadmissible dispossession,” since private capital financed itself with reserves the state had built up. He says Transener is too strategic to hand over “under speculative logic.”

Industry figures counter that the buyers simply purchased a company with the cash still inside it. Under that view, distributing it afterward was an ordinary corporate decision, not a public giveaway.

Why Transener Matters

Transener carries about 85% of the electricity that moves through Argentina’s high-voltage grid. Nearly every province depends on its lines to keep power flowing.

That scale is precisely why Lissalde and other critics say the sale deserves closer scrutiny. A misjudged sale price on an asset this large, they argue, is a costly mistake to make quietly.

What It Means

Nothing about the dividend changes who controls Transener or how the network is run day to day. The dispute is entirely about money, and about who ultimately paid for what.

Lissalde’s bill faces long odds in a legislature that does not control federal privatization policy. Its more immediate effect is to keep the Transener sale in the news months after it closed.

More: Argentina news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

How big was Transener’s September dividend?

Transener’s board approved 253.536 billion pesos, worth roughly US$165.7 million at the September exchange rate.

Who bought the state’s stake in Transener?

Edison Energía, controlled by the Neuss brothers, and the renewable energy company Genneia bought it jointly.

How much did the buyers pay in April?

They paid US$356.17 million combined for the state’s 50% stake in Citelec, Transener’s parent company.

Why did the government delay the dividend?

Officials wanted bidders to value Transener’s accumulated cash as part of the sale, rather than discount it in advance.

Who is criticizing the deal?

Buenos Aires provincial deputy Ricardo Lissalde has filed a bill seeking to reject the privatization entirely.

World.title: Britain Defies Argentina With New Falklands Business Guide
World.content:
ARGENTINA · SOUTH ATLANTIC

Key Facts — What happened Britain published new guidance for firms doing business in the Falkland Islands on 15 September.

— The message It states Argentina has no jurisdiction there and cannot apply its own laws.

— The companies Rockhopper Exploration and Navitas Petroleum, partners in the Sea Lion oil project, are named directly.

— Argentina’s reply The Foreign Ministry issued a “most vigorous repudiation” and repeated its claim to the islands.

— The backdrop Milei’s government sanctioned companies operating near the islands earlier this month.

— The catch Neither statement moves a single barrel of oil or changes who runs the islands today.

Stanley Harbour, the Falkland Islands capital. Britain’s new guidance defends companies operating on the islands.

London has answered Javier Milei’s sanctions threat with an official guide, not a concession. It tells companies that Argentine law does not reach the Falklands, whatever Buenos Aires says.

Britain’s government published formal guidance for companies operating in the Falkland Islands on Tuesday. It arrives two weeks after President Milei threatened sanctions on firms drilling near the islands.

What Britain’s Guide Says

The document is called Doing Business with the Falkland Islands, published on the gov.uk website. The Foreign Office and the business ministry issued it jointly on Tuesday.

It states plainly that Argentina does not exercise sovereignty or jurisdiction over the islands. Argentine domestic law, it adds, simply does not apply anywhere on the islands.

London says it backs all legitimate economic activity on the islands, including oil exploration. It adds that islanders alone should decide how their resources are managed.

The guide also spells out how companies should respond if they receive notices from Argentine authorities. It tells them London will treat such notices as having no legal effect.

Two Weeks of Escalation

The dispute has moved quickly and publicly since the very start of September. Argentina opened sanctions proceedings, Britain hardened its public language, and both sides have since traded formal statements.

Tuesday’s guidance is the first written document either government has published on the dispute this month. It sets out London’s position in detail rather than through a minister’s spoken remark.

Why Now

The timing is not accidental, since Sea Lion has moved from years of delay toward real construction financing.

A field that never gets built would cost Argentina nothing at all. One that starts pumping oil creates a fact on the water, and revenue for the islands’ own government.

Rockhopper holds 35% of Sea Lion and Navitas holds the remaining 65%, according to company filings. Both companies have chased financing for the project for more than a decade.

The Companies Named

Two companies, Rockhopper Exploration and Navitas Petroleum, sit at the center of the dispute. Both hold stakes in the Sea Lion project, an oil field north of the islands.

Rockhopper Exploration is a British company, while Navitas Petroleum is based in Israel. The Sea Lion field itself sits roughly 215 kilometers north of the islands.

Argentina has already barred Rockhopper from operating in the country for twenty years. It had already declared Navitas clandestine back in 2022, years before the current dispute.

Argentina’s Response

Argentina’s Foreign Ministry rejected the British guidance within hours of its release. It called the islands an integral part of Argentine territory, occupied by Britain since 1833.

The ministry warned that companies there still face administrative, diplomatic and judicial consequences. It said Argentina remains willing to negotiate the islands’ status directly with Britain.

Officials also promised to expand their complaints against companies working near the islands. No new company names had actually been added as of Tuesday evening.

Argentine officials have not said whether they will pursue Rockhopper or Navitas further under the new law. For now, the exchange remains a war of official statements rather than of enforcement actions.

The Sanctions Behind It

Argentina’s government opened its current sanctions campaign in the first days of September. It targeted companies it says are operating illegally on the disputed continental shelf.

President Milei has vowed to use every diplomatic, economic and legal tool available. The escalation followed remarks from President Trump questioning Britain’s ability to defend the islands.

A Legal Standoff With No Referee

Both governments are, in effect, applying their own law to the same patch of ocean. Argentina says its own rules bind any company operating on that continental shelf.

Britain says those rules carry no legal weight whatsoever on its overseas territory. Neither side has a court that can bind the other, so both simply state their position.

Argentina also cites a 1976 United Nations resolution urging both sides to avoid unilateral moves. Britain counters that the islanders’ own right to self-determination overrides that call.

The dispute is, for now, being fought with paperwork rather than warships.

What Happens Next

Sea Lion remains years away from producing its first barrel of oil. Both governments are, for the moment, arguing over a resource that does not yet exist.

The practical test is whether Argentina’s sanctions actually deter the investors Britain is trying to reassure. Neither government has signaled much interest in negotiating that particular question directly.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Britain publish on 15 September?

Britain published guidance called Doing Business with the Falkland Islands, defending firms operating there.

Which companies are involved?

The guidance centers on Rockhopper Exploration and Navitas Petroleum, partners in the Sea Lion project.

How did Argentina respond?

Argentina’s Foreign Ministry rejected the guidance and repeated its claim that Britain occupies the islands illegitimately.

What triggered the latest dispute?

Argentina sanctioned companies operating near the islands in early September, prompting Britain’s response.

Has the dispute affected Sea Lion’s timeline?

No changes to the project’s schedule have been announced by either Rockhopper or Navitas.

CHILE · OBITUARY

Key Facts — Who Patricio Guzmán, Chilean documentary filmmaker, born in Santiago in 1941.

— Died September 15, 2026, in Paris, at age 85.

— Known for Chronicling Chile’s 1973 coup and its long aftermath on film.

— Defining work “The Battle of Chile,” “Nostalgia for the Light,” “The Pearl Button.”

— Recognition Cannes Golden Eye, Berlin Silver Bear, Chile’s National Arts Prize.

— The catch Detained after the coup, he finished his trilogy in exile abroad.

Patricio Guzmán, Chilean Filmmaker Who Chronicled Coup, Dies at 85

He filmed a government being overthrown, then spent the rest of his life explaining what that meant. Chilean cinema has lost its most persistent witness.

Patricio Guzmán, the Chilean filmmaker who chronicled the 1973 coup for decades, died in Paris on September 15, 2026, at 85. Chilean and international outlets, including Infobae and Chile’s Culture Ministry, confirmed his death the same day.

His cause of death was reported as cardiorespiratory arrest. He had lived in France since the 1980s, after earlier years of exile in Spain and Cuba.

Guzmán remained a Chilean citizen throughout his decades abroad, returning periodically to film but never to reside permanently. Colleagues described him as someone who carried Chile with him wherever he worked.

From Santiago to Film School

Guzmán was born in Santiago, Chile, in August 1941. He studied theater, history, and philosophy before turning his attention fully toward cinema.

He trained at Madrid’s Official Film School in the late 1960s, then returned home with technical grounding few Chilean directors had. That training would soon meet a country entering a period of extraordinary political upheaval.

His early documentary “El Primer Año” followed the first year of Salvador Allende’s socialist government, elected in 1970. It established the observational, patient style that would define his later career.

Filming a Revolution, Then a Coup

By 1973, Guzmán was filming what became “La Batalla de Chile,” a sweeping account of the political conflict consuming Allende’s government. His crew kept shooting through strikes, shortages, and mounting street violence.

General Augusto Pinochet’s military coup struck on September 11, 1973, toppling Allende and ending the project’s original plan. Guzmán was detained afterward at Santiago’s National Stadium, used as a mass detention site for suspected government sympathizers.

He was released and soon left Chile, carrying his footage into exile rather than abandoning it. Smuggling the reels out of the country became its own quiet act of resistance.

A Trilogy Finished in Exile

Guzmán completed “La Batalla de Chile” in three parts between 1975 and 1979, editing much of it while based in Cuba. The finished trilogy became one of the most widely distributed Latin American documentaries of its era.

It could not be shown openly inside Chile until years after Pinochet’s dictatorship ended in 1990. For many younger Chileans, it later became a primary visual record of a period their own textbooks barely covered.

Guzmán revisited that gap in “Chile, Obstinate Memory,” a 1997 film showing the trilogy to young Chileans for the first time. Their reactions became a study of a country still learning its own past.

Guzmán settled first in Spain and then, from the 1980s onward, in France. He never again lived permanently in the country his films kept returning to.

Memory as a Filmmaking Method

Guzmán’s later films built what critics call an unofficial memory trilogy, linking Chile’s landscape to its buried political history. His 2010 film “Nostalgia for the Light” connected astronomers scanning the Atacama Desert to women searching its sand for disappeared relatives.

“The Pearl Button,” from 2015, turned to Chile’s coastline to explore indigenous history and the dictatorship’s ocean disappearances. It won the Silver Bear for best screenplay at the Berlin Film Festival.

“The Cordillera of Dreams,” from 2019, turned to the Andes as a witness to national memory. It earned Guzmán the Golden Eye documentary prize at the Cannes Film Festival.

His final feature, “My Imaginary Country,” appeared in 2022 and examined Chile’s mass protest movement that began in 2019. It closed a filmography built almost entirely around the country he had been forced to leave.

Awards and Institutional Recognition

Guzmán founded Chile’s International Documentary Film Festival, known as Fidocs, in 1997, giving the genre a permanent home in Santiago. He also taught documentary workshops to younger directors across Europe and Latin America for several decades.

Chile awarded him its National Arts Prize in 2023, one of the country’s highest cultural honors. He had earlier collected European Film Award recognition in 2010 and multiple Goya nominations over his long career in Spanish-language cinema.

British film magazine Sight and Sound later placed “Nostalgia for the Light” among its selection of the greatest documentaries ever made. International critics frequently ranked him among the handful of directors who defined Latin American nonfiction cinema.

Tributes Following His Death

Chile’s Culture Minister, Francisco Undurraga, said Guzmán’s work had shaped generations and carried Chilean cinema onto the world stage. He added that the filmmaker’s influence would keep marking national culture for years to come.

Colleagues across Latin American cinema echoed that assessment, describing him as the region’s most persistent chronicler of memory and loss. Few filmmakers anywhere built an entire career from a single, unresolved national wound.

Guzmán spent nearly fifty years asking Chile to look directly at 1973 rather than away from it. His death leaves that body of work as the fullest cinematic record the country has of what it lost.

ARGENTINA · OBITUARY

Key Facts — Who Griselda Gambaro, Argentine playwright and novelist, born in Buenos Aires in 1928.

— Died September 15, 2026, in Buenos Aires, at age 98.

— Known for Founding voice of Argentina’s theater of the grotesque and cruelty.

— Defining work “El Campo,” “Información para Extranjeros,” and “La Malasangre.”

— Recognition Konex award, National Theatre Prize, and an honorary doctorate.

— The catch Her breakthrough novel was banned, pushing her into exile in Spain.

Griselda Gambaro, photographed by Sara Facio, whose plays turned Argentine stages into mirrors of state violence (Photo, internet reproduction).

She wrote about cruelty before Argentina had a name for what was coming. Decades later, the country called her a founder of its modern theater.

Griselda Gambaro, the playwright who reshaped twentieth-century Argentine theater, died in Buenos Aires on September 15, 2026, at the age of 98. Her death was confirmed by major Argentine outlets including La Nación, Infobae, and the playwrights’ guild Argentores.

No cause of death was made public in the announcements that followed. Tributes arrived quickly from across the Argentine cultural world, where she was seen as a founder of postwar dramatic tradition.

A Childhood in La Boca

Gambaro was born in July 1928 in the working-class La Boca neighborhood of Buenos Aires, to a family of Italian immigrants. She completed primary school locally and secondary studies in the nearby district of Barracas.

She chose not to pursue a university degree, preferring instead to read widely and begin writing on her own terms. That self-taught path shaped a voice that later resisted easy classification within Argentine letters.

Her first staged work reached audiences in 1965 at the Instituto Di Tella, then the country’s leading showcase for experimental art. Director Jorge Petraglia brought her early scripts to a stage already associated with the avant-garde.

Recognition followed almost immediately, and a municipal theater prize arrived in 1968, just three years into her career on stage. Critics of the period noted an unusually assured and unsettling new voice in Argentine drama.

A Theater Built on Cruelty

Gambaro belonged to a generation of writers who used absurdist and grotesque imagery to describe violence that was becoming disturbingly real. Critics later grouped this current under the label Argentina’s theater of cruelty, a lineage running through much of her work.

Her 1967 play “El Campo,” or “The Camp,” placed ordinary characters inside a setting that revealed itself as a concentration camp. It remains one of her most widely studied and translated works.

“Información para Extranjeros” pushed the idea further, staging scenes of torture and abuse across several rooms that audience members walked through together. The format turned spectators into uneasy witnesses rather than distant observers of the violence on display.

Her 1976 novel “Ganarse la Muerte” depicted institutional cruelty toward women in unsparing detail. Argentina’s military government formally banned the book the following year, at the height of state repression.

The ban came as the country’s Dirty War intensified under a dictatorship that abducted and disappeared thousands of its own citizens. Gambaro soon left with her family for Barcelona, joining a wave of Argentine artists forced into exile.

She spent several years living in Spain before returning to Argentina in the early 1980s, while the military government still held power. Friends later said she felt writing from outside the country had become unsustainable for her.

Teatro Abierto and a Return to the Stage

In 1981, Argentine theater workers organized Teatro Abierto, a defiant collective season of new plays staged as protest against dictatorship-era censorship. Gambaro contributed her play “Decir Sí” to that founding cycle of resistance.

The festival continued despite official harassment and an arson attack that destroyed its original venue partway through the run. It is remembered today as one of the clearest acts of cultural resistance in modern Argentine history.

Her later play “La Malasangre,” staged in 1982, used a tyrannical father figure to evoke dictatorship without ever naming it outright. The play remains among her most frequently performed works in Argentina and abroad.

After democracy returned in 1983, Gambaro kept writing steadily for both the stage and the page, rarely slowing her pace. Her novel “El Mar que Nos Trajo” appeared in 2001, decades into an already substantial body of work.

Awards and Later Recognition

Argentina’s National Theatre Prize arrived in 1994, formal recognition from a democratic state that had once censored her writing outright. The playwrights’ guild Argentores honored her work on four separate occasions between 1976 and 1997.

The Konex Foundation awarded her a special career prize in 2014, marking five decades of continuous work in Argentine theater. Three years earlier, the National Arts Institute had granted her an honorary doctorate for her contribution to national culture.

Her final play, “El Don,” premiered at the Teatro Nacional Cervantes in 2015, closing a five-decade body of stage work. Critics described it as a fitting, quietly powerful conclusion to her theatrical career.

Gambaro was married to sculptor Juan Carlos Distéfano, who died in July 2026 at age 92, just weeks earlier. The couple had two children together during a partnership that lasted several decades.

A Legacy Across Latin American Theater

Playwright Mauricio Kartun described her as a true illuminator of Argentine drama in comments following news of her death. Argentores, her longtime guild, issued a formal farewell the same day, calling her one of the country’s essential dramatic voices.

Gambaro’s plays are now standard reading in university theater programs across Latin America and Spain. Scholars regularly place her alongside earlier Argentine writers as one of the clearest voices to confront state violence directly on stage.

Her work never let audiences look away from cruelty dressed up as ordinary life. That refusal, sustained across six decades of writing, is the legacy Argentine theater now carries forward without her.

The Medellín Flower Fair 2027 — the 70th Feria de las Flores — will once again fill Colombia’s second city with flowers, parades and free concerts for eleven days around the turn of August. Official dates are yet to be announced, but the fair holds one of the most fixed slots in the country’s festival calendar. This guide covers the expected dates, the signature events, the lessons of 2026 and how to plan a visit.

Medellín Flower Fair 2027: expected dates and the 70th edition

The Feria de las Flores has run every year since 1957, when it was created to honour the region’s flower growers and the silleteros who carried their blooms down from the hills of Santa Elena. The 2027 fair will be the 70th edition.

Official dates are yet to be announced by the Alcaldía de Medellín. Following the established pattern — the 2026 fair ran from 31 July to 9 August — event calendars point to 30 July to 8 August 2027, closing with the parade on the final Sunday.

The fair is the biggest event of Medellín’s year, drawing visitors from across Colombia and abroad. Hotels in the popular districts sell out weeks ahead, so the fixed calendar window matters for anyone planning a trip.

The Desfile de Silleteros: the heart of the fair

Everything builds to the final Sunday, when the silleteros carry towering flower arrangements on their backs along a city route. The 2026 parade, the 69th edition, fielded around 530 silleteros on a 2.4-kilometre course over five afternoon hours; the 2027 parade will be the 70th.

The silletas — wooden frames evolved from the chairs once used to carry people and goods over the mountains — can weigh up to 70 kilos. They are built in the days before in Santa Elena, the flower-farming corregimiento above the city, which visitors can tour during fair week.

Watching from the route is free; grandstand seating is sold separately and tends to go early. The exact 2027 route and start time will be published by the city a few days beforehand, as happens every year.

Beyond the silleteros: parades, orchids and music

The fair runs several major parades, not one. The Desfile de Chivas y Flores brings the decorated party buses onto the streets, and the Desfile de Autos Clásicos y Antiguos draws some 300 vintage vehicles — a spectacle watched by crowds that organisers have counted near a million people.

The Jardín Botánico hosts Florecer, the fair’s calmer counterpoint, an exhibition of more than 500 native Colombian orchid species alongside flowers and crafts. Music fills the city through free tablado stages across the comunas, plus a headline stadium concert and the National Festival of the Trova.

Looking back: what the 2026 fair delivered

The 69th Feria ran from 31 July to 9 August 2026, opening at the Obelisco and closing with the Silleteros parade on the final Sunday. Our 2026 fair guide tracked the eleven days of events across all 16 comunas.

More than 200 events filled the programme, over half of them free, including 21 tablado stages and the headline concert at the Atanasio Girardot stadium. Our guide for foreign visitors covered the practical side, from road closures to where to base yourself.

The 2026 edition also showed the fair’s growing international pull: a dedicated security operation ran through the fortnight, and the city’s hotels hit their annual peak. Expect the 70th edition to be staged at the same scale or larger.

Planning a visit: where to stay and how to get around

Most foreign visitors and residents base themselves in El Poblado or Laureles, both on the Metro and within reach of the main venues. Book accommodation well ahead: fair fortnight is the year’s peak demand window, and prices rise accordingly.

On parade days, expect road closures and heavy foot traffic along the routes. The Metro is the most reliable way across the city when streets are shut, and the Metrocable line to Santa Elena offers the easiest route to the flower farms.

Treat the fair like any large public gathering: keep valuables close, agree meeting points in dense crowds, and confirm times against the official programme, which can shift. We will update our Colombia coverage once the Alcaldía confirms the 2027 dates.

Programme: More than 200 events expected, over half free — parades, orchid exhibition, tablado stages, stadium concert, trova festival. Where to stay: El Poblado or Laureles, on the Metro; book well ahead for the peak fortnight. Side trip: Santa Elena, where the silletas are built, reachable by Metrocable. Official dates are yet to be announced by the Alcaldía de Medellín. The Desfile de Silleteros closes the fair on the final Sunday.

Is the Feria de las Flores free? Mostly, yes. The 2026 fair offered more than 200 events, over half of them free and open to the public, including the tablado stages and street parades. Watching the Silleteros parade from the route is free; only grandstand seating and select premium events charge a fee.

What is the Desfile de Silleteros? It is the fair’s signature parade and closing event, in which flower-bearers from Santa Elena carry elaborate arrangements on wooden frames called silletas along a city route. The 2026 parade fielded around 530 silleteros; the 2027 edition will be the parade’s 70th.

Where should visitors stay during the fair? El Poblado and Laureles are the usual bases for foreign visitors, both served by the Metro and close to the main venues. The fair fortnight is Medellín’s peak demand window of the year, so booking well ahead is essential, and prices rise accordingly.

Is Medellín safe during the Flower Fair? The fair draws huge crowds and a heavy police presence, and the city runs a dedicated security operation through the fortnight. Normal big-crowd precautions apply: guard your phone and valuables, avoid empty streets late at night, and use the Metro to move around on parade days.

Key Facts —Event — The Tango BA Festival y Mundial returns to Buenos Aires in August 2027, billed as the world’s largest tango event. —Dates — Expected in the second half of August 2027; the city government has yet to announce official dates. —Championship — The Mundial de Tango returns for its 24th edition, in the Tango de Pista and Tango Escenario categories. —Cost — Admission is expected to remain free across almost all events, as in every recent edition. —Scale — The 2026 edition drew nearly 800 competing couples from more than 45 countries and around 2,000 artists. —Organiser — The Buenos Aires city government stages the festival every year, with programming on tangoba.org. —Booking — August is Argentina’s low season; flights and hotels are cheapest when booked months ahead.

The Buenos Aires tango festival 2027 will once again turn the Argentine capital into the world capital of the 2×4 for two weeks in August, with free concerts, milongas and the planet’s most important tango championship. Official dates are yet to be announced, but the festival’s late-August slot is one of the most fixed points in the city’s cultural calendar. This guide gathers what is confirmed, what the 2026 edition tells us to expect, and how to plan a trip around it.

Buenos Aires tango festival 2027: what is known so far

The Tango BA Festival y Mundial is an annual event run by the Buenos Aires city government, and it has taken place every August for more than two decades. The 2026 edition ran from 19 August to 2 September; the 2027 edition is expected in the same late-August window.

Official 2027 dates are yet to be announced. The city typically confirms the programme in the first half of the year via the festival’s official site and the Buenos Aires tourism board, with the full grid of venues and reservation slots following closer to August.

What is certain is the shape of the event: two weeks of free concerts, dance classes, exhibitions and milongas across the capital, closing with the finals of the Mundial de Tango, the world tango championship, around the turn of September.

Two events in one: festival and championship

The festival half brings orchestras, singers and staged shows to venues across the capital, from the Teatro Colón to neighbourhood cultural centres. The 2026 edition spread across more than 50 venues in 34 neighbourhoods, with around 2,000 participating artists.

August in Buenos Aires is, in effect, a month of tango. In 2026 the celebrations opened with the eighth Semana de las Milongas, a week of dances, classes and open activities across 59 milongas, before the main festival even began. A similar warm-up week is expected for 2027.

Admission follows the established pattern: free across almost the entire programme, with the most in-demand events — such as the championship finals — requiring a free online reservation, usually released up to 72 hours ahead.

The Mundial: tango’s world championship

Two titles are at stake. Tango de Pista judges social floor-craft exactly as it would be danced at a real milonga: close embrace, musicality and navigation of a crowded floor. Tango Escenario is the theatrical stage style, with lifts, acrobatics and choreography.

The 2026 championship, the 23rd edition, drew nearly 800 couples from more than 45 countries, with a prize of ARS 6 million per winning category. The 2027 Mundial will be the 24th edition of the contest.

The finals traditionally close the festival at a grand downtown theatre — in 2026 the Teatro Gran Rex on Avenida Corrientes, on 1 and 2 September. The 2027 venue is yet to be announced.

Looking back: how the 2026 edition unfolded

The 2026 festival opened on 19 August at La Usina del Arte, with singers Vicentico and Abel Pintos backed by the city’s tango orchestra. Our 2026 festival guide covered the full programme and how the free reservation system worked.

It closed with the two championship nights at the Teatro Gran Rex on 1 and 2 September. In Tango de Pista, 300 couples reached the quarterfinals and 150 the semifinals; in Escenario, 90 and 45 respectively, as our finals report recorded.

The event’s pull goes beyond dancers. Past finals have filled arenas and public spaces — in 2022 the closing rounds were staged outdoors by the Obelisco and drew more than 20,000 spectators, a sign of how the festival doubles as one of the city’s biggest tourism drivers of the winter.

Planning a trip for August 2027

August is the tail end of the Argentine winter — low season for tourism, which means cheaper flights and hotel rates than in the summer months. Booking three to six months ahead secures the best fares around the expected festival window.

Even outside the festival, the city’s milonga circuit runs year-round, so a tango trip never depends entirely on the official programme. Neighbourhoods such as San Telmo, Almagro and Palermo host social dances every night of the week, with classes for visiting beginners.

Winter in Buenos Aires is mild rather than harsh, with average August highs around 17°C, but evenings on the way to milongas call for a coat. We will update our Argentina coverage as soon as the city confirms the 2027 dates and championship schedule.

Where: Venues across Buenos Aires — the 2026 edition used more than 50 venues in 34 neighbourhoods. Championship: 24th Mundial de Tango, in Tango de Pista and Tango Escenario; finals expected around the turn of September. Entry: Free across almost all events; top events via free online reservation up to 72 hours ahead. 2026 scale: Nearly 800 couples from more than 45 countries; around 2,000 artists; ARS 6 million prize per category. Frequently Asked Questions

When is the Buenos Aires tango festival 2027? The Tango BA Festival y Mundial 2027 is expected in the second half of August 2027, in the same window as the 2026 edition, which ran from 19 August to 2 September. Official dates are yet to be announced by the Buenos Aires city government; they are typically confirmed in the first half of the year.

Is the Buenos Aires tango festival free? Yes. Admission to almost all events is free, including concerts, classes and milongas across the city. High-demand events, such as the championship finals, require a free online reservation, usually released up to 72 hours before each event.

What is the Mundial de Tango? The Mundial is the world tango dance championship held within the festival each year. Couples qualify through rounds in Argentina and cities worldwide, then compete in Buenos Aires in two categories, Tango de Pista and Tango Escenario. The 2027 edition will be the 24th.

What is the difference between Tango de Pista and Tango Escenario? Tango de Pista is judged as social dancing: close embrace, musicality and navigation on a crowded floor. Tango Escenario is the stage style, allowing lifts, acrobatics and theatrical choreography. Separate champions are crowned in each category.

When should I book travel for the 2027 festival? August is low season in Buenos Aires, so flights and hotels are cheaper than in summer. Booking three to six months before the expected late-August window secures the best availability, and final dates can be checked against the official programme once the city publishes it.

World.title: Retire in Belize at 40 — US$2,000 a Month, Duty-Free Import and a Work Ban With One Exception
World.content:
BELIZE · RETIREMENT

The Qualified Retired Persons Programme is the main legal route to retire in Belize. It grants a great deal, and it draws a line at earning inside the country.

The swing bridge in Belize City, Belize
