World.title: 'Silk Road spirit' meets supply chains at Korea-Central Asia summit
World.content:
South Korea and the five Central Asian republics held their first heads-of-state summit in Seoul on Wednesday, adopting a 30-year cooperation framework targeting critical minerals, energy, supply chains and emerging technologies against the backdrop of a shared Silk Road history.

 

The declaration established a leaders’ summit that brings together South Korea, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan every two years, and a new mechanism that brings together the six countries’ industry ministers.

“The ‘Silk Road spirit’ of Central Asia that connected people, technologies and cultures of the East and West as one is needed more than ever,” South Korean President Lee Jae-myung said.

The six countries share common goals: Seoul needs more diverse sources of critical materials and more resilient supply chains, while Central Asian governments want technology, investment and a larger role in manufacturing the products made from their resources.

On critical minerals, South Korea is looking to diversify supplies for industries including semiconductors, batteries and electric vehicles, while Central Asian countries want more processing and manufacturing to take place inside the region.

The Seoul Declaration, which builds on a dialogue launched at the vice-ministerial level in 2007 and later elevated to the ministerial level, calls for “mutually beneficial value chains” that combine Central Asian resources and local production with Korean technology and manufacturing expertise.

“Today, Central Asia is no longer merely a supplier of raw materials,” Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev said. “Our countries are actively integrating into global value chains while expanding opportunities for innovation and technological cooperation.”

The leaders of South Korea and the five Central Asian states pose for a group photo at the first Korea–Central Asia Summit in Seoul, 16 September 2026. Press office of Kazakhstan President

President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said Kazakhstan has all 10 minerals classified by South Korea as strategic, and called for cooperation extending into semiconductors, batteries, electric-vehicle components and robotics.

Mirziyoyev proposed a Regional Investment Alliance for Critical Minerals covering the full production cycle, and set a $20 billion (€17.3 billion) target for trade between South Korea and Central Asia by 2030.

Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov pushed the regional approach further, proposing a joint investment fund to finance priority projects and make it easier for Korean companies to enter Central Asian markets.

Transport chain reaching Europe

Transport was another key segment to the summit, with Tokayev proposing an “end-to-end transport and logistics chain extending from Korea, through Central Asia, to Europe”.

Central to that idea is the Middle Corridor, formally known as the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route. It moves freight through Central Asia, across the Caspian Sea to Azerbaijan and Georgia, and onwards towards European markets through Turkey or the Black Sea.

The corridor has attracted growing attention as companies and governments seek alternatives to routes through Russia. Tokayev said its freight volumes had increased fivefold over the past six years.

Mirziyoyev also described Central Asia as an emerging “hub of global connectivity”, while Japarov highlighted the China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan railway and invited Korean companies to participate in industrial and logistics facilities along the route.

Turkmenistan put transport, logistics, energy and industrial cooperation among its priorities for deeper ties with South Korea.

Tajik President Emomali Rahmon, meanwhile, focused on water security, climate change and sustainable development.

From political strategy to business

The regional agenda moved from the leaders’ table to the business community later in the day, when more than 500 government and company representatives gathered for the first Korea–Central Asia Business Summit.

Government and business leaders attend the first Korea–Central Asia Business Summit in Seoul, 16 September 2026. Centre for the Production of Content of Mass Media under the Administration of the President of the Republic of Uzbekistan

Lee Jae-myung described the priorities in practical terms: broader trade and investment, cooperation across the critical-minerals value chain and new infrastructure connecting the region with international markets.

Tokayev pointed to Central Asia’s combined GDP of nearly $550 billion and growth of more than 6%.

“Combining these advantages with Korea’s industrial, technological and financial capabilities opens up broad prospects for mutually beneficial cooperation,” he said.

Mirziyoyev similarly urged Korean companies to view Central Asia as a single market of more than 80 million people, with opportunities in AI, semiconductors and advanced manufacturing.

Tokayev, meanwhile, pointed to transport infrastructure and technology as areas where Korean investment could strengthen connections across the Eurasian continent.

Nineteen memorandums of understanding were signed during the regional business summit in sectors including critical minerals, industry, infrastructure and digital technologies. They set out areas for future cooperation but are not, in themselves, final investment contracts.

The regional meetings in Seoul ran alongside separate bilateral talks and business programmes between South Korea and individual Central Asian states.

Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan were among the countries announcing national agreements and investment projects during their leaders’ visits.

The new C5+Korea format will meet again at the leaders’ level in Kazakhstan in 2028.

World.title: Hackers impersonating government agency hit Revolut customers in the UK
World.content:
Hundreds of European customers of digital bank Revolut had their personal information handed over to hackers after they impersonated a government agency, the company said on Wednesday.

 

Revolut said it had identified a “sophisticated external impersonation scam” in which an unauthorised third party used an email address from a legitimate government agency domain to submit fraudulent requests for customer information.

According to the Financial Times, the attack was carried out by Italian hackers who used a compromised Italian government email account to pose as officials seeking customer information.

The hackers obtained data including customers’ addresses, verification photos, identity documents and information about bitcoin activity.

Related This AI is combating money laundering and keeping out Russian oligarchs

A source familiar with the matter said around 680 Revolut customers across several European countries were affected.

Revolut is a British company, but its European banking operations are legally based and licensed in Lithuania, with more than 50 million customers across Europe.

Revolut said its systems and customer funds were “unaffected” and that it had contacted those affected to inform them and provide support.

“Upon detection, we immediately blocked the address and alerted the relevant government agency as well as enforcement agencies, data protection and financial regulators,” Revolut said.

Britain’s data protection regulator, the Information Commissioner’s Office, confirmed that it had received a report about the incident and was assessing the information provided.

Europe's fintech unicorn

The incident comes as Revolut expands further into the global banking sector, more than a decade after it was founded in 2015 as a fintech start-up.

The company was valued at $115 billion (€98.7bn) in a secondary share sale in July.

It secured a long-awaited banking licence in its home market of the UK in March, lifting restrictions on its ability to compete with established retail banks, and bagged a full French banking licence in August.

This month, Revolut also secured conditional approval for a US banking licence, while on Tuesday it filed an application for a banking licence in Switzerland.

Revolut initially built its business around smartphone-based currency exchange and money transfers before expanding into a wider range of financial services.

It now has more than 80 million customers globally and is targeting 100 million customers across 100 countries.

World.title: Danish pharma giant Novo to use Anthropic’s Claude to advance AI drug discovery
World.content:
Novo, previously Novo Nordisk, the Danish pharmaceutical company behind Ozempic, has partnered with Anthropic to accelerate the development of new medicines using artificial intelligence.

 

“Joining forces with Anthropic will supercharge our R&D organisation and help us on our mission to bring new, transformative health solutions to people living with chronic diseases,“ said Mike Doustdar, president and CEO of Novo, in a press release Wednesday.

The pharmaceutical giant will use Anthropic’s models and Claude Science to advance scientific reasoning for Research and Development (R&D), the company announced.

Beyond increasing productivity in R&D, Novo’s CEO said AI tools can offer “completely new scientific opportunities” and help reasoning and understanding of human biology and drug mechanics.

"AI’s increasing capability brings with it the potential to compress a century’s worth of biological and medical breakthroughs into a decade," said Dario Amodei, co-founder and CEO of Anthropic.

He added that by giving leading researchers access to safe, capable, and trusted frontier models, it is possible to shorten research timelines, improve outcomes, and discover medicines and treatments that significantly improve human life.

This partnership comes amid Novo’s bet on AI to fast-track drug research. The pharma giant is already using OpenAI’s science GPT-Rosalind, after sealing the deal in April to use advanced AI to analyse complex datasets, identify potential drugs, and cut the time between research and patient access.

In 2024, the Novo Nordisk Foundation partnered with Nvidia and the Export and Investment Fund of Denmark (EIFO) to establish the Danish Centre for AI Innovation, which operates Gefion – Denmark's first AI-ready supercomputer.

Anthropic is also expanding its work in the life sciences sector. In May 2026, the tech company announced a collaboration with Bristol Myers Squibb to deploy Claude across the company's research, clinical development, manufacturing, commercial, and corporate functions.

World.title: Edgar Barrera leads 2026 Latin Grammys with 10 nominations
World.content:
The Latin Recording Academy released the full list of nominees for the 2026 Latin Grammy Awards on Wednesday, and one name appears more often than any other: Edgar Barrera.

 

The Mexican songwriter has picked up ten nominations, most of them linked to work he did for Karol G and Carín León, and he features in all three of the night’s general categories: Record, Album and Song of the Year. The ceremony, the 27th in the history of the awards, will take place on 12 November at the MGM Grand Garden Arena in Las Vegas.

Behind Barrera comes a tightly packed group with seven nominations each: Ca7riel & Paco Amoroso, Jorge Drexler, Karol G and Rosalía. Silvana Estrada and Mon Laferte have six apiece, and Argentine producers Rafa Arcaute and Federico Vindver each notch up five.

These are, to a large extent, the names that have shaped the Spanish-language music conversation over the past year: from LUX, by Rosalía, recorded with the London Symphony Orchestra and sung in thirteen different languages, to Rawayana’s album, which in June reached number one on Billboard’s ranking of the best Latin albums of the year.

Ten albums in the running for Album of the Year

The flagship category brings together ten very different releases: 'EQUILIBRIVM' by Anitta; 'Free Spirits' by Ca7riel & Paco Amoroso; 'Taracá' by Jorge Drexler; 'Vendrán suaves lluvias' by Silvana Estrada; 'Tropicoqueta' by Karol G; 'Femme Fatale' by Mon Laferte; 'Muda' by Carín León; 'La vida era más corta' by Milo J; '¿Dónde es el after?' by Rawayana; and 'LUX' by Rosalía.

In Record of the Year, the standouts are '¿Cómo se ama?' by Jorge Drexler; 'Dime' by Silvana Estrada; 'Coleccionando heridas' by Karol G together with Marco Antonio Solís; 'Femme Fatale' by Mon Laferte; 'Desde que te tengo' by Carín León; 'La Perla' by Rosalía with Yahritza y su Esencia; and 'Alma' by Elena Rose.

The Song of the Year shortlist, the award that honours songwriters, comprises ten tracks, among them 'Hasta Jesús tuvo un mal día' by Ca7riel & Paco Amoroso featuring Sting, and 'Mi gran amor' by Santana together with Becky G. Also included are 'Humano' by Juanes and Vivir Quintana, and 'Nilo' by Zanna, alongside the already mentioned songs by Drexler, Estrada, Laferte, Karol G and Rosalía.

The Best New Artist category arrives without any obvious favourites: a group of eleven artists are competing, Delilah, Fabian, Loulu Gilberto, Arath Herce, Macario Martínez, Maye, Sofía Monroy, Kendall Peña, Dora Sánchez, Aria Vega and Zeca Veloso, who have yet to break into the awards’ general categories.

World.title: Russia used Claude AI for espionage, disinformation and drone swarms
World.content:
Russia used Anthropic's Claude AI model to accelerate cyber-espionage operations against Ukrainian and European government targets, run disinformation campaigns in Africa and Moldova, and develop targeting software for autonomous kamikaze drone swarms, the US company said in a report published this month.

 

Anthropic said it had blocked all malicious activity identified in the report, used the findings to strengthen its security systems, and shared the information with government bodies and industry partners.

In one major case, a hacking group designated GTG-20006 used Claude to automate operations against more than 20 organisations, including government ministries, defence and intelligence agencies, embassies, think tanks and defence-industrial companies, Anthropic said.

Ukraine was the primary target, with suppliers of military drone technology and their supply chains also among those attacked. The group also targeted Middle Eastern and Asian government departments with links to maritime activity.

Anthropic said GTG-20006 is linked to Midnight Blizzard, a hacking group Western intelligence assessments attribute to Russia's foreign intelligence service SVR.

The group used Claude across a range of operational modes: as an engineering assistant for writing malware, phishing kits and surveillance tools, as an executor of commands on victims' networks, including collecting credentials and extracting data under human direction, and in fully autonomous operations with minimal human oversight.

Disinformation in the CAR and Moldova

Working alongside investigators from the All Eyes On Wagner project, Anthropic identified and removed an account operated by a Russian-speaking individual in Bangui who was running a disinformation operation for Radio Lengo Songo, a station set up and financed in 2017 by the Kremlin-run mercenary Wagner group.

The operator prepared daily pro-Russian content for the station in coordination with Russian state outlets RT, Sputnik Afrique and TASS, and with the local "Russian House" cultural centre — part of a network Russia uses as a political and influence hub abroad.

Content consistently promoted the CAR government and Wagner, and attacked France and domestic opposition figures, according to the All Eyes On Wagner investigation.

The operation was designed to appear locally run, with one person coordinating output while contracts, scripts and publications were presented as the work of a Bangui-based radio station.

Anthropic investigators identified the individual through invoices for a Claude subscription issued in central Madrid.

The operator was linked to Africa Politology, aka "The Company," the information and political technology arm of the African Corps — the successor to Wagner in Africa — which is reportedly controlled by the SVR.

In Moldova, a former regional head of the Russian state-run Sputnik media network used Claude as a content-production tool, adapting news, polling data, and opposition material to fit pro-Kremlin narratives, Anthropic said.

Autonomous swarm drone warfare

Anthropic identified and shut down a group of Russia-linked developers who used its Claude Code tool to write software for kamikaze drones, including an autonomous targeting system tested on real hardware.

The developers trained AI models on footage from combat operations in Ukraine and used a fixed location in the Donetsk region as a demonstration strike target.

The project's stated goal was a fully autonomous swarm of FPV kamikaze drones.

Anthropic linked nine accounts involved in the project to a regional Russian university and a federal research centre connected to the Russian Academy of Sciences, without naming either institution.

Claude is officially unavailable in Russia, with access to Anthropic's website and API blocked and Russian bank cards not accepted for payment. The developers bypassed these restrictions by routing traffic through commercial virtual private servers (VPNs).

World.title: Shock and anger in Kosovo as former president convicted
World.content:
The conviction in The Hague of former President Hashim Thaci and three former Kosovo Liberation Army leaders has caused consternation in Kosovo — both among political leaders and on the streets. DW reports from Pristina.

The announcement of the verdict was greeted with shock and profound disappointment in Pristina.

Thousands of citizens had gathered in the main square of Kosovo's capital, many waving flags of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA), to follow the announcement live on large screens. Similar gatherings took place across the country in Kosovo's main cities.

When it became clear that the Kosovo war crimes tribunal in The Hague had found former President Hashim Thaci, and former Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) leaders Kadri Veseli, Jakup Krasniqi and Rexhep Selimi guilty of war crimes, the crowd fell silent.

The initial silence was then followed by calls for justice and chants of support for the four men.

Groups of citizens began trying to demolish sections of the perimeter wall surrounding EULEX, the EU Rule of Law Mission in Kosovo, which was deployed in Kosovo after the country's declaration of independence from neighboring Serbia in 2008 and continues to operate to this day.

Thousands of people gathered in Pristina to watch a livestream of the verdict in the war crimes trial at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague Image: Valdrin Xhemaj/REUTERS

Large numbers of Kosovo police officers and special units intervened to prevent further damage and incidents.

Political leaders in Kosovo respond

But it wasn't just the people on the streets who were disappointed; the country's political leaders were quick to respond to the news from The Hague.

Kosovo Foreign Minister Glauk Konjufca, who was present in the courtroom in The Hague when the verdict was announced, said that "the conviction of the former KLA leaders is a terrible judgment for Kosovo, for our liberation war," describing it as "a major blow to the state and to the domestic narrative."

"Kosovo experienced the war itself. We know what the KLA war was about and we know that there was no criminal mechanism to harm any population. It is a sad, unjust and undeserved decision," he said.

Kosovo Prime Minister Albin Kurti labelled the verdict an "unacceptable injustice."

"The conviction and such a severe sentence for four former leaders of the Kosovo Liberation Army is an unacceptable injustice, a great and harmful punishment," he said on Wednesday.

This man is wearing a T-Shirt with the images of four men and a bandana with the logo of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA/UCK) Image: Florion Goga/REUTERS

The Democratic Party of Kosovo (PDK), a party founded immediately after the war by Hashim Thaci and several other former KLA leaders, described the guilty verdict as an "unjust and unacceptable judgment," stressing that "the battle for justice continues until the very end."

"In The Hague, the right of our people, who fought for freedom, survival and liberation from the Serbian state regime that killed, expelled and terrorized Kosovo Albanians, was dealt a severe blow. For us, this judgment represents a major injustice because it is based on allegations and material that we consider fabricated and which, over the years, have been promoted by the Serbian state apparatus and propaganda in an effort to criminalize the just war of the Kosovo Liberation Army," the PDK said in a statement.

The response from Kosovo's acting president, Albulena Haxhiu, was similar. She described the convictions of the four men as "a severe blow to their families, deeply shocking news for the Republic of Kosovo and a grave moment for the Albanian nation wherever it lives."

"On a day like this, the weight of this decision cannot be separated from the history from which we have emerged," Haxhiu wrote in her statement. "Kosovo experienced first-hand the violence of a state apparatus that killed civilians, committed massacres, expelled hundreds of thousands of Albanians from their homes and left behind thousands of people killed or missing. This experience is an indelible part of the memory of Kosovo and the Albanian nation."

Charges of crimes against humanity dismissed

More than three years after the start of the trial and nearly six years after the four men were charged with war crimes and crimes against humanity committed during the 1998–99 Kosovo War, the panel of judges at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague handed down guilty verdicts against former KLA leaders Hashim Thaci, Kadri Veseli, Jakup Krasniqi and Rexhep Selimi.

Supporters of Hashim Thaci listen to the announcement of the verdict against the former president and three other former KLA leaders Image: Valdrin Xhemaj/REUTERS

While the three-judge panel dismissed the charges of crimes against humanity, the four men were convicted of war crimes against civilians and political opponents who did not support the KLA during the war.

Hashim Thaci, who was indicted while serving as president of Kosovo, was sentenced to 25 years in prison. Jakup Krasniqi, who served as a KLA spokesman and later as speaker of Kosovo's parliament on several occasions, was also sentenced to 25 years in prison. Kadri Veseli, who headed the KLA intelligence service during the war, was sentenced to 18 years in prison, and Rexhep Selimi, who served as chief inspector of the KLA military police, was sentenced to 13 years in prison.

Defense lawyers for the men said they would appeal the verdict.

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers, which was set up by the Kosovo Assembly (parliament) in 2015, is staffed by international judges and based in The Hague. It deals exclusively with cases relating to allegations of crimes committed by members of the KLA during the Kosovo War.

Before returning to join Kosovo's struggle for independence in 1998, Hashim Thaci had been a student in Switzerland.

As a political leader of the former KLA, he received support from Western leaders, who invited him to participate in the 1999 peace talks in Rambouillet, France. At the time, Thaci was seen in Kosovo as a leader who could guide the country toward independence.

Around 13,000 civilians — most of them Kosovo Albanians — were killed and around one million people were displaced during the war, which saw Kosovo, at the time a Serbian province, fighting for independence from Serbia.

Protesters also gathered outside the building that houses the Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague after the verdict was announced Image: Omar Havana/REUTERS

Following NATO's intervention against Serbian forces and their withdrawal from Kosovo, Thaci founded his own political party and came to power, first as Kosovo's prime minister and later as president.

In 2008, Kosovo declared independence from Serbia, a move rejected and still not recognized by authorities in Belgrade, Moscow and Beijing. Kosovo's statehood is, however, recognized by over 100 countries.

Relations between Kosovo and Serbia remain tense, despite more than 15 years of negotiations between the two countries, mediated by the European Union and supported by the United States.

Thaci, who like the other three men, denied the charges against him, resigned as president of Kosovo in 2020 to face the charges and defend himself in The Hague.

Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan

World.title: British-American writer Bonnie Greer dies aged 77
World.content:
Chicago-born playwright Bonnie Greer, who became a familiar face in British political discourse later in life, has died. Her husband David Hutchins announced news of Greer's death.

Playwright and author Bonnie Greer died aged 77, her husband David Hutchins said on Wednesday in a statement to British media.

A celebrated writer born in Chicago who at first plied her trade in New York, Greer spent most of her adult life in the UK.

She took up dual citizenship and became a regular and prominent political commentator in Britain.

Greer attended the Frankfurt book fair in 2019 at the height of the post-Brexit debate for a panel on the topic Image: DW/E. Grenier

What did Greer's husband say about her death?

Greer's widower Hutchins hailed her as "an acclaimed playwright, author, critic, cultural and political commentator whose intelligence, courage and distinctive voice made an enduring contribution to British cultural and public life."

Hutchins said his late wife had suffered succumbed to a brief illness.

He said those closest to Greer would remember her warmth, humor, generosity and extraordinary ability to bring people together.

"To me, she was my partner, confidante and inspiration, and I feel profoundly privileged to have shared my life with her," Hutchins said. The pair married in 1993, seven years after Greer emigrated.

Greed became a prominent political commentator and activist in the UK [FILE: October 2017] Image: Jonathan Nicholson/ZUMA/IMAGO

Who was Bonnie Greer?

Greer was born in Chicago in 1948, the eldest of seven children from a family of Mississippi sharecroppers.

Her familial exposure to the UK predated even her birth — her father Ben was stationed in Britain during World War II and had taken part in the D-Day landings.

She gravitated towards creative writing amid the civil rights movement in the US after a college professor told her he did not believe women should pursue a legal career.

Having studied theater in Chicago she moved to New York as a young aspiring writer.

Greer settled in the UK in 1986 and worked mainly in theater with women and ethnic minorities.

She acquired British citizenship in 1997 and wrote a series of successful radio plays aired on the BBC and musicals. Her 1993 play "Munda Negra" exploring mental health problems among black women won the Verity Bargate Award for best play.

Greer also became a frequent contributor to political and social debate in Britain, frequently appearing on topical shows like "Newsnight" and "Question Time".

Greer was a prominent supporter of Barack Obama and wrote a memoir and personal musical history in 2009 called "Obama Music." She also campaigned against the UK's exit from the EU, Brexit, and Donald Trump's first term as US president at around the same time.

She held a series of cultural roles, including being president of the Bronte Society, chancellor of Kingston upon Thames University in London, a fellow of the Royal Society of Literature, and a board member of the Royal Opera House and the London Film School.

World.title: Gaza: At least 20 dead, including children, in building collapse
World.content:
The search for survivors has been hampered by Israeli restrictions on heavy machinery in the Gaza Strip. Authorities say 2,000 damaged buildings in the territory are occupied by families who have nowhere else to go.

At least 21 people, including six children, were killed in the Gaza Strip in the early hours of Wednesday morning when a war-damaged building collapsed, injuring at least 14 more people and trapping dozens of others beneath the rubble.

On Wednesday, rescue workers were still searching through the wreckage — in many cases with their bare hands given the lack of heavy machinery in the devastated Palestinian enclave.

"We are still hearing voices from under the rubble," said Raed Al-Dahshan, the director of Gaza City's civil defense service, adding that at least 10 families had lived in the collapsed building and expressing hope that more survivors could yet be found.

"My friend and neighbors live in this building," resident Mohannad Al-Mashharawi told the AFP news agency. "I came to help my friend retrieve some clothes and mattresses. He currently has no shelter or home."

The death toll is expected to rise as the search for victims buried in the rubble continues.

Gaza: Hundreds of buildings at risk of collapse

"The situation, you see, is tragic because we don't have the equipment and machinery that is needed," said Alessandro Mrakic, head of the United Nations (UN) Development Program's Gaza office. "So there are actually people ​are digging with their bare hands."

With wetter autumn and winter weather approaching, Mrakic warned that rain water could destabilize hundreds of other bombed-out buildings in the war-torn territory.

"There are approximately 400 buildings at risk of collapse," he said. "And we know that these buildings will collapse, especially now with the upcoming winter."

According to authorities, about 2,000 damaged buildings in Gaza are still inhabited by Palestinian families, many of whom have told the Reuters news agency that it is the only way to shelter from the wind and rain in the absence of sufficient tents.

"Today's tragedy underscores the grave risks faced by families living in these structures and the urgent need for safer alternatives," said Ramiz Alakbarov, UN Humanitarian ⁠Coordinator for ​the Occupied Palestinian Territory.

"No one should have to risk their life simply to find a safe place to shelter."

Israeli restrictions on heavy machinery

Palestinian and UN officials have blamed Israel's restrictions on Gaza for the lack of heavy machinery available in the enclave.

Israel says it wants to keep such machines out of the hands of Hamas militants, who used such equipment in their deadly raid into Israel in October 2023, prompting Israel's devastating assault on Gaza which has since killed over 73,000 Palestinians — the vast majority of them civilians.

More than 1,300 Palestinians, also mostly civilians, have been killed in Gaza since a US-backed ceasefire in October 2025, while the Israeli military says four of its soldiers soldiers have been killed.

World.title: Forgotten US court of 'secrecy' could mean more deportations
World.content:
The use of a secretive and long dormant court in the deportation of a woman from the US could have significant consequences. The Alien Terrorist Removal Court was just used for the first time in its 30-year history.

An estimated 4.5 million people have been deported from the US since 1996 . But until this month, not one of those cases had involved the Alien Terrorist Removal Court (ATRC).

Nazira Haji Zada, 47, from Afghanistan, lived in Texas and had legal US permanent residency. According to a statment released by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) on Wednesday, she has now returned to Afghanistan after she "conceded she is an alien terrorist and waived appeal of the removal order, terminating her previous status."

"This landmark case, resulting in the prompt removal of this alien terrorist to her country of origin, is a win for national security and the rule of law," said US Attorney General Todd Blanche.

US Senate confirms Trump lawyer Blanche as attorney general To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

However, Zada's public defenders Matthew Farley and Mary Manning Petras earlier said that the case "should not be seen as an endorsement of this court’s legitimacy."

The court, founded as part of a raft of anti-terror measures after the 1995 Oklahoma City bombing, was set up to deal with non-US citizens facing terrorism-related charges on which the evidence is confidential or somehow related to national security.

ATRC never needed before

Hiroshi Motomura, a law professor at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), told DW that it appears the Donald Trump administration is using the ATRC as the latest tool in its deportation toolkit.

"This is a very elaborate procedure. There are so many other ways that you can essentially get someone out of the United States by using the word terrorism in the context of removal proceedings," he said.

"From a very practical perspective, the government's non-use reflects its view over the last 30 years that 'we don't need this court because we can essentially deport people without it.'"

Zada was accused by prosecutors of being the "matriarch" of a family in which two men — son, Abdullah Haji Zada, and son-in-law, Nasir Ahmad Tawhed — had been found guilty of plotting to carry out a mass shooting on election day in 2024. Earlier this year, Blanche described the family as "ISIS-sympathizing."

For Motomura, who has written a number of books and teaches on immigration and citizenship, one of the key distinctions between the ATRC and regular means of deportation is that those on trial do not have a chance to view the evidence against them. Their lawyers may be able to in some cases.

Secrecy inherent in operation of ATRC

"I'm speculating, although I think not unreasonably, that this is someone against whom they cannot invoke terrorism or other grounds without the kind of disclosure in court that they would not want to have," Motomura said.

DHS said in the statement released on Wednesday that they provided Zada and her lawyers with "half a terabyte of documents," though it did not disclose what these showed.

"So they would rather go through a more elaborate procedure and disclose it in chambers to a judge as opposed to having it be potentially more public," Motomura said. "Because the procedure that this court provides is a procedure that calls for some disclosure, but also calls for some secrecy."

The ATRC consists of five federal trial court judges selected by the chief justice of the US Supreme Court, John Roberts, who was appointed by George W. Bush in 2005.

The government must first apply to the court demonstrating it has probable cause to suggest a person is an "alien terrorist" under the immigration law definition. It must also lay out why proceeding through standard deportation procedures would be a national security risk. In Zada's case this happened in July.

Then comes the hearing, in which the government need only prove their case "by the preponderance of the evidence", a lower bar than usually applied to such cases. Zada's decision to leave the country without the hearing means that the feasibility of the government using the court in future remains somewhat in the balance due to a constitutional point that was not tested.

Due process constitutional question yet to be resolved

"Dragging lawful permanent residents into court but refusing to show them or their attorneys the evidence that will be used against them is a plain violation of due process. We are confident that the Alien Terrorist Removal Court will be struck down as unconstitutional as soon as a judge is asked to address the issue," said Zada's lawyers in a statement to the Washington Post.

US Attorney General Todd Blanche hailed the deportation as a "win for national security" Image: Rod Lamkey/AP Photo/picture alliance

An amendment to the US constitution states that no state can "deprive any person of life, liberty, or property, without due process of law." Whether this applies in cases such as Zada's is not yet clear, something Motomura said may frustrate the Trump administration.

"I bet they were disappointed. I don't know this, but it would not surprise me if they're disappointed that the case never got litigated in court on the constitutional issue because it would allow them a different opportunity to limit the rights of people in the United States under the US Constitution," he said.

Given the Trump administration's stated "zero tolerance" policy on immigration — which has also included deporting people to so-called ‘third countries' they have no connection with and the widespread deployment of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents — it seems likely it won't be 30 years before another case is brought before the ATRC. And that could have significant implications for justice.

"I think it's very hard to view this situation accurately without seeing it as part of a broader effort by the administration to limit access to courts and to legal counsel and access to evidence on multiple fronts," concluded Motomura.

Edited by: Carla Bleiker

World.title: After Neuer: Who will be Germany's new No. 1 goalkeeper?
World.content:
Following Manuel Neuer's retirement, there are many candidates to succeed him, but which goalkeeper will Jürgen Klopp choose? What factors will play a role? And will Neuer's future have an indirect influence?

Manuel Neuer retired from international duty after Germany's early exit from the 2026 World Cup, opening the door for a new No. 1.

Jonas Urbig appears the obvious choice, but Neuer is still the starter at Bayern Munich, which severely limits Urbig's playing time. If the 23-year-old was Bayern's first choice, he would likely be Germany's number one too. As it stands, though, it appears doubtful that Germany's new coach Jürgen Klopp will even call him up to his first squad. On September 17, he will announce his squad for four UEFA Nations League games against the Netherlands, Greece, and Serbia. And no position in the current Germany team is more up for grabs than goalkeeper.

Oliver Baumann: The automatic Neuer replacement?

Oliver Baumann represents exactly the kind of selfless No. 2 who could be the next No. 1. The Hoffenheim goalkeeper even commendably dealt with the humiliation of being replaced by Neuer just before the World Cup.

Baumann appears unlikely to be Germany's new No. 1 under Klopp Image: Michael Memmler/Eibner-Pressefoto/picture alliance

Klopp isn’t just tasked with celebrating short-term success with Germany, however. His remit is to bring about lasting change making Germany favorites for a World Cup and a Euros once again. Oliver Baumann turned 36 this summer. The Bundesliga veteran will be 38 at the next Euros, 40 by the 2030 World Cup. His age might count against a sustainable rebirth of the Germany team.

The Hoffenheim goalkeeper, who has 13 caps, spoke to Bild in the days leading up to the squad announcement about his exchange with Klopp: "Yes, I was in contact with him. He'll say everything else on Thursday. We'll see about the rest—that’s for him to handle."

Ter Stegen: Back in Germany colors via Ajax?

Since Klopp prefers a highly attacking style of play in which all players press high up the field, he might opt for a goalkeeper who can also take on the duties of a field player. Marc-André ter Stegen would fit this profile better than Baumann. Ter Stegen is also two years younger than his competitor, though his career has been hampered by injuries.

Perhaps ter Stegen will find his way back to the Germany team via Ajax Image: Van der Velden/Fotostand/picture alliance

After several serious injuries and a legal dispute with Barcelona, ter Stegen has gone on loan to Ajax, improving his chances of returning between the posts for Germany.

"As far as ter Stegen is concerned, I assume he’ll definitely be in the mix," Lothar Matthäus recently wrote for Sky. "If he continues to perform well in Amsterdam, he's a candidate for the number one spot."

Alexander Nübel: Out of the spotlight in Turkey

Alexander Nübel was Germany's third-string goalkeeper at the World Cup. He had been consistent at Stuttgart but moved to Besiktas this summer, where he has made a strong start. However, former national team goalkeeper Toni Schumacher sees the move as a disadvantage for the 29-year-old.

"His move to Turkey has taken him out of the spotlight," Schumacher, who also played for Fenerbahce for three years during his playing days, told Bild. "It simply has a positive effect when you play in your own country week after week and thrill the fans with your saves."

Loris Karius: History with Klopp at Liverpool

A goalkeeper who has never been called up to the Germany team but shares a history with Klopp is Loris Karius.

Once considered one of Germany's most promising goalkeepers, Karius appears to now, aged 33, have a real chance of being in the Germany setup Image: Norbert Schmidt/picture alliance

Karius, who has been at Schalke since January 2025, was at times Klopp’s No. 1 at Liverpool. However, he made two critical mistakes in the 2018 Champions League final against Real Madrid and was subsequently dropped.

Back in the Bundesliga aged 33, Karius is delivering consistent performances and may have played his way back into the spotlight.

"When people associate me with that, it's a testament to the performance I’m putting in. That's great," Karius said recently in an interview with Sky.

Keepers who could play for Germany or elsewhere

If none of the obvious candidates gets selected, there are a number of other good goalkeepers who might be considered. First among them is Noah Atubolu. The 24-year-old Eintracht Frankfurt keeper, who has Nigerian heritage, was the number one for Germany's U21s from 2022 to 2025, and was called up to the senior squad once last October.

Dahmen (left) and Atubolu (right) are both young keepers with potential Image: Sebastian Räppold/Matthias Koch/picture alliance

Freiburg's Mio Backhaus is another promising talent. The 22-year-old’s mother is from Japan, meaning Backhaus is also eligible to play for Japan. He even played for the Japanese U15 team, but has since progressed through Germany's youth teams up to the U21 level.

In addition to Atubolu and Backhaus, there are also Augsburg's Finn Dahmen (28), Stuttgart's Dennis Seimen (20) and Diant Ramaj (24), who left recently relegated Heidenheim to join Copenhagen.

If Klopp wants to rely on one of the five, it might be worth playing them sooner rather than later in a competitive game. After all, just like Atubolu and Backhaus, the other three are also eligible to play for another country due to their heritage. Dahmen could also play for England, Seimen for Romania, and Ramaj for Kosovo.

Köpke: 'Develop a young goalkeeper as the No. 1'

"I think they need to develop a young goalkeeper as the No. 1 right now," Andreas Köpke, the goalkeeper on Germany's 1996 European championship team, told Bild.

Germany's former goalkeeping coach pointed to Bayern's backup goalkeeper, Urbig, alongside Backhaus and Atubolu — though only as and when Urbig plays regularly at club level.

And, given his standing at Bayern, that's bound to come down to how long Manuel Neuer chooses to continue to play.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: How the Houthis are also putting Egypt under pressure
World.content:
The Houthis, a Yemeni rebel group, are expanding their control of maritime corridors in the Red Sea area. Their target is their avowed enemy Saudi Arabia. But the military moves also endanger Egypt.

Any and all ships may pass, at least at first. That was how the spokesperson for Yemen's Houthis rebel militia put it. Transit through the Red Sea would be safe, with one exception: According to the Houthi spokesperson, ships from Saudi Arabia would not be allowed to pass this stretch of the sea.

The comments came during a time when the Houthi militia has been fighting to increase its presence at the southern entrance to the ocean passage. The Houthis now control the tiny volcanic island of Mayun, also known as Perim, at the entrance to the Red Sea, as well as other parts of the Yemeni coast and some small islands.

With these moves, pressure is growing on Saudi Arabia, the country that opposes the Houthis and previously fought a war (unsuccessfully) with them.

Red Sea strains rattle energy markets To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

But pressure is now also increasing in Egypt. Every decrease in shipping traffic through the Red Sea also impacts one of that country's most important sources of national income, the Suez Canal.

As yet, maritime traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait has not been significantly reduced. According to news agency Reuters, last Saturday 24 ships passed through it and on Sunday, 27 did so. That is around the same as the 10-day average. The Houthis appear to want to signal that their plan is not stop traffic altogether. The Bab el-Mandeb Strait is a chokepoint between Yemen and and the Horn of Africa. Ships have to pass it to enter the Red Sea.

Boats that are not Saudi Arabian can still pass the Bab al-Mandeb Strait (file photo from April 2026) Image: REUTERS

In general though, maritime traffic has decreased here, according to maritime intelligence organization Kpler. On Monday, 21 ships went through the strait. But in the middle of July, the average number of ships passing through was 47.

How will things develop from here?

"The Houthis could actually interrupt, or at least significantly disturb, the connection between Asia and Europe," says Stephan Roll, a senior fellow with the Africa and Middle East division at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, or SWP, in Berlin. "So first we have to wait and see how big the actual disruption to the Suez Canal will be."

Even complete control of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait doesn't automatically mean control of the Suez Canal. But it does give the Houthis a further opportunity to indirectly threaten traffic.

For Egypt, this new disruption comes at a particularly unwelcome time. Houthi attacks at the end of 2023 had already disrupted business at the Suez Canal. According to the International Monetary Fund , earnings at the canal in 2024 fell by around $6 billion (€5.2 billion). Before the current security crisis, Egypt had been making between $9 billion and $10 billion from the Suez Canal annually.

More recently things had actually been improving again.

"The situation is certainly problematic compared to 2023," Roll told DW. "But it is not so clearly negative compared to the situation one, two or even three months ago."

Important source of income: opening of the Suez Canal in 1869 Image: akg-images/picture alliance

Thanks to rising oil prices and the resulting higher cost of circumnavigating Africa, shipping companies had been using the Red Sea as they travelled between Asia and Europe.

The Suez Canal's finances had recently improved. The Suez Canal Authority, which manages the passage, reported that during the 2025-2026 fiscal year, revenues had risen by 23% to $4.67 billion (€4.5 billion). Despite the various conflicts in the region, this actually represented a recovery for the Suez Canal.

Houthi offensive could change all that

There is also a second critical factor. After recent drone attacks that the Saudis blamed on Iraqi groups, Saudi Arabia's east-west pipeline to the coastal city of Yanbu will be out of service for at least several weeks. Between 4 million and 5 million barrels of oil were going through the 1,200 kilometer pipeline per day as the Saudis attempted to circumnavigate the Strait of Hormuz, blocked due to the US-Iran war. This latest damage could put as much as 4% of global supply at risk, according to Reuters.

An analysis by Qatar-based think tank, the Middle East Council on Global Affairs, warns of a scenario where the Persian Gulf and Red Sea are both likely to become more precarious. The East Asia Institute, a think tank based in Korea, has also written about the dangers of dual choke points.

Neither route can be seen as an independent alternative because flows of oil and trade depend on secure connections at several points.

Certainly for Egypt, this will increase economic pressure.

What can Egypt do about this?

In geopolitical terms, there is not a lot that Egypt can do. The Houthis in Yemen have only impacted the country indirectly.

"Egypt's military capabilities are very limited," Steffen Krüger, head of the Konrad Adenauer Foundation's Cairo office, explained.

Egyptian interventions in Yemen in the 1960s are still remembered in Cairo — back then, the country sent thousands of troops to support a new government in Yemen, in a war that would eventually last years — so Egypt would prefer to exercise restraint there.

"Although Egypt formally remains a member of the Saudi-led coalition against the Houthis, its participation is largely symbolic," Krüger told DW.

And there is no doubt that Egyptian officials have noted the lack of success other countries like Saudi Arabia and the US have had in their attempts to rein in the Houthis.

"The Egyptians simply have no real alternative," argues the SWP's Roll, adding that Egypt is likely to try diplomacy first. "Basically they have to try to put a positive spin on a bad situation and somehow negotiate appropriate arrangements with the Houthis."

That may already be happening. According to London-based media outlet The New Arab on September 14, the Houthis offered to talk directy to Cairo about shipping security via the International Chamber of Shipping in London. The same publication said Egypt had rejected the offer for fear of it being seen as recognizing Houthi authority.

The Strait of Hormuz has also been dangerous: This week the Panama-flagged El Gaia tanker was hit, although it is unclear by whom Image: IRIB/Handout/REUTERS

On Tuesday, Saudi Arabian leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, travelled to Cairo to try to get Egypt's support against the Houthis.

"The Egyptians are likely to wait and see," says Roll of the SWP about the next steps for Cairo.

Egypt has a difficult balancing act to perform. The country is closely allied with Saudi Arabia but is also bound to suffer economically in any further escalation between the Saudis and the Houthi group.

A decisive factor will depend on if, and how, the Houthis restrict maritime shipping, and if they go beyond vessels with Saudi Arabian ties, or whether they are just using their currenty improved military position to exert pressure on their enemies.

This story was originally published in German.

World.title: Iran: Activists sound alarm as regime seizes Baha'i assets
World.content:
Rights groups warn Iran is increasingly confiscating assets from government critics and members of the country's Baha'i faith, but also actors, athletes and journalists living abroad.

As Washington attempts to intensify economic pressure on Iran, ordinary Iranians are facing mounting financial distress.

Rights groups say Iranian authorities are increasingly using asset seizures against religious minorities, dissidents and government critics, adding a new layer of economic pressure for people already struggling with soaring living costs.

Members of Iran's Baha'i religious minority seem to be bearing the brunt of the crackdown.

The faith, which originated in 19th-century Persia — now Iran — is not officially recognized by the Islamic Republic. Unlike Christians, Jews and Zoroastrians, Baha'is are not protected under Article 13 of Iran's constitution, leaving them vulnerable to longstanding discrimination and persecution.

Baha'is portrayed as 'spies' for Israel

The US-based Human Rights Activists News Agency in Iran (HRANA) reported "a wave of arrests, searches of homes and businesses, and seizures of property belonging to Baha'i citizens" at the end of August.

Amnesty International said persecution of the Baha'i community has intensified since the 12-day war between Iran and Israel in June 2025, citing what it described as "a coordinated state campaign of incitement to hostility, violence, discrimination and disinformation falsely accusing Baha'is as spies and collaborators for Israel."

Bahai activist Padideh Sabeti says Tehran's 'discriminatory practices' deprive Baha'is of the ability to earn a living Image: privat

"Under current conditions, all people in Iran are facing economic hardship and extremely difficult living conditions, barely putting food on the table for their families," said Padideh Sabeti, spokesperson for the International Baha'i Community.

However, Baha'is suffer even more from the country's economic situation, "as the government's discriminatory practices deprive them of the ability to earn a living," she added.

Sabeti added that the judiciary uses poverty as leverage, demanding exorbitant bail "which is sometimes equivalent to a hundred years' wages for an average citizen."

Regime goes after prominent critics

The apparatus of repression does not only target religious minorities. The government has announced judiciary orders identifying and seizing assets belonging to over 400 individuals living abroad who authorities described as "supporters of the enemy," including actors, athletes and overseas journalists.

Domestically, Sadegh Saedinia, manager of the "Saedinia" chain of cafes, received a 12-year prison sentence, a two-year operating ban and total asset confiscation for posting content related to anti-government protests in Qom, a conservative city considered sacred to Shiites.

The growing number of confiscations has led some observers to ask whether property seizures are also aimed at filling state coffers at a time of economic strain.

The resources gained through seizures are 'very, very insignificant' compared with Iran's massive budget deficit Image: Privat

Economics of confiscation

Arezoo Karimi, a London-based economic analyst, said the financial impact is likely to be limited. The resources gained through seizures are "very, very insignificant" compared with Iran's massive budget deficit, she said.

According to Karimi, confiscated properties are often auctioned off below market value to individuals with political connections.

Sajjad Khodakarami, a Paris-based journalist, said targeting diaspora dissidents sends a clear psychological warning.

"This tool — which the Islamic Republic previously tested on a segment of society — is now being deployed on a broader scale against its opponents," he said.

"Today, this instrument of repression targets not only parts of the Baha'i community, but also various strata of society, including journalists, social and human rights activists, and artists who oppose the ruling political establishment," Khodakarami added.

"When the Islamic Republic targets the assets of hundreds of people, it sends them a message: Even when you are beyond our physical reach, we will continue to apply pressure on you from all sides."

Toys, wedding rings seized by law enforcement

International human rights monitors reported security forces taking gold, electronics, work tools, wedding rings and children's toys during recent home raids.

Khodakarami views the confiscation of everyday household items as a dark indicator of the regime's trajectory.

"When government agents stoop so low as to confiscate a couple's wedding rings or a child's toys, it is a sign of barbarism," said Khodakarami. "Moreover, this behavior is not merely a message to the Baha'i community, but a broader warning to all dissidents."

Khodakarami said post-protest Iran is witnessing 'both the securitization of the economy and the economization of repression' Image: Privat

Khodakarami argues that the government is placing a growing share of the economic burden on ordinary citizens rather than on powerful state institutions.

"As the regime's resources shrink, it tightens the screw on the people's livelihoods," Khodakarami said.

Can Iran avoid hyperinflation?

According to economic analyst Karimi, the government is relying on money printing and subsidy rollbacks to compensate for declining foreign currency revenues. The analyst warned that current fiscal policies risk pushing the country into galloping inflation.

"On one hand, banks are creating money, while on the other, production is effectively paralyzed," said Karimi.

"If we continue down this path at the current pace, I foresee a day when hyperinflation hits Iran — a day when people pay one fare to commute to work in the morning, but have to pay up to double that for the ride back home, just like what we witnessed in Venezuela and Zimbabwe."

While seizing personal assets may serve as a tool of intimidation and generate limited funds for the security apparatus, analysts say it cannot fix Iran's underlying economic problems and is unlikely to ease the financial pressures facing ordinary Iranians.

Edited by: Keith Walker

World.title: Poland reaffirms support for Ukraine after drone strikes
World.content:
After Russia's recent drone attacks on targets close to the Ukraine-Poland border, Warsaw has doubled down on its support for Kyiv and pledged a "nonprovocative but serious response" to Moscow.

Russia's war against Ukraine is moving ever closer to the border with Poland.

After a drone attack by Russia destroyed a gas station and the locomotive of a passenger train near the Dorohusk-Yahodyn border crossing between Poland and Ukraine early Sunday, Warsaw has demonstrated its determination in the face of the immediate threat.

"Border crossings in Poland — as has previously been the case in Moldova and Romania — are being targeted in an attempt to discourage people and deter countries from supporting Ukraine," Deputy Prime Minister and Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz told the private broadcaster TVN on Monday.

"Support for Ukraine is part of Poland's reason of state," Kosiniak-Kamysz said. He added that Poland's own security situation would be worsened should Ukraine lose the war.

Poland prepares response

Early on Monday, Prime Minister Donald Tusk met with the ministers responsible for Poland's security. Senior military commanders also attended the meeting. "We discussed further measures to strengthen the security of our borders," Tusk subsequently wrote on the social media platform X.

Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski provided more details.

"Poland will provide a nonprovocative but serious response to Russia's escalation, such as the attack on the train in Ukraine near the Polish border, one that will strengthen security," Poland's top diplomat told TVN Monday evening.

This truck was destroyed in a Russian drone attack near the Dorohusk-Yahodyn crossing on the Poland-Ukraine border Image: Sylwester Uchanski/REUTERS

On Sunday, Tusk spoke of an "escalation of activities" by Russia. The prime minister also announced that he would discuss the incident with Poland's allies in Europe.

"There is no doubt that we, if necessary, must be prepared, together with them, to deliver a coordinated response," Tusk said after a special session of the Government Centre for Security.

Drone attack on Kyiv-Warsaw train

Russian drones attacked a passenger train on the Kyiv-Warsaw line just short of the Polish border on Sunday morning. The train's locomotive was destroyed in the attack. All passengers and crew were evacuated in time.

Two special trains carrying high-profile participants returning from a security conference in Kyiv were nearby at almost the same time as the attack.

Among those on board were former Swedish Prime Minister Carl Bildt, former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson, former Finnish Prime Minister Sanna Marin, former Polish President Aleksander Kwasniewski and Günter Sautter, foreign and security policy adviser to German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

Polish political scientist Katarzyna Piskorska, who has organized the Warsaw Security Forum in the Polish capital for years, was also on the train.

"Our train was stopped beforehand, and the passengers were evacuated," she told TVN. "The situation was very tense, but everyone remained calm. We were given an evacuation plan and knew exactly what to do."

Russia turns to jet-powered drones to wear Kyiv down To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"The Russians wanted to intimidate us, but they achieved the opposite: The participants affected by this incident are determined to step up their support for the country that was attacked," she said.

Piskorska said the mood in Ukraine was "worse than at any time since the start of the war." She pointed to a new generation of drones equipped with jet engines that can reach their targets much faster.

Support for Ukraine slipping in Poland

Despite numerous acts of sabotage assumed to have be carried out by Russian agents and incidents involving Russian missiles and drones, Poland's government has remained firm in its commitment to supporting Ukraine.

Foreign Minister Sikorski has even called for support for Ukraine to be doubled, arguing that doing so is in Poland's own security interest.

But the government in Warsaw also has to consider the shift in Polish public opinion.

In a survey conducted in mid-July, 52% of respondents said they were in favor of continued military aid for Kyiv; 45% opposed it. These figures stood at 77.5% and 18.3%, respectively, after Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

"Russia has won the propaganda war in Poland," Piskorska said. "It is absurd that we are taking the side of the aggressor and claiming that this is not our war," she said, appealing to fellow Poles to "finally wake up."

Defense Minister Kosiniak-Kamysz has also expressed concern about what he described as a "radical shift in sentiment."

Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski has called for support for Ukraine to be doubled, arguing that this is in the interest of Polish security Image: Christoph Soeder/dpa/picture alliance

"In the past, there was consensus on this issue. Today, we are seeing great skepticism toward Ukraine," Kosiniak-Kamysz said. "There are forces in Poland that are spreading Russian propaganda," he added.

Polish media sound alarm

The Polish media, too, are sounding the alarm.

"Putin is sending out a signal that he is prepared to kill our citizens," Bartosz Wielinski wrote in the Tuesday edition of the Polish daily Gazeta Wyborcza. The Kremlin, he wrote, had sent a message that Poland is "the next country in line."

"These are no longer arson attacks or cyberattacks. These are acts on the threshold of war," he wrote.

Polish daily Rzeczpospolita said that "Putin is knocking on NATO's door."

"The attack on the Warsaw–Kyiv railway line was not just another Russian provocation. It was an attempt to intimidate Poland and the West. The response from Poland's politicians will show whether they are capable of assuming responsibility for the country's security," wrote editor-in-chief Michal Szuldrzynski.

Incidents involving Russian drones are now almost a daily occurrence in Poland. On Monday, a drone washed up on a beach near Jaroslawiec on the Baltic coast. A preliminary investigation indicates that the aircraft was unarmed and appeared to be intended for reconnaissance rather than combat.

"We do not know where Russia believes the limits of the escalation spiral lie," Kosiniak-Kamysz said. "But we do know that the Russians are prepared to go even further."

This article was originally published in German.

World.title: Von der Leyen endurece su discurso sobre migración a raíz de la crisis de Ceuta
World.content:
La presidenta de la Comisión ha propuesto un “protocolo de seguridad” que se active cuando un Estado sienta una amenaza contra su seguridad, como incursiones de drones, ciberataques o sabotajes “que están creciendo cada día”

La crisis migratoria de Ceuta marca el inicio del curso en la Unión Europea. La entrada irregular este verano de decenas de miles de personas en la ciudad autónoma española desde Marruecos ha dado pie, además, para romper otro tabú en el sistema de asilo europeo. La presidenta de la Comisión Europea, Ursula von der Leyen, ha propuesto este miércoles ante el Parlamento Europeo una nueva regulación que permitiría a los Estados miembros suspender —“flexibilizar”, lo ha llamado ella— las reglas migratorias, en casos de crisis. La propuesta de la conservadora alemana durante su discurso sobre el estado de la Unión constata un nuevo endurecimiento de la postura sobre asilo de una UE que se blinda y busca ya lanzar centros de deportación fuera de sus fronteras.

Las imágenes de decenas de miles de migrantes cruzando desde Marruecos a Ceuta, sacudieron la UE este verano. Apenas han ocupado unas líneas del discurso de 22 de páginas de Von der Leyen, una alocución llena de anuncios y guiños al espíritu europeo. Pero la conservadora alemana ha hablado de esa y otras crisis migratorias (como las de los bálticos) y ha culpado a las mafias de tráfico de personas y a los “adversarios” de la UE de utilizara “personas vulnerables” contra el club comunitario. “La frontera de Ceuta es una frontera europea porque Ceuta es España, Ceuta es Europa”, ha declarado, solemne.

Von der Leyen ha asegurado que la respuesta a la migración es el pacto de migración y asilo, que entró en vigor en junio y que endurece las condiciones para los solicitantes de asilo que llegan a Europa. Pero también ha dejado claro que ese conjunto de normas se podrá suspender con ese “nuevo marco europeo de respuesta ante emergencias” con el que, ante situaciones parecidas, se podrá “de forma temporal” dar “flexibilidad en los procedimientos estándar” de las normas europeas sobre migración.

La presidenta de la Comisión Europea, Ursula von der Leyen, dirigiéndose al Parlamento este miércoles. RONALD WITTEK (EFE)

No ha dado más detalles, pero parece claro que lo que planteará en ese nuevo marco será la suspensión “por un tiempo limitado y de forma estrictamente definida” de las reglas migratorias con el fin de acelerar y facilitar los retornos. “Los acontecimientos de este verano demuestran que nuestras herramientas deben evolucionar, sobre todo en situaciones de emergencia. Europa necesita los medios necesarios para proteger sus fronteras en todo momento. Especialmente en situaciones en las que los movimientos masivos se organizan y se utilizan como arma”, ha justificado Von der Leyen, después de destacar que “la frontera de Ceuta es una frontera europea, porque Ceuta es España, Ceuta es Europa y Europa está ahí para vosotros”.

Los argumentos usados para andar por esta senda también descansan en la seguridad exterior: “Desde nuestras fronteras orientales hasta las costas de Creta y a lo largo de todo el Mediterráneo. Y, por supuesto, con la crisis de Ceuta. Estos sucesos son de naturaleza diferente. Pero tienen dos cosas en común. La primera es que se está explotando a personas vulnerables por parte de traficantes y contrabandistas sin escrúpulos, y por parte de nuestros adversarios”, ha subrayado en una clara referencia a episodios como lo sucedido hace varios años en la frontera de Polonia y Lituania, cuando Rusia y Bielorrusia usaron migrantes en una suerte de ataque híbrido a sus fronteras.

“Protocolo ante emergencias”

Moscú ha estado muy presente en su discurso. La invasión de Ucrania hace ya más de cuatro años disparó todas las alarmas de seguridad y defensa en la UE y estas cada vez suenan con más fuerza. Los fallidos ataques con drones sobre el aeropuerto de Leipzig en Alemania este verano han elevado todavía más esta alerta. Y por eso, y por la desconfianza justificada en el histórico aliado estadounidense, Von der Leyen ha puesto sobre la mesa la creación de un “protocolo de seguridad ante emergencias” cuando uno de los Estados sienta que hay una amenaza exterior sobre su seguridad: incursiones de drones, ciberataques, sabotajes. “Amenazas que están creciendo cada día”.

La presidenta de la Comisión Europea, Ursula von der Leyen, dirigiéndose al Parlamento este miércoles. Yves Herman (REUTERS)

“Nos estamos enfrentando a un mundo abiertamente hostil”, ha advertido. Y eso le ha llevado a ir más lejos en este punto que en migración. Lo ha hecho poniendo un ejemplo de cómo funcionaría ese mecanismo: como el artículo 4 de la OTAN, en el que se contempla la que los aliados se consultarán cuando uno de ellas se sienta en peligro. La presidenta de la Comisión ha huido de dar la idea de que su propuesta va separada de la Alianza Atlántica. “Estamos reforzando nuestro trabajo con la OTAN”, ha proclamado.

En el capítulo comercial también ha tenido un lugar considerable China. Von der Leyen ha destacado que el déficit comercial (diferencia entre importaciones y exportaciones) para la UE ronda los 1.000 millones de euros. Para corregirlo, ha recordado que se está negociando con el gigante asiático, pero que eso no basta: “Las palabras son buenas, pero los hechos son mejores”, ha dicho. “Usaremos todas las herramientas a nuestro alcance para reequilibrar la relación”, ha agregado, sin dar más detalles.

World.title: Madrid se reinventa desde el norte: así será la capital del futuro
World.content:
Madrid Nuevo Norte se extenderá a lo largo de 5,6 kilómetros. En la imagen, simulación de una vista aérea del proyecto una vez finalizado.

El proyecto Madrid Nuevo Norte plantea un revolucionario cambio de enfoque en la transformación urbana: se regenerarán 2,3 millones de metros cuadrados de suelo para adaptarlos a los grandes retos sociales, ambientales y económicos del nuevo modelo de ciudad del siglo XXI

Habla

A pocos metros de la estación de Chamartín-Clara Campoamor, punto de conexión ferroviaria de Madrid con el norte de España, se está gestando la mayor transformación urbana del país y una de las más ambiciosas de Europa. El proyecto Madrid Nuevo Norte, aprobado definitivamente por la Comunidad de Madrid en 2020, y en obras desde comienzos de este año, trae consigo un singular cambio de enfoque en el urbanismo: la tendencia actual es que las grandes ciudades no se expandan, sino que regeneren espacios urbanos dentro de ellas que han quedado en desuso. Se trata de una apuesta deliberada para repensar cómo deben crecer las grandes metrópolis y afrontar los retos del siglo XXI con la mirada puesta en la sostenibilidad, la movilidad y la cohesión vecinal.

El proyecto se extiende a lo largo de 5,6 kilómetros desde la plaza de Castilla, al norte de la ciudad, hasta la autopista M-40, conectando la capital con el monte de El Pardo y abarca más de 2,3 millones de metros cuadrados de suelo que serán regenerados para aprovechar al máximo su potencial.

Transformar esa superficie es el principal objetivo de la mayor iniciativa de colaboración de instituciones públicas y privadas que proyecta la capital. “Es mucho más que un desarrollo urbanístico o inmobiliario”, explica José Ignacio Morales, consejero delegado de Crea Madrid Nuevo Norte, la compañía que lidera esta propuesta desde la iniciativa privada. “No estamos hablando simplemente de construir nuevos edificios, sino de crear una nueva centralidad para la ciudad capaz de generar actividad económica, oportunidades y calidad de vida”.

La próxima revolución urbana de Madrid Un impacto de miles de millones de euros Según los estudios realizados por la Universidad Autónoma de Madrid, por encargo de Crea Madrid Nuevo Norte, el proyecto aportará a lo largo de su desarrollo 15.000 millones de euros al producto interior bruto (PIB) nacional y generará 350.000 empleos.



Fotos: Simulaciones cedidas por Crea Madrid Nuevo Norte. Un jardín con su propio microclima Se crearán 400.000 metros cuadrados de zonas verdes. Entre ellas, el denominado Jardín del Viento (en la imagen), una estructura en forma de espiral que se erigirá en uno de los parques y quedará cubierta por vegetación, haciendo circular el viento y aportando humedad al ambiente lo que contribuirá a producir su propio microclima y reducir las temperaturas en verano. Puentes para comunicar las ‘orillas’ El proyecto va a subsanar una de las principales demandas vecinales: comunicar las dos orillas que separan las vías del tren de la estación de Chamartín y Fuencarral. Para ello, al sur de la M-30 se creará un gran parque que cubrirá la playa de vías de la estación de Chamartín-Clara Campoamor y al norte, ya en Fuencarral-El Pardo, levantarán cinco puentes, un túnel y una pasarela peatonal. 10.500 viviendas nuevas En el conjunto de Madrid Nuevo Norte se van a construir 10.500 nuevas viviendas. Del total, 4.000 inmuebles -el 38%- estarán en manos del Ayuntamiento de Madrid, para destinarlos a distintas fórmulas de acceso a un hogar. Un centro de negocios integrado en el barrio Se construirá un complejo de edificios de oficinas con un innovador enfoque: frente a la habitual dinámica de levantar distritos empresariales, aislados o incluso fuera de las ciudades, el nuevo centro negocios estará completamente integrado en el barrio junto a viviendas, comercios y espacios públicos para favorecer que exista actividad durante todo el día. Refuerzo de la movilidad Madrid Nuevo Norte incluye una línea de metro de tres kilómetros de longitud y tres nuevas paradas. Se sumará también una nueva estación de cercanías, Fuencarral Norte (en la imagen, una recreación), y se proporcionará un sistema de Bus Prioritario (BRT) con plataforma propia y más de tres kilómetros de recorrido. El nuevo centro de la Alta Velocidad El proyecto incluye la renovación de la estación de Chamartín-Clara Campoamor para convertirla en el centro de la alta velocidad del país.

Miguel Hernández, arquitecto y director de Estrategia de Crea Madrid Nuevo Norte, ha formado parte del equipo del proyecto desde su concepción. “Tradicionalmente, los urbanistas imaginaban la ciudad futura, la dibujaban, la sociedad se lo creía y todo se desarrollaba en función de ello”. Y para ilustrar el cambio de mentalidad que supone Madrid Nuevo Norte, explica: “Aquí decidimos hacerlo al revés, consultando a la ciudadanía y a expertos en distintas materias, para detectar necesidades reales de hoy y los posibles retos de las próximas décadas y diseñar una ciudad centrada en las personas y adaptable”.

Madrid Nuevo Norte es una operación estratégica que va a permitir a la ciudad afrontar los grandes retos de las capitales del mundo José Ignacio Morales, CEO de Crea Madrid Nuevo Norte

El resultado de este proceso integra “la vida de barrio”, es decir, las viviendas, los servicios públicos o los comercios, junto al nuevo centro de negocios con oficinas y sus trabajadores. “Nadie sabe realmente cómo va a ser el futuro, y una vez ejecutado el urbanismo, es muy difícil de modificar. Puedes cambiar el uso a un edificio, pero no puedes mover de lugar una calle”, concluye Hernández.

Madrid Nuevo Norte está diseñado para ir más allá de un concepto que se ha popularizado en los últimos años: la ciudad de los 15 minutos, un sistema de planificación urbana por el que la mayoría de las necesidades básicas que tiene un ciudadano se cubren en una distancia que pueda recorrerse a pie en un cuarto de hora. ”A nosotros nos gusta más hablar de la región de los 45 minutos”, comenta Hernández. “A 15 minutos se pueden tener las necesidades básicas, pero es imposible ubicar las mejores oportunidades de empleo, que es lo que va a proporcionar Madrid Nuevo Norte, a esa distancia para todos los ciudadanos”, explica.

Y aquí es donde juega un papel determinante la estación de Chamartín -Clara Campoamor, que ya está acometiendo su completa transformación y que está llamada a convertirse en el mayor nodo de hiperaccesibilidad en transporte público de Madrid.

“Según nuestros estudios”, continúa el arquitecto, “alrededor de 4 millones de ciudadanos de toda la Comunidad de Madrid van a poder acceder hasta este punto en transporte público desde sus casas en menos de 45 minutos”.

Nos gusta más hablar de la región de los 45 minutos que de la ciudad de los 15, porque es imposible que las mejores oportunidades de empleo estén a 15 minutos de todos los ciudadanos Miguel Hernández, director de Estrategia de Crea Madrid Nuevo Norte

Gracias a las ventajas que ofrece Madrid por su calidad de vida y su conexión internacional, el nuevo centro de negocios de Madrid Nuevo Norte atraerá no solo talento nacional, sino que permitirá crear un hub de talento internacional en la capital. Los cálculos de Crea Madrid Nuevo Norte apuntan a que habrá un tránsito de millones de pasajeros al año cuando la nueva city empresarial funcione a pleno rendimiento. Como respuesta a las exigencias de este objetivo, se reforzarán las conexiones de la Chamartín-Clara Campoamor con el aeropuerto de Madrid-Barajas-Adolfo Suárez.

Un nuevo concepto de movilidad

Responder a las grandes demandas de movilidad era uno de los grandes desafíos. En este apartado, el planteamiento también fue “a la inversa”, explica Jorge Serrano, director técnico de Crea Madrid Nuevo Norte. Primero diseñaron las fórmulas más sostenibles para que los ciudadanos puedan desplazarse a pie, en bicicleta o transporte público, y, a partir de ahí, definieron la estructura de las calles y la distribución de los edificios e integraron los nuevos trazados para el vehículo privado.

El resultado, según Serrano, se traduce en “calles más equilibradas, con mayor calidad urbana donde moverse deja de ser únicamente una cuestión de circulación para convertirse en una herramienta con la que mejorar el espacio público”. Con esa premisa integraron todos los sistemas de movilidad como una experiencia completa del usuario. “Hemos trabajado para que las conexiones sean más rápidas, intuitivas y cómodas, con el objetivo de reducir al máximo las fricciones entre modos de transporte”, argumenta Serrano.

En el proyecto primero se tuvieron en cuenta las fórmulas de movilidad sostenible, como los desplazamientos a pie o en transporte público (en la imagen, una simulación de un bulevar), y posteriormente se integraron los trazados para los vehículos privados. CREA MADRID NUEVO NORTE

Entretanto, los esfuerzos se centran ahora en que las obras afecten lo menos posible al día a día de los vecinos. Serrano da la clave: “Anticipar. En proyectos de esta escala es muy importante planificar con mucho detalle antes de comenzar a construir”. Algo que requiere una coordinación permanente con administraciones, operadores ferroviarios, empresas constructoras y equipos técnicos durante todas las fases de desarrollo. Y, a los vecinos de la zona, “mantenerlos informados de cualquier novedad y de las medidas de control”.

Como ingeniero urbano, Serrano considera que la mayor innovación es abordar de forma conjunta aspectos como la sostenibilidad, la infraestructura verde, el gasto de energía o la digitalización. “Esto ha sido posible gracias al trabajo desde el inicio con equipos multidisciplinares, con una visión transversal que será una de las principales referencias para las grandes transformaciones urbanas del futuro”.

Unanimidad política

Madrid Nuevo Norte consiguió salir adelante gracias a un consenso político tras 26 años de bloqueo por falta de acuerdo entre los partidos del Consistorio madrileño. El 29 de julio de 2019, el pleno del Ayuntamiento de Madrid, que en ese momento regía la alcaldesa Manuela Carmena, reunió la unanimidad en el voto de todas las formaciones políticas y dio luz verde al inicio del proyecto.
