World.title: Iraq seeks to diversify oil export routes away from Hormuz
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi announced that he discussed increasing his country’s oil exports to Europe during his visits to France and Germany to diversify export routes and reduce reliance on the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran closed following the start of a military conflict with the United States and Israel.

Al-Zaidi said during a joint press conference with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Berlin that Iraq wants to expand and diversify its oil export sources.

In light of the disruptions to maritime shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, al-Zaidi noted that Iraq cannot continue to rely on a single waterway.

The prime minister explained that he discussed oil exports to Europe with Merz, as well as with French President Emmanuel Macron, whom he met on Monday in Paris.

Crude oil sales constitute about 90 percent of Iraq’s revenue, but its exports have been disrupted since the outbreak of the war between Iran, the United States, and Israel last February.

Before the war, Iraq produced about four million barrels per day and exported an average of 3.4 million barrels, mostly through the Strait of Hormuz. The majority of its oil exports went to East Asia, with China and India being its largest importers.

The disruption to marine shipping has compelled Baghdad to transport crude oil using tanker trucks to the Baniyas port in Syria and through a pipeline to the Turkish port of Ceyhan. However, these alternative routes can only handle a small fraction of the export volume that was previously managed via sea transport.

Al-Zaidi said that Baghdad could largely increase its oil exports via the Mediterranean to supply European and American markets.

The Iraqi government seeks to raise oil production to ten million barrels per day, believing that a large part of it, or nearly half, could go to European and Western countries.

Iraq and Germany are expected to reach an understanding regarding crude oil exports in exchange for German technology and equipment, according to al-Zaidi.

Mertz noted that the economic sector is the main drive of cooperation between the two countries. He added that several German companies are currently involved in the development of Iraq’s energy industry.

World.title: Ammonia gas leak kills two, injures 114 in southern Iraq
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The Iraqi Ministry of Health announced on Monday the death of two people and the injury of 114 others following an ammonia gas leak at a fertilizer plant in the southern province of Basra.

The spokesperson for the Health Ministry, Saif al-Badr, told the state-run Iraqi News Agency (INA) that all the injured received the necessary medical treatment, and their conditions were monitored under the direction and supervision of Health Minister Abdul Hussein al-Moussawi.

Over 50 ambulances were dispatched to the scene of the incident to provide first aid and transport the injured to hospitals, according to al-Badr.

The Iraqi official explained that 21 of the injured remain hospitalized in different hospitals, with the majority of them in stable condition.

The initial reports of the incident emerged on Sunday evening following claims of suffocation and breathing difficulties caused by an ammonia leak from the factory.

Iraqi authorities have yet to reveal the source of the leak, the volume of gas discharged, or the duration of the incident.

Ammonia is widely used in fertilizer production. Exposure to high concentrations of the gas can cause eye and respiratory irritation and severe breathing difficulties. Extremely high levels of the ammonia gas can be life-threatening.

Authorities are awaiting the results of a technical investigation to determine whether the leak was caused by equipment malfunction, operational error, or another factor.

World.title: Powerful explosion rocks Soran in northern Iraq
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – A powerful explosion was reported near the Soran district in Erbil in the Kurdistan region of Iraq on Tuesday evening, according to Al-Arabiya News.

Locals and reporters confirmed that a big explosion rocked the district. Media outlets first stated that the cause of the explosion was unclear, while preliminary local reports pointed to possible suicide drone activity in the area.

Soran and the greater Erbil area have experienced increased instability. On Monday morning, rocket attacks targeted three residential camps belonging to Iranian Kurdish opposition groups east of Sulaymaniyah in Iraqi Kurdistan.

Iraqi Kurdistan’s security agency, the Asayish, said that five rockets landed in different areas of the region around 3:10 a.m. local time, noting that no injuries were reported.

The Asayish did not specify the type of rockets used or who launched them, and no group has yet claimed responsibility for the attacks.

Official Iraqi or Kurdish security has yet to provide a definite statement confirming the actual number of casualties, the targeted facility, or the precise source of the Tuesday evening explosion.

World.title: UAE’s ADNOC becomes largest buyer of Iraq’s crude in August, September
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The UAE’s state-owned Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC) has expanded its position as a trader by purchasing millions of barrels of discounted crude from Iraq due to supply interruptions caused by the conflict in the region.

Two sources in Iraq’s oil sector told Reuters that the UAE was the largest buyer of Iraqi crude in August and September, boosting Iraqi exports that had been severely constrained in the early months of the conflict.

ADNOC purchased 32 million Iraqi barrels in August with reductions ranging from $24.90 to $27 a barrel. In September, ADNOC purchased an additional 40 million barrels, including 10 million barrels at an $18 discount and 30 million barrels at a $25 discount.

While Iraq’s State Oil Marketing Organization (SOMO) offered ADNOC 32 million barrels in August, the UAE company only lifted 20 million barrels due to export limitations and the Basra Oil Company’s (BOC) inability to supply the required quantity.

One of the sources explained that ADNOC has shipped 14 million Iraqi barrels in September alone.

A third source said that ADNOC purchased around 20 million barrels of crude from SOMO in tenders at a discount of $25 to $27 per barrel for the September through October lifting period.

Other corporations are also purchasing Iraqi crude. SOMO discounted August-loading cargoes, attracting bidders such as PetroChina, Zhenhua Oil, TotalEnergies, Vitol, Trafigura, Mercuria, and Cathay ​Petroleum.

In August, Iran approved an Iraqi request to allow oil tankers to sail through the Strait of Hormuz after repeated requests from Baghdad.

World.title: Al Shorta hosts Oman’s Al Seeb in AFC Champions League opener in Baghdad
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi powerhouse Al-Shorta SC kicks off its continental campaign in the AFC Champions League Two (2026–2027) on Wednesday evening, September 16, 2026, hosting Omani champions Al-Seeb Club at Al-Zawraa Stadium in Baghdad for their opening Group D fixture.

Scheduled for a 9:15 PM kickoff local time, the Green Harp enters the clash determined to secure all three points early and set a commanding tone for their continental season with home-turf support behind them.

Al-Shorta management confirmed that ticket booths across the stadium perimeter will open to spectators at 6:00 PM, establishing a standardized admission fee of 5,000 Iraqi dinars.

The club issued an open appeal urging its loyal fanbase to pack the stands of Al-Zawraa Stadium in force, emphasizing that vocal home support will be pivotal in driving the squad forward through their continental opener.

The AFC group-stage draw placed Al-Shorta in Group D alongside Al-Seeb (Oman), Al-Hussein Irbid (Jordan), and East Bengal (India), with the top two finishing clubs securing qualification to the Round of 16.

The Baghdadi club heads into Wednesday’s Asian fixture holding fifth place in the Iraq Stars League standings with 12 points following the conclusion of Matchday 5, aiming to translate steady domestic form onto the continental stage.

World.title: Iraq PM returns to Baghdad concluding historic France-Germany tour
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Faleh Al-Zaidi returned to Baghdad at dawn on Wednesday, September 16, 2026, wrapping up an official European tour to France and Germany aimed at expanding bilateral partnerships in energy, defense, digital transformation, and capital investment.

According to an official statement issued by the Prime Minister’s Media Office and carried by the Iraqi News Agency (INA), the tour yielded a series of high-level diplomatic meetings, bilateral summits, and strategic agreements across Paris and Berlin.

In Berlin, Al-Zaidi engaged in head-of-state talks with German Federal President Frank-Walter Steinmeier and held bilateral negotiations with Federal Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

Following an expanded bilateral delegation session and a joint press conference with Chancellor Merz, the Prime Minister addressed the Iraqi-German Business Dialogue Forum to pitch direct foreign investment into Iraq’s manufacturing and infrastructure sectors.

On the commercial front, Al-Zaidi met with executive leadership from Siemens Energy, overseeing the signing of the fourth-phase Energy Cooperation Principles Agreement to modernize and expand Iraq’s electrical generation and grid infrastructure.

The Berlin stop followed an active diplomatic and commercial program in Paris, where Al-Zaidi met with French President Emmanuel Macron at the Élysée Palace and engaged with prominent French business leaders, including the head of TotalEnergies, the chairman of Rothschild & Co, representatives from major industrial firms, and the President of the Arab World Institute. The French leg concluded with the execution of six major memoranda of understanding and strategic declarations:

World.title: Anbar Health Directorate clarifies pork-breeding rumors amid recent Najaf case
World.content:
Anbar (IraqiNews.com) – The Anbar Health Directorate issued an official denial on Tuesday, September 15, 2026, firmly debunking viral social media claims alleging that its oversight teams had raided an illicit pig-breeding facility and confiscated pork intended for commercial distribution within the governorate.

In a formal statement received by Shafaq News Agency, health authorities stressed that the rumors circulating online are entirely groundless, fabricated, and completely disconnected from any inspection operations or actions executed by the directorate.

Health officials warned that amplifying such sensationalized misinformation fuels public panic and directly undermines institutional trust in state healthcare and food-safety regulators.

The directorate urged citizens, digital outlets, and news organizations to exercise journalistic due diligence by sourcing public health updates exclusively through accredited, official institutional channels while refraining from amplifying unverified social media posts.

The rumor mill in Anbar appears to have mirrored a verified, high-profile incident in Najaf governorate, where intelligence squads arrested a local butcher on Wednesday, September 9, for hunting wild boars in the marshlands of Al-Hurriya subdistrict, Kufa district, and processing the meat into minced beef products for unsuspecting consumers in central Najaf.

Judicial authorities in Najaf confirmed on Saturday that the butcher’s criminal dossier was formally referred to the Najaf Criminal Court after investigators compiled comprehensive forensic evidence, with the defendant now awaiting trial and sentencing under the provisions of the Iraqi Penal Code.

World.title: ‘You are Iraqi in any language’: PM Al Zaidi affirms pluralism in Berlin
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – A candid exchange between Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Faleh Al-Zaidi and an Iraqi Kurdish journalist captured widespread attention during the Iraqi-German Business Dialogue Forum in Berlin on Tuesday, September 15, 2026.

When the journalist stood up to address the forum and apologized for not speaking Arabic professionally, Al-Zaidi interjected with a smile: “In whatever language you speak, you are Iraqi.”The gesture drew spontaneous applause across the hall, reframing a routine press exchange into a high-profile affirmation of civic identity.

The encounter resonated deeply against Iraq’s complex social tapestry, highlighting that national identity transcends linguistic or sectarian boundaries.

Iraq remains an ancient crossroads of diverse ethnicities, religions, and native languages, where Arabs, Kurds, Turkmen, Syriac-Assyrians, Yazidis, Armenians, and Shabaks form the core fabric of the nation.

The Prime Minister’s spontaneous remark served as a reminder that every citizen—whether communicating in Arabic, Kurdish, Syriac, Turkmen, or an international tongue—holds an equal, indivisible place within the Iraqi state.

World.title: "Additional achievement": Uttar Pradesh CM inaugurates Charitable Blood Centre; praises IMA's healthcare efforts in Gorakhpur
World.content:
GORAKHPUR: Uttar Pradesh chief minister Yogi Adityanath on Wednesday lauded the contribution of medical professionals towards public welfare, highlighting the Indian Medical Association (IMA) for extending its role beyond clinical practice by establishing charitable blood banks and free outpatient departments (OPDs) in Gorakhpur.

Speaking at the inauguration of the Charitable Blood Centre at the IMA Building in Gorakhpur, Adityanath emphasised that institutional participation in community healthcare marks a significant milestone in social responsibility.

He said, "Indian Medical Association is not only an all-India organisation of practising doctors. It has also fulfilled its social responsibility by starting blood banks and free OPDs in areas of Gorakhpur."

The Uttar Pradesh CM further noted that while individual medical practitioners serve through state-run and private systems, collective initiatives by professional bodies can strengthen the grassroots healthcare framework.

"While doctors may practise individually through government or private setups, an organisation collectively running free OPDs or blood banks is an additional achievement in itself," Yogi Adityanath said.





Earlier this week, a differently-abled family in Uttar Pradesh's Basti district received assistance from the state government for housing, education and basic amenities following the intervention of chief minister Yogi Adityanath, officials said.

The family of Ramkishan Pandey, which has four differently-abled children, was provided support under various government schemes after the district administration took up their concerns on priority following directions from the chief minister.

According to officials, the family had been facing difficulties related to housing, education and access to essential facilities. After the matter came to the notice of the administration, steps were initiated to provide assistance and improve their living conditions.

Under the Kanshi Ram Awas Yojana, the family was provided a house, helping resolve their concern of having a permanent shelter. The administration also arranged wheelchairs for the differently-abled children to support their mobility.

Officials said the elder son of the family, Ankur, was also provided the benefit of a disability pension. The move was aimed at extending financial assistance and ensuring regular support for the family.

The administration also focused on the education of the children and facilitated their admission to schools. Officials said efforts were made to ensure that the children continue their studies and get access to educational opportunities.

The initiative highlights the state government's efforts towards supporting differently-abled persons and economically weaker families by ensuring access to welfare schemes and essential services, officials said.

World.title: 'There's no Pak-China boundary': India tells Islamabad to drop 'theatrics', vacate occupied territory
World.content:
NEW DELHI: India on Wednesday rejected the so-called Pakistan-China Boundary Joint Commission, saying it has no legal basis and reiterated that Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh are integral parts of India.

Responding to media queries, the ministry of external affairs (MEA) spokesperson said, "We have seen reports in this regard. Our position on this matter is clear and consistent. There is no boundary between Pakistan and China. We reject the so-called Joint Commission, which is without any legal basis."

The MEA said the entire Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh "have been, are and will always remain integral and inalienable parts of India".

"Pakistan has no locus standi to enter into arrangements concerning Indian territory under its illegal and forcible occupation," it said.

India also reiterated that it has never recognised the so-called "China-Pakistan Boundary Agreement" of 1963 and has consistently maintained that it is "illegal and invalid".

"We resolutely oppose and reject any attempts to alter the status of these occupied territories or legitimise illegal occupation, impinging on India's sovereignty and territorial integrity," the MEA said.





It added that any "so-called boundary cooperation" between China and Pakistan concerning Indian territories would be "completely unacceptable" and would have no bearing on India's sovereignty over those territories.

"Instead of engaging in such theatrics, we call on Pakistan to immediately vacate from areas under its illegal and forcible occupation," the MEA added.

In recent years, China has maintained military pressure along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) with India, with border violations and unauthorised entries reported across all three sectors of the 3,488-km-long boundary between the two countries.

The coordination between China and Pakistan along the border in the Karakoram region of Pakistan-occupied Kashmir, which stretches over 590 km, also impacts India's historical and legal claims over the area.

World.title: Tejashwi targets Centre, says ‘no money for flood-hit, but lamps for PM’s birthday’
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Rashtriya Janata Dal (RJD) leader

on Wednesday hit out at the Centre over the flood situation in Bihar, alleging that the government had no money for flood-affected people but was ready to spend on Prime Minister Narendra Modiâs birthday celebrations.

"Govt has no money for the flood-affected people but they are ready to spend for PM's birthday by lighting lamps," Yadav said.

His remarks came amid the ongoing flood situation in parts of Bihar affecting nearly 50 lakh people across 15 districts of the state. Bihar has recorded 112.7 mm of rainfall so far this month, about six per cent above normal, according to the local weather office.

Earlier in the day, BJP appealed to people to light an âAashirwad Ka Diyaâ at their homes on September 17, marking Modi's birthday. BJP president Nitin Nabin, Union minister Kiren Rijiju and other party leaders have made the appeal through social media.

The lamp-lighting initiative is part of the BJP's month-long âSeva Sankalp Abhiyanâ, which includes service activities, welfare outreach and public-participation programmes across the country.

World.title: 'Callous and criminal conduct': Delhi HC on Satya Niketan building collapse that killed 7
World.content:
Delhi HC calls the incident 'callous and criminal' conduct

NEW DELHI: Delhi high court on Wednesday said the collapse of a multi-storey hostel building in Satya Niketan, which killed seven people including students, was "not an ordinary incident. "A bench of Chief Justice D K Upadhyaya and Justice Tejas Karia said four students who died had come to Delhi from small towns with hopes of building their careers. The court said their dreams were âshatteredâ because of the âcallous and criminal conductâ of certain persons.âFour students lost their lives in the mishap...very tragic. It's not an ordinary incident of any mishap. These four students had come to the capital with a lot of hopes and dreams, coming from small towns. All of that was shattered by such callous and criminal conduct on the part of (certain persons),â the court said.The building, which housed a boysâ paying guest accommodation near Delhi Universityâs South Campus, collapsed on September 6 while repair work was under way. Several people were injured in the incident.Additional Solicitor General Chetan Sharma told the court that authorities had taken several steps after the collapse, including mapping and identifying land and other facilities that could be used by students.The bench, however, said the shortage of hostel facilities in Delhi was not a ânew phenomenonâ.âWho doesn't know the problem of hostels in the city? Students are flocking to Delhi for higher education, and this is not a new phenomenon. It has been happening for the last 20-25 years in the hope that they will build their career. See what has happened,â the bench said.The court was hearing a PIL filed by Aakarshak Danveer Rathi seeking an independent probe into the collapse, inspection of all paying guest accommodations and a compensation and rehabilitation scheme for victims and their families.The high court said it would hear the PIL along with another pending petition on September 25.On September 7, the court had ordered a high-level MCD inquiry into the collapse and said the government could not evade responsibility.It had also said the incident raised serious concerns over inadequate housing and hostel facilities, student safety and the measures taken by the MCD and other authorities to regulate paying guest accommodations.

World.title: From ‘Ankur’ to ‘Malgudi Days’, Anant Nag’s five-decade journey earns Phalke honour
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Veteran actor

, whose career spans Kannada cinema, Hindi films and the much-loved television series âMalgudi Daysâ, will receive the Dadasaheb Phalke Award for 2024, the government announced on Wednesday, recognising more than five decades of work across languages.

The 78-year-old actor will be presented with Indiaâs highest cinema honour at the 72nd National Film Awards ceremony in Kevadia, Gujarat, on September 22, 2026. The recognition follows the Padma Bhushan conferred on him in 2025.

Announcing the selection, the government said Nagâs cinematic journey had âinspired generations of artists and enriched the cultural landscape of the nationâ. He was chosen on the recommendation of the Dadasaheb Phalke Award Selection Committee.

Nag made his film debut with the Kannada feature âSankalpâ and entered Hindi cinema with âAnkurâ. Over a career that marked its golden jubilee in 2023, he has appeared in more than 300 films across Kannada, Hindi, Telugu, Malayalam, Tamil and Marathi. His television work includes âMalgudi Daysâ, adding another dimension to a career distinguished by its range of characters and languages.

The award carries a Swarna Kamal medallion, a shawl and a cash prize of Rs 10 lakh.

World.title: Lazzari and Mohamedi: When two artists search for the same silence
World.content:
Installation view In-Rhythm, Bice Lazzari and Nasreen Mohamedi at KNMA Saket

BICE LAZZARI Courtesy_ Archivo

Nasreen Mohamedi , Photo by _Jyoti Bhatt, Courtesy_ Heirs of Nasreen Mohamedi

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

'In Rhythm' will be on view at the Kiran Nadar Museum of Art, Delhi, till 22 Dec.

Picture two works hanging side by side. For a moment, forget the labels. The lines are so deftly controlled, the spaces so carefully constructed, that it is easy to imagine they came from the same hand. But the artists are separated by continents, generations and circumstances. They never met, never knew of each other, and as far as records show, never encountered each other's work. But now they share a gallery in Delhi, in a conversation neither artist could have seen coming.'In Rhythm: Bice Lazzari and Nasreen Mohamedi', presented by KNMA in partnership with the Italian Embassy Cultural Centre and the Archivio Bice Lazzari, places the Italian painter Lazzari, known for her minimalist abstraction, in dialogue with the Indian artist Mohamedi, whose work carries a similar stunning subtlety. The exhibition delivers a compelling lesson in brevity, in the discipline of discarding the unnecessary.Lazzari (1900â1981) and Mohamedi (1937â1990) came from different artistic worlds, but both carved out singular places in the history of modern art. Lazzari, regarded as one of the founding figures of Italian postwar abstraction, moved from painting, murals and applied design to the spare, linear language of her late acrylics, created against monochrome grounds.Her work has since been the subject of major retrospectives in Washington, London and Rome, and is often discussed alongside that of artists such as Agnes Martin. Mohamedi occupies a comparably important place in Indian modernism. Trained in London and Paris before returning to India, she taught for years at the Faculty of Fine Arts in Baroda, developing a radical minimalism and an almost poetic engagement with the grid that had few precedents in Indian art. But the exhibition does not argue that one artist influenced the other; instead, it examines the resonance between two independent paths toward abstraction.The show is curated by Andrea Anastasio, director of the Italian Cultural Institute in New Delhi, and Roobina Karode, artistic director and chief curator at KNMA. Anastasio was drawn to the idea of pairing the two artists after encountering Mohamedi's work at a KNMA retrospective in 2012-13.Rather than proceeding chronologically, the show opens with each artist's late, most reduced work. "We decided to start with the end of their lives, when they achieved the essence of their practice," Anastasio says. "For both of them, lines, rhythm, space have a very important role to play. They are in a continuous dialogue," he says. Lazzariâs early work was far removed from the spare lines and grids of her later practice. The exhibition traces her beginnings through objects, textiles and paintings shaped by Futurism and domestic materials. Mohamediâs own trajectory was different. Her early work encompassed colour, collage, watercolour and figuration. Gradually, colour receded as line, geometry, space and interval took over.The word "subtracting" recurs throughout Anastasio's account of both artists. "Towards the end of their lives, in subtracting and subtracting, they come across very interesting... not similarities, but reverberations of each other's work," he says.The physical circumstances of their later years add another layer to the show. In her later years, Mohamedi developed a neurological disorder (Huntington's disease) that caused motor challenges, including tremors in her hands. She then adapted her technique, using precision drafting tools to continue working. Lazzari's own departure from oil paints and tactile mixed-media (like sand and glue) was a direct reaction to physical illness caused by chronic exposure to toxic paint solvents, leading to respiratory and eye issues that forced a complete overhaul of her materials, allowing her canvases more "light, space, rigour, structure, synthesis and a little poetry".Mohamedi's works ask for a different kind of attention. A room devoted to them in the exhibition is conceived almost as a meditation space. Spare lines from her poems unfurl across the walls, asking viewers to stare hard, to think, to find the maximum in the minimum, all of it forming a continuity, like the immense sea. She rarely signed or dated her work and the result is an abstraction that does not ask to be decoded. "The beauty of abstraction is that the artist tries to evoke, in the most subtle way, something that is seen first inwardly, more than outwardly," says Anastasio. That inwardness shapes the exhibition's treatment of space too. The curators build an intimate, almost domestic environment in one section before opening it out toward a larger sense of landscape and horizon.There is, finally, a parallel in how the two women came to be recognised. Lazzari was known within artistic circles during her lifetime but did not achieve mainstream recognition. The Guggenheim Foundation had acquired one of her works as early as the 1930s, but wider acknowledgement came much later.Mohamedi's posthumous recognition followed a similarly delayed arc.The exhibition is, in the end, more than a comparison of two artists who happened to use lines. It asks what happens when two women, working independently and without any direct exchange, arrive at a shared insistence on restraint.

World.title: Blueprint for Vizag’s water security may emerge during CM’s September 19 visit
World.content:
The ongoing drinking water crisis is set to take centre-stage during Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu’s proposed visit to Visakhapatnam on September 19. Local leaders are preparing to seek a comprehensive, long-term strategy from the Chief Minister to strengthen water storage and ensure water security for the city.

Speaking to The Hindu, TDP State president and Gajuwaka MLA Palla Srinivasa Rao said: ”Yes, we are preparing to bring Vizag's water issue to the notice of the CM during his visit to the city on September 19. There will be a possible meeting with all the major stakeholders.”

Highlighting a shift in planning he said; “Back in 2004, there was a proposal to spend ₹3,000 crore on building a pipeline from the Yeleru canal to prevent water evaporation, and reduce frequent desilting works. However, now our priority has changed. We want to invest such large amounts to creating dedicated water storage points for the city. This point will also be discussed in the meeting with the Chief Minister.”

History of vulnerability

Visakhapatnam has long faced recurring water shortages due to its heavy reliance on the erratic monsoon cycles. Because the city lacks perennial river sources within its immediate basin, a failed southwest monsoon regularly dries up local tanks like Meghadrigedda, triggering intense panic. This vulnerability was visible during the 2004–2006 drought, which forced prolonged rationing and left residents heavily reliant on erratic tanker supplies. Furthermore, rapid industrialisation—anchored by heavyweights like the Visakhapatnam Steel Plant—have increased pressure on the available water resources, leaving residential areas to bear the brunt of dry taps.

The 2027 Godavari Roadmap

To break the cycle of recurring water shortages, State authorities have mapped out an ambitious plan to bring the Godavari River water to Visakhapatnam via the Polavaram Left Main Canal by 2027. However, public skepticism remains high regarding its practical execution. Irrigation experts have also highlight strict hydraulic constraints that must be managed. Lift irrigation operations can only function effectively when the Godavari water level reaches a minimum height of 14 metres. Managing these minimum flow thresholds during lean periods is essential to keeping the inter-basin transfer project reliable and operational year-round.

Building a decentralised storage grid

Experts agree that long-distance canal transfers alone cannot secure urban taps without local retention systems. To solve this, officials have outlined a decentralised storage network across both sides of the Polavaram Left Main Canal.

This planned 27 TMC storage grid requires the integration of key storage nodes including—Tallapalem, Rangupolugedda, and Seshugedda in Yelamanchili, Cheedikada in Nakkapalli, Krishnapalem in Achyuthapuram, and urban reservoirs like Gambheram and Meghadrigedda.

According to irrigation officials, “The 2027 vision is a conditional equation. It will only succeed if lift thresholds, canal linkages, and the proposed 27 TMC storage grid are properly synchronised.”

World.title: It took two to tango to set stage for September 17, 1948 in Hyderabad
World.content:
A week before the tanks and armoured personnel carriers rolled into Hyderabad, Indian Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru made it clear on the floor of the Constituent Assembly: “India could never agree to Hyderabad having independent relations with any other power for that would endanger her own security. Historically, Hyderabad has at no time been independent. Practically, in the circumstances of today, it cannot be independent.” The message on September 7, 1948 was a much stronger message than the earlier missives.

Weeks earlier, on June 4, 1948, Deputy Prime Minister Vallabhbhai Patel in Dehradun wrote to Nehru. “I feel and feel very keenly that we should do nothing in Hyderabad whether in regard to its internal constitutional problems or in regard to its accession, which we cannot justify in all good conscience to the world and to our own people.”

This was the good cop-bad cop routine the two statesmen of India followed as the war in Kashmir turned into a diplomatic and security quagmire. Indian two leaders were worried about how it will look if they used strongarm tactics to bring in line the recalcitrant Nizam Mir Osman Ali Khan and his band of advisors and hatchet-men.

The Nizam’s government allegedly gave a $48,000, i.e. ₹20 lakhs a year deal to the United Press of America to broadcast Hyderabad version of news to the world. The Nizam’s government also financed films that were shot in Hyderabad to show peaceful life in the State.

In contrast, India resorted to diplomacy and letter-writing. In the run-up to the Operation Polo or Police Action, Patel was in touch with British diplomats as well. One of whom, Arthur Henderson, the Secretary of State for Air, UK wrote on June 26, 1948: “I still hope that it will be possible for a satisfactory agreement to be reached, both with regard to Kashmir and Hyderabad. Whatever form of political set-up there may be, both Pakistan and India have everything to gain by friendly co-operation and good neighbourliness. Hyderabad also will have much to gain by closer co-operation with India.”

The diplomacy wore thin. Patel was furious when it didn’t help. “Our attempt at a settlement, which so often came near to success, ended unfortunately in failure. There are forces at work which are determined not to allow any agreement to be reached between Hyderabad and the Indian Union, and which have progressively gained strength in Hyderabad and seem now completely to control the Government of the State.”

He was responding to a mail sent by Nehru on May 27, 1948 which said: “I feel that it would be of tremendous advantage to us if we could satisfactorily settle with Hyderabad and make it innocuous by bringing it effectively under our control.”

The diplomatic pretence worked so well that the CIA spooks in their weekly Intelligence summary on May 26, 1948, did not expect the Indian action in the middle of September: “India is not likely to take overt action to end Hyderabad’s independence before the ‘standstill agreement’ between India and Hyderabad expires on 15 November.”

This was not to be. Between September 13 morning and September 17 afternoon of 1948, India was in effective control of Hyderabad state. A State that existed continuously from 1724.

Even seasoned diplomats were surprised by the quick turn of events that was like a sea tide that subsided normally. Sir Walter Monckton, who advised the Nizam on the negotiations with the Indian government wrote to Patel. “I want to tell you how relieved I am that the action which you were eventually driven to take did not result in large-scale communal troubles. I know how anxious you were not to take the action at all, and how hard you struggled to avoid it. I honestly believe that moderate world opinion shared your view rather than the other.”

World.title: Koti Vishnu Nama Parayanam in Coimbatore on September 20
World.content:
The 17th edition of Koti Vishnu Nama Parayanam, involving the chanting of Vishnu Sahasranamam 10,000 times in a single day, will be held at VRG Thirumana Mandapam, Edayarpalayam, Coimbatore, on September 20 from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. The event is being organised by Vishnu Sahasranama Mandali, Kavundampalayam, Sri Maha Sasthru Seva Sangam, Tatabad, Sai Lakshmi Caterers, Ramnagar, and other Vishnu Sahasranama mandalis.

The chanting will begin around 7.45 a.m. after Ganapathi Homam, Gou Pooja and Maha Sankalpam. Devotees can participate virtually through the Mahasasthru YouTube channel. The organisers said online participants could communicate the number of chanting repetitions completed by 3 p.m. on the day. A book, Dharmacharyan, featuring rare stutis, information on temples based on the Shanmatha tradition, and aspects of Dharma Sastras, will also be brought out during the event.

World.title: Anant Nag brings Dadasaheb Phalke to Kannada
World.content:
In a big honour for Kannada cinema, veteran actor Anant Nag became the second artist from the State to win the Dadasaheb Phalke Award on Wednesday. The recognition comes a year after the actor was conferred with the Padma Bhushan.

After Dr. Rajkumar received the honour in 1995, no Kannada actor had bagged the country’s highest award in the field of cinema.

Anant Nag, who debuted with the 1973 Kannada film Sankalpa, has acted in more than 300 movies for over five decades in both mainstream and parallel cinema, with more than 250 of his performances being in Kannada. The actor, born Anant Nagarkatte in 1948 in Uttara Kannada district, began his acting stint with Kannada, Marathi, Hindi and Konkani plays, and has a rich background in theatre shaped largely in Mumbai.

Anant Nag is the recipient of five Karnataka State Awards, including the Lifetime Achievement honour. He will receive the Phalke award at the 72nd National Film Awards Ceremony on September 22, 2026 in Kevadia, Gujarat.

“It’s a great feeling to receive this honour. In a way, I feel the Padma Bhushan was a rehearsal for this big award, with all the excitement and anticipation that came with it. I dedicate this award to Kannadigas and Karnataka,” the actor told reporters in Bengaluru.

An official statement from PIB read, “On the recommendation of the Dadasaheb Phalke Award Selection Committee, the Government of India is pleased to announce that the actor will be conferred the prestigious Dadasaheb Phalke Award 2024 for his contribution to Indian cinema and an illustrious cinematic journey that has inspired generations.”

Prime Minister Narendra Modi congratulated the actor for “Infusing unparalleled performance and vitality in every role he played.” Mr. Modi took to social media, and said, “Over the past several decades, his natural acting, remarkable versatility, and exceptional artistic talent have left an indelible mark on Indian cinema, particularly in the Kannada film industry.” Karnataka Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar also took to social media to commend Anant Nag’s cinematic journey and the Phalke award.

Though cinematographer V. K. Murthy, from Karnataka, was honoured with the award in 2008, it was for his work in Hindi cinema, making the award for Ananth Nag only the second recognition for Kannada cinema.

World.title: A sea-facing life in Chennai: Murugavel Janakiraman, founder and CEO of Matrimony.com
World.content:
Chennai is a liveable city. People are nice and accommodating. The city has a wonderful mix of tradition and modernity. It is also a safe place to live in. I love the beaches in Chennai. I have always had a deep connection with the beach. I grew up in Royapuram, and later studied at Presidency College, which faces the beach. I then went to the University of Madras, which also overlooks the beach. Now, my office faces the sea. Earlier, beaches used to be quiet places. Now, you need to travel to resorts to find that kind of calmness. That has changed in the city. I like this place, Broken Bridge, which also faces the sea. I once had a brainstorming session here with my leadership team about Elite Matrimony.

Earlier, the city had fewer entrepreneurs. More entrepreneurs are emerging now. We may still lag behind Bengaluru and Delhi, but the ecosystem is steadily getting better. Dakshin at the Park Sheraton used to be one of my favourite places. Woodlands was another place, especially for coffee. I’m not a regular at either place, but I have always liked them.

Those days, matchmaking happened through marriage brokers, relatives, and family networks. Now most matchmaking happens online. There is also a growing amalgamation of cultures in weddings. Earlier, mehendi and sangeet were not part of Tamil weddings. Now weddings have become much more elaborate, with people adopting traditions from different cultures.

(As told to Sangeetha Kandavel)

World.title: India’s academic freedom ‘severely restricted’ under BJP government: report
World.content:
India’s academic freedom has been "severely restricted” under the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government, according to the annual “Free to Think 2026” report released by Scholars at Risk’s (SAR), an international network of higher education institutions that works to protect threatened scholars and promote academic freedom, headquartered at New York University.

Founded in 1999 at the University of Chicago, SAR comprises over 650 universities, academic associations, and educational organisations across 40 countries.

US-based lawyer and human rights advocate Rob Quinn heads SAR’s advocacy efforts. SAR’s Ambassadors Council features noted scholars and public leaders like former president of Pen America Dr. Anthony Appiah, prominent historian Ian Burma and former Canadian Minister of Foriegn Affairs Dr. Lloyd Axworthy.

According to the report, India’s Academic Freedom Index (AFI) score decreased from 0.16 in 2024 to 0.14 in 2026, with both values falling in the "severely restricted" category, next to its neighbours China (0.07) and Afghanistan (0.09), where academic freedom was in the "completely restricted" category. India’s AFI value has declined significantly over the last decade, from 0.41 in 2015.

The AFI is measured on a scale of 0 to 1 and assesses parameters like campus integrity, freedom of academic and cultural expression, freedom of academic exchange and dissemination, freedom to research and teach and institutional autonomy.

The report documents 382 attacks arising from 321 verified incidents in 59 countries and territories, as reported by SAR’s Academic Freedom Monitoring Project from July 1, 2025, to June 30, 2026. Of the 382, India accounted for the highest number of attacks, with 42 cases, the report noted. These attacks included violence, imprisonment or loss of position of academics or students.

Plummeting academic freedom under BJP government

The report states that India’s central government expanded its authority over higher education, influencing university governance, leadership appointments, and academic priorities. “University administrators took actions that stifled campus discourse, including dismissing faculty members, cancelling academic events, and enforcing new policies restricting student expression. Both students and police committed acts of violence at protests or other campus gatherings,” the report notes.

The report says that the ruling BJP government continued to deploy the University Grants Commission (UGC) as a primary vehicle for State influence over higher education. “The UGC faced scrutiny in recent years for policies perceived to tighten government control over universities, including loosening academic qualification requirements for university vice-chancellors and accelerating the casualisation of academic labour by removing the 10% cap on non-permanent, contract faculty,” it notes.

The report also notes that the government of Jammu and Kashmir banned the sale, distribution, and possession of 25 books by globally respected scholars, historians, and journalists which addressed Kashmir’s sociopolitical history, including discussions of enforced disappearances and feminist resistance. “Actions like these are particularly threatening because they provide a new model for the relationship between States and educational institutions that prioritises ideological compliance over independent thought,” the report notes.

Repression of Academics

On the targeting of academic faculty, the report cites the incident in which the Supreme Court issued a "life ban" on three academics from receiving public funding for curriculum development over the National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT) textbook’s reference to "corruption in the judiciary”. “One of the scholars, Michel Danino, a guest professor at IIT Gandhinagar and chairperson of the NCERT social science curricular group, was dismissed from his faculty position,” the report notes.

In another example, it notes that following a two-year suspension, South Asian University officially terminated professor Snehashish Bhattacharya in September 2025 for “misconduct against university interests”. Mr. Bhattacharya and fourteen other faculty members had signed a November 2022 letter expressing concern over the university’s handling of student protests in October 2022.

The report also mentions the case of SRM Institute of Science and Technology professor Lora Santhakumar, who was fired over social media posts critical of civilian casualties resulting from Indian military action in Pakistan.

The report also notes the case in which Jamia Millia Islamia, a public research university in Delhi, suspended Professor Virendra Balaji Shahre for administering an examination question that asked students to “discuss the atrocities against Muslim minorities in India” for his course “Social Problems in India”.

Penalising student protestors

Ideological polarisation between student groups, particularly the right-wing Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad (ABVP) and left-wing All India Students Association (AISA) and National Students’ Union of India (NSUI), transformed academic and cultural events into “political flashpoints,” the report says. “Policy shifts, academic decisions, and debates about national identity, caste, religion, and historical interpretation led to student protests. In some instances, demonstrations resulted in clashes between opposing student factions,” it states.

The report says student protestors on Indian campuses faced pressure from university authorities, police, and opposing student factions. Some institutions, such as the Tata Institute of Social Sciences (TISS) and Jamia Millia Islamia, cited a lack of official permission and “unauthorised” gatherings to penalise students engaging in peaceful protests. These include organising a “peaceful” memorial for G.N. Saibaba, an Indian scholar who died after repeated imprisonments. At TISS, police complaints were filed against students. After a peaceful demonstration on the fifth anniversary of the 2019 police crackdown related to the Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA) at Jamia Millia Islamia students were given show-cause notices, the report states.

On a broader scale, the University of Delhi implemented a temporary blanket ban on all public meetings, rallies, and demonstrations, which resulted in the cancellation of cultural festivals, press conferences, iftar gatherings, and any assembly of five or more people. “When the ban expired, the university notified the campus community that all future protests would require approval 72 hours in advance, warning that violators would risk expulsion or police action,” the report notes.

The report states that academic freedom has declined significantly in 50 of the 179 countries analysed over the past decade. The AFI rated 9 of the 22 countries or territories featured in this report—and 34 overall—as “completely restricted”: Afghanistan, China, Occupied Palestinian Territory (OPT): Gaza, Iran, Russia, Türkiye, Syria, Venezuela, and Zimbabwe. Another six countries or territories in this report—and 30 overall—were rated as “severely restricted”: Hong Kong, India, Indonesia, Pakistan, the OPT: the West Bank, and Ukraine.

World.title: Privatise Chennai airport at earliest, air passengers say
World.content:
A monkey’s entry into Chennai airport’s international terminal on Tuesday not only drew the ire of air passengers but also reignited the old debate over why the airport must be privatised as soon as possible.

Air passengers said that it is important to ramp up plans to bring in a private operator for the airport, given that the Parandur airport project has been dropped and plans to find an alternative site for the second airport are only in the earliest stages. Be it the delay in the inauguration of the T3 Terminal or the lack of adequate food and retail options, air passengers said they deserve to experience the standards of a private airport like Bengaluru or Hyderabad in Chennai as well.

“Take the case of the cab pick-up plaza. It was ready for the last nine months, but was inaugurated only recently after so much pressure from passengers. If it were a private operator, he wouldn’t wait so long to inaugurate a facility. Similarly, the deadline for the T3 Terminal has been extended so many times. Whatever the reasons may be, can an integrated terminal construction go on for nearly seven years?” Dayanand Krishnan, a frequent flyer, asked.

Sowdeshwar Sarveshakumar, another frequent flyer, said the ambience and maintenance that a private airport provides are definitely far superior. “There is a wide variety of eateries and retail outlets in a private airport. Time passes effortlessly before boarding the flight, but that’s not the case in Chennai airport. The ambience and architecture too are much more pleasant and beautiful in a private airport, and Bengaluru’s new terminal is a classic example. Also, the private airport manages to get more connectivity to many more destinations, which we are unable to. I hope the airport is at least privatised soon,” he added.

Sources in AAI said it is true that the planning and execution of some projects get delayed at times because they need permission from the headquarters in New Delhi. Such situations are less likely to happen for a private operator.

In addition to this, congestion at the cargo terminal is another key issue adding to the woes of the airport.

Dinesh Krishnan, National Treasurer, Air Cargo Agents Association of India (ACAAI), said, “The core reason for congestion at the Chennai Air Cargo Complex is the acute shortage of terminal space relative to export demand, compounded by operational productivity bottlenecks. While the airport’s passenger facilities have undergone significant rebuilding and expansion, the air cargo terminal has seen minimal upgrades to its floor area and handling infrastructure,” he said.

To resolve this crisis, the government must open terminal expansion to private sector participation, injecting the capacity and high-efficiency logistics practices the industry urgently requires to fix this problem long-term, he added.

Officials of AAI said that while the cab pick-up plaza has already been opened to passengers, the T3 Terminal will be ready in seven months. Officials also said that they have been continuously taking several initiatives to address the issues faced by passengers. As far as adding new retail and food and beverage outlets, officials said measures are underway to bring in a new master concessionaire and bring in more variety.

The cargo issue has primarily occurred due to the congestion on the GST Road, especially during peak hours, officials said. “Out of the two cargo terminal operators, one is operating way beyond its capacity. But AAI has acquired 19 acres of land, and this will avoid the congestion within the premises,” an official said.

AAI officials also said that they are working with Traffic Police and the State government to resolve the congestion.

World.title: DG ISPR says Makkah defence pact has 'no regional aspirations', intended for collective deterrence
World.content:
Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) Director General Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry has said that the Makkah Defence Alliance — a tripartite agreement between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye — has no “regional aspirations”, adding that it is intended for collective deterrence.

The military spokesperson made the remarks during an interview on Al Arabiya English’s programme ‘Global News Today’, during a conversation with the host, Tom Burges Watson.

During the show, aired during the early hours of Wednesday, Lt Gen Chaudhry was asked about Pakistan’s commitments under the agreement.

“It formalises Pakistan’s decades-old relationship with the kingdom of Saudi Arabia and the brotherly country of Turkiye in the domains of collective deterrence and defence,” he said.

Watson then asked whether the pact was primarily a defensive cooperation or the beginning of a broader strategic alliance. To that, Lt Gen Chaudhry asserted that the pact was defensive, as its name implied.

“It is defensive. There’s nothing aggressive. There are no regional aspirations. It is collective deterrence,” he said, adding that the agreement was also “complementary”.

Elaborating further, he said the countries part of the alliance had independent relationships with other nations, blocs and alliances.

“So this mutual defence agreement is complementary in nature. It is not competing with any other relationship of these countries,” he added.

At that, Watson asked, “But does it contain any mutual defence obligation?”

In his short reply to the question, Lt Gen Chaudhry remarked, “The text that has been made public by the leadership of the three countries enunciates that very clearly and it’s interpretation is quite clear.”

Asked how Pakistan would respond if one of the countries in the alliance came under attack, he said that the operationalisation of defensive commitments was never made public in any discourse.

“You see, you have multiple other agreements which are defensive in nature, which are committal in nature. But no country comes out and starts sharing its operational details […] What you’re asking is the how part — that how we are going to defend Pakistan against any aggression.

“That is always part of the operational classification and security […] What you’re asking is that how it will be done. It is for the three countries to decide, and it is for them to know and for them to actualise it,” he said.

Specifically asked whether the military spokesperson saw the alliance “complementing or competing” with Pakistan’s relationship with China, Lt Gen Chaudhry asserted that it complemented Islamabad-Beijing ties.

“We need to understand that the Pak-Saudi and the Pak-Turkiye relationship has not come out of the blue. The Chinese understand it. The world at large understands it. That’s how historic these relationships are. We have formalised that.

“Nobody has any problem with that. Everyone understands that this is defensive. Everyone understands it is for maintaining stability and peace in the region. And all the three countries that are part of it, they have a wonderful relationship with China,” he said.

During the interview, Lt Gen Chaudhry was also asked whether he saw the defence agreement becoming a part of the wider, Muslim-world security architecture.

He replied that there was nothing in the pact that stated that it was a Muslim alliance, adding that it was an alliance for regional stability.

“It is not a club that is being made for only Muslim countries,” he said, adding that decisions on its expansion were to be taken by the leadership of Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye.

“This agreement, this alliance can always encompass new, willing partners who also believe in regional peace, stability and security, [and] who have a shared vision of non-aggression, non-interference and collective deterrence.

“But that’s for the leadership of these three countries to decide; the how and when part,” he elaborated.

The joint defence pact was signed on Aug 7 and provides that an attack on one member state would be treated as an attack on all. Its inaugural meeting was held in Istanbul on Aug 31, where it was decided that Pakistan would initially head the alliance’s secretariat for three years.

Since its signing, there has been conversation about the possibility of its expansion, with Turkiye initially suggesting the possibility of Egypt’s inclusion. Though there has been no confirmation from Cairo.

From Pakistan, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar clarified soon after the signing that the pact was defensive in nature, with the latter saying that it was also “open to any country in the region” willing to uphold its fundamental principles.

However, when Foreign Office spokesperson Sajjah Haider Khan was asked about possibility of the pact’s expansion during a weekly media briefing last week, he said an expansion was not on the cards at that point.

The three countries first needed to solidify the new organisation before considering opening it to other states with similar threat perceptions and requirements, he explained.

US-Iran mediation and Pakistan’s ‘unique position’

During the interview, Lt Gen Chaudhry was also asked about Pakistan’s efforts to mediate between the United States and Iran and whether the Makkah Defence Alliance complicated Islamabad’s position towards Tehran.

Lt Gen Chaudhry replied such was not the case, adding that the alliance was based on decades-old strategic ties.

“This alliance is a formalisation of that strategic relationship in a peculiar environment,” he said, reiterating that the pact was based on collective deterrence. The defence pact, he said, had no offensive or aggressive element and was purely defensive in nature.

Asked why Pakistan had opted to play the role of a mediator in the ongoing Middle East conflict that began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in February, he succinctly stated, “For regional peace.”

Lt Gen Chaudhry then added that stability stemmed from peace and Pakistan was a proponent of peace in the region. Moreover, he continued, Pakistan had a “unique position” in this case because of its policy of alignment and engagement with countries across the world.

Hence, it could play the role of an “objective arbiter of peace and an honest broker of peace”.

To a question about progress on the mediation front and towards a settlement, Lt Gen Chaudhry explained that one of the prerequisites of good mediation was remaining objective and neutral.

“So it’s not for us as a mediator to start commenting on things that are happening or that are bound to happen,” he said, adding that Pakistan’s political and military leadership had been reaching out to all the parties so that “better sense prevails and, instead of a military solution, we come to a negotiated outcome of this very complex situation”.

Watson then pointed to the possibility of the US and Iran rejecting Pakistan’s proposal and asked whether Islamabad was prepared to continue its mediation in that case.

Lt Gen Chaudhry replied, “Is there any other way of resolving this conflict other than [through] mediation? Is there any other desirable way of doing that?”

He stressed the need for a “negotiated, peaceful outcome”, adding that those who could mediate objectively and sincerely between the two sides must continue their efforts.

Asked whether Pakistan was concerned about the conflict spilling over towards its western frontiers, Lt Gen Chaudhry answered that as far as Pakistan’s borders, territorial integrity and sovereignty were concerned, “we are very confident and very self-reliant on our security”.

There were always concerns of any conflict spiralling horizontally or vertically, he said, adding that not just Pakistan, but the entire world at large was feeling the impact of the conflict.

“So, there are [always] concerns in multiple domains”, but Pakistan was “fully confident of taking care of whatever nefarious designs come out of that towards” it, he said.

Asked whether Pakistan aimed to become a regional mediator or was simply trying to prevent a regional war from reaching its own doorstep, Lt Gen Chaudhry said, “Pakistan is interested in regional peace and stability, because peace and stability are essential for development, for human development, for prosperity and for the citizens of Pakistan and the region.”

And if the “mediation is for peace, […] and we’ll always be there”.

Prospects of dialogue with India

Watson then came to the brief military conflict between Pakistan and India in May last year, and asked what lessons Pakistan’s military had learned from the episode.

Lt Gen Chaudhry replied that what was more important were the lessons Pakistan and its military taught during that conflict. He said that a military conflict between two nuclear countries, especially neighbours, was “out of question”.

“It’s a sheer, I would say, a sort of mad idea,” he said, adding that Pakistan also showed that India made a “strategic folly” in May last year.

Asked whether he believed India had learned that lesson, Lt Gen Chaudhry replied it was for the Indian side to answer.

“Our job in Pakistan is to keep on reminding them of that lesson,” he said, adding that the other side had a “hubristic mindset” and the Indian military was “deeply politicised”.

In India, he continued, there was a propensity of externalising their internal problems, giving the example of minorities facing oppression.

On the other hand, he said, there was the Kashmir issue, which was an “external problem” that New Delhi wanted to “internalise through repression”.

The military’s spokesperson added that Pakistan continued to give out the message to India that it believed in “peace on equal terms” and that it was a rational and objective player.

Pakistan believes in regional peace, but if India has any “misconceptions about [imposing] regional hegemony through military aggression, results of that would be beyond their imagination”, he warned.

Lt Gen Chaudhry said Pakistan had showed India and the world in May last year that it had the capability and resolve to dominate and control an escalation.

“And we’ll do it again,” he added.

Asked whether there were any realistic prospects of restoring sustained military-to-military communication with India, Lt Gen Chaudhry said, “Yes, of course.”

He added that communication between the directors general of military operations had remained effective during the May conflict and beyond.

“Communication is always good. We must communicate, we must engage, but that engagement has to be done on equal terms while respecting each other’s integrity and sovereignty,” he said.

To a question about resuming dialogue with India, he said it was for the political leadership to decide. But dialogue, he said, had to be on equal terms.

“Dialogue cannot be, or engagement cannot be to provide a cover for the ongoing state-sponsored Indian terrorism in Pakistan, for the ongoing aggression,” he emphasised.

‘Only successful counter-terrorism campaign in the world’

Coming to Afghanistan, Watson asked about the Pakistani military’s preferred end state with the Afghan Taliban.

“I think the military’s end state is actually part of Pakistan’s end state that the political leadership sets. So, there is no separate military end state.

“So, there are Pakistan’s objectives and desire, which are primarily the domain of the Pakistan’s political leadership and an expression of the will of the people of Pakistan. And what that is that we want — no interference, no terrorism from Afghanistan in Pakistan. So that’s the foundation,” he said.

Asked what options Pakistan considered legitimate for preventing cross-border attacks in case of the failure of diplomacy, Lt Gen Chaudhry said, “Right of self-defence is enshrined in the Article 51 of the United Nations; right of self-defence is given to each nation state of the world.”

He added that the Pakistani state had an obligation to defend the lives, honour and property of its citizens. To that end, “all that is necessary will be done and is being done”.

In this connection, he detailed Pakistan’s counter-terrorism measures and said the country’s counter-terrorism campaign was the “only successful counter-terrorism campaign in the world”.

“Because we are the bulwark state against” terrorism emanating from Afghanistan, he said.

Lt Gen Chaudhry also mentioned that in the current year, 42,000 intelligence-based operations (IBOs) had been carried out and 2,100 terrorists had been killed.

Towards the programme’s end, Watson steered the discussion towards Balochistan, on which Lt Gen Chaudhry said there was no insurgency in the province.

“There’s just terrorism,” he said, adding that the military had clarity on that, tactically and strategically.

He said of the 42,000 IBOs, over 32,000 were conducted in Balochistan and security forces remained engaged in “taking out the so-called proxies who associate themselves with Balochistan and have got nothing to do with it”.

Regarding strategic clarity, he said the government, people of Balochistan and the military understood that the way to deal with terrorism was to kill terrorists and “embrace the people of Balochistan”.

World.title: Police refute KP CM's claim of 'murder' conspiracy in Wazirabad, say constable was on security duty
World.content:
Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi on Wednesday claimed that his security detail had apprehended a man allegedly sent to kill him. Gujranwala Police, however, refuted the claim, saying the detained man was a constable deployed for the chief minister’s security.

The KP chief minister has been visiting Punjab since Monday to mobilise party supporters ahead of the PTI’s nationwide protest scheduled for Sept 27.

Earlier on Wednesday, Afridi issued a video statement, which he said was recorded shortly before 5am, giving his version of events.

The KP CM alleged that hurdles were created during his stay in Sialkot, with power supplies cut off and the electricity generators at two residences he visited “ruined”. He subsequently travelled to Wazirabad.

“They had sent an assassin after us with the intention to kill. He was in civil clothes. When we arrived in Wazirabad, my security team apprehended this armed individual, recovered a pistol from him, and handed him over to the local SHO (station house officer),” he claimed.

Afridi reiterated his stance in an X post at 5:49am, saying his security team handed the “bearded man” over to SHO Saqlain after apprehending him.

The KP CM recalled that he was supposed to spend the night in Sialkot, but the electricity was “cut off”. He added that power at two other locations was also disconnected, after which he travelled to Wazirabad.

“Now, the electricity here has also been cut off. I cannot go anywhere else from here now,” the chief minister lamented.

However, in separate statements, Gujranwala Police and Wazirabad City police station said the man was Constable Muqadas Ali, who had been deployed on security duty for Afridi.

Gujranwala Police said the constable was “subjected to severe physical assault by members of the chief minister’s protection team”.

“Importantly, Constable Muqadas Ali was allegedly assaulted in the presence of the SHO City Wazirabad, who intervened and after considerable effort, managed to rescue the constable. The SHO’s presence can also be clearly seen in footage and images from the scene,” the statement said.

The police said the “misrepresentation of facts” and the constable’s “portrayal as a killer is a matter of serious concern”.

According to Gujranwala Police, following the incident, “claims portraying Constable Ali as a ‘killer’ emerged from representatives” of the KP CM.

“These claims misrepresent the facts, despite his identity having already been established at the scene and his departmental identity card having been presented.”

The police asserted that “any baseless and factually incorrect portrayal of its personnel is unacceptable”.

“Misrepresenting facts and portraying a police officer deployed on official duty as a killer is strongly condemnable,” it added.

“It is a matter of serious concern that, after the incident, the constable was allegedly portrayed as a ‘murderer’, despite his identity and official duty being established at the spot,” the statement from Wazirabad City police said.

Punjab Inf­ormation Minister Azma Bokhari also reiterated the police’s stance.

“God knows why such fits of madness strike them as soon as they reach Wazirabad,” she quipped.

On Nov 3, 2022, during PTI’s long march in Wazirabad, former premier Imran Khan and several others were injured in a gun attack, while one worker had lost his life. In 2025, a man was handed life imprisonment for the attack, while two others were acquitted.

Punjab visit

Wednesday was not the first episode of claims and counterclaims during the KP CM’s Punjab visit.

On Monday night, Afridi alleged he was “abducted” by authorities in Lahore and later “thrown” by the roadside — a claim the Punjab government swiftly denied.

In a video shared by Bokhari, Afridi could be seen voluntarily walking towards and boarding the police vehicle. He then refuses to dismount, while an individual can be heard asking the chief minister to “please leave the vehicle”.

Afridi turned his Lahore visit into a full-fledged political showdown, lashing out at the Punjab government, refusing security and vowing to rid the country of “fake rulers” through a nationwide street movement on September 27.

Speaking on Tuesday, CM Afridi alleged that Punjab police had blocked routes, arrested party workers and removed tents from a protest camp.

On its part, the Punjab government has imposed a ban on gatherings across the province from September 13 to 17.

District authorities had also issued preventive detention orders against dozens of PTI workers under Section 3 of the Maintenance of Public Order, including 31 in one Punjab notification and a further 14 in Toba Tek Singh.

Additional input from Asif Chaudhry

World.title: JI chief warns talks with govt may end after 4th round if decision on abolishing petroleum levy delayed
World.content:
KARACHI: Jamaat-i-Islami Pakistan (JI) Emir Hafiz Naeemur Rehman on Wednesday warned that ongoing talks with the government over the petroleum levy may end if the levy is not withdrawn soon.

The talks between the government and JI began on September 7 after the two sides agreed to form committees, comprising experts and leaders, to discuss recommendations for reducing the petroleum levy and providing relief to the public.

So far, three rounds of talks have been held, with the fourth round scheduled for 6pm today (Wednesday) in Islamabad.

According to a statement issued by the party, the JI chief spoke in Karachi earlier in the day, where he rejected the government’s fuel relief scheme and demanded that the levy be abolished, “rather than replaced with temporary relief schemes”.

“If the government continues delaying and does not abolish the petroleum levy, today’s talks will be the last round,” Rehman was quoted as saying, reiterating that the party will go ahead with its march to Islamabad on Sept 20.

As per the statement, Rehman said the government collected Rs1,567 billion through the petroleum levy annually but announced only Rs25bn in relief for the public.

He described the package as inadequate and questioned its proposed implementation through weekly fuel distribution, the statement added.

Rehman slammed “lockdown measures”. He added that the traders were “being pressured in the name of maintaining the system”.

As per the statement, Rehman “called for an end to the practice of revising petroleum prices daily”. He voiced concern at the “frequent revisions”, which he said created difficulties for consumers and businesses.

Speaking to the media, Rehman also outlined plans to hold “public meetings”, adding that a “large gathering” would be held in Karachi on Wednesday night, followed by rallies in Lahore on Thursday, and in Mardan and Peshawar on Friday.

“The Islamabad march will not stop,” he was quoted as saying. Rehman urged the government not to disrupt peaceful and democratic struggle, according to the statement.

Meanwhile, in a post on X, the party said that Wednesday’s round will be held in the Federal Secretariat at 6pm, with the JI delegation led by Liaquat Baloch and the government by Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal.

The government’s team will also include Adviser to the Prime Minister on Political Affairs Rana Sanaullah, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik and Minister of State for Finance Bilal Azhar Kayani.

JI has been staging regular sit-ins in Lahore, Peshawar, Karachi and dozens of other locations across the country since August 16 to protest the levy and IPP agreements.

The government levies Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel.

World.title: PHF requests AHF to shift Asian Champions Trophy out of India or relocate Pakistan matches
World.content:
The Pakistan Hockey Federation (PHF) has formally asked the Asian Hockey Federation (AHF) to move next month’s men’s Asian Champions Trophy out of India or shift all of Pakistan’s matches to a neutral venue, citing the “sensitive bilateral situation” between the two countries.

The request effectively rules out Pakistan playing their matches at the tournament’s scheduled venues in Jalandhar and Mohali unless the AHF agrees to the proposed change.

PHF president Mohyuddin Ahmed Wani, who is also federal secretary of the Ministry of Inter-Provincial Coordination, confirmed to Dawn on Wednesday that the federation had formally approached the AHF.

The development came two days after Wani had told Dawn that Pakistan’s proposed tour to India was subject to government clearance and that the PHF would abide by whatever decision the government took.

Sources in the PHF said the latest decision to seek a neutral venue had been taken on the direction of the federal government.

In an official statement issued on Wednesday, Wani said the request had been made to ensure a “safe, dignified and conducive environment” for Pakistan’s players and officials.

“The Pakistan Hockey Federation has formally requested the Asian Hockey Federation to relocate the Men’s Asian Champions Trophy 2026 tournament or shift all of Pakistan’s matches to a neutral venue,” Wani said in the statement.

The PHF chief, however, made it clear that Pakistan remained committed to the tournament and was willing to face India.

“Pakistan remains fully committed to participating in the Asian Champions Trophy and international hockey and is ready to play against all FIH member nations, including India,” he said.

The PHF president also said the federation hoped the AHF would consider the proposal positively to ensure Pakistan’s full participation in the tournament.

The request comes two days after Indian Punjab Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann said Pakistan would participate in the tournament, prompting the PHF to clarify that no decision had been taken on the team’s visit to India.

Mann, according to a Press Trust of India (PTI) report, had said Pakistan would be among the six teams competing in the Asian Champions Trophy, scheduled to be held from Oct 27 to Nov 5.

“There is no problem in multi-national tournaments. Maybe individual series [between India and Pakistan] cannot take place,” Mann said at an event in Mohali when asked about Pakistan’s participation and whether the requisite clearances had been obtained.

The tournament is scheduled to feature hosts India, Pakistan, China, Japan, Malaysia and South Korea.

Jalandhar is to host the opening ceremony and all league-stage matches from Oct 27 to Nov 2, while the semi-finals and final are scheduled to be played in Mohali on Nov 4 and 5.

Pakistan’s proposed match against India is scheduled for Nov 1 in Jalandhar.

The PHF’s latest move means that, while Pakistan is seeking to avoid playing its fixtures in India, it is not seeking to withdraw from the competition.

The federation has specifically stated that it is prepared to play India and other FIH member nations at a neutral venue.

Pakistan had also withdrawn from last year’s Junior World Cup in Tamil Nadu amid heightened tensions between the two countries.

World.title: CDF Munir, US-based POWERUS discuss defence technology, cooperation
World.content:
Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) and Chief of the Army Staff (COAS) Field Marshal Asim Munir on Wednesday discussed evolving trends in defence technology and potential areas of cooperation with United States-based defence and critical infrastructure company POWERUS, the military’s media wing said.

The meeting focused on opportunities for collaboration in defence procurement, production and capacity building, according to a statement issued by the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR).

The POWERUS delegation was led by Robert Bret Velicovich. During the meeting, CDF Munir also highlighted the “importance of technological innovation and advanced solutions in strengthening national security and resilience.”

The company, according to its website, “builds hardware and unified systems architecture that keep critical assets running in high-consequence environments.”

Both sides expressed interest in further developing engagement in areas of mutual interest, added ISPR.

In January, US and Pakistan army soldiers completed training at the National Counter-Terrorism Center during Exercise Inspired Gambit, which focused on combined infantry skills and tactics, and counterterrorism operations.

World.title: Indian delegates attempt to interrupt Ayaz Sadiq’s address at Commonwealth conference
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: Indian delegates reportedly attempted to interrupt National Assembly Speaker Ayaz Sadiq’s address at the 69th Commonwealth Parliamentary Conference in Cape Town, South Africa, as he spoke about climate adaptation and climate justice.

According to information available, the Indian delegates repeatedly sought to intervene during Sadiq’s speech, with footage showing attempts to get hold of the microphone and disrupt the proceedings.

Sadiq had raised the issue of “water terrorism” during his address without naming any country, in the context of broader concerns over climate change, water resources and climate justice.

The Indian delegates’ attempts to seize the microphone affected the atmosphere of the session, prompting direct intervention by the host and the Jamaican speaker, who asked them either to remain silent or leave the hall. Meanwhile, other participants advised the Indian delegates to listen patiently to Speaker Sadiq’s address.

Despite the disruption, the discussion on climate adaptation and climate justice continued.

In his address, Speaker Sadiq, without naming any country or delegation, presented a principled position on tackling climate change and stressed the responsibilities of the international community.

He raised issues, including the sudden surge of water in rivers and the withholding of water, without naming any country.

Speaker Sadiq said climate adaptation policies should be formulated with effective public participation, adding that oversight by democratic institutions was indispensable to policies aimed at addressing climate change.
