World.title: In praise of Mymensingh’s Bangla folk ballads
World.content:
Folk-ballads are living archives that represent the imagination, values, ideas, and aesthetics of the people to whom they belong. Bangla literature has a rich repertoire of folk ballads. We are, however, quite oblivious of this treasure trove and, therefore, there is a dearth of research on these folk elements.

Czech Indologist Dusan Zbavitel's Bengali Folk-Ballads From Mymensingh And The Problem Of Their Authenticity can be called a wonderful exception in this regard. It is considered to be the first literary study of the beautiful folk-ballads from Mymensingh. The study was published by the University of Calcutta in 1963.

A brief background of the book may not be irrelevant here. In 1923, Rai Bahadur Dineshchandra Sen edited a volume of epic songs from the Mymensingh District of the then Eastern Bengal under the title Maimansimha-gitika. The ballads were mainly collected by Chandra Kumar De, a literary activist from the area. In the following years, Dineshchandra published three more volumes of balladic texts containing epic songs from different parts of Eastern Bengal. The beautiful ballads received enthusiastic response and admiration in India and abroad. However, for some scholars these ballads were too good, and they shared doubts about the ‍antiquity, authenticity and folk character of these lores. Dusan Zbavitel found this uncertainty "highly regrettable" and undertook a study to assign to the ballads their proper place—"one of the high points of Bengali literature". Dr Zbavitel tried to find out: "what is it that makes them so excellent?"

Zbavitel confined his analysis to the study of the ballads originating in Mymensingh—41 ballads containing more than 21,000 verses. He took an arduous effort of analysing each of these 41 ballads to prove their originality and, I must say, he achieved his goal with marked success.

One key argument put forward by Zbavitel in favour of the originality of the gitikas from Mymensingh is that these ballads are not collected by a single person and, still, there are similarities among the ballads: identical images, and similar artistic approach and common inventory of similes and metaphors. So these ballads couldn't be the creation of a modern poet as suggested by some detractors.

According to Zbavitel, the most significant aspect of these folk ballads is that they are devoid of any religious implications. They generally show harmonious co-existence of the Hindu and Muslim communities, without religious bias on either side. Zbavitel points out the fact that most of the Hindu ballads were collected from Muslim singers, which shows, according to him, that these folk poems were enjoyed and appreciated by both the communities with the same eagerness. The secular outlook of the folk ballads is diametrically opposite to the explicit religious connotation of the classical Bangla literary texts such as Mangal-kavyas and Vaisnava literature.

Zbavitel extensively discusses the ideological and artistic approach of the ballad writers, verse and rhyme technique, and use of similes and metaphors in chapter three and four of the book. The most dominant motif, according to Zbavitel, is love. Even the historical and heroic epics can be grouped into this category.

As to the literary techniques, the ballad writers, being true to the characteristics of folk epics, do not try to introduce innovations in their lyrical dictions. They are content with the poetic means offered by their predecessors. They want to tell an interesting and touching story in a simple garb, fresh with country scenes and feelings.

Zbavitel also discusses the manner of preservation of the folk ballads—preserved, in most cases, in torsos. Referring to two versions of the same ballad, Maishal Bandhu, he argues, "The 'original' ballads [were] sometimes rewritten by another folk poet, or other poets, quite freely, without any scruples; whole portions, as well as individual couplets and verses, were taken over, others were replaced by newly replaced passages, and the story itself was often changed." The reasons behind such changes, according to Zbavitel, might be an effort to offer listeners a 'better' story than the original one.

Due to this oral nature of preservation, it is always difficult to prove the originality of folk elements. If we undertake an effort to study the folklore of Bangladesh, Zbavitel's book will be an invaluable companion guide.

Rabindranath Tagore wrote to Dinesh Chandra Sen in appreciation of the book Maimansimha-gitika, "Classical Bengali literary texts such as Mangal-kavyas are ponds dug on by order and at the expense of the rich, but Maimansimha-gitika is a source of exuberance from the deepest level of the heart of rural Bengal, a clear stream of genuine pain. There has never been such a creation of self-forgetting rasa [aesthetic joy] in Bengali literature." [translation by the author]

While celebrating the Bengali new year this Pohela Boishakh, may we remember the melody and the essence of communal harmony embedded in Maimansimha-gitika.

Shamsuddoza Sajen is a journalist and researcher. He can be contacted at [email protected].

World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

Supreme Court puts controversial parliamentary rules on hold

The court says two provisions in the House of Representatives rules may conflict with constitutional safeguards on amending the constitution and the authority of existing laws.

The Supreme Court building. File Photo

World.title: Sudurpaschim set to get cable car in its largest private-sector project
World.content:
Sudurpaschim set to get cable car in its largest private-sector project

The Rs7 billion Jalpa Devi Cable Car is expected to begin operations in November, linking Chisapani with Rajkanda in the Chure hills and opening up a new tourism destination in far-western Nepal.

The cable car will stretch 3.1 kilometres from Chisapani in Lamkichuha Municipality-3, Kailali, to Rajkanda in Mohanyal Rural Municipality-7. Post Photo

World.title: Deuba loses support as Nepali Congress factions realign
World.content:
Deuba loses support as Nepali Congress factions realign

The Thapa-led Congress has scheduled the 15th general convention for October 2-5, with ward-level conventions beginning on September 19. Deuba faction has its general convention scheduled for December 7-9.

More than 30 leaders who had been aligned with Deuba are moving towards the central working committee led by party president Gagan Thapa after the party agreed to accommodate members of the central committee elected under Deuba’s leadership. Photo: Nepal Photo Library

World.content:
Families of missing foreign nationals want answers Nepal can’t give

Hundreds of foreigners remain unaccounted for as families press for cross-border searches, clearer information and official confirmation of their relatives’ status.

Dmitrii Tretiakov, brother of missing Russian national Kirill Tretiakov, studies a map during a search for his brother following the recent floods. Photo: Courtesy of Vichitra jain

World.title: English village votes to ‘secede’ from U.K. over asylum center plan
World.content:
An English village of around 350 people announced Wednesday that a vast majority of residents had voted to exit the U.K. in an “independence referendum” in protest at plans to house over 1,200 migrants in a nearby facility.

Piddington in central England, 25 kilometers from the university city of Oxford, has grabbed headlines with its tongue-in-cheek breakaway vote.

The village’s parish council announced that with 312 ballots counted, 285 had voted to secede from Britain over plans to house asylum seekers in a nearby disused military site, in a symbolic vote with no recognized legal basis.

World.title: Former Philippine leader Duterte appears before ICC judges for first time
World.content:
Former Philippines President Rodrigo Duterte appeared in the courtroom on Wednesday for the first time since being transferred to the International Criminal Court 18 months ago to face murder charges regarding his war on drugs.

Duterte, 81, served as president from 2016 to 2022, before being charged with crimes against humanity for setting up, funding and arming death squads that targeted narcotics peddlers and users. He was arrested and taken to The Hague in March 2025.

Dressed in a black suit and white shirt, Duterte did not speak in court, but sat quietly sipping water during the proceedings. He stood and waved to family members in the public gallery.

“We’re happy that he has finally appeared and that he looks OK. In fact, he looks like he has put on weight,” said Llore Pasco, whose two sons were killed during Duterte’s war on drugs, watching a television broadcast of the hearings from Manila.

In court, presiding Judge Joanna Korner asked prosecutors to find ways to shorten the trial, set to begin in November, due to the defendant’s age and health.

“It’s important this trial goes ahead as quickly as possible,” she said, pressing parties to limit the number of witnesses and focus on key evidence.

Duterte’s attorney, Peter Haynes, called disclosure by the prosecution “enormous and impossible” and said his team could never examine tens of thousands of pieces of evidence in time.

“If I had a younger and healthier client, I would request pushing back the trial by six months,” he said.

Details of Duterte’s condition were not discussed in open court Wednesday, but his lawyers have said he suffers from cognitive decline that affects his memory and daily functioning, and is not well enough.

In January, ICC judges said Duterte’s health was good enough for him to follow proceedings and requested his presence in court, rather than by video link from the detention unit.

The warrant for Duterte says he was responsible for a widespread and systematic campaign that led to thousands of killings between 2011 and 2019, including his time as the mayor of the southern city of Davao.

ICC prosecutors have said as many as 30,000 people may have been killed in the crackdown.

Police said 6,200 suspects were killed during anti-drug operations. Duterte said he instructed police to act in self-defence and told supporters he was ready to “rot in jail” if it meant ridding the Philippines of illicit drugs.

World.title: Two firms show interest in spent nuclear fuel facility
World.content:
Kansai Electric Power and Tohoku Electric Power have expressed an intention to use an interim storage facility for spent nuclear fuel in Mutsu, Aomori Prefecture, people familiar with the matter said Wednesday.

The facility currently accepts spent nuclear fuel only from Tokyo Electric Power Company Holdings and Japan Atomic Power. Securing storage capacity for growing amounts of spent nuclear fuel has become an urgent issue as nuclear reactors resume operations across the country.

Tepco is expected to report the intentions of Kansai Electric and Tohoku Electric to local governments on Friday, but it is uncertain whether they will be allowed to use the facility.

Tepco and Japan Atomic said last December that they wanted to begin considering having the Mutsu facility accept spent fuel from nuclear plants operated by other companies, after they determined that spent fuel from their own plants would fall short of the amount expected to be stored at the facility under initial plans.

After Mutsu Mayor Tomoya Yamamoto gave the go-ahead with the move last month, Tepco and Japan Atomic asked eight other Japanese power firms that operate nuclear plants whether they wanted to use the facility.

But Aomori Gov. Soichiro Miyashita has said that adding companies to the list of nuclear plant operators that use the interim storage facility was “not envisaged under the agreement” with local governments hosting the facility.

Kansai Electric currently stores spent fuel in pools at its Mihama, Oi and Takahama nuclear power plants in Fukui Prefecture. Between 80% and 90% of the pools’ storage capacity is already filled, and the pools are expected to reach maximum capacity between fiscal 2028 and fiscal 2030.

The company plans to build a dry storage facility to secure sufficient capacity for the time being, and begin transporting the spent fuel out of Fukui by the end of 2035.

At Tohoku Electric, spent fuel pools at its Onagawa nuclear plant in Miyagi Prefecture are expected to reach maximum capacity around November 2028. The company plans to start building a dry storage facility this month and begin operating it in March 2028.

A nuclear fuel reprocessing plant in Rokkasho, Aomori Prefecture, to which spent fuel stored at the Mutsu facility is eventually expected to be transported, remains under construction and its completion has been repeatedly postponed.

World.title: LNG market faces extended Hormuz outage, Japanese shipper says
World.content:
Mitsui OSK Lines, a top Japanese shipping firm, doesn’t expect LNG shipments through the Strait of Hormuz to resume soon, signaling a prolonged disruption that could keep prices elevated and curb demand across Asia.

“As long as this situation continues, it’s almost impossible to carry the LNG cargoes” through Hormuz, Chairman Takeshi Hashimoto said on the sidelines at the Gastech conference in Bangkok on Wednesday. “At the moment, we are quite pessimistic about the near future.”

He said that a peace deal settlement among the parties looks “very, very difficult.” MOL, as the company is called, has stopped sending liquefied natural gas tankers through Hormuz, a strategic waterway that carried about a fifth of global supply before the conflict began.

The disruption has pushed Asian spot LNG prices to their highest level since 2022, with the potential for further gains as winter approaches and heating demand rises. The price surge is already prompting many buyers in Asia to scale back purchases, Hashimoto said.

“People are saying that there are alternative energy supplies possible from the U.S., Canada, Australia or parts of Africa,” he said. “But obviously it would not be enough to cover demand.”

World.title: False Tamaki info reposted mostly by X users outside Okinawa
World.content:
Almost all reposts of an online post containing false information about Okinawa Gov. Denny Tamaki, who failed to secure re-election in Sunday’s gubernatorial race, were made by social media users outside the prefecture, an analysis showed Wednesday.

The false X post made at around 10 a.m. on July 26 claimed that Tamaki had decided to relocate U.S. Marine Corps Air Station Futenma in the city of Ginowan to the Henoko coastal area in Nago.

The post in question also claimed that the campaign against the base relocation was a publicity stunt orchestrated by Tamaki.

It was also structured, at first glance, to make it appear, with a photo, that Tamaki himself had described the relocation decision as a “brilliant decision.”

The number of reposts stood at 54 in the first hour after the original post appeared on X, snowballing to over 1,300 reposts in three hours, over 3,600 reposts in six hours and over 9,000 reposts within 24 hours, according to a survey using social media analysis tool Brandwatch.

Locations of social media users could be deduced for a total of 1,927 reposts made within the first 24 hours through their profiles, social media messages and current location information.

A total of 98.8% of such reposts were made by social media users outside Okinawa, with those in Tokyo accounting for over 60%. The number of such posts made from Okinawa stood at only 24, or 1.2% of the total.

Contrary to what the post said, there is no evidence that Tamaki had decided to relocate the base. The “brilliant decision” remark was found unrelated to the base relocation.

While some social media posts were made the following day or after to point out the factual errors, even the most widespread such post only had about 600 reposts in the first 24 hours.

In August, Japan Fact-Check Center, a nonprofit organization, concluded that the post in question was “false.”

Genta Koja, who won the gubernatorial election and is set to become Okinawa’s new governor on Sept. 30, was also caught up in a social media misinformation issue.

His camp came out to say that it had not created an election poster-like image that was doing the rounds on X. The “poster,” with Koja’s photo, said that he would aim to create an Okinawa that serves the national interest.

During the election campaign period between Aug. 27 and Sunday, about 1.67 million posts on X contained the words “Okinawa gubernatorial election.” Of about 360,000 posts whose location of origin could be deduced, about 95% were from outside Okinawa.

World.title: AI can supercharge Putin’s goals, not his great-power ambitions
World.content:
When Russian President Vladimir Putin imposed harsh censorship laws in the wake of his 2022 invasion of Ukraine, a major Russian publishing house took drastic action.

Faced with trawling through the thousands of volumes it had published over the previous 20 years in light of the new restrictive criteria, the Eksmo-AST group trained an artificial intelligence agent to highlight books and passages that risked falling foul of the law so they could be removed from bookshelves.

The publisher conducted some 20,000 checks, and 600 volumes were handed over to external experts for additional reviews, Oleg Novikov, the group’s president, told Russian state television. “We’re here on the frontier of technological progress,” he said.

World.title: Drop in Chinese visitors drives decline in Japan’s inbound tourism in August
World.content:
Japan received 3.1 million foreign visitors in August, down 9.6% from the same month last year, mainly due to a sharp plunge of Chinese visitors, according to estimates from the Japan National Tourism Organization (JNTO) released Wednesday.

Arrivals from China, one of Japan’s largest tourism markets, fell by 59.0% to 418,000. JNTO said the decline reflected cuts to air services following a Chinese government advisory urging people to avoid travel to Japan, despite the high number of visitors from other countries during the summer school holiday period.

Some markets weakened because August is typically a quieter period for Japan-bound travel, with flight cancellations due to tropical storms, and reduced air services also weighing on arrivals, the organization said. Visitors from Australia fell 7.4% year on year, Thailand fell 9.3%, Germany declined 5.5% and the Philippines dropped 11.6%.

The sharp drop in Chinese visitors contrasted with continued growth from several other major markets.

South Korean arrivals jumped 28.7% to 850,500, the highest figure on record for August, helped by school holidays, increased airline capacity and sustained demand for travel to Japan, the organization said.

Visitors from Taiwan rose 7.3% to 666,000, while those from Hong Kong climbed 9.4% to 247,300, with both markets also posting August records.

The JNTO said 14 countries and regions recorded their highest-ever August visitor numbers, including Malaysia, India, the United States, Mexico, France and several European markets.

Italy and Spain posted their highest monthly visitor totals on record for any month. Arrivals from Italy rose 15.1% to 47,300, while Spain increased 14.1% to 36,500.

U.S. visitors edged up 1.5% to 197,400, while arrivals from Mexico surged 37% to 18,600.

The JNTO said the yen remained weak against many currencies through August, supporting demand from overseas. However, longer flight times from Europe caused by route changes linked to the war in Ukraine continue to act as a potential deterrent.

Separately, 1.59 million Japanese people traveled overseas in August, down 3.6% from a year earlier.

World.title: Over 60% of Japanese firms with foreign workers would struggle without overseas hiring: survey
World.content:
Nearly two-thirds of Japanese companies employing overseas workers say their operations would be disrupted if they became unable to recruit more, according to survey results released Tuesday.

The survey was conducted by the Japan Chamber of Commerce and Industry and the Tokyo Chamber of Commerce and Industry from July 21 to Aug. 21 among chamber-member companies across all 47 prefectures.

Of the respondents, 60.0% said they were short-staffed, with the highest rates found in construction (at 77.4%), transportation (72.2%) and nursing and healthcare (70.5%).

World.title: Hong Kong targets gold trading, FPS-UnionPay link to boost yuan use
World.content:
Hong Kong will expand the use of the yuan in areas including gold trading and cross-border payments, as policy blueprints call for the city’s biggest push yet to internationalise the Chinese currency.

Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu on Wednesday devoted part of the city’s first five-year plan and his annual policy address to developing a gold trading ecosystem and creating a regional intellectual property trading centre in the city.

“We will consolidate and enhance Hong Kong’s status as an international financial centre, and stay committed to our global positioning,” the city leader said.

“Hong Kong will deepen the development of its global offshore renminbi business and capital market, develop an international asset and wealth management centre and international risk management centre, enhance the securities market and expand fixed-income and commodity trading.”

World.title: Hong Kong aims to raise innovation spending to 3% of GDP by about 2030
World.content:
Hong Kong will strive to raise its expenditure on innovation activities to a level equivalent to 3 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP) by around 2030, nearly double the current rate, according to the city’s first five-year plan.

Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu unveiled the ambitious goal, together with measures to boost frontier technologies, including aerospace research, on Wednesday.

Among the 22 indicators laid out in the plan, the government aims to raise the ratio of total domestic expenditure on innovation activities to GDP from 1.63 per cent in 2024 to 3 per cent around 2030.

The government expects the increase in average annual expenditure on innovation activities to be around 10 per cent.

World.title: Police arrest man after wife found dead with knife wounds in Heng Fa Chuen
World.content:
Hong Kong police have arrested a man on suspicion of murder after his wife was found dead in a flat at a private residential estate.

The force said the woman, 53, was discovered with knife wounds to her neck in a flat in block 2 of Heng Fa Chuen in Chai Wan at about 7.50pm on Wednesday, a police spokesman said.

She was confirmed dead at the scene.

Hong Kong police arrive at the scene. Photo: Handout

Officers arrested the man, 52, and announced that an investigation was under way.

Heng Fa Chuen is a major private waterfront residential estate built directly above the MTR depot in Hong Kong’s Eastern district.

World.title: Hong Kong sets 5-year plan to double innovation spending, boost new industries
World.content:
Hong Kong’s leader has unveiled the city’s first five-year blueprint , aligned with China’s national development strategy, setting targets to nearly double innovation spending and raise the share of manufacturing and new industries to 5.5 per cent of the economy.

In a historically significant new approach, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu prefaced his annual policy address on Wednesday with a comprehensive set of binding and anticipatory or aspirational longer-term targets for Hong Kong up to the year 2030.

The two documents would go hand in hand, Lee said, promising to take the city’s economic development to the next level by creating a new innovation engine in the Northern Metropolis megaproject, while building on Hong Kong’s strengths in finance, aviation, maritime services, trade and technology.

He also focused on improving living standards and social well-being, announcing initiatives ranging from higher baby bonuses to encourage childbirth and increased healthcare spending to more subsidised housing and shorter waiting times for public flats.

World.title: Hong Kong leader vows support for media’s global reach, to review TV practice code
World.content:
Hong Kong’s leader has expressed renewed support for the local media industry, including strengthening its global reach and reviewing the code of practice for television to ensure it keeps abreast with the times.

Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu made the pledges in both the city’s first five-year plan and the policy address he unveiled on Wednesday.

In the section on “Develop an East-meets-West Centre for International Cultural Exchange” under the five-year plan, Lee said: “We will strengthen the global reach of the mainstream media”.

And in the part discussing measures to strengthen the city’s status as an international trade centre in the policy address, Lee said: “The government will continue to assist the local media to expand their network beyond Hong Kong, telling the good stories of Hong Kong.”

World.title: Hong Kong to offer ‘attractive’ merger deals for schools beyond those struggling
World.content:
Hong Kong education authorities will offer a “very attractive” proposal and policy support to encourage schools without survival issues to merge amid the shrinking student population, according to official sources.

The government said it might allow aided schools and semi-private Direct Subsidy Scheme (DSS) schools to merge and operate across two campuses, though all arrangements remained subject to the forthcoming announcement of further details.

Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu announced that the government would launch the “Confluence and Elevation – School Excellence Project” for publicly funded schools in the 2026-27 school year.

“This will encourage and support mergers of suitable publicly funded primary and secondary schools, consolidating resources and raising the quality of education,” he said.

World.title: Hong Kong’s new training visa could be available in first quarter of 2027
World.content:
A new visa intended to attract international talent to participate in short-term training programmes in Hong Kong could become available as early as the first quarter of next year, the South China Morning Post has learned.

The final policy address of Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu’s current term also put the spotlight on five existing or soon-to-launch academies that would seek to train overseas professionals and organise international events.

They and the new visa category were among a spate of talent-trawling measures unveiled on Wednesday, with the latter allowing non-locals to take part in government-recognised training programmes lasting less than 12 months.

“It will advance Hong Kong’s development into a regional training hub,” an insider said.

World.title: Hong Kong targets film tourism boom and higher-level tennis tournaments
World.content:
Hong Kong will introduce themed tourism routes showcasing the city’s most recognisable filming locations and explore upgrading Victoria Park’s Centre Court to host higher-level tennis tournaments, as authorities seek to significantly increase the sector’s economic contribution under the city’s first five-year development plan.

The 2026-30 blueprint aims to raise the tourism industry’s value added from HK$86.2 billion (US$10.9 billion) in 2024 to HK$126 billion by 2030 – an increase of about 40 to 50 per cent. It also targets increasing the proportion of non-mainland Chinese visitors among overnight travellers to 40 per cent by the end of the decade.

Among the more immediate measures unveiled alongside the plan in Wednesday’s policy address were a series of “+ Tourism” initiatives aimed at combining travel with mega-events, finance, industrial brands, ecological conservation and heritage.

02:32 Key takeaways from Hong Kong’s first five-year plan and 2026 policy address: from the Northern Metropolis to babies and employment

The government will also promote film tourism, yacht tourism, urban renewal and homestay accommodation on outlying islands.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019029/Token of Trust: Beijing Links AI Usage to Company Loans
World.title: Token of Trust: Beijing Links AI Usage to Company Loans
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019029/Token of Trust: Beijing Links AI Usage to Company Loans
World.content:
A zone in Beijing has launched a program asking several banks to extend billions of yuan in credit to multiple companies across the AI industry chain, partly based on their token usage.

Termed “token loans,” the financing scheme was recently implemented by the Beijing Economic and Technological Development Zone, also known as Beijing E-Town, in the city’s southeast, and involves extending nearly 2 billion yuan ($300 million) in credit to several AI companies, domestic media reported Monday.

A token is the smallest unit of data an AI large language model can process. In March, the National Data Administration officially adopted “ciyuan” — combining “word” and “currency” — as the Chinese term for “token.” The move was largely seen as putting an economic spin on AI-led computing power.

In June of this year, China’s daily token consumption already exceeded 500 trillion, according to data from the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology. A Saturday report by the China Telecom Research Institute estimates that that number could rise to 100 quadrillion, or 200 times that figure by year-end.

Six domestic banks, including the Agricultural Bank of China, China CITIC Bank, Industrial Bank, Bank of Beijing, China Minsheng Bank, and Huaxia Bank, provided the loans. The credit is intended for AI companies with “high research investment and high technological barriers,” as well as growing computing needs, but without the physical assets or profits typically required to obtain bank financing.

In addition to token consumption, the banks also awarded the loans based on technological barriers, team strength, and companies’ business development prospects.

Guoqi Zhikong, a developer of automobile-focused connected cloud platforms and autonomous driving vehicles, received a 30-million-yuan credit line from China CITIC Bank. Meanwhile, Shenzhou Guangda, which provides computing infrastructure and enterprise-level AI agent solutions, received the same credit amount from Industrial Bank.

The rapid growth of the AI industry has created a dilemma for tech startups, which often struggle to obtain traditional loans, an anonymous staff member from Beijing E-Town’s business and finance bureau told domestic media. Conventional lending models rely heavily on collateral and corporate profit statements, so even companies with strong technological capabilities often lack physical assets to pledge. In contrast, their opportunities for technological development and business expansion are constrained by profits that have yet to fully materialize.

In August, Bank of China’s branch in the southern city of Guangzhou launched the country’s first token loan scheme. Aimed at small- and medium-sized computing companies, it covers token supply, applications, and related services, with successful applicants eligible for up to 30 million yuan in credit.

Looking ahead, Lou Feipeng, a researcher at the Postal Savings Bank of China, said that before such loans can be adopted more broadly, the country must address several major issues, including exaggerated token-use data, inaccurate assessments of computing power consumption, and overestimation of borrowers’ repayment ability.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018999/From Monkey Kings to Little Demons: China’s New Age of the Supporting Character
World.title: From Monkey Kings to Little Demons: China’s New Age of the Supporting Character
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018999/From Monkey Kings to Little Demons: China’s New Age of the Supporting Character
World.content:
In the classic Chinese novel “Journey to the West,” little demons are nobodies. They serve powerful demon kings, perform menial tasks, and are easily dispatched by heroes like Sun Wukong, better known as the Monkey King. Most do not even have names.

But increasingly, these once-forgotten characters are moving to the center of the story. Across Chinese films, TV shows, games, and books, little demons are being transformed from anonymous supporting characters into protagonists in their own right.

Take Black Myth: Wukong, the Chinese AAA video game that became a global hit. The game features a compendium of 203 supernatural creatures, including 90 classified as “little demons,” each with its own biographical profile. It is almost like an archive assembled from the gaps in “Journey to the West,” a who’s who of forgotten characters.

Another example is 2024’s “The Great Nobody,” a Chinese comedy series spinoff that grew out of the variety show “Amazing Night.” In it, a group of little demons living on the fictional Flower Neck Mountain waits in vain for the monk Tang Sanzang and his disciples to arrive on their pilgrimage to retrieve Buddhist scriptures. The reworking of the classic tale becomes a commentary on supporting comedians struggling to make their mark in the entertainment industry.

But perhaps the most striking example is “Nobody,” a Chinese animated film that grossed 1.7 billion yuan ($240 million) at the box office last summer. Expanded from the first episode of “Yao-Chinese Folktales,” an animated anthology series released on the video platform Bilibili in 2023, the film follows a “knock-off” pilgrimage team of demons comprising a pig, a toad, a weasel, and a gorilla.

Seen in the broader history of “Journey to the West” adaptations, this renewed interest in little demons represents the third major approach to interpreting the classic since the turn of the millennium.

The first was what might be called “post-revolutionary interpretations.” Emerging in the late 1990s, this approach is represented by Stephen Chow’s “A Chinese Odyssey” (1995) and the online novel “The Legend of Wukong,” which began serialization in 2000. These works focused on Sun Wukong’s struggle for individual autonomy, symbolized by his decision over whether to don the golden headband, a device used by Tang Sanzang to rein in his mischievous nature. At their core was the tragic rebellion of the neoliberal individual against the grand narrative of the pilgrimage, as well as a playful deconstruction of earlier “revolutionary” interpretations of “Journey to the West.”

The second consisted of “gothic interpretations,” represented by films including “Journey to the West: Conquering the Demons” (2013), “The Monkey King 2” (2016), and “Journey to the West: The Demons Strike Back” (2017). Through digital spectacle, these films created fantastical worlds and recast the classic as a monster movie. Their dark, horror-filled atmosphere can be seen as a cultural expression of the crisis of neoliberalism.

The third approach is what I call “system-based interpretations.” These works portray the Heavenly Palace and Vulture Peak, the respective seats of the Taoist and Buddhist hierarchies, as parts of a vast network of relationships. Tang Sanzang and his disciples’ pilgrimage to obtain the scriptures becomes a meticulously planned project, while the 81 trials they encounter along the way are recast as conspiracies orchestrated by the powers that be.

Ma Boyong’s bestselling novel “The Annoyance of the Gods” (2023), for example, portrays Taibai Jinxing, a deity associated with the planet Venus, as a project manager exhausted by office politics. In doing so, the novel reframes the pilgrimage as an internal struggle within a sprawling bureaucracy characterized by maneuvering, competition, and checks and balances.

The focus on little demons emerged from this same “system-based” approach. Rather than subverting the logic of the original text, these works stand in the shadows of its grand narrative and construct detailed accounts of the lives of those who remain nameless.

This interpretation is closely connected to the current social mood. Since 2020, growing uncertainty has weakened faith in nixi, or the idea that ordinary people can beat the odds and dramatically improve their fortunes. As economic growth has slowed, such aspirations have increasingly given way to greater empathy for ordinary workers simply trying to get by.

If the era in which little demons were ignored corresponded to a period of economic expansion, when workers believed they too could “retrieve the scriptures and achieve Buddhahood,” then the era of empathizing with them belongs to the period after that peak. Ordinary people stuck on the periphery of systems recognize themselves in these little demons: operating at the margins, with limited control over events, and little guarantee that their efforts will be rewarded.

Take “Nobody,” for example. Close-ups of the little demons’ vacant eyes and sluggish expressions reflect the mental state of some workers today. Their circumstances , to a certain extent, closely mirror contemporary workplaces: routine and often modest tasks, represented by scrubbing pots and making arrows; shifting expectations and promises that do not always materialize; and the risk of being treated primarily as a functional part of a larger operation.

Identification with these little demons reflects a changing sense of where ordinary workers locate themselves within larger systems. Rather than always imagining themselves as protagonists destined to rise above their circumstances, they may find greater resonance in supporting characters who navigate constraints, make compromises, and carve out limited forms of agency within the roles available to them.

This sense of being a supporting character also underlies the popular idea that “the world is just a ragtag troupe.” Some individuals may struggle to fully identify with the current situation while also finding it difficult to imagine viable alternatives. For those who remain within these structures, a common response is to learn how the rules operate and navigate the available room within them in order to maintain a workable position.

This shift toward accepting a supporting role has already manifested in forms of spectatorship common online. “Roasting” other people’s stories allows individuals to mock them from a safe distance while releasing some of the psychological pressure they themselves face.

Posting “bullet comments” that scroll across videos in real time creates a more distanced form of viewing while giving spectators a sense of collective belonging. “Eating melon,” a Chinese internet expression for following gossip and online drama as a bystander, similarly turns public events into spectator entertainment. Rather than emphasizing individual agency, these forms of spectatorship encourage people to watch from the sidelines.

This consciousness has also spread into contemporary cultural production, with little demons being just one example. In the 2024 web novel “The Diary of a Female Zombie’s Hiking Adventure,” the protagonist has no desire to become involved in other people’s storylines and instead chooses simply to observe. Meanwhile, in the animated film “Chang An” (2023), the figure who guides the audience through the splendor of the Tang dynasty (618–907) is the diligent and orderly poet Gao Shi rather than Li Bai, the personality who most fully embodies the era’s poetic spirit. Through Gao Shi’s eyes, Li Bai’s wildness and romanticism are viewed with a sense of incomprehension and detachment.

The audiences for these works are people navigating rapid social change, uncertainty, and shifting forms of connection. They are not merely digital natives, but individuals searching for a sense of place and meaning in this “era of supporting characters.”

Translator: David Ball.

(Header image: Visuals from Douban and VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019024/After Beijing Bowel Accident, Hyrox Changes Its Rules
World.title: After Beijing Bowel Accident, Hyrox Changes Its Rules
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019024/After Beijing Bowel Accident, Hyrox Changes Its Rules
World.content:
Hyrox has amended its official rulebooks after the winner of a recent Beijing event experienced bowel incontinence mid-race yet continued competing. The incident sparked widespread debate in China over sportsmanship and the organizer’s handling of potential hygiene risks.

On Monday, Hyrox updated its online rulebook to state that a race director may withdraw an athlete if their “blood, vomit, urine, or faeces pose a welfare or contamination risk to the racer or to other racers.”

The change comes in the wake of controversy surrounding the women’s solo elite race on Saturday, in which Australian athlete and Hyrox world record holder Joanna Wietrzyk finished first with a time of 1:01:23. Footage circulating online showed fecal matter staining Wietrzyk’s clothing and legs as she performed various exercises.

Hyrox has recently surged in popularity across China. Founded in Germany, the sport features eight 1-kilometer runs, each followed by strength training stations including sled pulls, rowing, and burpees. China’s first official race was held in Beijing in 2024 and drew 1,700 entries. Participants at this weekend’s Beijing event exceeded 11,000, with standard individual registration costing roughly 800 yuan ($125).

Competitors and social media users questioned organizers’ decision to let Wietrzyk continue racing. The Women’s Pro division won by Wietrzyk began at 2:40 p.m. Saturday, with other heats scheduled until 8:40 p.m. and another full day of competition Sunday.

“As someone who works in the public health sector, my biggest concern is that if she had a bacterial or viral infection, contamination like this could spread pathogens very quickly,” a Beijing-based athlete in her 20s, surnamed Wang, whose race began about an hour after Wietrzyk, told Sixth Tone.

Toilets were available at the venue, she noted, but using the bathroom counts toward an athlete’s total race time.

In a post made via its official account on microblogging platform Weibo Saturday night, Hyrox’s China division said organizers had “immediately” closed and disinfected affected areas and removed contaminated equipment. Wang said she had seen nothing “noticeably unusual” on the course.

Wietrzyk later posted an Instagram Story of herself receiving an intravenous infusion from what appeared to be a hospital. An accompanying caption read: “a win is a win.”

This drew further criticism from some Chinese social media users, who saw the remark as dismissive of concerns over other competitors’ health and safety.

Italian Hyrox pro-athlete Sara Gandola, who competed in the same race, told Sixth Tone that Wietrzyk should not be blamed for the incident.

Gandola said the responsibility of athletes is to perform at their highest level within the rules, while “it is the sport’s responsibility to set those rules and define what is acceptable.”

“If you disagree with the rules, debate the rules,” she said. “But attacking an athlete for doing exactly what elite athletes are supposed to do is completely backward.”

On Monday, Hyrox’s global headquarters issued a statement on Instagram, describing the incident as an “unforeseen situation” and adding that those who threatened its athletes would be permanently banned from future events.

However, Chinese social media users criticized their stance for not directly acknowledging failures in how it handled the incident at the time.

Later that day, Hyrox China admitted on Weibo that the incident exposed “shortcomings” in its competition rules and said it had proposed revisions to its global headquarters. The previous Hyrox rulebook imposes a two-minute penalty for littering, spitting, or blowing one’s nose onto the floor, but does not address fecal incontinence.

Hyrox China added that the venue’s carpets had been replaced and that the entire venue had been deep-cleaned overnight, pledging to disinfect both venues before future events and any shared equipment.

Hyrox co-founder Moritz Fürste also issued an apology via Instagram on Monday, admitting that “Hyrox made a mistake by not reacting immediately during the race.”

In a Sunday commentary, Chinese state broadcaster CCTV said the incident highlighted a growing tension between the “rapid expansion” of commercial sporting events and “gaps in competition rules.”

Additional reporting: Xie Anran; editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019025/The Chinese Dating App Promising Marriage — or Your Money Back
World.title: The Chinese Dating App Promising Marriage — or Your Money Back
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019025/The Chinese Dating App Promising Marriage — or Your Money Back
World.content:
A new Chinese dating app is betting that AI can do more than keep users chatting — it wagers it can see them married in three years or less.

If it fails, the team behind Liangpei — roughly “good match” in Chinese — promises to refund the user’s one-time fee of 2,000 yuan ($275). The guarantee comes as marriage rates fall in China, with only 6.76 million couples tying the knot in 2025, about half the number a decade earlier.

Launched this past July, Liangpei begins with a roughly 20-minute voice conversation with an AI matchmaker. Users answer 25 questions about their relationship history, marriage plans, and even whether they intend to buy property. The system then uses their answers to build a detailed profile, calculate compatibility scores, and recommend potential partners.

Once two people match, they can talk only until one decides to move on, a restriction the app’s developers say is intended to keep them focused on one relationship rather than constantly searching for alternatives.

“We want to get the users off the platform as soon as possible,” founder Zeng Xinxun told Sixth Tone.

Before launching Liangpei, the 32-year-old worked on AI search technology at Kimi, one of China’s best-known generative AI platforms. His 18-person team now uses similar technology to draw out information that basic dating-app tags such as age, occupation, and location cannot capture.

Approximately 91% of users who start Liangpei’s interview finish it, Zeng said, going on to create profiles averaging 516 Chinese characters, about four times as long as those on several major Chinese dating apps.

About one in 10 users has reached an exclusive one-on-one match, according to Zeng. Those conversations last more than 10 days on average and run to more than 200 messages.

“One-on-one allows both parties to invest more focus and effort into building a relationship,” Zeng said. “Even if it doesn’t work out, it’s a conclusion reached after genuine communication.”

So far, he said, Liangpei has more than 9,300 active users across 300 cities. Men account for 57% of users, and women 43%. The two largest age groups are 26 to 28 and 29 to 31.

China’s established dating and social platforms operate at a much larger scale. Tantan, one of the country’s oldest dating apps, had 10.7 million monthly active users in March 2025, while Soul draws large audiences with broader offerings that combine dating, social discovery, entertainment, and shared interests.

Liangpei also requires real-name registration, a marital status check, and live photo verification. The company has blocked 487 people found to be married, Zeng said. It also uses AI to watch for signs of fraud once conversations begin.

Wang, a Shanghai-based user who asked to be identified only by her surname for privacy reasons, has tried more than 10 dating apps. Liangpei was the first on which she was willing to answer so many questions.

“It has helped me understand myself better and clarified exactly what I’m looking for,” she said.

Within a week, Wang entered an exclusive one-on-one match. She said the format made online dating less exhausting and allowed her to focus on getting to know her counterpart. But with no other matches to turn to, the arrangement depended on that person keeping the conversation alive.

“Once matched, your slot is locked,” Wang said. “If the other person isn’t proactive, you’re left waiting with nowhere for the conversation to go.”

On Xiaohongshu, the lifestyle app also known as RedNote, Liangpei has drawn sharply mixed reactions. Some users described it as a welcome option for people anxious about finding a spouse, while others questioned whether treating marriage as a fixed target made dating too rigid.

Free users can send only one “like” a day, according to posts reviewed by Sixth Tone. The app also prominently displays compatibility scores, which some users said made them more reluctant to start conversations.

Despite the compatibility score, several users admitted they still ended up judging potential partners by appearance.

Three-year itch

Six years ago, Zeng said he became frustrated trying to meet someone online — a period that lasted a year. He wrote a lengthy profile, but few people seemed to read it, and even fewer replied.

“Profiles were too bare to spark interest,” he said. Zeng eventually expanded his own to around 2,000 Chinese characters, then came across a woman whose profile was just as detailed.

“We quickly went from strangers to a close connection,” Zeng said. By the time they met in person, he thought the relationship might go somewhere.

They are now married. And Liangpei uses that same outcome as its measure of success.

His team had considered a first date or the start of a relationship instead. Marriage, Zeng said, was different: “It’s legally verifiable and undisputed.”

The three-year cutoff came after his team interviewed 150 couples obtaining marriage licenses at a civil affairs bureau in the southern city of Shenzhen. More than 70% said they had married within three years of meeting, Zeng said.

Liangpei has been operating for only a few months, so none of its users have yet to reach that deadline. For now, the company is reviewing the data it does have, including whether higher compatibility scores are associated with more likes, replies, and longer conversations.

“For example, among 1,500 users in Shenzhen, the AI can directly rank the top 10 people most likely to succeed with you,” Zeng said. “You don’t have to browse everyone — just start with the highest scores.”

To address relationship anxiety, Liangpei offers an “icebreaker” feature that suggests questions when a conversation stalls. An “AI wingman” can also analyze an exchange and offer advice.

But the “AI wingman” will not compose replies. Zeng said someone who struggles with online banter might still make a good partner in person, but AI should only carry early exchanges far enough for both people to find out.

Du Shichao, an assistant professor of sociology at Shanghai’s Fudan University, said Liangpei’s focus on marriage could appeal to people who already know what they are looking for. He also saw value in matching people using more than surface-level information.

“It may not address everyone’s pain points, but it can at least solve problems for some people and offer them more choice,” Du said.

But he was more cautious about AI taking on a larger role in relationships.

“This ‘enhancement’ can easily slide into ‘replacement,’” Du said. “When this kind of use is taken to an extreme, people need to be wary of ceding their capacity for emotional connection to technology.”

Whatever help an AI assistant can provide online, he said, people still have to learn about each other in person. “Ultimately, people must rediscover each other and themselves through real-world interaction.”

Du said technology may help with some of the difficulties individuals face in meeting and communicating with partners, but it cannot address the forces shaping marriage more broadly, including demographics, economic pressure, and family expectations.

“It may benefit some, but won’t significantly change China’s marriage patterns,” he said.

Zeng is making a more modest claim. “We don’t need to serve everyone,” he said. “We can’t help those with particularly poor prospects, or those with unrealistic expectations. If the people in between can find success in Liangpei, that’s good enough.”

Whether they do will become clear in 2029, when Liangpei’s first users reach the end of its three-year guarantee.

Additional reporting: Xu Ruishuo; editor: Apurva.

(Header image: Visuals from VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019020/China Approves Obesity Drug for Severe Fatty Liver Disease
World.title: China Approves Obesity Drug for Severe Fatty Liver Disease
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019020/China Approves Obesity Drug for Severe Fatty Liver Disease
World.content:
China has approved the weight-loss drug Wegovy, a brand name for the medication semaglutide, to treat a severe form of fatty liver disease, making it the country’s first and only glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) drug approved for the condition.

The drug, approved Sept. 10 by the National Medical Products Administration, covers adults with moderate to advanced liver damage from metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) — the result of inflammation caused by excess fat — but no cirrhosis, or permanent scarring.

The move comes as obesity drugs become more widely available internationally and growing competition pushes drugmakers to differentiate products to treat a broader spectrum of diseases.

China has one of the world’s largest burdens of fatty liver disease, affecting about one in three adults and over 80% of people with obesity. An estimated 6.7% of Chinese adults have MASH, the disease’s more severe form, and may not qualify for GLP-1 drugs under previous weight-management indications.

The share of global liver cancer cases caused by MASH is forecast to rise from 8% to 11% by 2050, according to a report by the Lancet Commission on liver cancer published last year.

Effective drug options for fatty liver disease have long been limited, with treatment until now largely dependent on patients making lifestyle changes, Jia Jidong, director of the Liver Research Center at Beijing Friendship Hospital, told domestic media. He added that approval of the drug could help to raise public awareness of fatty liver disease, as the illness can be “silent and asymptomatic” in its earlier stages.

Semaglutide was originally developed to treat diabetes but has become widely used for weight management in recent years. It does so by mimicking the hormone GLP-1, released in response to eating, binding to the hormone’s receptors and suppressing appetite.

The medication is sold by Danish drugmaker Novo Nordisk as Ozempic for diabetes and at a higher dose as Wegovy primarily for weight management. Wegovy was approved in China for weight management in June 2024.

The latest approval was based on a trial involving 1,197 MASH patients with moderate-to-advanced liver scarring. About two-thirds of patients who took semaglutide saw their MASH resolve, while slightly more than a third experienced reductions in liver scarring.

Other drugmakers are also exploring GLP-1 medications as potential treatments for fatty liver disease, with Chinese regulators fast-tracking approval for U.S. pharmaceutical giant Eli Lilly’s tirzepatide in January.

Chinese biotech firm Innovent Biologics has also reported fatty liver reduction with its drug mazdutide, which was approved in the country for weight management last year.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019019/A Crab Farmer and His Uninvited Guests
World.title: A Crab Farmer and His Uninvited Guests
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019019/A Crab Farmer and His Uninvited Guests
World.content:
Thanks to years of ecological restoration, endangered Oriental storks have been expanding their range around Gaoyou Lake in the eastern Jiangsu province. In recent months, dozens have descended on crab farmer Hu Dingsong’s ponds, bringing him online fame — and huge economic losses.

Hu first spotted two or three storks in April. After learning they were a nationally first-class protected species, he was delighted. “I even joked online that my pond had crabs to spare,” he said.

But the numbers quickly grew: over 20 by mid-May, to more than 40 by early June, to their present numbers of around 80. Hu estimates that the birds collectively eat roughly 2,400 crabs a day, costing him 30,000 to 40,000 yuan ($4,200-$5,600) daily. His agricultural insurance does not cover wildlife damage.

Forestry officials have also banned Hu from using firecrackers to drive the birds away, as they are a protected species. Netting such large ponds is also impractical, and offering the birds other food sources — such as fish — introduces disease risks, leaving him with little recourse.

Lu Changhu, a wildlife ecology professor at Nanjing Forestry University, said storks staying in the province during summer is not new. Once mainly winter visitors, more have begun staying around Gaoyou Lake and nearby wetlands as their population has grown. Some may skip migration when food is plentiful, he said.

Local officials have provided Hu with a drone to monitor the flock and are helping address his losses, but farmers currently lack official channels to pursue compensation for wildlife damage.

Hu is now urging authorities to work with farmers on solutions that protect both the birds and their livelihoods.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019013/Frog Gone: China’s Beloved Traveling Game Is Going Offline
World.title: Frog Gone: China’s Beloved Traveling Game Is Going Offline
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019013/Frog Gone: China’s Beloved Traveling Game Is Going Offline
World.content:
A mobile game beloved by millions of Chinese users about a traveling frog is set to shut down after the game operator and the IP holder failed to reach a licensing agreement.

Announced Tuesday by its official account on microblogging platform Weibo, the game, Travel Frog: China Journey, will discontinue on Dec. 8.

“This time, the little frog is going on a long journey, with no set date of return,” the announcement read. “But that quiet companionship will always remain in our hearts.”

A video game insider told domestic media that the IP holder, Japanese gaming studio Hit-Point, sought harsher terms from domestic operator Lingxi Games, including stripping it of its right to collaborate with other companies and sell game-related merchandise. After multiple rounds of negotiations, the companies could not reach an agreement, though the insider disclosed that they are in a final round of talks.

Travel Frog, released in 2017, is an idle game, meaning gameplay progresses with little player input. Chinese users began downloading the Japanese version before tech giant Alibaba secured authorization to publish it exclusively in the Chinese mainland under its gaming division, Lingxi Games, a year later. By then, the original version was already popular, with iOS downloads in China alone exceeding 30 million.

At its peak, the game was more popular than the domestic, Tencent-produced game Honour of Kings, topping the domestic App Store free chart. Lingxi Games was acquired by the private equity firm Trustar Capital in August this year.

In Travel Frog: China Journey, the protagonist, a frog who lives alone in a cave, passes its days reading, writing in its diary, eating, and whittling wood. It also travels around China, such as to the Great Wall in Beijing and West Lake in the eastern city of Hangzhou. While on the road, it meets fellow animal travelers, brings back local specialties, and sends home postcards, which devoted users post on WeChat.

After learning that the game would be discontinued, a graduate student in Shanghai surnamed Fang spent a day trying to redownload it. She had played since her first year of university but hadn’t reinstalled the game after changing phones, not thinking it would shut down permanently.

“(I will have to) think of it as a child growing up and setting off on a new journey — a solo trip where the parents don’t need to worry anymore,” Fang said. “I really loved my frog … It felt like a real little baby.”

Another player, surnamed Wang, in the southern city of Guangzhou, first tried the game’s Japanese version in 2018. The frog’s ability to travel, rest, and meet friends whenever it wanted — moved her, as she said that adult life is all about KPIs, responsibilities, and pressure.

When she learned the game would be taken offline, Wang told Sixth Tone that she was devastated. “This isn’t just a game,” she said. “It’s a second life.”

Online, some called the move the “tears of an era,” a Chinese internet slang term referring to something that evokes a strong sense of nostalgia. Others lamented that their “youth is over,” or said they could not bear to delete the game, hoping it might one day be restored.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A screenshot from Travel Frog: China Journey. From Weibo)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018994/She Preserved the Memory of the Mogao Grottoes. Now It’s All She Remembers.
World.title: She Preserved the Memory of the Mogao Grottoes. Now It’s All She Remembers.
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018994/She Preserved the Memory of the Mogao Grottoes. Now It’s All She Remembers.
World.content:
Chang Shana, one of China’s most treasured artists, is sitting on her living room sofa in Beijing, her eyes fixed on a TV documentary about Dunhuang, the northwestern oasis city where she spent much of her childhood. When a familiar face appears on screen, the 95-year-old breaks into a broad smile.

“That’s my father,” she says, pointing out Chang Shuhong, an accomplished painter best known for his research on the ancient Buddhist murals at the Mogao Grottoes.

Alzheimer’s disease, the most common cause of dementia, has robbed Chang Shana of most memories, yet her face still lights up the moment anyone mentions Dunhuang.

“Apart from Dunhuang, her family, and the caregivers who attend to her day and night, my mother has largely forgotten the people and things outside her immediate world,” says her son, Cui Donghui.

Gone are her memories of studying under world-renowned masters, of her mother walking out on the family, of helping design state gifts and landmark buildings like Beijing’s Great Hall of the People and the Cultural Palace of Nationalities, of losing her beloved husband, and of her tenure as the longest-serving president of the Central Academy of Arts and Design, now Tsinghua University’s Academy of Arts and Design.

On a desk in her bedroom is “Clothing Patterns of China Dunhuang Mural,” which compiles 328 color illustrations of cave murals and sculptures from various periods. “I drew this book. It’s all decorative motifs,” says Chang, standing up. After catching her breath, she points out another book: “This one, ‘Dunhuang! My Father’s Call,’ was written by my father, but I contributed many of the illustrations and written materials.”

Would she like to return to Dunhuang one day? “Yes,” she replies in a soft voice, without hesitation. Then, she slowly wanders back to the sofa to continue watching her documentary.

Life on the move

Chang Shana was born in Lyon, France, in 1931. Her father was among China’s first generation of French-trained artists, and both her parents went on to attend the prestigious Beaux-Arts de Paris school.

After being moved by a photobook about the Mogao Grottoes that he discovered in a secondhand book stall beside the Seine, Chang’s father returned to China alone in 1936 to head the fine arts department at the National Art School in Beiping, predecessor of Beijing’s Central Academy of Fine Arts.

However, as invading Japanese troops advanced toward Beijing, he was forced to flee, eventually moving with the academy to Nanjing in the eastern Jiangsu province — where he was joined by his wife, Chen Zhixiu, and daughter — and then to the southwestern city of Chongqing, which served as the nation’s wartime capital during the War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression. In 1943, the family relocated again to Dunhuang in the northwestern Gansu province, where Chang Shuhong was appointed director of the National Dunhuang Art Research Institute.

Chang Shana found it difficult adjusting to their austere life among the arid dunes. In her 2013 memoir, “Yellow Sands and Blue Sky,” the artist recalls that first winter night, eating cold noodles with only salt and vinegar, and her father promising, “Things will get better.”

Yet despite the lack of material comforts, she instantly found an abundance of inspiration at the Mogao Grottoes. On days without school, she would walk the dirt roads, past the shimmering poplars, and climb into the grottoes to copy the murals. “I loved going into the caves to draw. I was always eager to do it. My parents never had to tell me to go,” she wrote. She would also chat with the many visiting artists and scholars, laying a strong foundation for her artistic development.

Previously, students had typically copied the murals with tracing paper, which they secured to the walls with thumbtacks, leaving tiny holes. Chang Shuhong prohibited this practice to prevent further damage to the relics, meaning his daughter had to recreate the originals stroke by stroke through observation alone. Although laborious, it helped her develop extraordinary levels of precision.

But the desert took as much as it gave. Under the strain of his responsibilities, Chang Shuhong was often irritable, and his relationship with his wife became fractious. She eventually left him and moved back east in 1945.

Chang Shana was 14. She dropped out of school and stayed home to help with the housework and to knit sweaters for her 4-year-old brother.

That same year, the Nationalist government ordered the Dunhuang Art Research Institute to close. As funding dwindled and workers left, Chang Shuhong traveled extensively to enlist fresh support, eventually recruiting a group of teachers and students from art academies in Chongqing and Chengdu, capital of the neighboring Sichuan province.

With the institute’s future secured, he instructed his daughter to make copies of representative murals covering various Chinese dynasties. In her memoir, Chang recalls her work to recreate the figures of warriors from the Western Wei dynasty (535–556): “The lines followed my feelings; my brushwork was especially free and expressive.”

Finding faith

When Chang turned 17, a Canadian friend of the family sponsored her to study in the United States at what is today Tufts University’s School of the Museum of Fine Arts. There, she took classes in drawing, anatomy, art history, perspective, color, painting, and design.

Although confident in French, she initially struggled with some of the highly specialized English terminology. What baffled her most, though, was the painting course. With abstract expressionism on the rise, her professors required students to create work without recognizable forms or subjects. In a letter to her father, she wrote, “Perhaps I just don’t understand.”

According to her son, Chang’s diary entries from the early 1940s are filled with confusion and unease. She occupied her time with sketching and knitting, often questioning the meaning behind such pursuits. Yet her letters home in 1950 reveal “a completely different person,” he says.

In one, she wrote about “finally finding faith,” and expounded on her belief that art should be accessible and serve the people. In other letters, she displayed a weariness with life overseas. “Staying here, depending on others for everything, life feels so empty,” she wrote. “I have a perpetual sense that something is missing, like I owe a debt.”

Chang returned to China in December 1950 without completing her degree. She immediately began helping her father organize an exhibition of Dunhuang cultural relics in Beijing, featuring copies of murals she and several art researchers had made.

The following year, she was introduced to the influential architects Liang Sicheng and Lin Huiyin, who agreed to recommend her for a teaching assistant position at Tsinghua University’s School of Architecture. Under Lin’s guidance, she and two other students applied traditional cloisonné enamelwork techniques and motifs to everyday items such as table lamps, cigarette cases, and plates.

With a growing portfolio, Chang was commissioned to design themed gifts for the 1952 Asia and Pacific Rim Peace Conference, held in Beijing. She created a silk headscarf and large cloisonné plate with peace dove motifs, inspired by Dunhuang cave paintings from the Sui dynasty (581–618).

When China began reforming its university system in the early 1950s, she transferred to the Department of Applied Arts at the Central Academy of Fine Arts before ultimately joining the Central Academy of Arts and Design in 1956.

Gone too soon

Chang met her first husband while studying in the U.S. The couple married in China in 1953 but divorced after just a few years. The artist barely mentions this time in her memoir, not even naming him.

Her second husband, Cui Taishan, was a Japanese-language interpreter. They met while part of a Chinese cultural delegation to Japan in 1961 and were married two years later, spending 26 years together until Cui’s death in 1989.

The artist’s friend, Huang Xuanzi, recalls that Chang often talked to her late husband’s photo before she developed dementia. “She’d grumble at him for leaving her too soon, then turn to me and say, ‘Look at him, always smiling at me like that,’” she says, adding that Chang still sometimes recognizes him in photographs. “One day, she suddenly smiled and said to me, ‘Cui Taishan was very handsome.’”

Huang recalls a thick stack of flower studies Chang had painted when she was pregnant, each accompanied by a short poem handwritten by her husband. “They were never published, so almost no one outside the family knows about them,” she explains. “You can clearly feel the depth of their affection in those paintings and poems.”

In 1983, Chang was appointed president of the Central Academy of Arts and Design, leaving her less time for family. Around the same time, Cui was diagnosed with diabetes and then liver cancer. Even during his final days, she was unable to stay with him full time, yet he would always reassure her, “You go ahead with your work. I’m fine.” He was just 62 when he died.

The artist struggled to cope with the combination of grief and work stress. “There were photos of her husband everywhere in the house,” says her sister-in-law, Wang Fulan. “She would always say, ‘He left us too soon. He was so young.’ She felt that she had devoted herself entirely to her work and left household matters to her husband, and that was what had worn him down.”

In later years, Chang told a friend: “I have done right by everyone and everything in my life. My father Chang Shuhong wanted me to carry on the cultural legacy of Dunhuang, and I spent my life doing so. Lin Huiyin mentored me to become a designer, and I devoted myself to that career. The only person I failed was my husband, Cui Taishan.”

Forever home

Shortly after losing her husband, Chang’s father was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s. His condition remained largely stable until he took a serious fall at age 92. After that, his memory began deteriorating rapidly, and he passed away two years later in 1994.

Huang says Chang Shana was also healthy and mentally sharp until her early 90s. She might forget small things, but a little prompting was enough to bring her back.

During the pandemic, her son Cui Donghui couldn’t visit in person; he could see her only through the security camera installed at her home. When he checked late at night, he often saw her lying alone on the sofa watching television. When he was finally able to return, she opened the door, looked at him, and said, “Who are you?”

Leafing through his mother’s book, “Clothing Patterns of China Dunhuang Mural,” he proudly remarks, “This is her life’s work. She systematically cataloged the motifs from different periods and defined their evolutionary progression. This foundational body of work is still essential today, whether for research or for the development of cultural products.”

All the detailed illustrations inside were completed during a special trip Chang took to the Mogao Grottoes in 1959 with two colleagues. For the artist, it was a joyous return to the place she once called home.

“We were young then,” she wrote in her memoir. “We rode horses and camels, climbed the Singing Sand Dunes barefoot, and had an absolutely wonderful time.”

At 95, the journey to Dunhuang is impossible. Yet smiling at that flickering TV screen, she is already back among the caves. The memories are gone, but the patterns remain.

This article, reported by Li Mei, edited by Peng Wei, originally appeared in The Paper. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

World.title: Divine Adili’s parents accept teammates’ account of son’s death: ‘We have known the truth’
World.content:
Seeking answers, Elias and Ifeoma Adili visit the Philippines for the first time and hear firsthand from Divine's teammates what happened in the June 8 incident that claimed the lives of their son and Rene Baterbonia

MANILA, Philippines – The parents of late Ateneo big man Divine Adili can return home to Nigeria having known the “truth” about their son’s death.

Visiting the country for the first time in search of answers, Elias and Ifeoma Adili heard firsthand from Divine’s teammates what happened during the June 8 incident that claimed the lives of their son and Rene Baterbonia during a team-building activity in Dipaculao, Aurora.

“We talked to the teammates, because they are the ones that will tell us what happened, because they were present at the place of the scene. So they explained everything,” Elias said. “That was our purpose of coming — to see the team, to talk with them, to tell us the truth.”

“It’s only the truth that will set you free. Okay? So we have known the truth and I think I can now go back to my kinsmen and tell them that this is what happened.”

Play Video

Elias and Ifeoma were in attendance as the Blue Eagles opened their UAAP Season 89 men’s basketball campaign at the Mall of Asia Arena on Wednesday, September 16, exactly 100 days since the two student-athletes’ deaths.

And Ateneo did not disappoint, breezing past the UE Red Warriors in a 101-74 rout starring Kieffer Alas, Jared Bahay, and Grayson Rogers.

While they are grateful to finally see their son’s team play in person, the moment is inevitably bittersweet for the Adilis.

Divine, after all, had once promised to bring Elias and Ifeoma to the Philippines so they could watch him in action for the Blue Eagles — a commitment that, in the end, was never fulfilled.

“I’m delighted to be here, but I wish I am watching my son. But I really appreciate what I see because I know that my son is there. Divine and Rene, they are there. They might be invisible, but I know my son is there,” said Ifeoma.

“I wish to come to the Philippines to watch my son play because that’s what I’ve been desiring. And I know my son desired that, to bring us to the Philippines to come and watch him live, though we have been watching his games [online]. We have been watching every of his games since he came to the Philippines and he desired to bring us here.”

Moving on has also been particularly difficult for the Adilis, especially now that they find themselves surrounded by things and people that were once close to their son.

“To be honest with you, it has not been easy. I tried to move on. But honestly, it has not been easy for me. Even as I entered the Philippines, the moment I stepped in at the airport, I felt so emotional,” said Ifeoma. “I don’t want to cry. But unfortunately today, the moment I stepped into the playground, I saw myself crying. But it’s fine.”

Ifeoma also expressed her disappointment that former Ateneo head coach Tab Baldwin only reached out to their family much later.

“He spoke to us very late, about four days after the incident, which is not proper,” said Ifeoma. “I am not okay with that. To be honest with you, since then, we’ve not heard from him. And it’s okay, it’s okay.”

As painful as Divine’s death is, though, the Adilis know they have to live with it and find the strength to move forward without their son.

“There’s nothing we can do. We can’t bring him back. We have cried, we have shed tears, we have complained. But there’s nothing we can do. Thank God we saw his remains — seeing his remains and laying him to rest,” said Elias.

Elias and Ifeoma will also be around when the Blue Eagles battle perennial finalist UP Fighting Maroons on Saturday, September 19, at the Araneta Coliseum. – Rappler.com

World.title: Rodrigo Duterte attends ICC hearing | The wRap
World.content:
