World.title: ‘Poland is ready to support Armenia’s ambitious goal of joining EU’ — Marcin Bosacki
World.content:
Polish official on Armenia’s EU integration

“Being an influential member of the European Union, Poland can support Armenia in pursuing its ambitious goals, whatever they may be,” Polish Deputy Foreign Minister Marcin Bosacki said in an interview with the Armenpress news agency.

He noted that if Yerevan’s goal is to expand trade with the European Union and conclude a free trade agreement, Warsaw can support the process. The deputy minister also stressed that Poland can support the ambitious goal of joining the EU.

“It will not happen overnight, but it is entirely possible,” he said.

Marcin Bosacki discussed Poland’s experience of European integration, military-technical cooperation with Armenia, and efforts to establish peace in the South Caucasus.

EU membership would open new doors for Armenia

“European Union is a huge market for you. 460 million people, rich people, relatively speaking in terms of the world. And Armenia has some advantages from IT business and gaming even to agriculture, which fit quite nicely into European market. So, this is the big opportunity, and probably you need to diversify your economic ties and directions of export. So, European Union countries like Poland is a natural choice, but yes, there are two challenges, obstacles.

One is institutional, you know, European Union in its core is a free trade zone, which means we really trade freely, without any barriers between ourselves between twenty-seven members of the European Union, but we do have barriers for others.

So, to remove, or at least ease those areas is very important for Armenia, and we are in talks of that. Some of that already happened, like Poland imported one thousand tons of Armenian fruits this year, and temporarily this market was open for you in the scope of European Union. But we need to have trade deals, maybe pre-accession deals.

When you become a candidate for EU, if you become, then it will be much easier to open those doors for you, with the benefit of your producers, not only agricultural producers, but also industrial producers.”

“It is worth becoming a member of this club”: Poland’s experience of European integration

“Poland joined EU twenty-two years ago. So, twenty-three years ago, twenty-five years ago, twenty-seven years ago, we were a candidate country, and we know how to prepare for cooperation and possibly membership with European Union, and then how to negotiate with European Union. And I’m so proud that today with Deputy Minister Vahan Kostanyan, we opened the training of your diplomatic corps by Polish diplomats and experts who were active in those talks and negotiations with European Union when Poland wanted to join, 23, 25 years ag

There is one lesson. It is worth to be in this club. Thirty-five years ago, just after Poland, as one of the first actually as the very first country got rid of communism in 1989, Polish economic situation and Polish economic development was on par with Ukraine’s.

Now we are at least three times richer than Ukraine in terms of GDP per capita, purchasing power and we grew into the sixth biggest economy in the EU, twentieth economy in the world. And we are almost fifty percent richer than we would have been, if we were not members of EU. Polish economic success is magnificent. We didn’t have a year of recession since 1991.

The only year of recession was the year of COVID, 2020, but that was global. And Poles really are five to six times richer than they were a generation ago. It is not always easy. The first years are not easy of economic reforms and the preparations for joining EU, but the benefits for a hardworking, energetic, full of entrepreneurs country like Poland is, those benefits are enormous, and I firmly believe that Armenia will follow Polish path, because you are also a very energetic, very ambitious. And full of entrepreneurs, nation and country.”

Armenia–Poland military-technical cooperation

“In many areas. Yes, in many dimensions of this, yes, really recently opened an area, because just last May, our respective Ministers of Defense signed this agreement on cooperation in this sphere between Poland and Armenia. You know, Polish defense industry is an expert in transitioning of Soviet or post-Soviet armory into NATO standards, into Western standards.

So, we can help you with that if you wish so. Another one is that those two wars, Russian war in Ukraine, and between U.S. And Iran, really emptied the magazines for ammunition, from very simple one to the very developed anti-air and anti-ballistic missiles. We can help produce more of it in cooperation between Armenian and Polish industries, and those talks are already between our two countries.”

Supporting peace and stability in the South Caucasus

“Poland has been and is supporting peace and stabilization of South Caucasus region. We do support TRIPP project, we do support the reconciliation agenda between Armenia and Azerbaijan, and we strongly encourage our Turkish friends to normalize relations with your great country of Armenia, because we really believe that the world, based on peace and democratic values, and the protection of sovereignty of each particular country, is the world in which economy is booming, people are safer and more happy, and the world is more stable.

And therefore, we do wish Armenia all the best on your decisions to diversify, both economically and politically, your future. And we not only wish, but we will help how much you want us to help.”

Polish official on Armenia’s EU integration

World.title: ‘Suleyman’s community case’: Baku dormitories and courses become subject of legal proceedings
World.content:
Suleyman community case in Azerbaijan

Unregistered religious instruction allegedly took place at preparatory courses and student dormitories in Baku linked to the “Suleyman community”.

Witnesses in the case say they were provided with accommodation and three meals a day for 150 manats (approximately $88) a month. They also attended lessons on the Quran and Islamic prayer. The trial of Said Mikailov is ongoing.

What is the “Suleyman community”, what does Azerbaijan’s legislation say about religious education, and what questions about the case remain unanswered?

What happened?

Following an operation carried out by the State Security Service, Said Mehman oglu Mikailov was charged with a criminal offence. He reportedly presented himself as the “head of the Baku branch of the Suleyman community”. Authorities also took administrative measures against several other people.

The case is being heard by the Binagadi District Court in Baku. According to a court report by the pro-government APA news agency, investigators believe that religious rituals took place at premises operating in Baku as preparatory courses, a student dormitory and a kindergarten. The activities allegedly took place without approval from the State Committee for Work with Religious Organisations, and some involved minors.

Media reports do not specify which article of the Criminal Code Mikailov faces charges under, whether he is in custody or what position his defence has taken.

The next court hearing is reportedly scheduled for 30 September.

What do the witnesses say?

The testimony of three witnesses questioned in court suggests that similar arrangements operated at different addresses. They offered low-cost accommodation and meals, general education classes, and parallel lessons on the Quran, the Arabic alphabet and the rules of Islamic prayer.

Ibrahim Teymurov, a former head of the Nasimi student dormitory, said he returned to Azerbaijan after receiving religious education at courses run by the “Suleyman community” in Turkey. He said he initially worked at the dormitory as a supervisor and security guard. He later taught Quran classes two or three times a week and was eventually appointed head of the dormitory, replacing Said Mikailov.

According to Teymurov, each student paid 150 manats a month in cash in exchange for accommodation and three meals a day. He said the services were used mainly by children from low-income families who had come from the regions. The witness stated that the religious books in use were commercially available, but acknowledged that no government body had registered the religious instruction.

Another witness, Ismayil Serverli, said he managed an educational centre in the Bakikhanov settlement. According to him, five students lived at the centre, where they also studied literature, mathematics and English. Most teachers worked without employment contracts. Serverli attributed this to their unwillingness to pay taxes. He also said that income was insufficient to cover expenses, so the centre placed a donation box at the entrance.

Elton Abdullayev, a former head of another dormitory in Binagadi, said around 17–18 students lived there, each paying 150 manats a month. According to him, teachers with religious training who lacked permission to teach religion instructed students in the Arabic alphabet and the Quran. They also performed Islamic prayers together with the dormitory residents. The report says that this dormitory also installed a donation box to help cover expenses.

What is the “Suleyman community”?

The “Suleymanists”, or the “Suleyman community”, is the name of a religious community that brings together students and followers of Turkish religious figure Suleyman Hilmi Tunahan. Tunahan received religious education during the final years of the Ottoman Empire. In the first decades of the Turkish Republic, he taught the Quran and religious subjects.

According to a biography published in the Turkish Religious Foundation’s “Encyclopaedia of Islam”, as well as a 2024 academic study, the movement’s main activities included Quran courses and student education. After Tunahan died in 1959, his students continued this work by organising courses and dormitories, and later various educational and social institutions.

The model described during the trial in Baku — combining education with accommodation in dormitories — therefore resembles the organisational structure the movement has historically used in Turkey. However, this similarity alone does not prove that individuals in Azerbaijan received direct instructions or funding from the movement’s leadership in Turkey. The published trial materials contain no documents or information about financial transactions confirming such a connection.

What does Azerbaijani law say?

Article 48 of the Constitution of Azerbaijan guarantees everyone freedom of conscience, the right to determine their own attitude towards religion, and the right to perform religious rites individually or jointly with others. However, exercising this right must not violate public order or conflict with public morality. Article 18 of the Constitution separates religion from the state and establishes the secular nature of the state education system.

Article 6 of the Law on Freedom of Religious Belief allows citizens to study religion and receive religious education individually or jointly with others. However, establishing a religious educational institution or organising courses on sacred texts through religious organisations is subject to a separate procedure. A religious educational institution may be established by a religious centre with the approval of the relevant state body. Courses on sacred texts must follow the religious organisation’s charter, receive approval from the religious centre to which it is subordinate, and be reported to the authorised state body.

Under Article 6-1 of the law, mass religious rites generally take place in houses of worship and pilgrimage sites. Holding them outside such locations requires the consent of a state body. At the same time, Article 21 allows religious rites to take place in dormitories at the request of their residents.

The key legal question in this case, therefore, is not simply whether people read the Quran together. The court will have to establish whether the activity constituted individual and voluntary religious practice or systematic religious instruction organised without the required authorisation. The assessment may also take into account the participation of minors, the official designation of the premises, and the mechanisms used to manage and finance the activities.

Parents have the right to raise their children in accordance with their religious beliefs. However, the law prohibits forcing a child to practise a religion and requires religious upbringing not to harm their physical or mental health. Open sources do not specify how many minors are involved in the case, how old they are, whether their parents gave consent, or which religious rites they took part in.

Receiving religious education abroad is not, in itself, a violation of the law. In 2024, the State Committee for Work with Religious Organisations reported that Azerbaijani citizens who had received religious education abroad could attend an interview and receive official appointments as religious figures. At the time, the committee said that 19 people with foreign religious education had received such appointments.

Parallel investigation in Turkey

Several months after the trial began in Azerbaijan, Turkey also launched a major investigation into the community’s leadership. Ankara’s Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office describes the case as an investigation into the activities of a “criminal organisation led by Alihan Kuriş and established for the purpose of financial gain”. Authorities detained 38 suspects. On 16 August 2026, a court remanded 32 of them, including Alihan Kuriş, in custody. It placed the other six under house arrest as a judicial-control measure.

Turkish media report that the investigation concerns alleged fraud, tax evasion and the laundering of criminal proceeds. According to Anadolu Agency, investigators also found 200 kilograms of gold bars during one of the searches. Their origin remains unknown.

At present, open sources contain no information about a direct procedural link or evidence connecting the Baku case with the investigation in Ankara. The two proceedings can be viewed as parallel investigations into the activities of the same religious network. However, there is currently no basis for treating them as part of a single case.

Suleyman community case in Azerbaijan

World.title: Ruling Georgian Dream adds another party to lawsuit seeking opposition ban
World.content:
Gakharia’s party ban

Georgia’s ruling Georgian Dream party is asking the Constitutional Court to declare the parliamentary opposition Gakharia – For Georgia party unconstitutional and ban it, parliamentary majority leader Irakli Kirtskhalia said.

The party’s leader, exiled former Prime Minister Giorgi Gakharia, responded: “Even with a parliamentary majority, the Ivanishvili regime could not tolerate the presence of even one opposition party in parliament because it has no answer to criticism.”

Georgian Dream previously asked the Constitutional Court to declare four opposition groups unconstitutional and ban them: the United National Movement, Coalition for Change, Strong Georgia – Lelo and the Federalists.

Georgian Dream alleged that the parties had “been involved in unconstitutional activities, including sabotage against the Georgian state, and had adopted essentially identical positions for many years”.

The Gakharia – For Georgia party will now be added to the revised submission.

Kirtskhalia said the party had not initially been included because Georgian Dream wanted to give it an opportunity to participate in parliamentary work, “despite its past ties and direct coalition with the ‘collective National Movement’” (the ruling party’s term for the country’s entire opposition – JAMnews).

He said the revised application seeking to ban the opposition parties would be submitted to the Constitutional Court this week.

Kirtskhalia said the decision to include the party in the case was prompted by its conduct in parliament and its public statements.

“The case is based on numerous indisputable facts,” he said. “Look at how openly, crudely and brazenly they refuse to recognise the country’s constitutional order, and at their numerous destructive actions in parliament and public comments.”

He again accused Gakharia – For Georgia of links to the “collective National Movement network” and said that, in his view, the party “serves the same insidious cause”.

Kirtskhalia added that the case did not seek to strip Gakharia – For Georgia representatives of their seats in either parliament or local councils.

Former Prime Minister Giorgi Gakharia and his party

Gakharia’s party joined three other opposition groups in boycotting parliament after the 26 October 2024 parliamentary elections, alleging that the vote had been rigged.

However, in November 2025, the party decided to take up its seats in parliament and municipal councils.

According to the Central Election Commission, Gakharia – For Georgia holds 12 seats in parliament and 26 seats on municipal councils across the country.

Giorgi Gakharia is living in forced exile after two criminal cases were brought against him.

1. “Gavrilov’s Night”, or the “20 June case”. On the night of 20-21 June 2019, security forces violently dispersed a large protest in Tbilisi. Investigators allege that Gakharia, then interior minister, ordered riot police to use crowd-control weapons without warning or giving peaceful protesters an opportunity to leave the area. Dozens of people were injured by rubber bullets, including two who each lost an eye, while five others suffered serious injuries.

2. The “Chorchana episode”. Investigators allege that in August 2019, Gakharia, then interior minister, unilaterally ordered the installation of an additional police checkpoint near the village of Chorchana in the Georgian-Ossetian conflict zone, without coordinating the move with the prime minister or the State Security Service and without informing the EU Monitoring Mission. The move sharply escalated tensions in the conflict zone.

Giorgi Gakharia’s statement

Following the ruling party representative’s announcement, Giorgi Gakharia, who now lives in Germany, posted his response in English on X.

Giorgi Gakharia: “Despite severe restrictions, we have consistently contested every election, regarding elections as the only peaceful and democratic path to political change.

Our party remains the only opposition force represented in parliament.

“By targeting us, Ivanishvili is seeking to ban the country’s only genuinely functioning parliamentary opposition.

“Even with a parliamentary majority, the Ivanishvili regime could not tolerate the presence of even one opposition party in parliament because it has no answer to criticism.

“This is another step by the Ivanishvili regime towards formally establishing authoritarian rule in Georgia and suppressing the political opposition.

“Whether we are banned or not, we will not abandon our goal of restoring democracy in Georgia and defending its European and Euro-Atlantic course,” Gakharia wrote.

News in Georgia

World.title: Azerbaijan joins Central Asian security chiefs’ key forum in Kazakhstan
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 16. A delegation from the State Security Service (SSS) of the Republic of Azerbaijan took part in an international forum of intelligence agencies in Kazakhstan.

This information was released by the press service of the State Security Service.

Colonel General Ali Naghiyev, head of Azerbaijan’s State Security Service, led the agency’s delegation at a meeting of the heads of special services from Central Asian states and the Republic of Azerbaijan, dedicated to the theme “Ensuring Regional Security in the Face of Modern Threats.”

Speaking at the event, Colonel General Ali Naghiyev emphasized that the participation of the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan, Ilham Aliyev, in the Consultative Meeting of the Heads of State of Central Asia clearly reflects the strategic nature of bilateral and multilateral ties. He noted that Azerbaijan’s full-fledged participation in this format has elevated relations with the countries of the region to a qualitatively new level, marking a historic step toward strengthening peace and stability.

The head of the State Security Service identified international terrorism, religious extremism, the activities of transnational criminal groups, and the illicit trafficking of drugs and weapons as key risks to regional security. Particular attention was paid to cybercrime and risks to critical infrastructure. A. Naghiyev expressed concern over the active use of modern information technologies by criminal and terrorist elements to target transportation and communications facilities.

The head of the service expressed confidence in the further strengthening of fraternal relations and an atmosphere of mutual trust between the countries.

Following the meeting, the parties reached an agreement to continue close cooperation between their intelligence services to maintain stability in the region.

World.title: Tajikistan presents transport investment opportunities to South Korea
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 16. Tajikistan considers transport and communications among the strategic areas of cooperation with the Republic of Korea.

According to the press service of the President of Tajikistan, President Emomali Rahmon made the statement on September 16 at the first Korea - Central Asia Business Summit in Seoul.

"Today, the Government of the Republic of Tajikistan is taking the necessary measures to develop strategic sectors, in particular energy, transport and communications, industry, digitalization, agriculture and tourism," the statement said.

During the forum, Rahmon presented Tajikistan’s opportunities in the transport sector and identified this area as one of the promising fields for attracting investment.

The president expressed the development of strategic sectors is in line with national development programs and the interests of the peoples of the Central Asian countries and the Republic of Korea.

Meanwhile, Tajik President Emomali Rahmon is participating in the first Central Asia-Republic of Korea Summit in Seoul on September 16-17. The summit brings together the leaders of South Korea and the five Central Asian countries - Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan - marking the first elevation of the Korea-Central Asia dialogue to the leaders’ level. The meeting is focused on expanding cooperation in areas including trade and investment, industry, energy, transport, digitalization, technology and human capital.

During his visit to South Korea, Emomali Rahmon is presenting Tajikistan’s investment opportunities and highlighting areas with potential for greater cooperation with Korean businesses, including critical minerals, mineral processing, energy, infrastructure, technology and agriculture.

The summit provides Tajikistan with a regional platform to promote its investment potential and discuss opportunities for attracting Korean capital, technologies and expertise. It also offers a framework for expanding practical cooperation between South Korea and the Central Asian countries in strategic economic sectors.

World.title: Saudis pound Yemen as Houthis fire back, further widening Middle East war
World.content:
Saudi warplanes have intensified their strikes on Yemen as Iran-backed Houthi fighters launched another salvo of drones and missiles at Saudi cities, as a new front in the Middle East conflict continues to grow.

The rebel movement announced renewed strikes on the Kingdom in a move threatening to exacerbate a global energy supply shortage first triggered by the US and Israel's decision to launch a war on Iran.

In a sign of the worsening conflict in a new theatre, the United States tightened its travel warning for Saudi Arabia, banning government employees from travelling within 32 kilometres of the Yemen border.

The Houthis, who since last week have swept through Yemeni towns along the Red Sea coast and seized islands in the Bab el-Mandeb strait at its mouth, released battlefield video overnight of fighters seizing armoured vehicles from Saudi-backed forces.

Warplanes flew overhead and huge explosions billowed into the sky from desert dunes, the video showed.

Houthi military media broadcast footage purporting to show their fighters attacking Saudi-backed forces in Yemen. (Houthi military media via Reuters)

Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had launched fresh drone and missile strikes on the major Saudi Red Sea oil port of Yanbu, and at a southern Saudi airbase at Khamis Mushait.

Saudi officials and oil company Aramco did not immediately respond to emails seeking comment.

Mr Saree said the Saudis had carried out as many as 450 air strikes on Yemen this week.

Officials in the Saudi-backed government that controls southern Yemen have acknowledged that their forces and those of Saudi Arabia were conducting air strikes on Houthi positions, though Riyadh itself has not confirmed them.

Houthi rebels have frequently targeted Saudi oil facilities in Jizan, Jazan province, Saudi Arabia. (European Union/Copernicus Sentinel-2 via Reuters)

Danger of global energy shortage worsening

The Houthis have fired repeatedly into Saudi Arabia over the past week causing alarms over cities in the south and west.

An attack blamed on Iran-aligned fighters in Iraq last week also knocked out Saudi Arabia's East-West Pipeline, the main route used to divert oil exports from the blockaded Strait of Hormuz.

Riyadh said its air defences had shot down a Houthi drone south of Mecca on Tuesday before it entered prohibited airspace over the holy city, an attack it said crossed a "red line" of threatening shrines sacred to all Muslims.

The extension of the war into Yemen threatens to worsen the global energy supply shortage caused by the six-month-old US-Israeli war on Iran, which has disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

The price of Brent crude hovered around $US108 ($151) a barrel on Wednesday, close to its highest levels since May.

The politically sensitive average retail price of diesel fuel in the United States hit another all-time high above $US6.30 a gallon for the first time.

Traders say a prolonged closure of Saudi Arabia's East-West Pipeline could cut off as much as 4 per cent of global oil supply.

Saudi Arabia has not said when operations might resume, but US Energy Secretary Chris Wright told CNBC on Tuesday that crude oil should be flowing through the pipeline within days.

Reuters

World.title: Duterte appears in person at The Hague over 'war on drugs' killings
World.content:
Former Philippines President Rodrigo Duterte appeared in the courtroom for the first time since being transferred to the International Criminal Court 18 months ago to face murder charges regarding his war on drugs.

Mr Duterte, 81, served as president from 2016 to 2022, before being charged with crimes against humanity for setting up, funding and arming death squads that targeted narcotics peddlers and users.

He was arrested and taken to The Hague in March 2025.

ICC hearings on Rodrigo Duterte An International Criminal Court prosecutor tells judges that former Philippines president Rodrigo Duterte personally instructed members of a death squad to kill suspected criminals and drug users.

Dressed in a black suit and white shirt, Mr Duterte did not speak in court, on Wednesday, local time, but sat quietly sipping water during the proceedings.

He stood and waved to family members in the public gallery.

"We're happy that he has finally appeared and that he looks OK. In fact, he looks like he has put on weight," said Llore Pasco, whose two sons were killed during Mr Duterte's war on drugs, watching a television broadcast of the hearings from Manila.

In court, Presiding Judge Joanna Korner asked prosecutors to find ways to shorten the trial, set to begin in November, due to the defendant's age and health.

"It's important this trial goes ahead as quickly as possible," she said, pressing parties to limit the number of witnesses and focus on key evidence.

Mr Duterte's attorney, Peter Haynes, called disclosure by the prosecution "enormous and impossible" and said his team could never examine tens of thousands of pieces of evidence in time.

"If I had a younger and healthier client, I would request pushing back the trial by six months," he said.

The court heard arguments about Rodrigo Duterte's health and ability to stand trial. (Reuters: Piroschka van de Wouw)

Details of Mr Duterte's condition were not discussed in open court Wednesday, local time, but his lawyers have said he suffers from cognitive decline that affects his memory and daily functioning, and is not well enough.

In January, ICC judges said Mr Duterte's health was good enough for him to follow proceedings and requested his presence in court, rather than by video link from the detention unit.

The warrant for Mr Duterte says he was responsible for a widespread and systematic campaign that led to thousands of killings between 2011 and 2019, including his time as the mayor of the southern city of Davao.

ICC prosecutors have said as many as 30,000 people may have been killed in the crackdown, the details of which were reported in a Reuters investigation.

Police said 6,200 suspects were killed during anti-drug operations. Mr Duterte said he instructed police to act in self-defence and told supporters he was ready to "rot in jail" if it meant ridding the Philippines of illicit drugs.

Reuters

World.title: Tiny cells and creatures dazzle in microscopic video competition
World.content:
A video of tiny hair-like structures fluttering in the airways of a child with a rare genetic disease has won an international microscopic imagery contest.

The video, taken by Ning Xu, a researcher at Tsinghua University in China, is one of dozens highlighted by the 2026 Nikon Small World In Motion competition.

The competition is open to anyone around the world with an interest in film or time-lapse photography through a microscope.

Dr Xu's video, magnified to 100 times in size, shows cilia that line airways to clear out mucus.

In people like this child with primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD), they move strangely and make it harder to keep lungs clear.

Dr Xu used a series of complicated light waves to illuminate different parts of the sample in colour, allowing researchers to gain a better understanding of PCD.

Surprise roundworm altercation

Vietnamese researcher Nguyen Nam Nhat was awarded second place for a video of a microscopic roundworm, or nematode, encountering a single-celled organism called a Dileptus.

Loading...

Mr Nguyen said the footage was a chance observation.

"I had intended only to film Dileptus specimens from a naturally collected water sample in order to study their morphology," he said.

But a rogue roundworm appeared, pressing itself up against the Dileptus. The Dileptus lost a chunk of its tiny body in the struggle to escape.

"After examining several similar cases, I found that pressing against or immobilising other organisms appears to be one of the typical defensive behaviours employed by nematodes," Mr Nguyen said.

Baby jellyfish in ocean drops

Microscopic photographer Benedikt Pleyer won third place for a video of various types of jellyfish larvae.

Loading...

Mr Pleyer set up the shots by suspending water droplets on a string over a petri dish, sliding tiny larvae into the drops.

Most jellyfish-containing droplets splashed into the petri dish too quickly to film, so it took months to collect the footage.

"This is a game of patience," he said.

Sea slug, fungus take honourable mentions

Other entrants received honourable mentions such as a video of the Cyerce kikutarobabai sea slug, which is native to the western Pacific Ocean.

Loading...

Animals weren't the only things on display, with one video showing the growth of the Penicillium venetum fungus, which can cause rot in garlic.

Loading...

Another video showed the formation of crystals of the food additive monosodium glutamate (MSG).

Loading...

Bioluminescent sparkles

Mr Pleyer also received an honourable mention for a video of tropical phytoplankton he had collected and cultured.

Loading...

The phytoplankton, which are magnified to 200 times their size, glow when they are physically disturbed.

"The biggest problem with this bioluminescent reaction is how to trigger it and to at the same time get a clear shot," Mr Pleyer said.

Jostling the phytoplankton to get a reaction makes the camera shake too much at this resolution, so Mr Pleyer used glycerol to fix them in place, and a small electric charge to trigger the bioluminescence.

Tardigrades, animals half a millimetre in size, featured in several other videos.

Loading...

Mr Pleyer said amateur microscopy enthusiasts had an important role to play in science.

"The microcosmos is a vast field and we don't know much about it yet," he said.

In the past decade, it's become much easier and cheaper to see moving things at the micro scale.

"With the digital revolution, a sensor, a camera, you can just go," Mr Pleyer said.

" You will come across things that probably have not been observed. "

The full list of winners and honourable mentions are published on the competition's website.

World.title: Canada in the EU and other takeaways from State of European Union
World.content:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has laid out her bold vision for a strengthened, revitalised, united Europe and has invited a new name to the party: Canada.

Ms von der Leyen covered a large range of topics in a 73-minute annual "state of the union" address to the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France, leading off with the opening line from Charles Dickens' Tales of Two Cities, which she said also described the world today.

"It was the best of times, it was the worst of times," she said.

Here are five key takeaways from her speech.

Oh, Canada!

Ms von der Leyen said the European Union was opening the door for Canada to become its first associate member.

"We want to bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible," she said.

"So, I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to be the first associate member of the EU."

Mark Carney received a standing ovation from the European Parliament. (Reuters: Yves Herman)

Ms von der Leyen walked up to and embraced Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who she had invited to the address, after mentioning Canada's "associate membership" and he received a standing ovation from the chamber.

It will be up to the 27 EU member states whether Ms von der Leyen's proposal goes ahead.

The US-Canada 'divorce' The US and Canada are often referred to as North American cousins, but the family feud has turned bitter as their trading relationship falls apart.

The EU has historically resisted such types of flexible alliances that have no legal status.

EU members were lukewarm in reacting to Germany's proposal in May of associate membership for Ukraine as a stepping stone to full membership.

New security council

The European Commission chief also pitched setting up a "European Security Council" with countries including Britain and Ukraine, as the continent grapples with the threat from Russia.

"For a long time, we have discussed a leaders' format focused on the security of our continent, with partners like Canada, Norway, Ukraine, the United Kingdom and others involved," Ms von der Leyen said.

"This is even more urgent now, given the nature and scale of the risks at play.

"This is why we will set out our ideas to make a European Security Council a reality."

Russia and Ukraine continue strikes on energy The US president declared both sides would refrain from striking energy-related targets as petrol and diesel prices rise.

Europe is grappling with what it calls a campaign of "hybrid attacks" by Moscow aimed at undermining support for Ukraine, including recent attacks on Lithuania, Denmark and a Russian strike on the Ukraine–Poland border that just missed a train carrying diplomats, including former British prime minister Boris Johnson and former Swedish prime minister Carl Bildt.

"We should be under no illusions about what is happening here: hybrid threats facing Europe are less and less hybrid and less and less threats," Ms von der Leyen said.

"Europe needs its own counter-hybrid playbook.

"We urgently need a consensus on how to respond to certain incidents: Those which fall below armed aggression but clearly threaten our national security."

The European Commission president said she wanted to establish an "emergency security protocol" that would allow any EU member state to convene urgent talks in case of crisis.

'Strongest ever' support for Ukraine

While the EU is struggling to counter Russian activities, Ms von der Leyen pledged that the bloc would ramp up support for Kyiv as Russia steps up bombardments ahead of the winter.

"We will give our strongest-ever support to Ukraine over the toughest winter of the war," she said.

"Together with our partners, we will provide humanitarian aid and reinforce Ukraine's supplies of power and heating."

Ursula von der Leyen has invited Canada to become the first associate member of the European Union. (Reuters: Yves Herman)

Ms von der Leyen backed plans to jointly "develop with Ukraine an affordable, modular missile-defence system".

She said that Europe would also step up its efforts to develop its own key military capabilities, pledging a "new European instrument for strategic enablers".

Strengthened trade and manufacturing

Ms von der Leyen said she would like Europe to build "an alliance for the future, to create a common prosperity" and economic security.

"We will work on intelligent manufacturing," she said.

"We will create a tech alliance. We will integrate defence industrial bases.

"We will make the Arctic a flagship joint project."

While Ursula von der Leyen was laying out her vision, animal rights activists demonstrated outside the European Parliament. (Reuters: Yves Herman)

She said the EU would work on energy critical minerals and batteries, on AI, quantum, cyber and economic security.

"This is not a partnership against anyone else, but for our common strengths," Ms von der Leyen said.

Slow down on AI and social ban for kids

Despite calling for more European technological advances, Ms von der Leyen said she supported the recent calls from tech leaders for a slowdown on AI.

Last week, AI researcher Jacob Coxon quit tech company Anthropic, saying those building the technology "earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade".

And earlier this week, AI pioneer Geoffrey Hinton and Anthropic's Dario Amodei both called for a global slowdown in AI development.

"Models being developed will allow hacking on a level we never thought possible," Ms von der Leyen said.

Anthropic researcher says AI 'could kill us all' A researcher for AI developer Anthropic has quit the company and is calling on the industry to slow down.

"And they will soon be in the hands of adversaries who see the world very differently from us."

She pointed to recent incidents of rogue AI agents and warnings from developers.

"CEOs of the most advanced companies tell us that it is time to slow down on the self-recursive models, to pace the frontier," Ms von der Leyen said.

"If the people developing the technology are clear, then we should be too."

Landmark EU rules governing the use of AI adopted recently put Europe in the position to shape global efforts to tackle the risks, Ms von der Leyen said.

She said Europe would work with like-minded partners such as Canada, the United Kingdom and others to take measures such as model evaluation, verification and AI security.

"I will invite the main frontier labs for a discussion on how we can support ongoing industry efforts to pace the frontier," von der Leyen said.

She also proposed a social media ban for children under 13 — similar to Australia's world-first ban for kids under 16 — and no personal accounts for people under the age of 15, saying that platforms have to prove that they are safe for children.

ABC/Reuters/AFP

World.title: Former Kosovo president Thaci sentenced to 25 years' prison for war crimes
World.content:
Former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci has been found guilty of war crimes, including murder, torture and illegal detention by the Kosovo war crimes tribunal in The Hague.

Thaci, 58, was sentenced to 25 years in prison for crimes committed as top commander of the ethnic Albanian Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) during the territory's violent break from Serbia in the 1990s.

The tribunal said he was guilty of the murder of 96 political opponents and perceived collaborators with Serbian security forces by Kosovo Liberation Army forces during the conflict.

He was also convicted of arbitrary illegal detention of 385 people, torture of 303 people and cruel treatment of about 50.

The court said Thaci had "actively participated in and encouraged crimes".

"The scale and nature of the crimes committed were very serious," presiding judge Charles Smith said.

"The so-called intelligence on which many of these victims were arrested, detained and killed was little more than unverified rumours. Based on that information, victims were called and described as spies and collaborators and violently treated."

Thaci had denied all charges.

Supporters gather in Pristina

Supporters of former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci protested after he was found guilty. (Reuters: Valdrin Xhemaj)

The ruling was closely watched in Kosovo and Serbia, where the legacy of the 1998-99 conflict and Kosovo's 2008 declaration of independence remain a source of tension between ethnic Kosovo Albanians and Serbs.

Thaci remains a revered figure for many Kosovo Albanians, while the tribunal itself is deeply unpopular in Kosovo.

In Pristina, Kosovo's capital, thousands of people watching the verdict on a big screen booed the verdict and chanted "Thaci, Thaci" as some burst into tears.

One billboard showed the faces of the defendants, which read: "In the name of the people you are declared innocent".

Albania's Prime Minister criticised the verdict with a picture posted on social media of a circle of barbed wire across a map of Europe and one word: "Unbelievable".

Former Kosovo leader pleads not guilty on war crimes The former president and three others charged led a pro-Kosovo guerilla faction during the break-up of Yugoslavia.

Prosecutors had sought a 45-year sentence against Thaci and three other former top commanders of the KLA.

But the three-judge panel dismissed six charges of crimes against humanity.

However, they ruled that Thaci and his co-accused were part of a joint criminal enterprise, with a common plan to take control of Kosovo politics following its independence by targeting political opponents.

Thaci's lawyers had argued the accusations were unfounded, amounted to an attempt to rewrite history and there was no evidence to directly link Thaci to any of the alleged crimes..

Reuters

World.title: Perth city 'landmark' sign badly damaged by fire at Yagan Square
World.content:
A popular sign at tourist attraction Yagan Square in the heart of the Perth CBD has been badly damaged in a fire, as authorities investigate its cause.

Yagan Square's social media account announced the news in a statement this evening.

"Farewell to an icon," the post read.

"Today, we share the news that the PERTH Sign at Yagan Square was badly damaged by fire.

"For eight loyal years, it has been the backdrop to countless photos, cultural celebrations and memorable Perth moments.

The sign, pictured prior to the fire. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"It has well and truly earned its place as one of our city's most-loved landmarks."

The square's social media account invited users to share their favourite photos of the sign, with social media users expressing their sorrow and devastation.

Blaze quickly extinguished

The fire was reported to the Department of Fire and Emergency Services at 2:30pm today, and extinguished by 2:50pm.

A worker at a nearby bar told the ABC he saw the fire once it had already started.

He said there were plenty of people around until security moved onlookers away.

Once firefighters arrived, he said the flames were extinguished within less than five minutes.

A closer look at the sign shows blackened areas where the fire has been put out. (ABC Radio Perth: Ashleigh Davis)

Development WA, which manages and maintains the square, said it would not comment on the incident as it was an active fire investigation.

Yagan Square is described as a transit area for thousands of city workers and Perth residents, situated between the Perth CBD and the city's Northbridge entertainment precinct.

It is surrounded by bars and restaurants, the new multi-million-dollar Edith Cowan University city campus, Perth Underground train station and Perth Busport.

The square is named after the 19th century Aboriginal warrior Yagan, and was officially opened in 2018, costing taxpayers tens of millions of dollars.

World.title: Pyne warns AI could be 'means of human race's destruction'
World.content:
Former Labor leader Bill Shorten and former Coalition defence minister Christopher Pyne have joined the chorus for a slowdown in the development of artificial intelligence (AI).

Both issued blunt warnings on 7.30 about the damage AI could do if guardrails are not introduced as Mr Shorten compared AI to nuclear weapons and called for an AI version of the nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NNPT).

That treaty was introduced in 1970 to stop the spread of nuclear weapons, promote peaceful use of nuclear energy and pursue negotiations towards disarmament.

"I think the more that we hear from the CEOs and the chief officers of these frontier laboratories of AI, I cannot help escape the conclusion that we may have built nukes with opinions," Mr Shorten told 7.30.

"This is a marvellous technology, but until we can regulate it, we need to slow down.

"What we're seeing at the cutting edge of AI laboratories is actually a technology which doesn't appear to need humans to make decisions. Once you eliminate human oversight, there's no guarantee that what we're designing will actually make decisions in the best interest of humanity."

Mr Shorten said he was not suggesting that building data centres or infrastructure was a problem but that generative AI needed more human oversight.

It was a sentiment Mr Pyne, who now holds a number of positions as a strategic advisor and consultant, including for the defence industry, echoed.

"AI has tremendous opportunity for the human race It has the capacity to make our lives much, much better, not just from a health perspective, but many others," Mr Pyne said.

Former Liberal MP Christopher Pyne runs lobbying firm Pyne & Partners. (Four Corners: Ryan Sheridan)

"But there is an inherent danger.

"Obviously human beings are the smartest being on the planet, we have dominion of the globe because we might not be the strongest, we might not be the fastest, but we're the smartest.

"And we've created something that's actually smarter than us and with regenerative self-improvement is going to get much smarter and much quicker than we ever can.

"So we could have actually created the means of the human race's destruction.

" I'm not saying next week or in 10 years, but I think you would be a brave person to predict that the human race will dominate the globe in 500 years from now. "

Pressed if that was something he expected, Mr Pyne pulled back.

"I'm an optimist. I think it will all be OK in the end, but we wouldn't want to underestimate what we've done," he said.

An AI non-proliferation treaty?

With that warning the pair were asked what could be done to bring the rapid development of AI under control.

It is the same question those in the industry have been facing.

CEO and Co-Founder of Anthropic Dario Amodei has called for a slowdown on AI advancement. (Reuters: Denis Balibouse)

First AI researcher Jacob Coxon, who left OpenAI to join Anthropic, decided to leave the industry, accusing both US companies of "gambling with our lives" in the race to develop models capable of self-improvement.

That sparked a deluge of calls to slow it down from Geoffrey Hinton, widely known as the "godfather of AI", Anthropic boss Dario Amodei, OpenAI head Sam Altman and Elon Musk, who owns xAI.

"We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models," Mr Amodei wrote in a post on his personal website.

Given the nuclear comparisons made earlier, Mr Shorten was asked if an AI version of the NNPT was needed.

"Dario [Amodei] has proposed a plan, which does involve independent verification," Mr Shorten said.

"It does involve, as technologies are being developed, that you have external observers like we have the International Atomic Energy Agency.

"So I do think it does need global action and I don't think we can afford, in Australia, to say the problem is someone else's.

"As a middle power we can help lead this debate, but it's pretty interesting that you have the technology leaders, the private sector saying, 'hey, we need help here. We need regulation'.

"So I do think there is some analogy between the proliferation of nuclear weapons and the proliferation of AI and maybe some of the solutions that were used for nuclear weapons need to be put into place here."

Mr Pyne agreed and while he said AI was a race between the US and China, he suggested that guardrails were necessary to prevent potential rogue actors from being involved.

"China and the United States are locked in a competition over AI for different reasons and it could be very dangerous," he told 7.30.

"But by the same token, we as humans need to live on this planet and we need them to come to an agreement that the rest of the world can then fold into."

Cutting immigration is 'economic self-harm'

With the issue of immigration dominating the political agenda after One Nation released their policy earlier in the week it was put to the two former senior politicians as to what should be done.

Tony Burke was due to outline Labor's migration policy last month, but postponed the speech. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Mr Shorten, who is the Vice-Chancellor of the University of Canberra, acknowledged the government had work to do but cautioned them against acting too harshly, especially when it comes to mooted changes to policy around international students.

"We don't need to be in a bargaining auction in a race to the bottom about the lowest possible number," he told 7.30.

"We need migrants for this country to do well. Migrants tend to pay, as a group they're more likely to pay tax."

He said that cutting international student numbers would become a potential economic nightmare.

"If some people are overstaying their visas, by all means clamp down but economic self-harm when it comes to cutting international students is a real problem.

"It's international students whose fees cross-subsidise us being able to support Aussie kids. It's international students' fees who allow us to be able to fund research, which the nation wouldn't otherwise get.

Bill Shorten, is currently Vice-Chancellor at the University of Canberra. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

"And in regional Australia ... if you take out international students, there will be job losses.

"So governments have got to have a migration debate, but it's not going to save a government or an opposition."

Asked for his take on the issue, Mr Pyne said "migration has built this country".

"Everything Bill said about international students is right.

"Saying that we're going to start curtailing international students is definitely an act of self-harm.

"Politicians need to do is actually start standing up for migration, a population that is sustainable and explaining the benefits that this brings.

"Australia is so powerful internationally because of its multiculturalism and all the people in Australia who do business with the countries that they came from or their grandparents came from because of the knowledge they have, the skills they gain, the language commonalities.

"These things are not something that we should be embarrassed about."

Watch 7.30, Mondays to Thursdays 7:30pm on ABC iview and ABC TV

World.title: Ninth person charged over fatal house party attack on 21yo man
World.content:
Police have charged a ninth person with murder over the death of a 21-year-old man at a Logan house party in July.

Jongkuch Kur Jongkuch died on August 1, days after being allegedly assaulted by a group of people at an out-of-control house party at Bahrs Scrub.

The Redbank Plains man was discovered unconscious with critical head injuries on Orchard Avenue just after 2am on July 26.

Last month, police charged eight teenagers aged between 17 and 19 with his murder.

The 21-year-old Redbank Plains man was found unconscious with critical head injuries on Orchard Avenue. (ABC News: Meghan Dansie)

On Wednesday, detectives charged a ninth person, a 17-year-old Inala boy, with murder.

Police have alleged the teenagers who fatally attacked Mr Jongkuch came to the party armed and "prepared to inflict harm" on the people there.

The 17-year-old arrested this week will face the Beenleigh Children's Court on Thursday.

Police acknowledged the assistance of residents, community leaders and representatives who encouraged members of the community to come forward with information throughout the investigation.

World.title: Do animals grieve? Rare footage of this mother and her calf may hold the answer
World.content:
NationalWhales Do animals grieve? Rare footage of this mother and her calf may hold the answer Angus Dalton September 17, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The sea was calm and the sky half-strewn with clouds on a winter’s morning at Palm Beach Reef, off the Gold Coast, when Andrew Mulville arrived by boat to check on two whales milling in the shallow water. Members of the public had become worried that one of the humpbacks was injured or entangled, and reported their concerns to Sea World. Mulville, a whale rescue boat captain with the organisation, happened to be fishing nearby. A mother and her calf – not involved in the new study – playing off Byron Bay. Humpbacks have strong maternal bonds and have now been observed displaying possible “grief behaviours” towards a dead calf. Danielle Smith The whales weren’t hurt, he found, but were behaving strangely. An amniotic sack – part of a placenta – floated to the surface. Mulville dipped his GoPro underwater, and captured what researchers believe is the first detailed documentation of possible grief in a humpback whale over a stillborn calf. Watched by a companion, the young female repeatedly dove to the bottom, lying next to the calf’s body on the sea floor. She nudged it gently with her head and touched it with her fin.



“There were what appears to be attempts at eye contact, just observing it to see whether, maybe, there was any sign of life,” said Griffith University whale scientist Dr Olaf Meynecke. “There was clearly vocalisation happening, calling between the escort and her. “She was going and literally lying on the bottom … she was definitely spending time with the deceased calf.” A new paper by Meynecke and Mulville about the incident, which occurred in July last year, argues the whale probably understood her calf had died, as there was no attempt to lift it to the surface to breathe. Based on sightings from the public, Meynecke believes the whales may have remained near the calf for almost three days.



“We think it was a younger female; she wasn’t that big,” he said. “It might have been her first.” The observation adds unique insight into rare “post-mortem attentive responses” in socially complex mammals – also called grief behaviours – which involve mothers carrying, nudging, circling and guarding their dead offspring. The behaviours have been documented mostly in toothed whales, notably the orca known as Tahlequah, who carried the body of a calf for 17 days in 2018 and was observed doing the same with another dead calf last year. There have been few observations of these behaviours in baleen whales such as humpbacks.



Whether these intelligent and social creatures truly mourn, or experience something we would understand as grief, is up for debate. “Of course, from a science perspective, we can’t prove it’s grief,” Meynecke said. “It’d be so much easier if you could just ask them.” The paper notes the behaviours could be explained by confusion, or misfired caregiving instinct. The orca known as J35 (Tahlequah) carries the carcass of her dead calf in the waters of Puget Sound off West Seattle, Washington. AP But after years of observing humpbacks respond to other whales entangled in nets, and even protect other species from predators, Meynecke believes they must experience an “emotional state that is not necessarily comparable to ours … but there is something there that is quite strong”.



“I don’t even want to think about how horrible or traumatic it might have been for the whales that survived whaling because clearly, they would have had emotional responses,” he said. Related Article Visual story

Whales The new whale watching: Why this epic migration is more astonishing than we ever imagined Brain studies have discovered “spindle neurons”, which underpin social awareness and empathy, in humpbacks alongside other species that guard and touch their dead, including elephants and chimps. “Marine mammals are closely related to us from an evolutionary perspective. If they have evolved similar responses that we have, it might explain some of our quite deeply embedded emotional connections.” Associate Professor Rebecca Dunlop, an expert in whale behaviour from the University of Queensland who wasn’t involved in the study, said “descriptive case studies reporting the potential for animal emotions run the risk of anthropomorphising” animal behaviour.



“However, the study does present a balanced argument of how the observed behaviour could be interpreted and notes that the terms ‘grief’, ‘emotion’, ‘distress’ must be used with caution since we cannot definitively assign these terms to the observed behaviour,” she said. “The issue is around comparing human definitions of ‘emotion’ to non-humans, since emotion is a human conscious experience, where a human subject self-reports their experienced feelings. Clearly, this is not possible for animals.” While this study meditated on the possible deep emotional lives of whales, another paper released on Wednesday showed their close cousins can be thugs. Bubbles the fish-bullying bottlenose dolphin. Tracy Olive, UniSC Australia Scientists from the University of the Sunshine Coast have documented a bottlenose dolphin called Bubbles repeatedly harassing and chasing fish until they regurgitated their food, so Bubbles could eat it.



Related Article Whales First drone footage of a humpback birth shows mum and bub thriving It’s the first detailed description of “kleptoparasitism” in a whale or dolphin – and provides another warning about viewing wild animals through a simplistic human lens. “This perception of dolphins as the ‘good guys of the sea’ has more to do with anthropomorphism – our tendency to assign human characteristics to them – and perhaps that’s because dolphins appear to be smiling,” research co-author Dr Asia Haines said. “Dolphins are predators and actively hunt their prey, whether it has been stolen from another species or not.” The Examine newsletter explains and analyses science with a rigorous focus on the evidence. Sign up to get it each week.

World.title: ‘Repay the faith’: How Dylan Moore has gone from the jailhouse to becoming a role model
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘Repay the faith’: How Dylan Moore has gone from the jailhouse to becoming a role model Jon Pierik Updated September 16, 2026 — 10:47pm ,first published 5:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

From jailhouse to role model, that’s the tale of redemption Hawthorn hard nut Dylan Moore has experienced over the past year. And, as the Hawks prepare for Saturday night’s preliminary final against the Brisbane Lions, teammates say there is no one they would rather go into battle with than the robust forward. A season that is now just one step away from a grand final could have been so different for Moore had he and the Hawks not handled his off-season indiscretion in the mature manner they did – Moore and teammate Connor Macdonald having spent a night in jail in Phoenix, Arizona, after trespassing and climbing onto a scissor lift suspended 2.5 metres in the air while on a boozy end-of-season trip. Dylan Moore remains one of the Hawks’ most respected figures. Eddie Jim They were arrested by Scottsdale police, the pair charged with third-degree criminal trespass for their antics. The obligatory mugshot followed, but, in July, Moore’s case was officially dismissed. Reflecting on that ill-fated trip this week, Moore, 27, said it had been a humbling experience.

World.title: Chalmers wipes more than $500b off nation’s debt – in four decades’ time
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalFederal budget Chalmers wipes more than $500b off nation’s debt – in four decades’ time Shane Wright September 16, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Hundreds of billions of debt that would weigh on future taxpayers is likely to be avoided, a long-term forecast on the state of the federal budget will reveal, even as the government faces growing spending pressures and a blowout in the nation’s interest bill. The seventh release of the intergenerational report, to be released by Treasurer Jim Chalmers on Monday, will show gross government debt far lower than expected and deep spending cuts in this year’s budget improving the budget bottom line into the 2060s. Treasurer Jim Chalmers will reveal a long-term improvement to the budget worth hundreds of billions of dollars. Alex Ellinghausen Yet the immediate pressure on the budget is growing with another step-up in the interest rate on Australian government debt amid a global repricing of public debt exposing fiscal problems in the United States. Then-treasurer Peter Costello introduced intergenerational reports in 2002 to provide an outline of the pressures on government finances over the next four decades. Costello’s first report warned that a surge in spending on health services and the age pension would drive the budget into the red all the way to the 2040s.



Chalmers’ 2023 update forecast that gross debt, which recently hit $1 trillion, would reach more than a third of GDP by the early 2060s. But the report to be released next week will show gross debt around a quarter of GDP. In 2062 nominal dollar terms, the smaller level of debt is worth more than $500 billion. Related Article Analysis

Government debt How did we get here? The 20-year journey to $1 trillion in debt The lower debt level is being driven by an improvement in the budget. The report will show the deficit to be 1.2 percentage points lower, at close to 1.5 per cent of GDP in 2062-63, than had been forecast by Chalmers in his previous intergenerational outlook. Every intergenerational report has predicted large budget deficits from the late 2030s out to the 2060s. Costello’s first report forecast a deficit of 5 per cent of GDP – the equivalent of $135 billion – by 2042.



Part of the improvement is due to stronger revenue over recent years. Chalmers released his first intergenerational report in August 2023, when he expected a $4.2 billion surplus for the just-completed financial year and a deficit of $13.9 billion for 2023-24. Instead, the 2022-23 surplus was eventually revealed to be a record $22.1 billion, which was followed by a $15.8 billion surplus the following financial year. Another improvement is expected to flow from spending cuts contained in this year’s budget, putting pressure on Health Minister Mark Butler to deliver his ambitious overhaul of the National Disability Insurance Scheme. Next week’s report will show spending as a share of GDP 1.3 percentage points lower than had been forecast in 2023, a saving in nominal 2062 terms of almost $100 billion. The report will also confirm tax collections are not expected to climb above the historical high of 24.2 per cent of GDP seen in 2005 and 2006. It is slightly lower than what Chalmers had forecast in 2023. Interest rates on US debt have climbed to a 19-year high under President Donald Trump. AP



Chalmers said savings such as those made on the NDIS not only improved the budget bottom line in the long term but helped reduce interest costs borne by taxpayers. “We’ve made a lot of progress in the budget – paying down the debt we inherited, finding savings, restraining spending and addressing structural pressures – but we know there’s more work to do,” he said. “By getting the budget in better nick, we can rebuild our fiscal buffers at a time of heightened global uncertainty as we make room for more of the things Australians need and deserve, like more investment in Medicare, aged care, housing and tax cuts.” But the immediate cost to taxpayers from higher interest rates is growing. On Wednesday, interest rates on 10-year US government debt rose above 5 per cent for the first time since 2007. American gross debt is expected to reach $US41 trillion by year’s end, with the Trump administration on track for a budget deficit of $US2 trillion.



Interest on US debt helps set rates on the global debt market, with all developed economies facing an increase in their bond yields. Related Article Exclusive

Australian recession Global debt worries grow as Trump promises $1 trillion in handouts On Wednesday, Australia sold $1 billion in debt that will be repaid in April 2037. The interest rate on that debt is 5.39 per cent, an increase of more than 8 per cent since early August. Chalmers told parliament that Australia was in a good position to deal with the growing economic uncertainty caused by the lift in yields on government bonds, the jump in Brent crude to $US108 a barrel, and likely higher rates in the US, Britain and Europe. But shadow treasurer Tim Wilson said Chalmers should be reducing government spending to take inflation pressures off the Australian economy. Whitmore (Bill Pullman, in Independence Day and Independence Day: Resurgence) delivers one of the most famous, rallying motivational speeches in cinema history, right before returning to the cockpit and sacrificing his life by detonating cold-fusion bombs to destroy the alien Harvester Queen. Gail Grogan of Toongabbie reckons Dave Kovic “would win an election hands down. The doppelganger played by Kevin Kline in Dave is presently what’s needed in every country.”

“Oh, David Prest (C8), lucky you,” says Maureen Donlon of Wagga Wagga. “My older brother told me you had to keep the tyre caps in your mouth so you didn’t lose them. The Pullman East Melbourne hotel. Star trio Isaac Heeney, Nick Blakey and Chad Warner, along with James Jordon and Riley Bice, were handed season-ending suspensions by the Swans for failing to meet the club’s standards by drinking, partying late and bringing exotic dancers back to the Pullman after their round 23 win over Essendon. Best-and-fairest nights are typically a celebration of a club’s season. Sydney awards have previously been presented by club legend Bob Skilton (or a family representative) and Adam Goodes, who have medals struck in their honour. World.title: Do animals grieve? Rare footage of this mother and her calf may hold the answer
World.content:
NationalWhales Do animals grieve? Rare footage of this mother and her calf may hold the answer Angus Dalton September 17, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The sea was calm and the sky half-strewn with clouds on a winter’s morning at Palm Beach Reef, off the Gold Coast, when Andrew Mulville arrived by boat to check on two whales milling in the shallow water. Members of the public had become worried that one of the humpbacks was injured or entangled, and reported their concerns to Sea World. Mulville, a whale rescue boat captain with the organisation, happened to be fishing nearby. A mother and her calf – not involved in the new study – playing off Byron Bay. Humpbacks have strong maternal bonds and have now been observed displaying possible “grief behaviours” towards a dead calf. Danielle Smith The whales weren’t hurt, he found, but were behaving strangely. An amniotic sack – part of a placenta – floated to the surface. Mulville dipped his GoPro underwater, and captured what researchers believe is the first detailed documentation of possible grief in a humpback whale over a stillborn calf. Watched by a companion, the young female repeatedly dove to the bottom, lying next to the calf’s body on the sea floor. She nudged it gently with her head and touched it with her fin.



“There were what appears to be attempts at eye contact, just observing it to see whether, maybe, there was any sign of life,” said Griffith University whale scientist Dr Olaf Meynecke. “There was clearly vocalisation happening, calling between the escort and her. “She was going and literally lying on the bottom … she was definitely spending time with the deceased calf.” A new paper by Meynecke and Mulville about the incident, which occurred in July last year, argues the whale probably understood her calf had died, as there was no attempt to lift it to the surface to breathe. Based on sightings from the public, Meynecke believes the whales may have remained near the calf for almost three days.



“We think it was a younger female; she wasn’t that big,” he said. “It might have been her first.” The observation adds unique insight into rare “post-mortem attentive responses” in socially complex mammals – also called grief behaviours – which involve mothers carrying, nudging, circling and guarding their dead offspring. The behaviours have been documented mostly in toothed whales, notably the orca known as Tahlequah, who carried the body of a calf for 17 days in 2018 and was observed doing the same with another dead calf last year. There have been few observations of these behaviours in baleen whales such as humpbacks.



Whether these intelligent and social creatures truly mourn, or experience something we would understand as grief, is up for debate. “Of course, from a science perspective, we can’t prove it’s grief,” Meynecke said. “It’d be so much easier if you could just ask them.” The paper notes the behaviours could be explained by confusion, or misfired caregiving instinct. The orca known as J35 (Tahlequah) carries the carcass of her dead calf in the waters of Puget Sound off West Seattle, Washington. AP But after years of observing humpbacks respond to other whales entangled in nets, and even protect other species from predators, Meynecke believes they must experience an “emotional state that is not necessarily comparable to ours … but there is something there that is quite strong”.



“I don’t even want to think about how horrible or traumatic it might have been for the whales that survived whaling because clearly, they would have had emotional responses,” he said. Related Article Visual story

Whales The new whale watching: Why this epic migration is more astonishing than we ever imagined Brain studies have discovered “spindle neurons”, which underpin social awareness and empathy, in humpbacks alongside other species that guard and touch their dead, including elephants and chimps. “Marine mammals are closely related to us from an evolutionary perspective. If they have evolved similar responses that we have, it might explain some of our quite deeply embedded emotional connections.” Associate Professor Rebecca Dunlop, an expert in whale behaviour from the University of Queensland who wasn’t involved in the study, said “descriptive case studies reporting the potential for animal emotions run the risk of anthropomorphising” animal behaviour.



“However, the study does present a balanced argument of how the observed behaviour could be interpreted and notes that the terms ‘grief’, ‘emotion’, ‘distress’ must be used with caution since we cannot definitively assign these terms to the observed behaviour,” she said. “The issue is around comparing human definitions of ‘emotion’ to non-humans, since emotion is a human conscious experience, where a human subject self-reports their experienced feelings. Clearly, this is not possible for animals.” While this study meditated on the possible deep emotional lives of whales, another paper released on Wednesday showed their close cousins can be thugs. Bubbles the fish-bullying bottlenose dolphin. Tracy Olive, UniSC Australia Scientists from the University of the Sunshine Coast have documented a bottlenose dolphin called Bubbles repeatedly harassing and chasing fish until they regurgitated their food, so Bubbles could eat it.



Related Article Whales First drone footage of a humpback birth shows mum and bub thriving It’s the first detailed description of “kleptoparasitism” in a whale or dolphin – and provides another warning about viewing wild animals through a simplistic human lens. “This perception of dolphins as the ‘good guys of the sea’ has more to do with anthropomorphism – our tendency to assign human characteristics to them – and perhaps that’s because dolphins appear to be smiling,” research co-author Dr Asia Haines said. “Dolphins are predators and actively hunt their prey, whether it has been stolen from another species or not.” The Examine newsletter explains and analyses science with a rigorous focus on the evidence. Next week’s report will show spending as a share of GDP 1.3 percentage points lower than had been forecast in 2023, a saving in nominal 2062 terms of almost $100 billion. The report will also confirm tax collections are not expected to climb above the historical high of 24.2 per cent of GDP seen in 2005 and 2006. It is slightly lower than what Chalmers had forecast in 2023. Interest rates on US debt have climbed to a 19-year high under President Donald Trump. AP



Chalmers said savings such as those made on the NDIS not only improved the budget bottom line in the long term but helped reduce interest costs borne by taxpayers. “We’ve made a lot of progress in the budget – paying down the debt we inherited, finding savings, restraining spending and addressing structural pressures – but we know there’s more work to do,” he said. “By getting the budget in better nick, we can rebuild our fiscal buffers at a time of heightened global uncertainty as we make room for more of the things Australians need and deserve, like more investment in Medicare, aged care, housing and tax cuts.” But the immediate cost to taxpayers from higher interest rates is growing. On Wednesday, interest rates on 10-year US government debt rose above 5 per cent for the first time since 2007. American gross debt is expected to reach $US41 trillion by year’s end, with the Trump administration on track for a budget deficit of $US2 trillion.



Interest on US debt helps set rates on the global debt market, with all developed economies facing an increase in their bond yields. Related Article Exclusive

Australian recession Global debt worries grow as Trump promises $1 trillion in handouts On Wednesday, Australia sold $1 billion in debt that will be repaid in April 2037. The interest rate on that debt is 5.39 per cent, an increase of more than 8 per cent since early August. Chalmers told parliament that Australia was in a good position to deal with the growing economic uncertainty caused by the lift in yields on government bonds, the jump in Brent crude to $US108 a barrel, and likely higher rates in the US, Britain and Europe. But shadow treasurer Tim Wilson said Chalmers should be reducing government spending to take inflation pressures off the Australian economy. World.title: Putting a sheen on the presidency
World.content:
As for a fictional politician joining the real electoral race (C8), Greg King of Springwood writes: “I’m sure everyone is suggesting The West Wing’s Josiah Bartlet as a fictional president who would do well in the polls. It’s worth noting that Aaron Sorkin was the creator and writer for both this show and The American President. A dab hand at ideal presidents.” For what it’s worth, Granny’s vote goes to Warren Beatty’s titular, darkly satirical Jay Billington Bulworth.

“Michael Douglas as Andrew Shepherd would definitely rate well in Australian opinion polls,” thinks George Zivkovic of Northmead. “But Thomas J. Whitmore (Bill Pullman, in Independence Day and Independence Day: Resurgence) delivers one of the most famous, rallying motivational speeches in cinema history, right before returning to the cockpit and sacrificing his life by detonating cold-fusion bombs to destroy the alien Harvester Queen. What a leader!” Good stuff, but The Donald claims that was him.

Gail Grogan of Toongabbie reckons Dave Kovic “would win an election hands down. The doppelganger played by Kevin Kline in Dave is presently what’s needed in every country.”

“Oh, David Prest (C8), lucky you,” says Maureen Donlon of Wagga Wagga. “My older brother told me you had to keep the tyre caps in your mouth so you didn’t lose them. Then again, he and my older sister also convinced me, every spring for a number of years, that soursob was really delicious! Then they would almost die laughing as they told me the flowers are yellow because of the dog pee. It’s lucky I survived childhood, and they are lucky I still speak to them.”

“You make me jealous, Judy Bower,” says Mary Carde of Parrearra (Qld). “Barry was the best-looking Bee Gee. But I’ve only ever admired him from the nosebleed section at their One Night Only Sydney concert. I can brag, however, that Lonnie Lee winked and smiled at me during a performance in Melbourne in the 1960s as he sang I Found a New Love. I was 16 at the time and my heart skipped a million beats.”

World.title: Why the Swans are set to avoid a Pullman Hotel return if they qualify for the grand final
World.content:
SportAFLSydney Swans Why the Swans are set to avoid a Pullman Hotel return if they qualify for the grand final Andrew Wu September 16, 2026 — 8:52pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

Sydney are highly unlikely to be returning to the Pullman Hotel in East Melbourne if they qualify for next week’s grand final. The Brisbane Lions are staying at the Pullman this week for their preliminary final with Hawthorn and were also based at the venue for their premiership last year. An industry source with knowledge of the situation, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Chris Fagan’s men are highly likely to return to the venue in grand final week, should they qualify. The Pullman East Melbourne hotel. Simon Schluter The AFL does not usually book two clubs at the same accommodation simultaneously due to the logistical challenges for hotel staff to satisfy the specific catering needs of two large groups.
