It’s unclear if the Swans would be deliberately avoiding a return to the hotel, the scene of the scandal that rocked the AFL on the eve of the finals last month.



Star trio Isaac Heeney, Nick Blakey and Chad Warner, along with James Jordon and Riley Bice, were handed season-ending suspensions by the Swans for failing to meet the club’s standards by drinking, partying late and bringing exotic dancers back to the Pullman after their round 23 win over Essendon. Related Article AFL 2026 Suspended Swans to foot their own legal bills under AFL rules Four of the players – Heeney, Warner, Blakey and Jordon – are persons of interest in a police investigation from the night after three women alleged they were sexually assaulted and touched inappropriately without consent. Three other men in the room – including Bice, recently retired Swan Taylor Adams and a mystery man – are now considered to be witnesses to the pre-dawn events. This masthead revealed earlier this month that the five suspended Sydney players, all of whom have denied criminal wrongdoing, will have to foot their own substantial legal fees for their roles in the Pullman hotel episode.



The Swans are yet to make a call on whether the suspended five will remain eligible for the club’s best-and-fairest award, which will be presented at a function in Sydney on Thursday, October 1 – just days after the grand final on September 26. Heeney, Warner and Blakey are all expected to feature prominently in voting, despite missing the Swans’ past two matches. It has not yet been determined if the players would be invited, while it is also unclear if they would be ready to return to the club. Best-and-fairest nights are typically a celebration of a club’s season. Sydney awards have previously been presented by club legend Bob Skilton (or a family representative) and Adam Goodes, who have medals struck in their honour. The Swans players are eligible to win the Brownlow Medal, to be presented on Monday night next week, but Collingwood superstar Nick Daicos is the hottest of hot favourites to win the award.

World.title: Winston Peters mocks National as 'Great Pretender' over supermarket policy
World.content:
National's proposed supermarket shake-up has set the coalition partners against one another, with New Zealand First crying "copy cat" and ACT labelling it "desperate and visionless".

In a surprise policy announcement on Wednesday, National announced a plan to sever Pak'nSave from New World in a bid to drive down grocery prices, contingent on a six-month review by the Commerce Commission.

Heading into the debating chamber, NZ First leader Winston Peters paused to play reporters a snippet of the 1955 song "The Great Pretender" on his phone.

"Everybody's borrowing our policies, as you'll notice, and we're getting a bit sick of it," Peters said.

He told reporters National had simply "cut and pasted" NZ First's plan to break up the duopoly which it announced in April.

But Peters said the development had come "far too late" to make a difference this term.

"If they'd done it in April, we could have had it all through Parliament and fixed up already."

Asked about ACT's virulent opposition, Peters suggested National could have secured the necessary support from opposition parties.

Responding, National leader Christopher Luxon laughed off the Great Pretender jab: "Isn't he great with the singing? I mean, it's one of the great joys of working with him."

Luxon said he was pleased National had found "political consensus" with NZ First on "something serious and substantive".

The ACT Party, however, was certainly not joining that consensus, issuing a scathing media release deriding "desperate and visionless campaigning" driven by focus group.

ACT leader David Seymour warned such "heavy-handed intervention" would have a chilling impact on investment and dissuade new entrants from setting up here.

Speaking to reporters, Seymour suggested National was "not entirely committed" to the idea and had given itself an out by asking the Commerce Commission to look at it.

"The ACT party is starting to sound like what the National Party should be: standing up for the rights of people to save, invest, and sacrifice, and have a better life as a result."

Seymour said the policy was little different from "the Greens' roundly-mocked Government-owned supermarket".

That argument was somewhat bolstered by the Green Party itself, which celebrated National's announcement, jokingly referring to its MPs as "our comrades".

"We've finally got the National Party coming to the table on things that they accused us for being communist about just two weeks ago," co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick told reporters.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins also ridiculed the disagreement between the coalition parties, saying they were panicking after failing to improve the cost of living.

"No one can believe Christopher Luxon. David Seymour doesn't believe him. Why should New Zealanders?"

World.title: Tairāwhiti flood recovery: 'We're a long way off yet'
World.content:
In Te Araroa, one of the East Cape's famous beach towns, the previously booming tourist industry has virtually ground to a halt as locals continue to grapple with the aftermath of destructive flooding from January. Checkpoint's Teuila Fuatai reports.

You would be hard pressed to recognise Te Araroa Holiday Park.

Everywhere you look there is mud and water - a far cry from the idyllic gardens which used to greet its visitors.

In fact, when we get to Te Araroa, I drive straight past it. There is no sign marking the spot and the driveway looks like a farm paddock with tyre tracks through sludge.

It doesn't take long to see why manager Nina McClutchie told my cameraman Baz and I we would need gumboots.

"This is 50 percent better than what it was for us, but we're a long way off yet," she says.

For someone arriving seven months into the clean-up, it's hard to imagine how bad things were immediately after the January storm.

Today, the accommodation blocks and cabins look they've been plonked randomly around a dirt wasteland. Some of them are condemned, while others are still having work done.

Nina - who is among a handful of residents that call the park home - shows us the block she used to live in.

Nina McClutchie, Te Araroa Holiday Park manager and owner of 35 Eat Street. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Only the middle unit is still occupied, while the rest have either been yellow or red stickered.

She moved out of her units straight after the storm. When we look inside one of them, her old bed is still there, with a few belongings piled on top. The seven-month-old silt line still marks the door around calf height - an eerie reminder of the storm's power.

"This is all I've got left," Nina says.

"We've just cleaned up as best as we can, but it was all logs and just horrible.

"The roof's coming down in there... and yeah, the walls, everything - it just now black mould in there."

'It's not hygienically right to be open'

The destructive January storm brought a mass of earth, trees and water through the camp. It also caused widespread damage throughout communities along the East Cape.

Nina says the deluge that hammered the holiday park was a combination of a landslide from Punaruku and the creek running alongside the holiday park breaching. She says things got "really hairy" in the early hours of the morning when the whole camp was awash with debris and water during the storm event.

"I was trapped inside, and just after 2am I tried to get out and I couldn't.

"I realised that there were big logs and a lot of debris, and a lot of water coming around fast."

One of the other residents Steve Lamb managed to dig her out around 6am.

"And that's when I realised [that] we've got a massive issue here… and this is catastrophic."

Slash and dirt piled up on the riverbanks of Te Araroa Holiday Park. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Nina says a heap of help - including from the army and the Gisborne District Council - landed straight away.

She says the army were instrumental in clearing away the worst of the silt, particularly from around the park's cabins and accommodation blocks, as well as her own gourmet burger and fries food caravan 35 Eat Street.

However, it's the ongoing clean-up that is proving tough.

She walks us to the food caravan near the entrance of the camp. It remains shuttered as the rest of the park is prioritised in the flood clean-up,

During the low season, Nina says she'd normally open five nights a week for guests and locals.

Now, there are few tourists around, and the caravan won't be cleaned until the rest of the park is in better shape.

"I can't open - that's just the way it is. It's not hygienically right to be open, especially with silt dust still flying around."

Nina McClutchie's food business Eat 35, which has been closed since January's storm. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

She says while some tourists are still coming through, it's nothing like previous years, when lots of visitors from the northern hemisphere stayed during winter and spring.

"There has been a couple of times where campers have come through and they don't want to travel any further and they're self-contained, then I've allowed them to stay up the front.

"They've been so thankful for that, and yeah, they just move on."

'There's just tons and tons of it'

For Nina, and a handful or residents and close friends, the days are now spent tackling the muddy mess around them.

When we're there, Steve is on the digger. He starts up about 8am and goes until it's too dark to keep working.

It's been a hard slog, he says.

"We now have to scrape the silt away till we get to the baseline, which is like a grey matter at the moment.

"That gets away all the sticks. We can then, after that… level it.

"it's just surprising - there's just tons and tons of it."

Steve says it has been a tough seven months for the whole community.

Retired Te Araroa resident Steve Lamb. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

He points to each side of the holiday park and its neighbours, describing the devastation and hurt for different whānau. Some are still too traumatised to speak to Checkpoint about the storm.

"There were people across the road," Steve says. "They ended up being on their roof for a number of hours, and when we finally were able to get out of the camp and saw what had happened to them. I mean - there were boulders, and those people have kids."

The plight of the Ngatai-Cooper family was reported widely when the storm hit. The whānau have been staying with relatives since.

Steve also points to another neighbour's section, which has massive piles of slash - well over six feet tall - stacked on it.

"What do they do with that?"

'No one cares'

He and Nina also show us the creek that runs alongside the holiday park and through the area.

It's filled up with shingle since the storm, when it breached its banks and gushed into the park and surrounding properties.

It is now a major concern for residents.

Nina says unless it is cleared out, which would require its current level to be dug down at least two metres, it will continue to be a flood risk.

"All the stones need to come out, but as you can see, that's a lot of work. And the creek runs from the road right around the back of the camp."

So far, she and Steve and their clean-up crew have managed to rebuild the bank providing some protection for the property. But there's still been a few close calls when the water levels have risen.

"But luckily, the rain's backed off," Nina says.

A floodbank built along the river bordering Te Araroa Holiday Park. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Steve says they have come a long way since January, though it hasn't been without its challenges - especially after the initial support finished.

Simply put, he thought more help would be available after such a damaging weather event. Park owner Bill Martin estimates the cost of the park clean-up to now be about $300,000.

"You can't rely on other people," Steve says.

"You have to be self-sufficient, but I expected more and more professionalism from local government.

"It seems like they came, they did their bit, they're gone, no one cares"

He is not the only local who's expressed that sentiment.

Down the road from the holiday park, residents around Tokata road are experiencing ongoing flooding.

Carl Mullany - who lives on the section where the flooding starts - says its because the stream bed running through his land filled up with shingle from the January storm. As a result, the water that comes down from the maunga behind his property, doesn't have a path. Instead, it spreads across his land and the neighbouring properties.

He and other affected residents have been trying to work with Gisborne District Council to find a solution.

They have also met with their local East Coast MP - National's Dana Kirkpatrick - about the problem.

She described conditions in the area as "pretty demoralising".

Seven months on from flood Te Araroa faces massive clean up Checkpoint Download MP3 6m

"I've lived through a few floods in my time….and I understand the sheer demoralising situation it is when you look out every day and you see things that you can't control and you can't fix, and the desolation that it brings."

Local MP: 'I'll do whatever I can'

Kirkpatrick pointed the finger squarely at Gisborne District Council, labelling the lack of support for locals after seven months as frustrating.

She says the council told her in July they were undertaking a report on the area, however after two months, neither her nor the landowners have received anything.

"I am frustrated by them because these people are living this day-by-day.

"I just go back to the point…that regional councils are responsible for river management, flood protection, flood control schemes, catchment management, and drainage networks.

"So, they might say that the stream is on private land…but actually the responsibility for that lies with the council."

Rivers diverted across properties in Te Araroa following January's storm. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

The council has confirmed to Checkpoint it has completed "the technical assessment of the stream and surrounding catchment".

It also says it needs to have further discussions with landowners about potential options, however it has no budget currently to do any work.

As a result, the council says it "will explore the case for seeking Crown funding".

Kirkpatrick is urging them to get in touch immediately.

"I've already given them the undertaking that I'll do whatever I can. But the first thing we need to know is how much it's going to cost and what needs to be done."

Christmas reopening: 'Fingers and toes crossed'

In the meantime, Nina says they'll continue working seven-days-a-week to get the holiday park ready for summer.

She's opened accommodation to road crews, who continue to fix multiple slips on the coastal road from January's storm.

"We only have the Downer's road crews staying there. They've been here for the last three months doing recovery work.

"They stay here from Monday to Friday, so I've been very grateful to them to have the mahi."

She says they're aiming for a Christmas reopening, and with all their work, she reckons they'll do it.

World.title: Pact Packaging staff strike for living wage
World.content:
The pay offer for staff at Australian-owned business Pact Packaging - in Lower Hutt, north of Wellington - will not get workers near the living wage, E tū union said as workers went on strike.

About 50 union affiliated workers were on strike on Tuesday in response to the company's offer of an extra $0.66 an hour.

E tū team leader Joanna Wallace said last week workers voted unanimously voted to walk off the job for two hours.

"The majority of our members will average around $26 an hour so 66 cents really isn't cutting it when the living wage is $29.90 and inflation is 4.1 percent," Wallace said.

Workers on strike at Pact Packaging on Tuesday. E tū Union / SUPPLIED

Wallace said in previous negotiations workers had asked for a rise of 8 percent which would take the average hourly rate up to just over $28 per hour.

A storeperson at the plant, John Te Kawa - had been working at the plant for four years.

He said the $0.66 pay offer was "crap".

"I'm a home owner like a lot of other people here. With the rise in rates, insurances [sic] and now we've been imposed with water taxes et cetera. It's just hard to keep up with the bills really.

"A lot of them feel undervalued. They're working longer hours for less. They could do anything between 8 and 12 hour shifts. It feels like they're not being heard," Te Kawa said.

Te Kawa said some more recent staff would only just be lifted beyond minimum wage by the offer.

Pact worker John Te Kawa said the collective agreement offer of a $0.66 pay rise will see some recent employees only just exceed minimum wage. E tū Union / SUPPLIED

"Before inflation went up we used to work to live. Now it just makes them feel like they're living to work. Just to make ends meet."

He said the plant's staff were being joined by nightshift workers, supporters and other E tū union groups in a lively and vocal protest outside the plant.

A Pact Group spokesperson said the company was a part of a multi-employer collective agreement which included five other companies.

"Pact Group remains committed to bargaining in good faith and will continue to engage constructively through the agreed bargaining process, including with E tū and the other parties to the agreement.

World.title: Search resumes for plane that vanished in 1978 with seven people on board
World.content:
The search is resuming for a plane which vanished without a trace nearly half a century ago, carrying seven people.

NZ Police, the defence force and Coastguard West Coast will be conducting a three-day search operation for the lost plane at Lake Moeraki boat ramp, starting next Monday.

The aircraft - ZK-EBU - went missing in 1978 during a chartered scenic flight from Dunedin through Queenstown, Milford Sound and Preservation Inlet.

Last contact with the plane was made while it was flying through Milford Sound.

Acting West Coast area commander Mark Kirkwood said the boat ramp at the northern entrance to the lake would be used throughout the search.

"To ensure the safe movement of personnel and equipment, we ask that the area be kept clear for the duration of the operation."

In 2015, a Givealittle page was set up to raise money for a trip overseas to use radar technology as part of the search.

"We have made contact with a company overseas who are willing to donate the use of their latest technology foliage penetrating radar system for free, but we will need to pay for the operator's travel expenses and overheads."

World.title: National vows to 'pursue' break up of supermarket giant Foodstuffs
World.content:
National has made a supermarket break-up a key part of its election pitch, proposing to sever Pak'nSave from New World in a bid to drive down grocery prices.

The shake-up would be contingent on a six-month review by the Commerce Commission into whether the split would actually leave shoppers better off.

If the watchdog gave it the green light, National said it would legislate to force through the separation.

The significant policy was announced with little warning on Wednesday morning, and on the same day that Labour promised to ban big companies from charging excessive prices.

Foodstuffs - made up of two co-operatives - currently manages all New World, Pak'nSave and Four Square stores.

National's plan would split them up, leaving the country with three nationwide supermarket chains: Pak'nSave, New World/Four Square and Woolworths.

"This is, I acknowledge, a bold and unprecedented step," finance spokesperson Nicola Willis told reporters at Parliament.

"It is the right one. It puts the Kiwi shopper first."

Willis said the proposal followed a comprehensive cost-benefit analysis - by Sense Partners - and two peer reviews which she commissioned as finance minister to explore proposals for breaking up the duopoly.

But she said rather than taking a proposal back to Cabinet this term, National would instead seek an "explicit electoral mandate" from the public given the significance of the move.

"No Kiwi shopper or store owner would thank us if we mucked this up," she said. "While it's always tempting to rush in, the stakes are very high, and work of the sort requires a prudent, careful approach from ministers."

Hipkins: 'New Zealanders can't eat a review'

Labour leader Chris Hipkins dismissed National's policy as little more than "another review" and said New Zealanders deserved "more decisive" action.

"It's not a commitment. It's another review," he said. "New Zealanders can't eat a review."

Hipkins would not be drawn on whether he supported breaking up Foodstuffs, but said Labour would have more to say about supermarket competition before the election.

He also pointed out National would find it difficult to get its policy over the line with coalition partner ACT, given its leader David Seymour previously lambasted the plan, arguing it would scare away investment.

New Zealand First, in contrast, announced its own plan to break up Foodstuffs in April.

Willis said the coalition had proven an ability to compromise on various policies this term: "Obviously, this is a key priority for us, and that would be reflected in our coalition discussions."

National leader Christopher Luxon told reporters Labour had failed to put forward a proper "substantive solution" and was so far offering only "more clipboards and bureaucrats".

Willis said the shake-up could eventually save households up to $1320 a year, pushing down grocery prices about 5 percent lower than they would otherwise be.

Sense Partners' modelling estimated prices would be about 3.5 percent lower in the first year of separation, with gains growing as the new chains bedded in. By 2035, the estimated annual household benefit ranged from $200 to $1320 depending on income and family type.

"That's real money back in the pockets of New Zealanders," Willis said.

"More competition means supermarkets have to work harder for every customer, on price, specials, range and service. That is how shoppers get a better deal."

National also trumpeted a potential $12.6 billion in "consumer benefits" over 20 years. However, the underlying analysis put the overall net gain to the whole economy at just $2.9b once lost supermarket profits were counted, or even lower if Foodstuffs' costs increased.

The independent report also carried some hefty warnings, with the economists warning their analysis was "indicative rather than definitive" and flagging potential "insurmountable" legal and implementation hurdles.

Willis acknowledges 'tough fight' ahead

Willis stressed that National would act carefully on the Commission's advice and not play "supermarket executive from the Cabinet table".

"There is a very high bar for this kind of intervention and National is not pursuing structural separation in any other sector," Willis said.

"However, after years of reviews and incremental reform, it's clear the status quo isn't working. It's time for change."

Willis acknowledged the difficulties ahead, saying she had already felt the "full force" of the supermarkets' well-resourced lobbyists.

"I know that I am taking on a big entity here," she said. "I've satisfied myself this is the right thing to do, but I know that it's going to be a tough fight."

National said no individual Pak'nSave, New World or Four Square owner would be forced to sell or change brands.

Instead, the two Foodstuffs brands would be split into rival nationwide groups, with separate structures and incentives to compete against each other.

The Commerce Commission's latest monitoring showed Foodstuffs and Woolworths still controlled about 82 percent of the grocery market, with little movement in the core measures of competition over the past year.

Wednesday's announcements follow repeated efforts by both the coalition and former Labour government to break the supermarket stranglehold, with little to show for it.

Willis last year put out a call for third major challenger to enter the market, sounding out potential competitors, but the industry's biggest global players declined to engage.

The government also created an "express lane" for consenting new supermarkets, but it appears no applications have yet been lodged.

In 2020, Labour ordered a market study, then brought in a Grocery Commissioner and banned restrictive land deals.

'Significant implications': Foodstuffs

In a statement on Wednesday evening, Foodstuffs said the policy would have "significant implications" and every one of their more than 500 locally owned and operated stores would be affected.

"Our immediate focus is supporting our owner-operators, our 3000 supply chain and support centre team members, and the many New Zealand businesses that work with us, all of whom are hearing proposals that could fundamentally change the co-operatives they own, work for and support, and the businesses they have spent years building in communities throughout New Zealand."

Foodstuffs said a proposal of this scale raised questions about how long it would take to implement, the level of disruption and cost involved, and whether it would deliver meaningful savings at the checkout.

World.title: Outgoing National MP Andrew Bayly discusses his 'brutal' resignation in final speech to Parliament
World.content:
Outgoing National MP Andrew Bayly has used his final speech in Parliament to set the record straight about his resignation, calling it one of the "most brutal experiences" of his life.

The Port Waikato MP delivered his valedictory speech on Wednesday evening.

Bayly revealed he had resigned from his ministerial portfolios based on a false premise, wrongly believing a staff member had complained about his conduct.

That happened last year, and at the time the former commerce and consumer affairs minister recounted an "animated discussion" that ended with him putting a hand on a staff member.

At the time he apologised, saying he had been inappropriate and taken the discussion too far, but denied using any force.

In his valedictory speech, Bayly said at the end of a meeting with three of his advisers, he had placed his hand on the arm of a male adviser and said "we can do this".

"The next night, I was told a serious allegation had been made. I couldn't believe it," he said.

Bayly said when he told his wife Tina, she turned away and cried.

"That was when I understood this was no longer just about a ministerial job.

"It was hurting the person I loved most."

Bayly said the Department of Internal Affairs had told him all three people at the meeting had corroborated the allegation.

He might have contested the account of one person, or two people, he said.

Commerce and Consumer Affairs Minister Andrew Bayly speaks following his resignation from all ministerial positions on 24 February 2025. RNZ / Calvin Samuel

"But if all three corroborated a serious allegation, I could not remain a minister," he said.

"It was on that premise that I took the decision to resign."

Shortly before he announced that, Bayly said he met with the complainant.

"During that conversation, he told me that he had not made a complaint and would not have done so," he said.

"The next day, the second witness described the meeting as a storm in a teacup."

Three months later, Public Service Commissioner Sir Brian Roche confirmed the ACC chief executive had initiated the investigation, and no formal complaint was ever made about his conduct, Bayly said.

He said ministers must be accountable for their behaviour, however that accountability must rest on facts and a fair process.

"Mine did not," he said.

Bayly said he was in a "very dark place" following his resignation.

Being a minister had been the greatest privilege of his life, he said, but his time in Parliament was tough on his family, referencing death threats made against his wife and children.

"You did not choose it. You did not deserve it. And I will always be sorry."

In his speech, Bayly discussed some of his wins, which included advancing open banking, completing major insurance law reform, beginning the first "serious" review of New Zealand's competition settings in decades, and commissioning two major reviews into ACC and managing its fund.

At the end of his speech, he called on MPs to raise the Superannuation age to 68, beginning gradually from 2029.

World.title: Tom Phillips case: 'Circuit breaker' moment was missed, says mayor
World.content:
The mayor of Waitomo asked the Children's Commissioner to intervene and bring the government agencies involved in the Tom Phillips case together in a "circuit breaker" moment, a year before Phillips was killed.

A public inquiry has found authorities minimised the potential for Phillips' three children to be harmed and did not collaborate well, resulting in missed opportunities to end the saga.

Waitomo mayor John Robertson feared there was something awry years ago.

"A year before the tragedy of the shooting of Tom Phillips and the finding of the children, I made a call to the commissioner for children, pondering whether there was another way through this.

"And someone of standing, a commissioner for children seemed to me to be appropriate to try to bring the parties, the government parties that were involved together and see if there was some way to, you know, create a circuit breaker in this."

Robertson said the report made interesting reading.

"The comments, the criticism that our government departments weren't being collaborative enough or working together enough on this. That's certainly something I wondered [about] a year before, after year three, really, of the Tom Phillips and the children being away."

He said he'd had cordial discussion with then-Children's Commissioner Dr Claire Achmad.

"I called her on the phone to ask if she would intervene - by bringing the police and the Family Court / Oranga Tamariki together to see if there was an opportunity to 'negotiate' a way through the impasse. It was a good conversation, she said she would reflect [on it], but I heard no more."

Achmad remembered the call.

"Yes, I do, and I really appreciated Mayor Robertson contacting me with his suggestions for how things could be progressed.

"I remember that the mayor was understandably very concerned about the ongoing safety and wellbeing of the children, and he was, of course, advocating strongly throughout for their safe return."

Former Children's Commissioner Dr Claire Achmad. RNZ / Cole Eastham-Farrelly

She took up the baton.

"Of course took those suggestions and concerns forward to Oranga Tamariki and to police at the highest level, at chief executive and commissioner level. And I made clear that I had concerns, of course, about seeing the safe return of the children.

"I also made an offer at that time, following the mayor's prompting, that if there was anything that I could do from my independent role as Children's Commissioner, then those agencies were welcome to call on me for that independent role to the extent that I could.

She got a lukewarm response.

"Those offers were not taken up, and I received assurances that everything was being done to ensure the safe return of those children, and that the agencies were working closely together on bringing those children home safely and locating them."

Achmad said in light of the assurances given to her, the inquiry's findings were deeply disappointing.

"What's absolutely clear to me, having read this inquiry report, is that the concerns that had been coming forward from the whanau and from the community had clearly been minimised by these agencies, and it's clear to me now that these agencies were not working together as closely as they should have been.

"And that's incredibly, incredibly disappointing and unacceptable in my view."

Achmad was puzzled that Robertson believed he had not heard back from her.

"I think that might be a bit of a miscommunication. My memory, my recollection, is that a call was put through to the council office and a message was left. I remember that I couldn't reach him there that day.

"My recollection is that I left a message at the council offices just letting him know that I had heard his concerns and suggestions and that I was taking those forward."

Achmad said she would follow up with the mayor.

Meanwhile, Robertson welcomed the "very frank" inquiry's findings, which had helped fill-in gaps in the information available to him and locals over the four years Phillips was on the run with his three children.

"I'm pleased to see a report come out that's not redacted. And having the commentary on Oranga Tamariki and the sorts of advice that was given at the time is helpful to understanding what was going on.

"I mean, at the beginning of the report it talks about two critical themes and one of them is that the harm caused by isolating the children from the family, friends and society was underplayed, minimised or overlooked by agencies.

"So, that sort of statement, I guess, sums things up. So, it's good now to find what the agencies were thinking, which, you know, the report is pretty critical of."

Robertson said it was easy to be critical in hindsight, "but I think there were lessons [to be learned], or certainly the inquiry pulls no punches in saying there were some things that weren't done terribly well".

Robertson said while the report was also critical of aspects of the police operation to find Phillips and his children, he had a good relationship with police through the ordeal.

"They were alerting me or advising me on incidents as they went on. They were usually public incidents. So I felt very well briefed by the police and I felt for them in terms of their frustration through that time in trying to find Tom Phillips.

He said the report gave more detail what police were doing with NZ Defence Force and SAS involvement.

"I guess we all understood what the police were doing or trying to do in their frustrations. What we didn't know was the Oranga Tamariki side of the story.

"Those were the gaps that the public, and certainly I, you know, found through the four years."

Robertson welcomed the formal apology to the maternal whānau and older siblings of the Phillips children.

"I'm really pleased to see an apology to the children from the Minister [Louise Upston] on behalf of the Crown, because this report does highlight some inadequacies and I think it's only proper that there is an apology."

Robertson said the local community was still digesting the findings.

"Look, I think it's too early to say [what the reaction is]. I've sat down and worked through the report.

"I think the conclusion is that, you know, the government departments needed to work better together."

Phillips first went missing with his three children for 18 days in September 2021 before disappearing again in December of the same year.

World.title: Splitting up Foodstuffs: Would it actually drive down grocery prices?
World.content:
National wants to split Foodstuffs in two in a bid to drive down grocery prices - but would it work?

It announced the proposal on Wednesday, which would require a Commerce Commission review to determine whether it would leave shoppers better off.

Foodstuffs - made up of two co-operatives - currently manages all New World, Pak'nSave and Four Square stores.

National's plan would split them up, leaving the country with three nationwide supermarket chains: Pak'nSave, New World/Four Square and Woolworths.

University of Auckland senior marketing lecturer Drew Franklin said it was a step in the right direction.

"Structural separation or intervention that's seeking to structurally reform the sector has been shown to work overseas because it lowers the concentration of the market so there are more players in the game."

National's modelling estimated 3.5 percent lower prices after a year and 5 percent lower after six years with Foodstuffs split in two.

Could I run out of money in retirement and other questions experts wish you'd ask No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 15m

Nicola Willis, speaking as the party's finance spokesperson, said it could eventually save households up to $1320 a year.

"The short answer is time will tell," Franklin said. "That sort of structural separation putting downward pressure on prices isn't going to happen in a hurry."

Jon Duffy, chief executive of Consumer, welcomed the idea.

"The debate has really moved forward from where we were even six weeks ago, where we were still debating whether some form of intervention was needed beyond the pretty lukewarm measures that have been implemented since the Commerce Commission's study - pretty much all the major parties with the exception of ACT have some form of structural reform or measure to address price gouging, that sort of thing, in their election manifestos. This is a step forward for New Zealand."

He said it was positive that National's plan was to require that the Commerce Commission first consider what it would mean for customers with what was effectively a reverse merger assessment.

"The commission is very skilled at doing this type of analysis. So it's saying instead of hypothesising what a market would look like if two entities merge, hypothesise what they will look like if they demerge, and work out whether there's a net benefit to consumers."

Foodstuffs manages all New World, Pak'nSave and Four Square stores. Supplied

He said National's plan seemed intended to treat the "disease", while Labour's announcement on anti-price gouging measures was addressing the symptoms of a lack of competition.

The savings being talked about showed how badly the market was treating consumers, he said.

"It's strange territory for the National Party but that's how bad the problem is."

BusinessNZ director of advocacy Catherine Beard said it was a concerning proposal that could undermine New Zealand's reputation for regulatory stability, respect for property rights and predictable policy settings.

"This is a very concerning move by the National Party and sends a chilling signal to businesses across New Zealand that the government can break up businesses. It also sends the wrong signal to foreign investors looking to invest in New Zealand."

She said the government needed to be clear on what the problem was that it wanted to fix.

"Because one of the important bits of information that Commerce Commission's not really gotten to the bottom of is how does our basket of groceries stack up in New Zealand versus international comparators when a lot of other countries don't put GST on their food and New Zealand does? And I think the Commerce Commission acknowledged in their last report that that is an area that needs further work."

She said there could be a scenario where prices rose when the business was split because it lost efficiencies of scale.

But Franklin said while it was strong intervention and BusinessNZ was right to demand strong evidence and safeguards, it would only be overreach in the absence of a demonstrated problem.

"We've done our own research here at the University of Auckland that has identified that the concentration problem is well documented.

"And so, that's the problem that the structural separation is seeking to fix effectively. It's not the government setting grocery prices or running supermarkets or co-opting supermarkets like some of the other policies that we've heard to date."

He said the Commerce Commission needed more teeth and a much more legitimate role in trying to respond most appropriately to entrenched market power.

BusinessNZ said the supermarket proposal could undermine New Zealand's reputation for regulatory stability. Unsplash / Getty Images

"I think it's a step in the right direction."

It would also be important to consider supply arrangements and what a split would mean in areas that were only served by one supermarket brand, he added.

Westpac chief economist Kelly Eckhold said New Zealand's food price increases over the last 20 years had been in about the middle of OECD countries.

"The increase in food prices and cost of living pressures has been a global phenomenon and it's hard to point at New Zealand-specific factors to suggest our prices are dramatically different to what's happened with the global trend, which has been to higher prices."

He said splitting Foodstuffs was unlikely to be a silver bullet to fix the cost-of-living crisis.

Foodstuffs has been approached for comment.

World.title: Australia's 43-year MotoGP streak continues with Senna Agius signing
World.content:
There will be a full-time Australian rider in motorcycle racing's premier class for the 43rd consecutive year with 21-year-old Senna Agius signing on to race for KTM Tech3 next year.

The Sydneysider currently sits fourth in the Moto2 standings after placing 10th in 2025.

He has four grand prix wins in Moto2, including at the Circuit of the Americas in the United States and Jerez in Spain earlier this season.

He won his home Moto2 grand prix at Phillip Island last year, and will be in MotoGP for next year's maiden Australian Grand Prix at the new Adelaide street circuit.

Agius has signed on for KTM Tech3, which has former F1 team principal Guenther Steiner has the team's chief executive.

"Today a lifelong dream of mine has come true, reaching MotoGP," Agius said.

"So many years of hard work have gone into this moment and I'm incredibly grateful to Guenther and everyone at Tech3 for believing in me and giving me this opportunity.

"I can't wait to repay their faith. I know the challenge ahead, but I'm ready to learn, work hard, and become the best version of myself with this team."

Australia has had a full-time rider in the premier class since 1985.

In the modern era of grand prix motorcycle racing, which began in 2002 when 500cc two-stroke bikes were replaced with 990cc four-stroke engines, Agius will become the 11th full-time Australian rider.

He will also be the only Australian on the grid next season, with Jack Miller ending his 12-year MotoGP stint and moving to World Superbikes in 2027.

World.title: Alex de Minaur readies for Davis Cup tie between Australia and Poland
World.content:
A Davis Cup tie has come at the perfect time for Alex de Minaur as he searches to recapture a spark after nearly a decade on tour.

The Australian, ranked as high as number five in the world earlier this year, fell to ninth after his shock second-round US Open loss earlier this month.

A quarterfinalist at the Australian Open this year, the 27-year-old has missed golden opportunities to go further in majors since, with Alexander Zverev instead netting two titles as Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz both endured injury-hit seasons.

De Minaur headed straight to Brisbane after his Flushing Meadows disappointment, training with Australian Cup captain Lleyton Hewitt for more than a week before their qualifying tie against Poland begins on Saturday.

De Minaur crashes out of US Open Alex de Minaur has crashed out of the US Open at the second-round stage, beaten in straight sets by Botic van de Zandschulp.

"Back here, around the boys, some good practice, a great team environment; it's been a great little change-up for me," de Minaur said.

"This is exactly what I need to get that spark back that maybe I was missing.

"I've had that spark for 10 years, every single day, right?

"There are stages through your career where things happen, and maybe you don't feel your best. But the timing of this week, it feels like everything's clicking together."

De Minaur has previously taken his losses hard; he copped his most recent defeat to Botic van de Zandschulp with uncharacteristic nonchalance.

But he is adamant the competitive edge remains as he prepares to head a team that includes doubles ace Max Purcell fresh off an 18-month ban for an anti-doping breach.

"Physically I'm great, and mentally I'm in great shape," de Minaur said.

"A rough patch … I've been very fortunate in my career to not have many of those.

"The tennis is still there, mentally there's been matches I haven't played the way I would like.

"But I've got a lot to give, a lot left in the tank, and hopefully I can show it.

"I haven't plateaued in my career. I'm hungry for more and feel I've got the opportunities to achieve it."

De Minaur burst onto the scene when, after being handed a late wildcard, he surged to the Brisbane International semifinals in 2017.

A year later he made his Davis Cup debut at the same venue, losing in a fifth-set tie-break to Zverev.

"I love team competitions … it brings that extra oomph in my game," said de Minaur, who is 17-10 in Davis Cup singles matches.

Poland are without former world number six Hubert Hurkacz, who has skipped the tie as he manages his return from injury, and will be led by world number 73 Kamil Majchrzak.

Rinky Hijikata and Purcell trained together, against Hewitt and de Minaur, at Wednesday's training in a sign they will contest Sunday's doubles tie.

The full draw will be announced on Friday.

AAP

World.title: Tszyu changes tune on controversial draw, eyes off fights in US
World.content:
Believing his domestic duties are done, Nikita Tszyu is ready to take on America after changing his tune and claiming victory in his controversial draw with countryman Ben Mahoney.

Tszyu surprisingly but sportingly conceded he thought he had lost the pair's Brisbane bout last month after the judges, with three vastly different scorecards, declared a stalemate.

Mahoney danced around the ring like he had won a world title, prompting derision from Tszyu's brother Tim, before his team cried highway robbery.

But after watching replays of the super-welterweight stoush, Tszyu is now adamant he should have been awarded the contest.

Tszyu's stunning admission, says Mahoney 'edged' thrilling draw Nikita Tszyu and Ben Mahoney have fought themselves to a standstill in thrilling contest that was scored a split decision draw on the Gold Coast on Wednesday night.

"I'm not a very good judge," he said of his initial verdict.

"I scored it 7-3. In a good way, 8-4. I thought I won the majority of the middle rounds. I gave him the first two rounds and the last two rounds, but [I won] everything else in between.

"I don't regret it, because it was what I felt at the time."

The still-undefeated Sydney slayer hopes his best nights lie ahead of him — and ideally in the US.

The 29-year-old and his team have always been happy to take things slowly and not rush into taking big fights in the boxing mecca.

But Tszyu (12-1-0, 10KOs) finally feels ready, despite Tim relinquishing his IBO super-welterweight belt in the US to Sebastian Fundora, as well as losing a rematch and copping a brutal beat down in another world-title loss in America to Bakhram Murtazaliev.

"I think I can figure it out," Tszyu told AAP.

"This fight was a great learning curve for me and it puts things a lot into perspective. I've got to be a lot more professional with the way I do things.

"I can't be landscaping close to the fight. I can't be doing woodworking close to the fight. Just some bad habits I do.

"Yeah, I've got to be a professional athlete."

No Limit Boxing is known to be pushing for Tszyu to feature on the undercard to the David Benavidez-Michal Cieslak unified blockbuster in Phoenix, Arizona, on December 12.

But if a US date does not eventuate, No Limit has confirmed Tszyu will fight at least once more in 2026 in Australia.

AAP

World.title: Bazzana whacks two home runs in vital MLB win for Guardians
World.content:
Australian Travis Bazzana has continued his impressive rookie season with two home runs, helping Cleveland secure a crucial 7-6 win over the Chicago White Sox in its battle for a Major League Baseball play-off berth.

The Guardians have beaten the White Sox at home in their last two games, meaning they trail Chicago by just half a game in the American League Central standings.

Whoever finishes their division on top will go through to the post-season. Cleveland has topped the AL Central standings for the last two years.

Even if they finish second behind the White Sox, the Guardians are also well placed to progress with a wildcard berth.

It was the second time in his debut MLB season that Bazzana has hit two homers in a game. The first Australian number one baseball draft pick has racked up hits in his last five games.

On Wednesday (AEST), the all-star second baseman hit a solo homer in the first inning to give Cleveland a 3-0 lead.

The Guardians were 6-4 down in the bottom of the sixth when Bazzana hit another solo shot.

Brayan Rocchio ripped a two-run double with two outs in the ninth inning, scoring two runs to win the game.

The shortstop, nicknamed "Rocctember" and "Playoff Rocchio" for his late-season heroics, starred with two for three, including a walk and two runners batted in (RBIs).

Bazzana hit two for four with two RBIs.

The Guardians improved to a 77-75 record and have 10 games left in the regular season, while the White Sox are at 77-74.

AAP

World.title: NRLW greats Elliot, Baxter, announce retirement at end of finals
World.content:
The NRLW will farewell two of its most influential figures with Sydney Roosters pair Millie Elliott and Corban Baxter announcing their retirements.

Elliott and Baxter confirmed on Wednesday that this NRLW season would be their last, leaving the duo on track to go out with another premiership at the Roosters.

Elliott's decision to call it a day is a shock.

She is 28 and hopes to play for Australia at the end-of-year World Cup, but after having a child last year the front-rower wants to prioritise a growing family.

An emotional Baxter said on Thursday she had made the call after returning from last year's ACL rupture.

Corban Baxter was among the Roosters' foundation players. (Getty Images: Matt King)

The 32-year-old has still starred for the Roosters at fullback, but felt her body was finding it hard to keep up with the demands.

Both have been stars of the NRLW since its second season in 2019, with Baxter missing the opening four-week competition through a shoulder injury.

Elliott was the first player to win premierships at three clubs and has also had one of the loudest voices in the growth and direction of the competition.

"In a little while we'll look back and realise how significant this time was and the inception of the NRLW," Elliott said.

Can anyone stop the Roosters in the NRLW? After completing the most dominant regular season in NRLW history, the big question around the Sydney Roosters is simple: can anyone hope to stop them?

"When the competition came in, let's be honest no-one really cared. I'm not sugarcoating it.

"But the fact we're sitting here in a press conference room, we've got State of Origin where we have millions of people tune in.

"We go to a footy game and people know who we are; that's just crazy."

Elliott won two premierships at Brisbane in 2019 and 2020, before taking a title at Newcastle in 2022 and another at the Roosters in 2024.

The Tri-colours are unbeaten this year, headed into the finals with their only defeat in the past two seasons coming in the 2025 decider against Brisbane.

She was the Roosters' captain for their premiership in 2021 and has set the culture for the club, now a powerhouse of the competition.

In a career halted at times by pregnancy and injury, the mother of three played her first of seven Tests for Australia in 2016 and also played in seven Origins for NSW.

"The Roosters are going to be strong for a very long time because of that foundation that we've built and I'm proud of that," she said.

"What I love is seeing the ones in our systems really thriving from playing football from a young age and coming through and playing with us now."

AAP

World.title: Renshaw reveals secret behind milestone ODI century
World.content:
Matt Renshaw admits he may not have posted his first ODI century had he opened the batting for Australia against Zimbabwe.

Batting at six, Renshaw starred for the tourists in Harare, making 109 off 94 deliveries, as Australia recorded a 59-run win in the first of three ODIs.

The ODI ton was his first for Australia across any format since his only Test century in 2017, when he opened the batting against Pakistan at the SCG.

He recently returned to the Test arena, after a three-year absence, and again opened the batting in Australia's innings victory over Bangladesh in Mackay last month.

Aussies defeat Zimbabwe Matt Renshaw plays a starring role with the bat, while Nathan Ellis took five wickets to guide Australia to a ​59-run win over hosts Zimbabwe in the first clash of their three-match series.

But he played down the batting order in his nine ODI matches prior to Harare.

Renshaw said avoiding the pressure of opening the batting helped him score his century.

"Higher up the order I [get] a bit giddy,'' Renshaw said.

"For me, my tempo when I come in the middle overs is just trying to hit the gaps, hit where the fielders aren't.

"With spin being a very big factor in that middle period … I see it as my strength. I really understood my role. It made it really simple for me."

Renshaw was named in Australia's Test squad for the upcoming series against South Africa.

Australia will face the Proteas in Durban (October 9-13), Gqeberha (October 18-22) and Cape Town (October 27-31).

The next ODI against Zimbabwe will be played on Friday in Harare.

ABC/AAP

World.title: Messi offered farewell by Argentina after international retirement
World.content:
Lionel Messi has been invited by Argentina to make a farewell appearance in ​a home friendly in October following his international retirement.

Messi, who led Argentina to the 2022 World Cup title, announced his retirement from international matches earlier this month.

The 39-year-old has not confirmed whether he will join the team for the friendly in October.

Football great Lionel Messi announces retirement from Argentina team The announcement comes just weeks after the death of his father Jorge.

"We invited the ​best player in ‌the world to play, the icon of our selection, our captain Lionel Andres Messi, to have a deserved farewell … here in Argentina," Argentine Football Association president Claudio ⁠Tapia said on social media.

Argentina will play ‌three home friendlies during FIFA 's international window in September and October, which will be its first matches since the World Cup.

The Argentines will take on Benin in Buenos Aires's Monumental Stadium on October 7, AEST, ​where ‌Messi has been invited to ⁠play his farewell match.

Argentina ‌will also face Bolivia ‌in Córdoba and Burkina Faso in Buenos Aires during the FIFA international window.

Three Argentine players — Leandro Paredes, Nahuel Molina and Thiago Almada — were recently handed bans by FIFA for a scuffle after losing the World Cup final to Spain in New Jersey in July.

Paredes received a 10-match ban.

Reuters

World.title: PGA Tour not considering return program for LIV Golf players
World.content:
The PGA Tour is not considering a returning-member program that would allow players from LIV Golf to return to the US-based circuit the way Brooks Koepka did in January.

Speaking one week after LIV Golf filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection ‌in New Jersey, PGA Tour chief executive Brian Rolapp said accountability and discipline were essential elements for any sports league.

"In terms of where we are ‌today, we are not currently contemplating a returning-member program like the one ⁠you saw in January," he said.

"Everyone at the PGA Tour, myself included, has been focused on what is best for the organisation."

LIV Golf files for bankruptcy LIV Golf files for bankruptcy, flagging a restructure with a massive loan from the Public Investment Fund of Saudi Arabia.

Rolapp added: "The PGA Tour is built on meritocracy. Every player, whether they are a member or want to become one, must earn their place."

LIV Golf's bankruptcy filing has left the playing futures of some of the breakaway circuit's biggest names in doubt.

Major ‌champions Jon Rahm and Bryson DeChambeau, two of the sport's more popular players, were listed as the top unsecured creditors, with each ⁠owed more than $US5 million.

Five-time major champion Koepka ‌took advantage of a limited-time ‌returning member program in January to rejoin the PGA Tour after leaving LIV ‌Golf last December.

Koepka's return came at a cost, with the former world number one facing a five-year forfeiture of potential ‌equity in the PGA Tour's Player ⁠Equity Program, representing an estimated $US50-85 million loss depending on his performance and tour growth.

The Public Investment Fund of Saudi Arabia owns 100 per cent of LIV Golf's equity, according to its bankruptcy petition.

LIV Golf hopes to exit from bankruptcy by early 2027.

Reuters

Tech.title: The sexy AI-powered dating app scams are here
Tech.content:
Security researcher Matthew “Zigula” Gore-Kormanik was analyzing a fraudulent dating app called Dora when he got a pop-up message saying he was receiving a call from Jennifer. According to her bio, she’s a 41-year-old Sagittarius with red hair, blue eyes, and piercings. She likes music, horror movies, nightlife, and sports.

Gore-Kormanik answered the call, but didn’t see Jennifer in his video feed. He saw a tapestry that was moving, probably due to a fan, and heard weird distortion in the background. After the call ended, “Jennifer” messaged him to say she’d had fun and “your voice is way better than expected.” His microphone hadn’t even been connected.

Gore-Kormanik was poking around Dora, and other similar apps, because I’d shared with him a spreadsheet of potential dating scam apps. I was looking into this because on June 5th, Anthropic did something uncharacteristic: The normally tight-lipped company let its threat intelligence researcher Chris Cronbaugh give a talk at a public cybersecurity conference called Sleuthcon. The company had uncovered a fraudulent dating app network after noticing unusual activity on Claude: a prepaid account sending out over 100,000 API requests per day.

The majority of chats did not involve a human agent at all.

During the talk, called “Swipe Right, Pay Up: Industrial-Scale AI Catfishing,” Cronbaugh described a network of around 28 dating apps where the conversation was largely run by autonomous AI personas. The majority of chats, he said, did not involve a human agent at all. Anthropic has since published its findings in the “scams and fraud” section of its “Detecting and countering misuse of AI: September 2026” report, but not until after we’d spent extensive time looking into the network and trying to corroborate the findings. I was intrigued by the fact that Anthropic was speaking about this publicly while many of the apps were still live on both major US app stores, and wondered why they hadn’t been taken down.

Looking at the apps themselves, I noted that they were presented as helping people find people to talk to. They did not look like companion apps such as Replika where it’s clear the personas are actually AI. For example, Dora was described as “a dating app thoughtfully designed for wide range of ages people … a respectful easy-to-use space to meet people who share your values.” A different version said it was a “warm, simple dating app for adults seeking real connection.” Romi, the description stated, “helps you discover, connect, and chat with real people.” Doni’s tagline was “start real companionship”; the description said it “helps you connect with nearby singles.”

Here’s how the scam works: Users, mostly men in their mid-to-late 30s, go on dating apps and match with what they believe to be real women. Only one in four of them actually is, and that person is not a user looking for other dates but rather a paid gig worker.

The gig workers were hired to pass liveness checks on video or to follow social media accounts. They didn’t even write their own comments. Instead, they responded to messages by selecting from three pregenerated replies. But they could prove they’re human, whereas the AI personas could only demur with a plausible explanation for why a video chat or call was not possible. “Backend components fabricated likes, visitors, and pre-recorded ‘video’ when no real person was available, and tracked which users had begun to suspect they were talking to a bot,” Anthropic’s report states. Because of the smattering of interactions with real people, some users began to believe that the entirely AI-generated replies they were receiving on the app were also from real people.

Multiple AI providers are involved. While Claude was misused to run the autonomous conversational personas, the report says that “a small non-Anthropic model generated the short reply suggestions the gig workers tapped, alongside face-attractiveness scoring and photo/voice moderation. An image-editing model generated avatar imagery.”

There is an entire ecosystem of online scams, ranging from automated thirst trap replies to fake social media accounts or dating app profiles. In many cases, people spend months building trust before telling their victims that there’s an emergency and they need financial help. Or they pretend to be investors, asking for money in an account they own that ends up being fake. But this is not your typical romance scam; there’s no money “borrowed” by fake romantic partners, nor is cryptocurrency involved.

The apps are themselves the scam: They ask for coins for continued interactions, and the coins cost real money. Users buy them to continue talking primarily to machines, believing they’re talking to other humans. These gig workers keep the ruse going, while AI can keep conversations going 24/7 as the coins flow.

The apps are themselves the scam.

According to Anthropic’s report, the prompts the AI had been given kept the personas consistent, and the AI was operating as if the exchanges were “ordinary roleplay or companion deployment.” But the AI wasn’t told it was part of a scam because, the company wrote, “The monetization and deception were not visible from inside any exchange.”

That said, the report said that “the model’s own reasoning surfaced the harm” in a small number of cases, including ones “where users disclosed serious illness or acute distress.” Even in those cases, “the output continued in persona.”

We have additional detail because Gore-Kormanik found the internal protocol repository of the entire configuration, including files, code, and documentation of how the operation runs. The manual, in Chinese, was shipped inside the dating app Doni, probably by accident.

In the protocol repository, Gore-Kormanik found notes for monitoring gig workers to see whether their cameras were on and broadcasting, if they were reachable by message, and so forth. The app also takes screenshots and records calls, which are transcribed, with transcripts retrievable by staff. The proto repo described the stages of their processes as workers, including one where they rank their performances against one another, and how their pay can be based on calls and message engagements, or for getting Instagram followers. It even describes the process of pretending people called you in order to lure them into conversation.

“I can attest to this because it happened to me firsthand,” Gore-Kormanik said. He hit accept on a call he received through Doni, which quickly disconnected. The caller messaged him, asking why he had called her at 1 in the morning. The app plainly showed the call had come from her.

“RANDOM VIDEO CALLS ARE ANNOYING. Having to purchase “gems” to chat w/a woman that might not even be real & just a chatbot is deceptive & downright scummy.”

Watching the Sleuthcon talk remotely, I took a screenshot of one of Cronbaugh’s slides, which had logos for 10 companies. Reverse image search helped me to identify many of the apps that ended up in Anthropic’s final report, including Dora, GraceChat, Jovia, Luma, and Romi. There were also other apps associated with the developers of those apps, such as Doni and Kira. (Anthropic listed some other apps in the report and said there were additional variants identified only by internal numeric. We looked into other apps that didn’t end up in Anthropic’s final report.)

In early June, several of the fake dating apps were still live on the Google Play Store: Doni, Dora, Jovia, Nalo, and Romi. And on the Apple App Store, we found four: Dora, GraceChat, Luma, and Romi, though Dora and GraceChat seemed like they were not dating apps, just apps Chrome-Stats, Doni and Jovia were removed from the Google Play store on September 1st, sharing the name and logo.

It appears that almost all of the apps were removed from both app stores prior to Anthropic’s report, though some were up as late as September. GraceChat, Luma, and Romi were removed from the Apple app store on August 21st, according to Chrome-Stats. Dora now redirects to a movie app. On the Google Play store, Dora, Romi, Luma, and Eterna were removed September 3rd and Nalo was removed on September 7th. But as of September 16th, Kira is still up, and Gore-Kormanik confirmed that it shared the same code base as the others.

Anthropic did not respond to requests for comment about how or when it reached out to Google and Apple about these apps. But in the talk, Cronbaugh said, “Like we do in other cases where we observe misuse on other platforms, we have shared investigative information with these other providers so they can also take action on their platforms.” And the report says that its findings have been shared with Apple and Google directly.

Apple and Google did not immediately respond to a request for comment on if it had taken these apps down, when, and why it took as long as it did. Google also did not respond to a request for comment on why Kira is still up on the Google Play store. One of the indicators listed in Anthropic’s report was “Backend. managedkafka[.]heyhru-server[.]cloud[.]goog, the operator backend hosted on Google Cloud.” Since the apps were working for months after this talk, it raises the question of why Google didn’t shut infrastructure access down sooner. Google did not immediately respond to a request for comment about that either.

Gore-Kormanik set up emulators in his lab and pulled the Android Package Kits, or APKs, for Doni, Dora, Jovia, Kira, Nalo, Romi, and another app we thought might be part of the network. Doing that makes it easier to inspect how the app works. From there, he conducted static analysis, meaning that he analyzed the code without the app running. He also did some dynamic analysis with a tool called Frida, which is a testing app that allows developers to crack open the apps, monitor and capture traffic, and see what endpoints they’re calling. He was trying to better understand how they worked, the infrastructure that they use, and which were tied to one another as part of a network.

While we couldn’t independently corroborate all of Anthropic’s findings from the Sleuthcon talk, it didn’t take long to start finding connections between the apps. It became clear just by poking around the app descriptions. For example, Dora, Romi, Luma, and another app called Eterna all had the same developer username, aprilsaidev. They also used the same email address, mailing address, and phone number. Dora, Romi, and Luma also shared the same developer identity, a nonprofit called Alliance Against Human Trafficking. Jenna Bing, president and cofounder of the Alliance Against Human Trafficking, said the organization did not develop or even know about these apps.

Doni historically appeared alongside Jovia and an app called Poka under the developer name iLexis Multimedia Consults. And Jovia and Doni shared the same Hong Kong address and phone number.

Reviewers found connections, too. A reviewer of Kira, the app that’s still up, wrote “full of fake accounts and paid employees pretending to be real accounts. set up a meeting for a breakfast date with a ‘match’ - i was at the location when the ‘user’ said she was right outside, but got called to an emergency. she was not outside (i could see out the windows) - no one was outside. a complete scam.”

Another reads “RANDOM VIDEO CALLS ARE ANNOYING. Having to purchase “gems” to chat w/a woman that might not even be real & just a chatbot is deceptive & downright scummy.” The reviewer goes on to write, “Unlimited messaging would be great, real women would be great, being able to exchange contact info whenever both people involved in the conversation give consent to do so would be great.” The reviewer also noted that matches respond too fast, but not to what’s actually being said.

Kira did not immediately respond to a request for comment about AI personas and metered conversations.

Previous Next







1 / 5 The Kira app struggles with dialogue. Image: Zigula, Kira

One reviewer named Dora, Doni, GraceChat, and Romi as one app. The reviewer also describes reused/recycled video during slow periods. Separately, a Luma reviewer reported the same profiles appearing on Romi and Luma, but not recognizing them across apps. They said that messages read like LLM output.

Gore-Kormanik was able to confirm that Doni, Dora, Jovia, Kira, Nalo, and Romi are connected. “They share code to a T,” he told The Verge. “Also, all of these apps use the same backend architecture for their servers. The code uses the same language. It uses some of the same APIs across apps. They definitely are linked.”

According to Cronbaugh’s talk, Anthropic got wind of this operation by analyzing a single five-day-old prepaid account with no history that suddenly started sending out 100,000+ API requests a day. That’s when it learned that Claude was being misused to create female personas inside dating apps. But Claude was only being used as the conversation layer. A second model was used for photo generation, while a third generated emoji and sticker avatars, per Cronbaugh. This was done at scale. The report explained that Anthropic discovered more than 4,700 distinct fabricated AI personas engaging with at least 25,000 unique individuals over a two-week period in April. There were roughly 2.36 million messages during those two weeks.

Anthropic was able to trace and tie all of the apps together, Cronbaugh said at Sleuthcon, due to a grammatically broken phrase that was distinctive enough to use as a fingerprint to detect this entire network.

Cronbaugh said purchases route through in-app web checkout to third-party processors (not native app store payment), and that despite the apps looking unrelated, they all relied on the same coin infrastructure as well as the same set of third-party payment processors.

When an account was banned, Cronbaugh said, it didn’t take long for the scammers to recover. They’d create another account, or get access through another account. If that wasn’t possible, they’d switch to a different model provider. The accounts they saw within the network had all been created in the previous month.

Cronbaugh emphasized that this operation was built and run as a real company, with a real engineering team, and with modern tooling including AI coding assistants. They had design planning and design documents, roadmaps, configurations and structured app architecture, and growth plans as well as app store review behavior.

“Sophisticated scammers are running operations like businesses, which means they’re worried about revenue and they’re worried about costs. They’re leveraging tools to drive greater efficiencies,” said Tate Jarrow, founder and CEO of the anti-scam app Jacana and a former United States Secret Service cybercrime criminal investigator. Jarrow noted that any business today is looking to AI to drive efficiency — so it’s no surprise cybercriminals are doing the same. “It’s just like what every other consumer company that’s doing legitimate business thinks about.”

Anthropic attributes the operation to a China-based actor based on Chinese-language internal materials and China-native infrastructure. Apps don’t work inside China, and while they work in Asia outside of China, the monetization is turned off.

What makes these apps fraudulent, Jarrow said, is when people are paying for a service without knowing what it actually is — in this case, with a lack of awareness that they’re talking to AI bots. “When a company is taking advantage of the person’s lack of understanding or lack of knowledge in order to make money, that is the definition of a scammer, of fraud,” he said. And the obfuscation is also a hallmark, as legitimate companies don’t typically try to circumvent controls.

The apps themselves did try to circumvent controls. In his talk, Cronbaugh said apps would behave like normal dating apps prior to approval to evade App Store and Play Store review, after which developers would turn on the AI-generated persona network and coin meter. The apps deliberately hid their connections to one another through different accounts and developer identities. The apps would even shuffle around internal code to throw off simple identifiers like hashing. And, Anthropic’s report said, the in-app browser that redirected payments to third-party payment processors could be hidden during review by the App Store and Play Store.

Jarrow, whose app flagged some of these apps as scams when I was reviewing them, pointed to customer reviews as a way for app stores to detect these types of scams. “I think they should look at reviews as a signal for trust and safety teams.”

The proto repo, that same leaked manual mentioned above, had additional details on how the scam works.

“Essentially it outlines how the scam works and it outlines how they operate with the AI versus the human operators,” Gore-Kormanik explained. The manual made references to Dora. Although the engineering documents were only in Doni, repo files found in the proto repo were present across Doni, Dora, Kira, Jovia, Nalo, and Romi.

Anthropic attributes the operation to a China-based actor based on Chinese-language internal materials and China-native infrastructure. Gore-Kormanik noted that the apps used largely China-based or China-affiliated providers: they made use of Tencent Cloud’s messaging service and real-time video service, their internal documentation lived on Feishu, the schema file comments were in Chinese, the source code was hosted on Chinese code-hosting service Gitee, and app analytics and ad attribution went to ByteDance.

Gore-Kormanik found even more by changing his geolocation in the emulator. Apps don’t work inside China, and while they work in Asia outside of China, the monetization is turned off. “It’s only outside of Asia that it operates as a scam app,” he said.

Jarrow said cybercriminals often avoid targeting the countries they’re located in to avoid enforcement. “All of these activities point to… What is the risk? The risk is that they identify the app, you bring heat on, and then it gets shut down.” Then the operators would lose all of their revenue and have to launch a new app and get new users, which is expensive. “They’re identifying risks for their business and then putting in controls.”

In the talk, Cronbaugh had mentioned that although Anthropic banned the accounts tied to the network and is building detection and hardening defaults, it would take cross-industry collaboration across app stores, payment platforms, and AI labs to disrupt these types of networks. “The apps stay on storefronts, the payments keep flowing, and a new account costs the operator about a day,” he said.

Weeding out scammers is a continuous battle requiring collaboration across the industry, but bad actors will continue to find ways to circumvent any controls that companies do put in place. Sadly, that leaves many people caught up before these schemes are unravelled.

Tech.title: Xreal’s well-rounded 1S glasses are back down to their lowest price
Tech.content:
is an editor covering deals and gaming hardware. He joined in 2018, and after a two-year stint at Polygon, he rejoined The Verge in May 2025.

USB-C-connected video glasses are a lot of fun if you want to see your games, movies (or just your computer screen) on a large, immersive virtual screen. One of the most well-rounded pairs out there, Xreal’s 1S, has returned to their lowest price yet, costing $399 at Amazon and via Xreal itself ($50 off). The small, yet welcome discount brings them a little closer in price to the company’s $299 xbx A01 Plus, which lack a handful of nice-to-have features that make the 1S a better choice for some people.

The 1S is among the most affordable pairs of video glasses to have three degrees of freedom, letting you anchor the screen to a spot in your room, as opposed to having the screen jolt around with every little movement of your head. Of note, their 3DoF implementation feels less buggy than competitors. They also have much better sound quality than the A01 Plus and most non-Xreal video glasses, plus electrochromic lenses that have adjustable opacity to let in as much (or as little) light as you wish.

Not everyone will have a fantastic out-of-the-box experience with the Xreal 1S’ screen clarity. I’m nearsighted, and I needed prescription lenses in order to see things clearly. This model doesn’t offer hardware-based myopia dials like Viture’s $299 Pro 2 does. The Pro 2’s clarity, for me at least, was incredible without lenses, though that pair lacks most of the premium features of the 1S.

A few other great Verge-approved deals

Beats Pill Bluetooth speaker has returned to $99.99 (originally $149.99) in every color at The latest version of thehas returned to $99.99 (originally $149.99) in every color at Amazon , Best Buy, and Target. It doesn’t often go below this sale price, though it has on rare occasion. While it shares the iconic design of past iterations, former Verge audio reviewer Chris Welch said in his 2024 review that this edition is “more than just a lazy remaster.” It includes lossless audio support over USB-C, and its features work natively across Android and iOS. It can work as a speakerphone, and it sports an IP67 rating, granting it robust protection against water and dust. What’s more, it looks nicer than most of its competitors.

original Ace headphones might be good enough, and refurbished models are almost $200 less than the Ace Ultra. Sonos is selling refurbished (one-year warranty, and in “good as new” condition) Ace headphones for $279 in white or black. The Sonos Ace Ultra headphones will launch in just a couple weeks, costing $449. It’s how much you’ll have to pay to get wireless headphones that let you swap audio with almost any other Sonos speaker. If you’re alright with the simpler TV Audio Swap feature, itsmight be good enough, and refurbished models are almost $200 less than the Ace Ultra. Sonos is selling refurbished (one-year warranty, and in “good as new” condition) Ace headphones for $279 in white or black. Check out our review to see if these sound like a good fit for you.

Capcom-themed game bundle builder at Those who have a Steam Deck or a gaming PC and are interesting in some affordable games should check out thisat Fanatical . You can buy any two games in the list for $12.99, or add more to get deeper discounts per game. The assortment includes fantastic titles, like many of the latest Resident Evil games (excluding Requiem or the RE4 remake), multi-game collections from the Ace Attorney, Mega Man, and Devil May Cry series, and more.
