It’s a good opportunity to get caught up on a bunch of Steam games, or round out your collection with two extras.

Tech.title: A brief history of AI executives calling for regulation
Tech.content:
is a senior editor and founding member of The Verge who covers gadgets, games, and toys. He spent 15 years editing the likes of CNET, Gizmodo, and Engadget.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Over the past few days, a lot of people who stand to make a lot of money from AI all publicly agreed that it’s time to make everyone slow down before we lose control — including OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Google DeepMind cofounder Demis Hassabis, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, and X CEO Elon Musk.

When people who profit from something declare that it’s dangerous and needs to be regulated, there’s always reason to be skeptical. But whatever their reason, this is far from the first time AI thought leaders have sounded the alarm.

Charles Darwin’s theory of evolution prompted author Samuel Butler to warn about intelligent self-replicating machines replacing humans back in 1863 — and in his follow-up 1872 book Erewhon, he describes visiting a fictional society that has already regulated machines out of existence to avoid humanity’s collapse. Computing pioneer Alan Turing famously warned in a 1951 lecture that artificial intelligence would “meet with great opposition,” because undying machines “would not take long to outstrip our feeble powers” and would eventually “take control.”

Calls for intervention, too, aren’t new. In 2000, Sun Microsystems cofounder and chief scientist Bill Joy wrote that self-replicating robots could be more dangerous than nuclear weapons, partly because they’re being developed “within the now-unchallenged system of global capitalism” rather than in tightly controlled government labs. And in 2009, Microsoft researcher Eric Horvitz, who now serves as the company’s chief scientific officer, brought leading AI researchers together to consider “creating policies that might constrain or bias the behaviors of autonomous and semi-autonomous systems so as to address concerns.”

But modern AI bigwigs warning that their investments should be controlled? That trend appears to have begun with Elon Musk, who invested earlier than most.

July 2017: Elon Musk says we need to regulate AI before it becomes a danger to humanity

By the time Elon Musk told a gathering of US governors that they needed to regulate AI right away, the SpaceX and Tesla CEO already had skin in the game. He’d already invested $38 million in OpenAI, as well as stakes in at least two other AI companies, and he’d publicly spoken about the dangers of AI for three years.

“AI is a rare case where we need to be proactive about regulation instead of reactive. Because I think by the time we are reactive in AI regulation, it’s too late,” Musk told a gathering of US governors at the July 2017 National Governors Association summer meeting. In March 2018, he added: “AI is far more dangerous than nukes. So why do we have no regulatory oversight?”

March 2018: Mark Zuckerberg is ‘actually not sure we shouldn’t be regulated’

In the wake of Facebook’s Cambridge Analytica data scandal, the Meta founder suggested his company should be regulated — if it’s the “right” regulation. It was largely not about AI, but he did go there:

Now that companies increasingly over the next five to 10 years, as AI tools get better and better, will be able to proactively determine what might be offensive content or violate some rules, what therefore is the responsibility and legal responsibility of companies to do that?

In March 2019, he added that the internet needs a “more active role” for regulators.

December 2018: Microsoft sounds an alarm over facial recognition technology

Earlier in 2018, Microsoft began taking fire for working with ICE on facial recognition technologies, at a time many tech CEOs had condemned Donald Trump’s policy of separating children from parents who are arrested at the US border.

While this form of AI isn’t quite the same as self-replicating intelligence, Microsoft president Brad Smith opened the door to voluntary regulation in a speech at the Brookings Institution, saying, “We believe it’s important for governments in 2019 to start adopting laws to regulate this technology. … We believe that the only way to protect against this race to the bottom is to build a floor of responsibility that supports healthy market competition. And a solid floor requires that we ensure that this technology, and the organizations that develop and use it, are governed by the rule of law.”

January 2020: Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai says there is ‘no question’ that AI needs to be regulated

“[T]here is no question in my mind that artificial intelligence needs to be regulated. It is too important not to,” wrote Pichai in an editorial for the Financial Times. “The only question is how to approach it.”

“Companies such as ours cannot just build promising new technology and let market forces decide how it will be used,” he added. Like with Microsoft a year earlier, these comments emerged around fears about AI facial recognition specifically.

March 2023: Elon Musk and top AI researchers call for pause on ‘giant AI experiments’

In 2023, as generative AI fervor began to reshape the entire tech industry, scientists began suggesting that companies should slow down their research — or else.

“If such a pause cannot be enacted quickly, governments should step in and institute a moratorium,” the letter, published by the nonprofit Future of Life Institute and signed by Musk, among others, reads.

Two weeks later, Musk announced he’d created his own new AI company. Two years later, he would use DOGE to dismantle chunks of the federal workforce instead of helping to regulate anything.

May 16th, 2023: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman asks Congress to regulate AI

Brought before the US Senate for a series of AI hearings, Altman agreed that Congress should create a new agency to regulate artificial intelligence. “We believe that the benefits of the tools we have deployed so far vastly outweigh the risks,” he argued. “However, we think that regulatory intervention by governments will be critical to mitigate the risks of increasingly powerful models.”

In another hearing on May 25th, Anthropic’s CEO warned US senators that AI could help create bioweapons.

May 25th, 2023: Microsoft president Brad Smith ‘details five ways governments should consider policies, laws, and regulations around AI’

When OpenAI’s CEO was before Congress, we noted that the tone was friendly and they seemed to be trying to shape legislation together; here is an example of Microsoft trying to shape future regulation as well.

One regulatory example: “New laws would require operators of these systems to build safety brakes into high-risk AI systems by design. The government would then ensure that operators test high-risk systems regularly to make certain that the system safety measures are effective.”

May 30th, 2023: Top AI researchers and CEOs warn against ‘risk of extinction’ in 22-word statement

“Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war.”

While the 22-word statement doesn’t explicitly ask the government to step in, it’s hard to think world leaders wouldn’t raise their eyebrows even higher than before. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and then-Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis were among the cosigners.

September 2023: Mark Zuckerberg wants everyone to ‘work together’ on regulation

In a private Senate meeting, closed to the public and media, tech CEOs reportedly agreed that the AI industry needed regulation. One set of remarks was not so private: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said that “Congress should engage with AI to support innovation and safeguards.”

“We think policymakers, academics, civil society, and industry should all work together to minimize the potential risks of this new technology, but also to maximize the potential benefits.”

Between July 2023 and May 2024, tech companies signed a flurry of nonbinding agreements with governments that would supposedly keep them in check:

July 2023 : Meta, Google, and OpenAI promise the White House they’ll develop AI responsibly

September 2023 : More companies commit to the White House AI safety accord

November 2023 : At UK’s AI Summit developers and govts agree on testing to help manage risks

May 2024 : AI Seoul Summit: World leaders agree to launch network of safety institutes

Also in September 2023: A book from Inflection AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman — who is now Microsoft’s AI chief — argued that governments should regulate.

August–September 2024: Elon Musk and Anthropic come out in favor of California’s AI safety bill

“This is a tough call and will make some people upset, but, all things considered, I think California should probably pass the SB 1047 AI safety bill,” Musk posted in August. Anthropic originally came out against it in July, as did OpenAI in August, but Anthropic changed its tune in September. California Gov. Gavin Newsom vetoed SB 1047, though, stating that “I do not believe this is the best approach to protecting the public from real threats posed by the technology.”

October 2024: Anthropic calls for ‘targeted regulation’

“Governments should urgently take action on AI policy in the next eighteen months. The window for proactive risk prevention is closing fast,” Anthropic wrote in an open letter (bolding theirs).

“It is critical over the next year that policymakers, the AI industry, safety advocates, civil society, and lawmakers work together to develop an effective regulatory framework,” the company added.

January 2025: OpenAI submits its ‘policy proposals’

The document begins by suggesting the UK stunted the development of its own automobile industry with regulation, while proposing “democratic AI” instead: “Rules and regulations for the development and use of AI should be based on the democratic values the country has always stood for.”

June 2025: Anthropic CEO: Don’t let AI companies off the hook

In a guest essay for The New York Times, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wrote: “Federal law does not compel us or any other A.I. company to be transparent about our models’ capabilities or to take any meaningful steps toward risk reduction. Some companies can simply choose not to.” The essay is against the Trump administration’s proposed 10-year moratorium on US states regulating AI.

He wasn’t arguing for a slowdown, though, but rather a “national transparency standard” that “would help not only the public but also Congress understand how the technology is developing.”

September 2025: Anthropic endorses California’s SB 53

As California tried to regulate its AI giants again, Anthropic threw its support in early, and this one actually became law. It’s a transparency standard, like the one Anthropic was asking for, with safety reporting requirements and whistleblower protection. OpenAI lobbied against it.

September 2026: The AI industry seemingly agrees to slow down — while Trump calls AI fears ‘a sick conspiracy’

Now, suddenly, the AI industry has seemingly agreed to slow down the pace of development. More:

Is this a new call for regulation? From Anthropic’s CEO, it seems to be. In his essay “We Must Pace the Frontier,” Amodei writes that “The most effective method of pacing is via regulation that targets all US frontier AI companies, as that covers even those who are unwilling to cooperate voluntarily,” and he suggests governments might embed people inside AI companies to help prevent incidents.

It’s not clear every AI company wants to go that far. “Where we will need the help of our government is for international coordination. But first we should do what we can ourselves,” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman writes. But Altman does say that he’ll commit to “independent evaluators with employee-like access” as well.

Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg also doesn’t seem to be aligned. On September 15th, he posted that each company has its own individual responsibility to move at the right pace and that Meta is already doing so. He also prominently linked back to his manifesto from August, which contains this line: “Any policy that slows American model releases -- even by a month -- could add significant risk to American leadership while letting foreign models race ahead.”

Regardless of what tech leaders are saying, regulation seems highly unlikely to come under the Trump administration, which has signaled it wants the industry barreling full speed ahead.

Even if these companies don’t actually want the regulation they seem to be asking for, this is one of the loudest alarm bells they’ve sounded so far — and the world is watching.

Tech.title: Nintendo opens up Fire Emblem with the gigantic Fortune’s Weave
Tech.content:
Nintendo has gotten quite good at making open-ended games. The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild upended the idea of what a Zelda game could be by giving the player free rein to tackle any part of the map, a philosophy iterated upon with Tears of the Kingdom. On the Switch 2 this idea expanded to Mario Kart World and Donkey Kong Bananza. Now, Nintendo has brought this philosophy to Fire Emblem with Fortune’s Weave. It works really well; with its many ways to progress through the game and tailor teams to your liking, Fortune’s Weave has become my favorite game on the Switch 2 so far.

Fortune’s Weave’s structure is a big reason why it feels so open: Instead of locking you to one path, Fortune’s Weave is designed so that you can experience multiple stories in one massive playthrough. There are four main hero routes and a final act that ties things together, giving you several opportunities to start over from scratch and master the dizzying amount of mechanics and meta-strategy involved in winning fights and building up your group. From early on you can swap between heroes and storylines at will, and it’s even possible to merge stats from characters you use in multiple routes to make one supercharacter later. The systems go really deep, but Fortune’s Weave gives you many ways to customize things exactly to your liking.

The game is split into a few sections. There’s a brief prologue that introduces the main protagonist and your mission to save the world and defeat an evil demon lord. To aid in your quest, you can recruit the four missing heroes from the recent past by playing through their individual stories in two parts. Part one features the hero of your choice as they compete in a grand tournament in the city of Dagsion, while part two carries over your hero’s squad to fight in a war. If you complete a hero’s path, you can take them and any of their allies into part three, where the true protagonist leads an effort to fight the undead.

Parts one and three give you a lot of leeway to train up for battles and build your teams as you’d like. You’ll quickly fall into a rhythm of splitting time between the main story battles, running around Dagsion to prepare for fights, enlist allies, and explore a vast map to gather resources and fight in small skirmishes. There’s a calendar system that counts down the days toward the next main story event, but you have the freedom to spend your days however you’d like. I fell into a comforting pattern where I’d explore a map for one in-game week, come back to Dagsion to complete weekly activities like training up skills and sharing meals with people in town to build rapport, and then back head out to the map to tackle more quests or grind out some XP. (Part two is pretty much all about battles, as you’re mostly just playing one big fight after another with very little pre-battle prep.)

The main battles are your typical Fire Emblem turn-based strategy. You can choose which allies you want to use, and then you spend each turn deciding how to best attack your enemies or buff your team with healing spells and other support moves. Each of your characters has a different class, and a diverse squad is key; as much as I’d love to run a team that consists just of flying units, if they came upon any archers, they’d probably be toast. Some battles have different objectives to mix things up, like tasking you with defeating thieves before they escape while simultaneously fighting giant birds. On the game’s standard difficulty, and with permadeath turned off, I didn’t have much trouble. But I often invoked the blessings of gods during battles, which give you handy abilities like rewinding back to a previous move if you make a mistake.

There are also battles that play out like a more typical turn-based RPG, which you’ll run into in dungeons on the map and with occasional story battles. I found these much less interesting than the strategy battles, and thanks to an autoplay feature, I usually skipped them altogether to get the experience and stat boosts.

I chose to finish all four hero routes in parts one and two so that I could bring them into part three. It was a herculean effort: Completing each hero’s path took me about 100 hours in total. And that was after reducing battle animations, skipping cutscenes I had already seen, and doing a lot of fast traveling. But with each hero’s playthrough, I better understood how to train characters, assign them advanced classes to build balanced teams, and use resources from the map to make my weapons more powerful.

Part three also adds one extra complication: Instead of roaming the map with a single character and their team, you can juggle multiple squads at a time. This initially felt daunting, but I quickly settled into deploying my squads to different corners of the map to finish quests, leveling up my whole team, and crushing a lot of bad guys.

Image: Nintendo

Not every hour of my playthrough, which ended at about 130 hours, was well spent. In parts one and two, I repeated a lot of quests, cutscenes, and exploration. Part two features the same levels, just with the characters swapped around depending on which hero you’re playing as. In part three, managing multiple squads simultaneously can feel like you’re inching across the map. And the strange, leery tea party minigame from Three Houses returns as “bird time,” where you talk with and “observe” other characters as the game’s main protagonist — who has taken the form of a bird — to build support. I promise the bird form makes sense in the context of the story, but it’s still weird.

But even with the repetition, I found myself completely immersed in Fortune’s Weave. The loop of leveling up my characters, preparing for battle, and routing my enemies was nearly perfect, and I couldn’t get enough. Reaching part three in particular felt like a significant reward for my hard work; after 100 hours, I was thrilled when I could bring all of my teams together for the final push.

Fortune’s Weave is just the latest example of how Nintendo adapts the idea of openness in a way that makes sense for each franchise. In this case, it doesn’t change the core game like how Breath of the Wild transformed Zelda. Instead, the game’s open-ended nature adds even more layers of strategy to a series that had already started pushing its own boundaries with titles like Three Houses. Fortune’s Weave feels like the culmination of what Nintendo has been building Fire Emblem to be.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave launches on the Nintendo Switch 2 on September 17th.

Tech.title: The iPhone 18 Pro’s big camera update is all about the small gains
Tech.content:
Last week, Apple announced an iPhone unlike any it has made in the past. An iPhone that has seemingly already led several other phone manufacturers to pursue entirely different designs for their flagship products. A remarkably distinct device with the kind of “I can’t believe they did that” software touches that Apple sometimes pulls off when it’s at the top of its game.

That phone is not the iPhone 18 Pro.

The 18 Pro and Pro Max are in the unusual position of being the second-most interesting iPhones that Apple is launching this year. The foldable iPhone Duo stole the show at Apple’s launch event, but it’s not arriving until next month. In the meantime, the 18 Pro cometh, and it is extremely familiar even with a totally new hardware feature in the camera.

It is so similar to the iPhone 17 Pro that it can use the same cases. Have you used an iPhone 17 Pro? Great, you now know what it’s like to use the 18 Pro. There are no surprises, and unless you’re a truly committed smartphone photographer, no hugely compelling reason to pick an 18 Pro over a 17 Pro if you can find one on sale. It’s what we’ve come to expect from what was the flagship iPhone: excellent and utterly iterative.

Inside, the iPhone 18 Pro has a revamped thermal management design that allows its new A20 Pro chip to sustain full performance for longer, but the biggest truly new idea is inside the main camera, where Apple has added a moving aperture to control how much light hits the sensor. This is a big deal, and also a small deal, which I promise makes sense.

With a few exceptions, phone cameras have fixed apertures. Their sensors and lenses are so small that most of your scene is in focus even when you’re shooting wide open, and it’s usually best to get as much light as you can on that tiny sensor anyway. But there are some edge cases where a narrower aperture is helpful, even on a phone camera. It could also be helpful in other situations, particularly in low light, to open up the aperture even further than the iPhone’s traditional f/1.8. So Apple seems to have said, “Screw it. Let’s have it both ways,” and put in a variable aperture.

With the right lighting and the help of a macro lens you can see those aperture blades.

So there are really two separate things happening here. The maximum aperture is now bigger, at f/1.48 vs. f/1.8, and has the ability to get smaller, with stops available at f/1.8, f/2.8, and f/4. And while both the larger and smaller apertures do offer marginal improvements to photo quality in some cases, the differences are generally marginal.

One of the reasons photographers like a wider aperture is for its ability to throw more of the background of a photo out of focus. But the small lens and sensor on a smartphone camera don’t allow for the same kind of soft background blur you get from a bigger camera system. At the iPhone’s old maximum aperture of f/1.8, most things are in focus most of the time, and going to the slightly wider f/1.48 doesn’t make a huge difference.

Previous Next

1 / 2 iPhone 18 Pro, f/1.48 cropped to 100 percent

A bigger aperture does offer an advantage for low light photography. On a traditional camera, letting in more light allows the system to keep noise down by using a faster shutter speed, a lower ISO, or both. It’s not quite the same on a smartphone camera that’s combining multiple frames at different exposures to create the final image, but broadly the concept of “more light = better photo” holds.

Maybe because phones are already so good at coping with low light through these computational methods, the low light gains in the 18 Pro look pretty minor. If I look closely at the detail in a shot at f/1.48 versus f/1.8, I can see a difference, but it’s subtle.

Previous Next

1 / 2 iPhone 18 Pro at f/1.8, cropped to 100 percent

The biggest advantage might be for Night Mode. At f/1.48, the system can use a slightly shorter Night Mode capture time compared to f/1.8. That’s less time you have to try and keep your hand still and less noise that the system needs to try and process out.

Previous Next

1 / 2 iPhone 18 Pro, f/1.48 and 1.4 second night mode capture, cropped to 100 percent

On the other side of the dial, a smaller aperture is useful for extending depth of field and keeping more stuff in focus, particularly if your subject is close to the camera. If you’re taking a close-up photo of a statue, at f/1.48 or f/1.8 the back part of it might look a bit soft. Stopping down to f/4 sharpens up the part in the background.

Previous Next





1 / 4 iPhone 18 Pro at f/1.48. For a subject close to the lens, the background blur is more pronounced.

That’s helpful! But once again, you’ll find these benefits on the margins. That’s because the iPhone’s new f/1.48 maximum aperture actually equates to about f/5 on full frame in terms of depth of field, which already puts a lot of the stuff in front of and behind your subject in focus. Unless you’re really close to your subject, most things are in focus or close enough when you photograph them with a smartphone camera.

If you don’t know or care about f-stops, you’ll still get along just fine with this updated camera. By default the aperture is set to automatically adjust based on lighting conditions, and it seems to stay at f/1.8 most of the time in good lighting. The aperture does open up to f/1.48 in dim light automatically, and will close down to f/4 when taking a group photo with someone who’s standing further back. And I saw it consistently dropping down to f/4 when I was taking a photo of some close-up text. That’s a situation where f/4 will help you get more in focus and make for a potentially more usable photo. But that’s an awfully narrow set of use cases, whether you’re the kind of person who wants to take manual control over the aperture or not.

That’s the big update, and the effect is a relatively small one. But it’s not the only camera update. Friends, in the year of our Lord 2026, you can finally change the exposure controls by yourself in the iPhone camera app. Apple has added pro controls for the aforementioned aperture as well as shutter speed, white balance, and focus. There’s also the exposure compensation control that existed before, though no direct ISO adjustment, which someone coming from a traditional camera system would probably look for. But there’s enough control here for anyone who is so inclined to get a little more creative and hands-on with the stock app than ever before.

I noticed that when I was using a manual shutter speed, the results appeared to have been less processed. Apple spokesperson Stephanie Ng confirmed that the camera is indeed capturing a single frame rather than using the typical multi-frame processing. That means you lose a bit of dynamic range, though the final image will still include a gain map if there are highlights bright enough to warrant it. That’s not ideal if you’re trying to capture detail in both highlights and shadows, but on the other hand, this is one way to get the less-processed iPhone photo that some folks have been clamoring for. It’s a bit hidden, but it’s finally here.

Previous Next

1 / 2 A photo taken with automatic exposure settings.

On top of that, there’s a new set of texture controls for Photographic Styles, with the ability to add a film-inspired glow to highlight areas of your photo, overlay film grain, or soften skin. It’s another first for Apple: the ability to make your photos a little bit worse. But you know, tastefully, Film simulation modes for digital cameras are as popular as ever, and Apple is trying to catch that wave. The recently released Pixel 11 series includes so many ways to customize the look of your photos that their camera team had an escalation meeting about it. Likewise, Samsung has added any number of ways you can restyle your photo into what you envisioned it would be. After basically a decade of pushing the technological envelope year after year, the major phone manufacturers seem to be opening up to other definitions of image quality.

If you put all these updates together alongside the less-important but completely underrated addition of a first-party wrist strap (!) accessory for Apple’s own 18 Pro cases, maybe there’s something more camera than phone here. When I got my hands on the 18 Pro last week, I wondered if I could convince myself that the iPhone is a camera camera now.

Previous Next



































1 / 19

I will go so far as to say that I had a better time shooting with the 18 Pro than I’ve ever had using an iPhone camera in the past. I shot sunstars peeking out behind some leaves in Battery Park. I took it to the US Open and documented the excitement of a night match at Arthur Ashe Stadium. I took a video of a sizzling fajita plate and converted it to a cinematic masterpiece* after capture. But I never forgot I was using a phone. The pro control icons are pretty small on the 18 Pro’s screen, and I had to focus just to hit them properly. I had to dismiss a spam call in the middle of a shoot. And after a morning of battery-draining photo and video shooting, it became really important to top the battery off so as not to lose my lifeline to the rest of the world. It’s a step closer, and the moving aperture is a bit closer to that dream of a phone that’s also a camera. But it’s still a phone.

*I use the term masterpiece loosely.

I’ll take a wrist strap over a crossbody any day.

Apple, Google, and Samsung have each achieved their own kind of excellence in shaping what a smartphone camera can be. So it’s interesting watching them pivot to flexibility and embracing some of the flaws that are turning people on to old digital cameras. But taking photos with one of their flagship phones still feels like using a phone, whether there are moving aperture blades inside or not. One of the reasons I found the wrist strap so appealing was that it made the process of handling the phone as a camera feel more like, well, a camera. I’m hoping for the day when one of the few phone makers who sell devices in the US at scale tries something like the Xiaomi photography kits or Vivo’s telephoto lenses. That would feel like a whole new camera experience.

Apple is also using the 18 Pro to introduce something it calls Reference Image, which is a method the company has developed for verifying the authenticity of a photo taken on the iPhone. Apple will start using Google’s SynthID standard to tag photos with AI edits, but Reference Image comes at the problem from the other direction: helping people to identify which photos are real. Apple designed a new main camera sensor for the 18 Pro and Pro Max that adds encrypted data to the images it produces, so it’s limited to photos taken with the main camera on those two models. It’s complicated and clunky right now, but it also seems to be a pretty robust system with a lot of room to grow.

Previous Next

1 / 2 In order to use the Reference Image feature, you need to turn it on in settings.

You need to enable it as a camera mode in the settings app in order to use it, and then actively switch the camera app to Reference mode to capture a Reference Image. The resulting image file contains the encrypted data from the main sensor, which means it’s bigger than a normal photo — a standard 4MB image I shot of a city street is an 8MB file when I shoot it in reference mode. If you send a Reference Image to someone who wants to verify that a Reference Image hasn’t been tampered with, they can push a button to send it to Apple’s Private Cloud Compute, where that encrypted data will be “developed” showing the image basically as it came off the sensor. (Apple’s metaphor here is having the original negative of a traditional film photograph.)

It’s hard to use at the moment, but the idea is that it’s almost impossible to tamper with. Apple is releasing an API for third-party developers to add an option to view reference photos when they’re attached to an image, and the company seems eager to push this into the wider ecosystem now that all of this has been announced.

The 18 Pro’s glacier color grew on me but nothing beats burgundy.

There are some meaningful updates on the video side of the aisle, too. There’s updated focus tracking that uses AI to stick to a subject. It’ll even pick them up if they leave the frame briefly and come back, but in my brief testing it seems to forget about someone if they’re gone for more than a few seconds. You can also convert video footage from the main camera to Cinematic after the fact, in the same way that you can convert regular photos to portrait mode after you take them. I often wish I’d taken video in cinematic mode but I never remember to in the moment, so this is a nice update. Video files don’t appear to be vastly bigger compared to similar clips from the 17 Pro, so this doesn’t come at a big cost to your storage space, either.

And that’s no small thing. The 18 Pro and Pro Max are each $100 more this year, with the 18 Pro starting at $1,199 with 256GB of storage. But each jump in storage tier will cost you dearly — all the way up to a $2,399 version for 2TB. Likewise, the Pro Max starts at $1,299.99 with 256GB of storage and goes all the way up to $2,499 for the 2TB version.

On the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, the Dynamic Island shrinks down when not in use.

You’re not getting nothing for that price hike. There’s a new chipset, the A20 Pro, plus an updated vapor chamber that’s supposed to move heat away from the chipset more effectively to help with sustained performance compared to the 17 Pro. I noted the phone getting pretty warm on my first few days of using it, which are usually pretty taxing as you’re going through setup, app downloads, and data indexing, but haven’t noticed it as a consistent problem.

Battery life is the eternally impossible question to answer about a phone after a week of using it. I haven’t experienced anything like a “normal day” for the past week, but I haven’t seen any surprising battery drain from the 18 Pro in my downtime, either. It survived a day of intense use during a video shoot without a recharge at any point, which is no small feat. Apple quotes a modest gain in battery life for the smaller Pro model — 36 hours of video playback, up from 33 hours on the 17 Pro. The 18 Pro Max offers a bigger increase: 45 hours of video playback compared to 39 on the 17 Pro Max. Verge editor-in-chief Nilay Patel has been testing the Pro Max, and he says it’s been lasting more than a day, although he also noted the same early setup vibes. He also points out his 17 Pro Max battery was a champ when it was new and now can’t make it through a day after a year of heavy use, so the real test here is going to come much later in this phone’s life cycle.

The real test here is going to come much later in this phone’s life cycle

The 18 Pro I’m testing uses Apple’s new in-house C2 modem, marking the first time that a Pro iPhone has shipped with an Apple-made cellular chip. It seems that the homegrown stuff has finally cleared Apple’s quality bar for inclusion at the very high end, and I can’t say I’ve found any reason to fault it over the past week. The C2 is paired with the N1 wireless networking chip, and the system overall seems quick to jump off a Wi-Fi signal when I’m in an elevator and just as eager to pick up a cell signal when I step out. Here’s hoping it’s just as quick to ditch my home Wi-Fi when I’m in the carport outside of my house trying to start GPS navigation — truly, the dream.

One other notable update here is that the Dynamic Island is smaller. On the 17 Pro, the black bar encompassed the Face ID sensor in addition to the front-facing camera. On the 18 Pro, the Face ID sensor is hidden under the regular part of the screen until that real estate is needed by the Dynamic Island. Apple went to great lengths to disguise the sensor under a unique pixel pattern that uses black pixels to allow the IR signals necessary for Face ID to pass through. Pretty cool, though I can’t say I noticed the Dynamic Island’s smaller size even a single time as I was using the phone, and jumping back to the 17 Pro’s larger Dynamic Island hasn’t bothered me. And I have yet to need three items in the Dynamic Island at one time, rather than two, but this is a new capability that exists on the 18 Pro.

Possibly an even bigger deal than the launch of a new $1,200 phone is the release of iOS 27, and with it the new-new AI Siri. We previewed it in detail earlier this summer, and it continues to impress me. Particularly, its ability to search across email and messages all at once — this keeps feeling more and more like a superpower the longer I use it. We also noted when it debuted that Siri as an AI chatbot is much less chatty and eager to keep you engaged than the likes of Gemini or ChatGPT, which is something I also appreciate the more I use it. iOS 27 has just gone fully public this week, and it will be interesting to see how people take to the new Siri. It has a lot of work to do to earn the trust of the public that it can do anything more complex than setting a timer reliably, but Siri seems to be on the right track at least. Finally.

The iPhone camera is more like a camera than ever before.

Unlike Siri, the 18 Pro’s big hardware update is much less visible. The aperture is hard to see without the right light and the help of a macro lens. It’s as small as my thumbnail, and it’s under layers of optical glass. Most people who buy this phone probably won’t go looking for it, and that’s fine. It’s the kind of feature that can live in the background and just jump in to help here and there, unseen, when you need it. You don’t need to know what it is or how it works. Which is kind of the point of personal technology, anyway.

So why make a big deal out of such a small thing? Is the defining feature of Apple’s new phones really an iris as thin as a human hair that most people will never see? I think two things are true at once: Adding a major new hardware feature to the world’s most popular camera is notable to those of us who pay attention to such things. But it’s also beside the point.

The iPhone camera’s most important job is to always take a usable photo, by default, no matter what. This new aperture mechanism provides some benefits to that end, and on top of that, allows a more hands-on photographer access to camera controls that weren’t there before. But the first part of that mission is the most important, and the 18 Pro upholds that mandate. Most people who use this phone will never touch the aperture control, and that’s fine. They might get a picture of a menu that’s fully in focus thanks to the camera dropping down to f/4, or a night shot that’s a little more detailed thanks to a brighter maximum aperture. Otherwise, it will feel like the same camera they’ve come to expect from a Pro iPhone.

As long as you don’t expect a revolutionary new camera experience, then the 18 Pro is what it should be: a little better than the version that came before it.

Tech.title: Meta is reportedly ready to launch less pervy smart glasses
Tech.content:
Meta may be ready to reveal a new pair of smart glasses with no camera at all, amid a PR crisis for the company caused by the video recording capabilities of its flagship smart glasses. A new report from The Information claims the camera-free glasses, codenamed Luna, could be revealed as soon as the Meta Connect event next week.

Instead of a camera, the Luna glasses will reportedly include six microphones that allow users to chat to Meta AI and the new Muse AI agent, along with speakers for audio playback. Stripping the camera out has apparently made it possible to make the glasses’ arms smaller, and closer to ordinary frames. Meta is reportedly targeting to ship the new glasses in October in two styles: Clubmaster and Burbank.

It’s a delicate time for Meta’s smart glasses. While its existing frames have proven popular, they’ve also sparked a privacy backlash caused primarily by the camera. Bad actors have used the glasses to surreptitiously record people, in some cases intentionally harassing them in pursuit of social media virality, and the glasses have been banned everywhere from New York courtrooms to Britain’s largest pub chain. While the glasses are equipped with a recording LED, and Meta says the camera will stop functioning if this has been tampered with, the company has been caught in a cat-and-mouse game with a small group of users developing workarounds to record with the LED off.

The Information reports that the camera-free Luna glasses will be joined at Connect next week by new augmented reality glasses, codenamed Phoenix, capable of bringing up a virtual workspace or movie screen in AR. Those are set to release in 2027, and follow a similar AR concept device from 2024.

Removing the camera may not entirely solve Meta’s privacy woes. The new Apple Watch models announced last week drew some criticism for their always-on audio recording capabilities. Meta’s new glasses could still trigger their own concerns thanks to the combination of microphones and a design that makes them harder to distinguish from regular glasses. And when it comes to trust, Meta rarely gets the benefit of the doubt.

Tech.title: The Boox Palma 3 gets stylus support and a sleek redesign
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Nearly two years after the last update to Boox’s smartphone-sized black-and-white e-reader, the company announced the Palma 3 with a sleek redesign, new functionality, and a handful of other small updates that may justify its significant price bump depending on how you plan to use it. While the Palma 2 launched in 2024 for $279.99, the Palma 3 will be $339.99 and is expected to be “available soon.”

The most obvious upgrade for the Palma 3 is the hardware itself. It still features the same 6.13-inch, 300ppi E Ink Carta screen as its predecessor (which is now quite a few years old), but it’s wrapped in a new anodized aluminum frame with a paperlike fiberglass backplate. The Palma 3 looks like a significant upgrade to the Palma line, even if under the hood you’ll find more of the same. The pocketable e-reader is powered by a Qualcomm Q-6690 octa-core processor with 6GB of RAM and 128GB of storage expandable with a microSD card. It also includes a 3950mAh rechargeable battery, a 16-megapixel camera on the back, and a fingerprint reader in the power button.

The original Palma and the Palma 2 came with Android 11 and Android 13, respectively, but the new Palma 3 ships with Android 16, which is just one generation behind the latest version of the OS. That should help it feel like a more modern mobile device. And like the color screen Palma 2 Pro, the Palma 3 supports the Boox InkSense Plus active stylus so you can use the e-reader as a digital notepad with your preferred note-taking app. But it’s not included. The stylus is an optional upgrade that will add another $46 to the cost of the Palma 3, pushing it closer to the price of premium e-notes like the Remarkable Paper Pure.

Tech.title: The EOS R8 Mark II is Canon’s lightest full-frame camera with stabilization
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Canon announced the second-generation of its EOS R8 with a new retro-inspired redesign and the addition of in-body stabilization. That feature was one of the most notable omissions from the original R8 that launched in 2023 as a smaller, cheaper, and more accessible alternative to the Canon R6 Mark II for photographers wanting a larger full-frame shooter. While the new EOS R8 Mark II is slightly heavier than its predecessor at 1.2 pounds thanks to the additional stabilization functionality, it’s lighter and cheaper than last year’s EOS R6 Mark III.

The Canon EOS R8 Mark II is expected to be available sometime in late October for $1,899 for the body only, or $2,099 bundled with a Canon 24-50mm stabilized lens. That’s more expensive than the original R8 that launched at $1,499, but more accessible than the $2,799 EOS R6 Mark III thanks to some lower specs and omitted features.

Like its predecessor, the R8 Mark II features the same 24.2-megapixel full-frame CMOS sensor as the R6 Mark II, while the R6 Mark III got a bump to a 32.5-megapixel sensor. The new R8 Mark II still exclusively uses an electronic shutter instead of an additional mechanical one, with high-speed captures maxing out at 40fps again. To ensure you’re not too late to a critical moment, a pre-continuous shooting mode captures up to an additional 20 shots before you press the shutter button.

Image: Canon

The new five-axis in-body stabilization offers up to 7.5 stops of shake correction that can be expanded by pairing the camera with a lens featuring its own stabilization. The R8 Mark II also features Canon’s Dual Pixel CMOS AF II system with what the company describes as “more tenacious tracking” than what the R8 offered. The autofocus system can also recognize animals, vehicles, and people, with the option to register up to 10 different people by their faces and rank their priority.

Video capabilities max out at 4K/60fps, but frame rates can be boosted to up to 180fps by dropping the resolution to 1080p. As Canon is targeting the R8 Mark II as a potential full-frame option for amateur photographers, the camera includes 16 different color filters, an easy to way to increase or decrease depth of blur that handles settings like f-stop and shutter speed automatically, and creative bracketing that takes three photos with different brightness and color tones.

Image: Canon

Following other companies drawing inspiration from older film cameras for the design of new digital shooters, the R8 Mark II eschews the curves of the original R8 for a more boxy and angular body. Canon credits the nearly 40-year-old EOS 650 and its pentaprism housing on top as the inspiration for the R8 Mark II. Other hardware upgrades include a new multi-controller joystick above the camera’s screen, which makes it easier to select focal points, and its single SD card slot repositioned on the side of the camera so it’s still accessible when using a tripod. Canon will also sell a matching $99.99 accessory that extends the R8 Mark II’s grip, making it easier to hold when using larger lenses.

In October Canon is also releasing a free new Windows app called Dual Pixel 3D Converter that leverages additional info captured by Canon’s dual-pixel autofocus system to generate 3D imagery from the 2D photos the camera takes. You can use the app to create a 3D photo with a background you can move around, a 3D model with the background completely removed, or short 3D videos demonstrating an animated perspective adjustment of close-up subjects.

Tech.title: Hear why Neuralink co-founder Max Hodak says the screen era is ending at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026
Tech.content:
When you imagine working with a computer, you likely think of keyboards, clicks, or typing on your phone. Science Corporation CEO Max Hodak has spent the last several months advancing a different vision. His company has enlisted a top neurobiologist to lead the first U.S. human trials for its biohybrid brain-computer interface. Hodak shares what his company has discovered so far with the 10,000+ tech leaders, founders, and investors at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026.

At his Beyond Screens session on the Disrupt Stage, Hodak will make the case for why the next era of technology could be built upon a different kind of interface, one that adapts to us from brain-computer interactions to create new ways of engaging with machines.

Image Credits:TechCrunch

Join Disrupt as it returns to Moscone West in San Francisco on October 13-15, bringing together more than 10,000 founders, investors, and startup community members across more than 250 sessions. This year, we have a particular focus on building sustainable AI companies, with AI-centric programming extending across six industry stages.

Secure your Disrupt pass today to save up to $200 on your ticket and hear one of Silicon Valley’s most ambitious founders explore a post-screen future.

Hodak’s path toward reinventing interfaces

Hodak’s career reads like a running bet that the interface between humans and machines has plenty of room for improvement. Having started programming at six years old, he studied biomedical engineering at Duke Pratt School of Engineering, and worked his way into Miguel Nicolelis’ brain-computer interface lab, interests that inform his work to this day.

He originally co-founded Transcriptic, a robotic cloud laboratory for the life sciences. But most famously, he co-founded Neuralink in 2016 and served as its initial president, helping build the company that put brain implants into the public imagination. Then in 2021, he founded Science Corporation to develop advanced neural engineering and brain-computer interface technology. The company has a particular focus on applications to aid those in need of help with vision, cognition, and mobility.

And it’s not all speculation: Science Corp’s PRIMA implant has already restored eyesight in people with severe vision loss, using a pair of glasses with a tiny camera that beams a captured scene onto a chip implanted in the retina. Since its founding, it’s raised $230 million in a Series C round at a $1.5 billion valuation, and the company’s ambitions go beyond interfaces. Hodak sees additional applications of Science Corp’s brain-implanted sensors helping heal damaged brain cells, warning about seizures, and maybe even helping treat conditions as severe as Parkinson’s disease.

Hear from one of Silicon Valley’s most ambitious founders, only at Disrupt

This is your best chance to learn how Hodak thinks the interface between people and machines is about to change, and the many ways that could impact your startup, your role, and maybe your life.

Take a look at the Disrupt agenda and choose your Disrupt ticket before savings of up to $200 expire September 25. Save up to 30% if you register as a group.

Tech.title: May Mobility is going public in a $1.4B SPAC deal
Tech.content:
Autonomous vehicle company May Mobility is merging with a special purpose acquisition company (SPAC) and will become a publicly traded company. It’s a deal that could raise more than $300 million for May Mobility at a valuation of $1.4 billion, the company said Wednesday.

Once the merger is complete, May Mobility said it will be the first public company in the U.S. that is focused entirely on autonomous ride-hailing vehicles. This is meant to differentiate it from a number of other public companies working on autonomy, including Tesla, Rivian, Alphabet (with Waymo), and trucking-focused Aurora and Kodiak.

The move sets up May Mobility to be a test of the stock market’s appetite for pure-play robotaxi ventures.

It will also be a test of May Mobility’s approach to autonomy, which it pitches as “asset-light” and “partnership-first.” Instead of owning and operating the robotaxis, May Mobility’s business revolves around selling its autonomous vehicles to its fleet partners over time while maintaining control of any remote supervision and software updates. In exchange, May Mobility receives either fixed fees or per-trip licensing fees.

Founded in 2017, May Mobility currently operates autonomous Toyota Siennas in three locations in the U.S. It has a partnership with Lyft in Atlanta, and offers rides in two cities — Eden Prairie and Grand Rapids — in Minnesota.

These deployments helped May Mobility generate around $10 million in revenue last year, with a cash burn of around $93 million. It has offered more than 550,000 paid autonomous rides to date, covering more than 1 million miles. The company recently spun up its first trial deployment in Japan and is planning commercial launches in Arlington, Texas, with Uber, at the end of this year or in early 2027.

May Mobility is merging with ACP Holdings Acquisition Corp., a special purpose acquisition company established by Houston, Texas-based investment management company Atlas Credit Partners. The merger will involve a $120 million “private investment in public equity” transaction, and up to $217 million from a trust account maintained by ACP Holdings — though shareholders in the SPAC may choose to redeem their stock at the time of the merger, which could reduce the amount of money going to May Mobility.

May Mobility said Wednesday that it will use the proceeds to fund more research and development, especially around removing its safety drivers, as well as supply chain investments to reduce its bill-of-materials costs. The company is also targeting new geographic deployments, some of which it expects to announce later this year.

Tech.title: Robots are waiting for a ChatGPT moment: Nvidia’s Les Karpas explains why at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026
Tech.content:
The world hasn’t been the same since ChatGPT made its debut in November 2022, when seemingly out of nowhere, a means of engaging with large language models propelled AI beyond hype and into day-to-day reality.

Robotics, like AI, has been discussed, built upon, and in some ways adopted for a long time now, but it’s yet to have that big breakthrough moment. Tech.title: Google says some Pixel phone owners were hacked in zero-day attacks
Tech.content:
In Brief

Google says that a bug in its Pixel smartphones’ software was exploited in limited and targeted cyberattacks. The company said Tuesday that the bug, tracked as CVE-2026-58704, has now been patched.

According to the limited details about the vulnerability, the bug was found in Pixel phones’ modem, which lets the device connect to the internet. Exploiting the bug could allow an attacker to gain access beyond the sandboxed walls of the modem and into the broader phone’s data, a vulnerability known as privilege escalation.

The bug can be exploited silently and without any interaction from the phone owner in what’s known as a “zero-click” attack, meaning a victim does not need to click on a link or open a file.

Google did not say who was exploiting the bug, and a spokesperson for Google did not return a request for comment. It’s not uncommon for bugs like this one to be abused by surveillance vendors, such as spyware makers, who sell access to their data-stealing software to governments and law enforcement agencies.

Tech.title: Amazon gives its workers a raise of $1 per hour
Tech.content:
In Brief

Amazon is raising the minimum starting pay for its U.S. core operations workers — like delivery drivers and fulfillment center employees — to $20 per hour and its average hourly pay to nearly $24 per hour. The company notes the higher pay represents an increase of $1 per hour for eligible employees.

“When you add in the value of our industry-leading benefits, average total compensation comes to more than $32 per hour,” Amazon Senior Vice President Udit Madan wrote in a blog post.

The investment in these raises comes out to over $1.5 billion, or about 0.06% of its $2.68 trillion market cap.

In addition, Amazon says it will now also provide employees with access to a low-cost banking system called Day 1 Financial, a membership in First Tech Federal Credit Union, as well as a 20% discount on purchases bought in-store at Whole Foods Market, the premium grocery chain that Amazon owns. If employees order groceries online via Amazon, they will also get a 10% discount.

Amazon already offers its employees free Prime memberships, prepaid education programs, and healthcare coverage, among its benefits.

On a subreddit for Amazon fulfillment center employees, people seem less than enthused. Regarding the Whole Foods discount, one worker commented, “So it would make it cost almost the same as a regular store, then? Hahaha,” a reference to Whole Foods’ historically higher prices.

Tech.title: Threads’ new features let podcasters promote shows and reach listeners
Tech.content:
Meta announced on Wednesday that its social network and X rival Threads is rolling out new tools that will allow podcast creators to promote their shows, grow their audiences, and engage existing listeners directly on the platform.

The news comes as X has also more recently been encouraging its creators to directly post videos on the platform, especially podcasts, to earn revenue and grow engagement. While Threads is not yet looking to host podcasts, it wants to make its platform a hub for posting and discussion.

To start, Threads will display a podcast profile card and banner on a creator’s profile and in their posts. Plus, when creators post episode links, they appear as tappable cards in the post, allowing users to easily listen.

Image Credits:Threads

The feature also lets podcast hosts directly post transcripts for listeners to read along with the episode, and they can tag featured guests, which displays a card related to that. Users can save any of these posts, making it easy to listen to the episode at a later time.

Threads will additionally be able to send reminders to creators when their new episode drops to post on Threads, which could help boost their engagement with listeners. The social platform is also providing tools that offer insights into how the audience is engaging with creators’ posts, with metrics like views over time by followers, non-followers, and all.

Image Credits:Threads

Last year, Threads rolled out new tools to increase discussion around podcasts, with features like better link cards and linking their profile with their podcasts. Threads is now close to X in terms of users, as Meta’s social network reached 500 million active users in June.

Tech.title: Chipotle Is Working With Palantir to Track Food Safety Risks
Tech.content:
Fast-casual burrito chain Chipotle is working with the data infrastructure giant Palantir.

The company is working on a “food safety risk platform” hosted on Palantir’s flagship software platform Foundry, according to screenshots viewed by WIRED. The platform appears to analyze factors like a store’s health department scores, pest incidents, and employee illnesses to assign a food safety score—basically, the store’s risk level.

Chipotle spokesperson Erin Wolford confirmed the initiative, but declined to comment further. Palantir did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.

It's not known exactly when the partnership started or how widely the platform has been deployed, but it comes amid a particularly disastrous period for food safety. The Food and Drug Administration identified more than 12,800 illnesses tied to foodborne outbreaks so far this year, most from a massive cyclospora outbreak connected to iceberg lettuce.

Chipotle was not directly impacted by the turbo diarrhea outbreak or the related recall, since it doesn’t serve iceberg lettuce. In July, however, it proactively stopped serving jalapenos from a particular supplier that was linked to a salmonella outbreak that went on to sicken more than 430 people.

Palantir has substantial offerings aimed at food-and-beverage companies, with contracts with poultry and beef supplier Tyson, cereal giant General Mills, and the independent purchasing co-op for the fast-food chain Wendy’s. Companies can use Foundry to manage inventory, automate ordering and delivery, and track their supply chains. At Wendy’s, for example, Palantir’s software is used to spot potential ingredient shortages before they occur.

Palantir’s work with corporate America now accounts for nearly half of its US business. In August, the company reported US commercial revenue reached $764 million in the most recent quarter, a 149 percent year-over-year increase.

The company has also done significant work with government entities focused on supply chains and food safety, including a $22 million contract with the FDA in 2022.

But Palantir remains best known for its other government contracts, including its work with Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the Department of Homeland Security. Last year, ICE awarded Palantir a $30 million contract to build a surveillance platform that provided visibility on people self-deporting.

Palantir’s work with ICE has the potential to be particularly controversial in the restaurant industry, where immigrants make up roughly a fifth of the workforce. In 2010 and 2011, Chipotle fired hundreds of workers who were ineligible to work in the US, following an ICE audit.

In 2025, Chipotle CEO Scott Boatwright said it would be “naive” to believe that Chipotle employees would not be impacted by the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown, “whether that’s directly or psychologically.”

“I think it’s a really important moment for us to connect with all individuals in our organization, as a mental check in, to say, hey, how are you doing, how are you feeling, is there anything we can do to help or support?” Boatright told NBC News at the time.

Tech.title: Apple iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max Review: For Camera Fiends
Tech.content:
Battery life has been stellar on the Pro models over the last few years, and that remains true here. The Pro Max is the more notable of the two because it packs a denser battery. With average use (around 5 hours of screen-on time), I hovered around 50 percent by the end of the day, and easily made it through day two on a single charge. I spent a little less time with the smaller Pro, but so far it has also comfortably gotten me through a day with around 40 percent left by bedtime. Safe to say, most people will very much enjoy the battery life, but the update doesn't feel drastic.

Next, there's the processor: the A20 Pro chip. I hardly run into problems with Apple's flagship silicon, and that hasn't changed. The phones run every app fluidly, and my benchmark tests show a surprisingly sizable leap over the A19 Pro in the 17 series.

It runs Control—a AAA game from 2019 ported to iOS earlier this year—decently well. However, aggressive upscaling makes the graphics look grainy, and character movements can feel a little sluggish. (I maxed out the graphics settings.) It's certainly not perfect, but I still can't believe I'm playing such a demanding title on an iPhone.

Control on the iPhone 18 Pro Max. Photograph: Julian Chokkattu

More impressive is Apple's thermal management on these phones. The company has expanded the vapor chamber's surface area by three times—the phone's cooling technology that helps spread heat around—meaning the entire phone felt toasty after close to an hour of gameplay in Control, with no uncomfortable localized hot spots. This larger vapor chamber also lets you game longer before phone’s thermal throttling kicks in and slows everything down.

The iPhone 18 Pro models come with iOS 27 out of the box, which features the all-new Siri AI. Yes, Siri AI is infinitely more capable than any version of Siri that Apple has offered before. It still doesn't quite have the spark or versatility of other AI assistants, but you might be fine with that. If you throw Siri AI a question, there's a good chance it can actually give you a satisfactory answer now. Remember that Siri AI and other Apple Intelligence features aren't exclusive to the latest models, though you do need an iPhone 15 Pro or newer to access them.

Tech.title: 7 Best Android Phones of 2026, Tested and Reviewed
Tech.content:
If none of the smartphones in this guide strike your fancy and you want to continue searching, keep these specs in mind.

Display: Gone are the days of shoddy phone displays—almost every smartphone uses an OLED panel now. Cheaper phones still use LCD, which won't have as deep blacks and poppy colors, but even phones under $300 can sport OLED. You'll see some variations, like AMOLED or Dynamic AMOLED 2X, but that's mostly marketing jargon.

Screen size: You hold a smartphone all the time, so make sure whatever you pick fits your palms. Most small Android phones are around 6.1 to 6.3 inches (measured diagonally), whereas larger phones typically top out at 6.8 or 6.9 inches. Foldable phones will have a smaller outer screen and a larger display when opened. For example, the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8 we recommend has a 5.5-inch screen when closed and a 7.6-inch display when unfolded, but sizes vary by manufacturer.

Processor: Most smartphones use a Qualcomm or MediaTek processor. Google phones use the company's in-house Tensor chip, and some Samsung phones utilize Samsung's Exynos processor in select markets. It's hard to say how reliably a processor will perform without looking at reviews and benchmark results, so do your research. For reliable performance, try to stick to Qualcomm's Snapdragon 7 series or higher, or MediaTek's Dimensity 7000 series or higher. The 2026 flagship chip is the Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5.

RAM: You'll want at least 8 GB of RAM, though 12 GB is better. This lets you juggle multiple apps more seamlessly and run more intensive AI tasks.

Cooling: High-performing phones can be ruined if they get too hot because the processor throttles, causing slowdowns. This mostly applies to folks who game a lot, but it's worth checking whether the phone has a dedicated cooling system. You'll want to look for language like “heat pipes” or “vapor chamber cooling.”

Refresh rate: Most phones used to come with 60-Hz refresh rates, meaning the display refreshes at 60 frames per second. Nowadays, even cheap phones offer 90- or 120-Hz screens. The more frames refreshed in a second, the more fluid everything looks and feels. It might sound small, but it can make a big difference in whether your smartphone feels buttery smooth. We have a broader guide that explains this technology. Flagship phones have screens with variable refresh rates ranging from 1 to 120 Hz, which often makes them more battery-efficient (look for LTPO or LTPS).

Battery capacity: Smartphone batteries are measured in milliampere-hours (mAh). A big battery doesn't necessarily mean better battery life, because it depends on screen size and other technologies the phone is powering. Most phones should have 4,000-mAh cells or higher, and you typically won't see much above 5,500 mAh. Some phones now use silicon-carbon batteries, a new technology that allows them to be denser but thinner.

Charging speeds: Most Android smartphones can charge fast, but certain companies offer shockingly fast recharge times. That's usually because they require a proprietary charging brick. You can find charging speed information on a phone's product spec page. Just remember that these days, most smartphones do not come with a charging brick, just a cable. We have more details in this fast-charging guide.

Software updates: Software support is crucial. Your phone stays secure longer, and you'll get new features over time. Even if you trade in your phone, it may end up in someone else's hands, and a long update policy means the phone will continue to be supported. The gold standard in Android is seven years right now, thanks to Samsung and Google. However, if you replace your phone every two or three years, the shorter update policies of other Android makers might not be a deal-breaker.

Cameras: Camera specs are very misleading. A phone with a 108-megapixel (MP) sensor doesn't mean it will take better photos than a phone with a 50-MP sensor. The only way to know for sure is to read reviews. If the camera matters to you, check whether it has a versatile system. The best camera phones offer a primary wide camera, an ultrawide, and a telephoto zoom (usually 5X). Cheap phones tend to come with a lot of cameras, many of which are useless.

Extra features: Don't overlook the secondary features. Does the phone have a near-field communication sensor (NFC) so you can make contactless payments? Does it have a good IP rating that can survive a drop in the pool? (You'll want IP67 or IP68!) What about wireless charging (Qi2 or Qi)? Or a microSD card slot, dual-SIM tray, or headphone jack? Vet the phone's specs if you're after something specific.

5G service: Nearly all smartphones support 5G, the current generation of network connectivity. 4G LTE isn't disappearing, and you may still fall back to LTE when 5G isn't available. Avoid smartphones that don't offer 5G at all.
